talks.title: GeeCON 2026: Tomer Gabel - Mob Rules, or: how I learned to Stop Worrying and Love Technical Debt
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2026: Tomer Gabel - Mob Rules, or: how I learned to Stop Worrying and Love Technical Debt.
talks.summary:
Overview: Tomer Gabel presents at GeeCON 2026 on technical debt, reframing it through financial analogies and arguing for deliberate, manageable debt rather than denial or panic.

Key Topics: Audience polling on technical debt prevalence; debt as a legitimate tool for time-to-market; distinguishing strategic debt from uncontrolled accumulation; and mob programming rules as team decision-making metaphor.

Technical Details: Gabel compares startup capital loans to intentional technical shortcuts that accelerate product delivery, while warning against debt that compounds without repayment plans.

Takeaways: Technical debt is inevitable and sometimes strategic. Teams should consciously manage debt with repayment plans rather than allowing it to spiral unchecked.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Tomasz Sikora - Scaling Agile Teams: The Matrix Model for Scalable Autonomy
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2025: Tomasz Sikora - Scaling Agile Teams: The Matrix Model for Scalable Autonomy.
talks.summary:
Autonomy and Industry Context

Tomasz Sikora of The Travel Corporation discusses scaling agile teams while acknowledging limited true autonomy—teams deliver software but rarely drive independent business outcomes. He targets scrum masters and facilitators managing organizational growth.

Software Demand and Scaling Paths

GDP growth correlates with accelerating software demand across industries, with cybersecurity and compliance cutting across sectors. Companies scale through internal product development, third-party libraries, or SaaS—each carrying vendor-lock-in risks that must align with long-term strategy.

Barriers to Scaling

Key impediments include talent gaps, inherited technical debt from dependencies, process bottlenecks, and misalignment between business vision and engineering execution. Innovation and cross-domain learning between technology and business teams accelerate growth before formal scaling is possible.

Team Foundations

Sikora argues scaling begins with cohesive teams providing psychological safety and mutual support. Ecosystems like open source, cloud computing, and rapid-iteration environments demonstrate how shared infrastructure enables experimentation at scale.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Ron Veen - Java 25: Unleashing the Power of Streams
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2025: Ron Veen - Java 25: Unleashing the Power of Streams.
talks.summary:
Stream Gatherers in Java

Ron Veen opens at GeeCON by celebrating Java streams, which arrived with lambdas in Java 8 after a long wait, and introduces stream gatherers—previewed in Java 22–23 and finalized in Java 24—as the talk’s focus for Java 25-era development.

How Streams Execute

He revisits stream pipeline anatomy: sources, intermediate operations, and lazy terminal execution that pulls elements one at a time. He explains optimizations like fusion, short-circuiting, size-based splitting via spliterators, and the tradeoffs of parallel streams on small datasets.

Meet Gatherers

Gatherers extend the streams API with custom intermediate steps beyond built-in map and filter. Veen plans live coding a stateless alternative map, a stateful gatherer, and reimplementing a new default gatherer—grounded in understanding stateless versus stateful stream operations.

Why Internals Matter

Knowing how streams pull data and split work across threads helps developers write correct, efficient custom gatherers instead of treating streams as magic syntax.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Jaroslav Tulach - Functional Programming
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2025: Jaroslav Tulach - Functional Programming with JVM and Truffle.
talks.summary:
Speaker background

Jaroslav Tulach traces a path from 1990s functional programming through NetBeans (first Java IDE in Java), Oracle Labs/GraalVM work, and joining Enso after Oracle Labs recruitment.

Enso introduction

Enso is a dual textual/visual language with one-to-one switching, live programming with instant feedback, and JVM interoperability where Java is the system language. Target users are advanced Excel users, not traditional developers.

Live demo

Starting from a sentence component, he builds a visual pipeline: split on spaces, uppercase a word, repeat three times, reverse text, group steps into a reusable function, then map it across array elements. Edits propagate immediately across the project.

Talk plan

After the demo, the talk was set to cover lessons learned on functional programming atop the JVM. The truncated transcript ends before those JVM lessons are delivered in detail.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Victor Gamov - Stream Processing As You’ve Never Seen Before (Seriously): Apache Flink
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2025: Victor Gamov - Stream Processing As You’ve Never Seen Before (Seriously): Apache Flink.
talks.summary:
## Stream Processing Fundamentals

Confluent's Victor Gamov introduces Apache Flink at GeeCON through a coffee-shop analogy: stateful systems should remember your order like a regular barista, not treat every visit as stateless. Flink is a distributed stream-processing framework for high-throughput, low-latency analytics over unbounded data.

## Architecture and Use Cases

Flink executes dataflow programs modeled as directed acyclic graphs, processing events with exactly-once semantics where configured. It integrates with Kafka, data lakes (Iceberg, Paimon), and batch pipelines, serving fraud detection, real-time dashboards, and event-driven microservices at scale.

## When Not to Use Flink

Gamov cautions against deploying distributed stream processors for tasks CLI tools handle faster—grep and awk beat a cluster for simple file parsing. Network overhead and operational complexity demand genuinely large-scale, continuous workloads before Flink's benefits justify the infrastructure.

## Stateful Versus Stateless Processing

The talk contrasts stateless per-event handling with stateful operators maintaining windows, aggregations, and keyed state across sessions. Understanding this distinction guides architects choosing between Flink, Kafka Streams, and batch systems for coffee-order memory—or enterprise event pipelines.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Heinz Kabutz - The Hidden Art of Thread-Safe Progr.: Exploring java.util.concurrent
talks.teaser: The session maps java.util.concurrent internals, from Vector's deadlock history to queue benchmarks and synchronizer selection guidance.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames thread-safe Java as a practical study of `java.util.concurrent`, opened by audience questions that are answered at the start, middle, and end. It walks through decades of `Vector` fixes—unsynchronized reads, serialization races, nested-vector deadlocks, and later cloning and `forEach` hazards—to show how subtle concurrency defects can survive unit tests.

From there it ties behavior to the Java memory model and elusive JDK issues such as `LockSupport` unpark races, then argues for preferring heavily used synchronizers over obscure ones. Live demos compare `AtomicLong` and `LongAdder` contention, implement startup coordination with latches and AQS patterns, and benchmark `LinkedBlockingQueue` against related queues, including pitfalls that affect fixed thread pools. Deeper reads cover weakly consistent iterators, `ArrayBlockingQueue` iterator bookkeeping, and `CopyOnWriteArrayList` locking choices tuned for the JVM.

Closing answers stress minimizing shared mutable state, favoring virtual threads over reactive stacks where appropriate, and learning concurrency by reading JDK source patiently rather than restarting when timing looks wrong.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Tomer Gabel - History in the Making: On Computer Preservation
talks.teaser: Explores why computing history fades and how software, hardware, and documentation can be saved for later generations.
talks.summary:
The talk begins by framing computing as a field whose written and oral past is disappearing much like lost crafts such as Stradivarius violin making or the formula for Greek fire. Despite modern machines outperforming antiques, the exact methods and stories behind early work often vanish while misleading anecdotes spread.

The middle section challenges popular origin myths. The famous moth in the Harvard Mark II logbook is separated from Grace Hopper’s actual role, dates are corrected, and the engineering word “bug” predates that incident. Claims that ENIAC was the first digital computer are contrasted with Konrad Zuse’s earlier programmable machines and with Colossus systems at Bletchley Park, whose existence stayed secret until the 1970s. For future historians the speaker sorts computing heritage into software bits, physical hardware, and documentation ranging from manuals to forums. Material comes from corporate archives, former employees who kept plans despite secrecy, and private collectors—especially after the Soviet bloc opened parallel industries to view. Preservation means attaching provenance, scanning paper, copying degrading magnetic media—including raw floppy flux captures—and restoring yellowed plastics and dead electronics so machines can run again, often with modern adapters for storage and displays.

The close argues that computer museums deserve the same casual respect as art or science museums, notes examples in Poland, and describes a personal decades-long collection aimed at seeding a museum in Israel. Listeners are pointed toward enthusiast communities and restoration channels. The message for practitioners is that witnesses and media are finite: capture artifacts and context now so later generations can judge what mattered.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Piotr Przybył - To RAG or not to RAG
talks.teaser: Shows when RAG fixes LLM hallucinations versus when vector search alone suffices, using local bash and Elasticsearch demos.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a familiar failure mode: a local large language model confidently misexplains Java stream gatherers because its training predates the feature, even when wording sounds like official documentation. That sets up retrieval-augmented generation as a way to ground answers in material that postdates the model.

The core is a stepwise live path built from shell scripts and HTTP calls—no heavyweight application stack. A baseline generate call hallucinates; stuffing in fetched JEP HTML fixes the answer but cheats on discovery. The talk then covers why search quality matters, dense embeddings, fixed model choice for indexing and queries, chunking large bodies, enriching an index with vectors, and k-nearest-neighbor retrieval before prompting. A full pipeline crawl-indexes Java pages locally, finds relevant chunks for the same question, and produces a accurate explanation.

The conclusion is deliberately skeptical: not every interface needs generation on top of search. When ranked hits are fast, transparent, and good enough, skipping the LLM saves cost and latency. Hybrid search, tooling hooks, and sound relevance judgment matter as much as the pattern itself; practitioners should treat capable use of these systems as an engineering skill rather than a default checkbox.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Maurice Naftalin - If Streams Are So Great, Let's Use Them Everywhere... Right?
talks.teaser: A veteran Java author weighs when streams beat loops for maps, counting, exceptions, and the newer gatherers API.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by recalling why the stream API was introduced: lazy evaluation, map-filter-reduce, optional parallelism, and clearer bulk processing of in-memory data. The speaker walks through everyday patterns—splitting tokens, find-first, counting, collecting to lists, min and max with optionals, and flat-mapping optional process command lines—where streams often read linearly and stop early without manual break logic.

The middle turns to harder cases. Indexed search forces an index range over an array and sacrifices laziness; nested cross-products look clearer as nested loops than as nested IntStreams. A CSV city dataset drives Collectors.groupingBy versus Map.merge for country histograms, entry-set minima, and inverting keys to list all countries tied for the smallest bucket. Checked exceptions in functional lambdas lead through awkward filter-parse duplication, mapMulti, and libraries such as Sneaky Throw before a short gatherers tour: fixed and sliding windows, scan, fold, and mapConcurrent over virtual threads.

The close stresses using both tools, prioritizing readability and correctness over micro-optimizing non-parallel streams, and recognizing parallel streams’ narrow, compute-bound niche. Q&A notes debugging via staged locals, modest performance gaps versus loops, and that method references are syntactic sugar over lambdas.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Baruch Sadogursky - Coding Fast and Slow: Applying Kahneman's Insights to Improve Dev.
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2025: Baruch Sadogursky - Coding Fast and Slow: Applying Kahneman's Insights to Improve Dev.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON presentation, Baruch Sadogursky explores developer productivity and code quality through the lens of behavioral psychology, specifically the work of Daniel Kahneman (*Thinking, Fast and Slow*). Sadogursky explains how the human brain relies on two primary modes of thought—System 1 (fast, intuitive, emotional, automatic, and cheap) and System 2 (slow, deliberate, analytical, logical, and expensive)—and maps these systems to everyday software engineering practices. Because writing high-quality software requires the deliberate, analytical effort of System 2, understanding the biological and cognitive limits of mental fuel is critical to preventing poor engineering decisions.

### Key Topics
- **System 1 vs. System 2 in Software Engineering**: System 1 excels at rapid pattern recognition, while System 2 handles complex analytical tasks like architecture, design, and non-trivial coding. When developers exhaust their mental fuel, they unconsciously default to System 1.
- **The Danger of 'Okay Code'**: Code produced under System 1 is not necessarily outright broken; it compiles, passes happy-path tests, and appears fine on the surface. Sadogursky argues that "okay code" is more dangerous than bad code because it slips past fatigued code reviewers and automated pipeline checks, silently degrading software quality across the industry.
- **The Fallacy of Pure Coding Intuition**: While repetitive activities with immediate feedback loops (such as driving, sports, or firefighting drills) can transition from System 2 to System 1 via practice, large-scale software engineering decisions have delayed or absent feedback loops. Consequently, high-level software engineering cannot be safely reduced to pure System 1 intuition.
- **Cognitive Drains and Interruptions**: Research on attention (such as Dr. Gloria Mark's work) shows that context switching and interruptions severely degrade performance. Checking emails (averaging 77 times a day) or switching context during a build takes roughly 25 minutes to regain deep focus, draining finite mental fuel and breaking flow state.

### Technical Details & Mental Fuel Management
Sadogursky reviews biological research demonstrating that mental fuel has physical limits tied to cellular metabolism. To prevent depletion and stay out of automatic System 1 coding, he outlines several practical tactics:
- **Time and Interruption Management**: Implementing minimum time blocks (e.g., at least 25-minute Pomodoro sessions without premature switching if in flow), batching similar tasks, turning off constant notifications, and using dynamic scheduling tools (such as Reclaim AI) to defend focus time while maintaining availability.
- **Physical and Cognitive Well-being**: Prioritizing sleep as the only true way to fully restore cognitive batteries (recommending 7–8 hours), practicing downtime, and utilizing short "caffeine naps" (drinking coffee immediately before a 20-minute nap) to recharge midday.
- **Optimizing Developer Tooling & Automation**: Shortening build feedback loops (e.g., keeping builds close to 1 minute to avoid context switching), automating repetitive tasks, and delegating non-core, time-consuming responsibilities.
- **Delegation and AI**: Evaluating tasks via a structured framework: if a task is outside a team's core expertise, hard to learn, and time-constrained, it should be delegated. He discusses using specialized AI models and agentic tools (such as JetBrains, Windsor Cascade, VS Code Copilot agent, or quality-focused agents like Coder) or delegating complex specialized problems like library security patching (referencing TuxCare's Secure Chain for Java).

### Takeaways
Developers must recognize that cognitive energy is finite and that tiredness causes an automatic, unannounced shift to System 1, resulting in mediocre code. Maintaining high software quality requires actively protecting mental fuel through disciplined time blocking, reducing context switching, eliminating unnecessary notifications, getting adequate sleep, shortening feedback loops, and strategically delegating non-core tasks.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Andrzej Grzesik, Jarosław Pałka - Gentle Introduction to Lock-Free Programming in Java
talks.teaser: Introduces lock-free progress levels, Java atomics and CAS loops, queue algorithms, ABA pitfalls, and practical library choices.
talks.summary:
The session opens by separating obstruction-free, lock-free, and wait-free progress guarantees, stressing that lock-free does not mean avoiding locks entirely but ensuring system-wide forward progress. The presenters walk through why a plain increment is not thread-safe, how java.util.concurrent atomics map to single-location hardware operations, and what cache lines and bus locking imply on multi-core CPUs. Benchmarks on a four-thread laptop compare unsynchronized access, synchronized blocks, read-write locks, and atomic integers, showing much higher throughput for atomics in their scenario.

They implement a lock-free stack and a Michael–Scott-style queue with compare-and-swap retry loops, describe intermediate inconsistent states, and compare the pattern to version-control workflows. JCStress is introduced to hunt duplicate consumption and validate happens-before ordering. The ABA problem is explained with versioning via markable references and a Harris-style linked list, plus cautions about allocation under contention.

The close covers Java memory model effects on atomics, scaling limits and wasted work on highly contended CAS, and pragmatic guidance: prefer mature libraries such as JCTools or LMAX Disruptor, read JDK documentation, benchmark real workloads, and reserve hand-rolled lock-free code for learning rather than production.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Mihaela Gheorghe Roman - Java Streams: Evolution from JDK 8 to Today
talks.teaser: Traces how Java streams evolved from Java 8 to Java 24, with pipeline basics, version highlights, and common pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The talk traces the Java Stream API from its arrival in Java 8 through to Java 24, explaining why it was introduced. Streams let developers describe what should happen to a collection, such as filtering or mapping, instead of writing manual loops. The speaker compares an imperative loop that prints filtered names with a stream version, then walks through the pipeline: a source, lazy intermediate operations, and a terminal operation that triggers execution. Four kinds of streams are covered: object, primitive, parallel and infinite.

Next, the talk goes version by version. Java 9 added takeWhile, dropWhile and converting an Optional into a stream. Java 11 allowed var in lambda parameters, and Java 16 added a toList method that returns an unmodifiable list. Java 21 introduced mapMulti as a leaner alternative to flatMap, stream gatherers appeared as a preview in Java 22, and Java 23 added transform. Java 24 brought primitive flattening methods. Each change is shown with a short code example.

The closing section covers practical guidance. Streams should avoid side effects and mutation of external state, especially in parallel use, and collect or expressive terminal operations such as allMatch are preferred over forEach with a flag. Parallel streams suit large, independent workloads rather than small lists. A grouping example counts active adult users per country, and the talk ends with a note on the Flow API for backpressure-aware reactive processing.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Andrii Rodionov - A way for multi-language refactoring with OpenRewrite
talks.teaser: Shows how OpenRewrite builds lossless semantic trees and recipes to automate framework and Java version migrations at scale.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the problem of manual, months-long JDK and framework upgrades on large codebases, using OpenRewrite’s origins at Netflix and its open-source recipe ecosystem of thousands of migrations for Java, build files, and configuration. A live migration of a former employer’s project from Java 17 toward Java 21 illustrates bundled recipes, patch review, and a compile check as a first trust signal.

The middle explains the lossless semantic tree: why plain abstract syntax trees lose formatting and semantics, how type attribution pulls compiler and reflection data, and how recipes visit and rewrite tree nodes while preserving style. Simple Java recipe examples cover method replacement and JUnit migration via templating, plus test-driven recipe development.

The close covers multi-language expansion for Python, C#, TypeScript, and JavaScript, challenges per compiler, and a planned approach to serialize foreign-language LSTs into Java so existing recipes can run cross-language. OpenRewrite versus the commercial Moderne platform, offline operation, recipe browsing, and Q&A on banking adoption, selective recipes, and continuous recipe validation wrap the talk.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Daniel Kec - Brief history of Virtual Threads in Java
talks.teaser: Charts Java concurrency from green threads through reactive APIs to virtual threads, JVM scheduling, and imperative microservice servers.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames today’s virtual threads as the return of cheap user-level threading in the JDK, after roughly two decades of one-to-one kernel thread mapping, pooling, and reactive callbacks used to limit context-switch cost and memory overhead. It explains how virtual threads yield through continuations, how carrier threads and the fork-join pool schedule them, and how stack freezing, thawing, return barriers, and compression avoid moving full megabyte stacks on every switch.

A historical thread runs from JDK 1.1 green threads—many-to-one scheduling that could emulate parallelism until CPU-bound work exposed serialization—through the removal of green threads, reactive streams, and research lines that led to JDK 21’s many-to-many model. The speaker contrasts models with demos and Solaris-era documentation, then covers pinning on synchronized blocks, JFR detection, JDK 24 monitor fixes, and when offloading to platform threads still makes sense.

Helidon 4 is offered as a practitioner example: dropping Netty’s reactive stack for a blocking, virtual-thread-native web server tuned with Project Loom, with SE versus MP flavors and migration notes versus larger frameworks. The closing message is that blocking-style business code can match reactive throughput when the runtime handles scheduling, while long CPU work and some native I/O still belong on platform threads.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Tomas Rehak - Reasoning Models over Agents: Lessons from O3 & O4-mini
talks.teaser: Contrasts agent frameworks with O3 and O4-mini reasoning models using production customer-support lessons and demos.
talks.summary:
The presenter outlines work at a Czech legal-tech company where large language models support word-heavy domains, then contrasts classical multi-agent designs with newer OpenAI reasoning models O3 and O4-mini. He argues that divide-and-conquer agent graphs look elegant but often cycle, need heavy fine-tuning, and show poor reliability in cited benchmarks, while widely publicized large-scale customer-service agent rollbacks illustrate how hard broad agentic automation remains.

The middle of the talk walks through agent frameworks, ReAct-style loops, tool overload, and cascading failures, then explains how reasoning models pursue goals with internal reasoning tokens and chained tool calls until the original user goal can drop out of context. A customer-support scenario is demonstrated twice: a multi-agent ADK flow that routes billing questions but hallucinates a refund tool and crashes, versus a Java LangChain4j reasoning setup that can answer accurately yet still improvises refunds without backing APIs.

The closing lessons favor reasoning models plus a growing tool surface, including a scratchpad for human handoff, over elaborate agent graphs. Practitioners should benchmark changes, watch context-window behavior, treat write-capable tools as security risks, and prefer read-only or delegated workflows when models hit capability walls.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Pavel Lahoda - Mobile-First Security: A Tale of a Greenhouse and a Bunker
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2025: Pavel Lahoda - Mobile-First Security: A Tale of a Greenhouse and a Bunker.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Pavel Lahoda presents a comprehensive framework for application security centered on the concept of a "security chain"—the idea that security is only as strong as its weakest link. Using metaphors of a greenhouse (vulnerable) versus a hardened bunker (secure), Lahoda argues that most modern applications violate fundamental security principles by centralizing sensitive data, transferring secrets between clients and servers, and outsourcing critical security functions.

## Key Topics

**Security Chain Principles**
The talk outlines five stages of application lifecycle requiring security attention: account creation, authorization, device switching, account recovery/access loss, and account closure. Lahoda emphasizes that security must be holistic—adding a padlock to a greenhouse door is meaningless if the walls are glass.

**Account Creation and Identity**
Traditional "identity provider" models are fundamentally flawed because identity is created server-side as stored claims, not verified assertions about the user. Instead, Lahoda advocates for self-sovereign identity where cryptographic key pairs are generated on the user's device. The private key never leaves the device; only the public key and signed identity are sent to the server.

**Authorization and Authentication**
Password-based systems that transfer credentials over the network violate core security principles. Multi-factor authentication via SMS (using SS7) expands the attack surface without necessarily improving security. The speaker recommends:
- Memorable PINs or short passwords that users actually retain
- Biometric factors using face recognition via face detection libraries (achieving ~97% accuracy)
- FIDO2 standards, though they lack mandatory proof-of-identity factors
- Post-quantum cryptography (matrix-based algorithms) to prepare for quantum computing threats

**Device Pairing and Multi-Device Access**
When adding a second device, users should enter "pairing mode" and scan QR codes to establish cryptographic relationships. Both devices should maintain equal copies of the identity and key material. For less capable platforms (web apps), security can be proxied through a mobile device acting as an authenticator.

**Account Recovery and Restricted Access**
A novel approach involves granting temporary, restricted access similar to leaving keys with a neighbor. The second device receives "restrictions" (a recipe for permitted actions). Authorization updates require multiple factors: a PIN (something known), the device itself (something possessed), and a time window (something timed). The primary device receives push notifications and can approve, postpone, or deny access requests. This time-lock mechanism provides users oversight while enabling secure delegation.

**Account Closure and Data Control**
Instead of trusting servers to delete data, encryption should be controlled by the client. Using HKDF (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function) and elliptic curve encryption, clients generate one-time keys derived from a stored seed value. Data is encrypted on the server but inaccessible without the client-derived key. Even if decrypted, access can be staged to prevent server abuse.

## Technical Details

Several standardized technologies enable this architecture:
- **FIDO2**: Passwordless authentication via browser APIs and authenticators
- **HKDF**: Key derivation based on hash functions (RFC 5869)
- **Post-Quantum Cryptography**: Matrix-based algorithms replacing vulnerable elliptic curve methods; implementations available now despite 10+ year timeline cited by financial institutions
- **Face Recognition**: Third-party libraries (DeepFace) provide 128-integer vector representations (~97% accuracy) for biometric verification
- **Zero-Knowledge Proofs**: Transmit proof of credentials without exposing sensitive data

Mobile devices are central because they offer:
- Hardware-backed cryptographic storage (secure enclaves)
- Biometric sensors (face, fingerprint—though third-party access is limited on iOS/Android)
- Push notifications for real-time authorization flows
- Open-source verifiability (F-Droid on Android; deterministic builds on iOS via toolchain)

## Takeaways

1. **Never transfer secrets**: Passwords, tokens, and authentication codes crossing the network undermine security regardless of encryption claims.
2. **Embrace self-sovereign cryptography**: Users should generate and control their own key pairs; private keys must never leave the device.
3. **Use multiple factors strategically**: Rather than relying on a single second factor (like SMS) that expands attack surface, combine what you know (PIN), what you have (device), and timing (time locks).
4. **Control data, not trust**: Even data stored on servers can be protected by keeping decryption keys client-side and requiring client approval for each access.
5. **Mobile-first security is foundational**: Modern smartphones provide cryptographic, biometric, and notification capabilities that enable secure architectures impossible on other platforms.
6. **Plan for quantum threats now**: Post-quantum cryptographic algorithms are standardized and implementable today; waiting for quantum computers is unnecessary.

The speaker is conducting active research in this space and plans to publish implementations under a working name to be announced in the future.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Josef Goldstein - The Future of Data is Words
talks.teaser: Celebrates SQL's longevity while outlining how words, LLMs, and semantic layers may deliver self-service data at enterprise scale.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames SQL's 51st anniversary as a lens on a recurring problem: turning human intent into answers from data. It walks from IBM System R and the original structured English query language through commercial databases, open-source engines, and the big-data era, noting that analytical systems kept adopting SQL even when storage and compute no longer looked relational.

Modern SQL examples stretch the language into streaming pipelines, API calls, and LLM inference jobs. The speaker contrasts that power with lay users who still struggle to write SQL, and argues that large language models make natural-language questions viable if systems can resolve intent, find the right assets, plan joins, generate reliable queries, and return answers—not just result sets.

The forward-looking portion centers on three pillars: retrieval augmented generation to supply relevant context within token limits, semantic layers that encode joins and business metrics like revenue or active users, and rich metadata and glossaries so models do not guess definitions. The talk closes with bets that metadata will dominate, databases will embed semantic capabilities, agents may prefer APIs over handwritten SQL, and new stores may appear for unstructured conversational data queried via embeddings and inference inside the database.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025 Olga Gupalo - From JVM to Native: The Path to Efficient Java Containers
talks.teaser: Shows how to shrink Java containers and cut startup time by compiling Spring Boot apps to GraalVM native images.
talks.summary:
Cloud bills follow resource use, so the footprint of a Java container matters. The session looks at common pain points: slow startup, bulky images, memory tuning, and heavy base images. It then walks through a Spring Boot demo app, moving from a fat jar to a jlink custom runtime, then to ahead-of-time GraalVM native images built with Paketo buildpacks and with Maven.

Each build was compared by its final image size. A fat jar on a Temurin base came to roughly 491 megabytes, and a distroless Java 21 base brought that down to 235 megabytes. A jlink runtime reached 188 megabytes. The Paketo native executable measured 158 megabytes and started in a fraction of a second, against about one second for the JVM-based versions. Optimizing the native binary for size gave 125 megabytes, a mostly static build on a smaller base gave 113 megabytes, and a fully static binary on a scratch image gave 92.3 megabytes. Compressing the executable with UPX brought the final image to 34.5 megabytes, about fourteen times smaller than the first build.

The main lesson is that native image compilation gives a larger reduction than jlink alone, and that the choice of base image sets a floor on size. Minimal images have no shell, package manager or debugging tools, which makes troubleshooting harder. UPX is a final step the speaker did not officially support, and it hides what was stripped out. The demo is reproducible through workshop materials shared by the speaker.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Achim Wiedemann - The DNA of highly effective teams
talks.teaser: Explores feedback loops, psychological safety, clear rules, and SRE habits that help software teams decide better and ship sustainably.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames organizational culture as how work actually gets done, drawing on roughly eighteen years across several companies and teams. The session is organized around feedback, mindset, and long-term priorities rather than pure coding technique.

On feedback, the talk contrasts technical signals from observability and incident response with business metrics and social cues in meetings and retrospectives. Blameless postmortems with a dedicated scribe illustrate how teams capture incidents and turn them into improvements. A CMS migration anecdote shows how unspoken user resistance can waste investment when feedback never reaches decision makers. The mindset section ties psychological safety to assuming good intent, solution-focused language, empathy, and accountability balanced with grace. Clear engineering rules—such as keeping main always deployable behind flags—and explicit responsibilities, including a support rotation, are paired with listening, active clarification, careful naming, readable code, and units embedded in values, illustrated briefly by the Mars Climate Orbiter unit mismatch.

Closing themes cover team spirit, habitual quality practices, technical debt, a bugs-first sprint policy, and service level objectives to trigger stability work. Scenario thinking and parallel experiments—such as dual-writing to compare databases—support investment choices without overbuilding. The takeaway is that better feedback, safer collaboration, clearer agreements, and disciplined habits improve decisions and sustained delivery.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Mads Opheim - How 15 years in politics have made me a better programmer
talks.teaser: Political campaigning offers communication lessons that help developers tailor messages, win support, and prioritize team work.
talks.summary:
A Norwegian government developer who also serves as deputy chair of Oslo’s Red Party argues that long political involvement sharpens everyday engineering work. The opening frames programming and activism as unrelated on the surface, then asks what civic experience teaches about being a better developer or teammate, with the assumption that listeners already know how to code.

The core follows themed blocks on messaging, persuasion, direction, communication, and team habits. Advice mirrors campaign practice: tune language and depth to the audience, compete for limited attention, put the right topics on the agenda, frame problems deliberately, map who must agree and who should deliver the pitch, pick one battle at a time, accept trade-offs, avoid gloating, and do unglamorous blockers before rewarding features. Later sections cover open versus closed questions, filtering unhelpful feedback, kindness in disagreement, meeting agendas and time limits, invisible operational tasks, and accepting that work never fully finishes.

The close recaps prioritize important changes, tailor communication, and collaborate as allies. Audience questions touch on teaching these habits in developer education and escalating persistent hostile behavior through management. Skipped bonus topics include procurement versus campaigning and estimation versus polling; brief closing notes warn about UI distractions, slippery terminology, deferred decisions, and removing capabilities users still need.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Loic Magnette - Bridging the Gap: Full-Stack Development Without the Headaches
talks.teaser: Shows how Quarkus can serve a JavaScript front end alongside a Java backend, with live reload during development.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a common situation for Java developers who are asked to build a JavaScript front end next to their back end. Rather than adding scripts or task runners that each need learning, the speaker argues for handling everything through Quarkus, whose development mode offers automatic reloading and integrated dev tooling.

A live demo builds a small application that logs animals seen on a safari, with an Angular front end and a Quarkus REST back end using Panache for persistence. Two routes for the front end are compared. The Kinoa extension runs the npm build during packaging and copies the output into the jar, passing unmatched requests through to REST endpoints. The web bundler instead resolves JavaScript dependencies from Maven repositories as web jars and bundles them with ES build, which does not support Angular, so it suits frameworks such as React.

The speaker also shows that generated API clients from an OpenAPI specification keep the front end in sync, that a database container starts automatically in development, and that a native executable can be built. The main takeaway is that Kinoa suits any Node framework but still requires managing npm, while the web bundler removes npm at the cost of framework support.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Tomasz Manugiewicz - The powerful careers of quiet engineers
talks.teaser: Quiet engineers learn how introversion shapes technical strengths, leadership, and career tactics that build trust with executives.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the speaker’s mistaken belief that talkativeness meant extroversion, and how an MBTI assessment and readings from Jung, Jonathan Cheek, Susan Cain, and others reframed introversion as a continuum—including social, thinking, restrained, and anxious types—rather than a fixed label.

The middle maps those traits onto engineering and leadership: deep focus, analytical work, quality delivery, thoughtful team leadership, mediation without dominating conversations, and “critical mission” roles where trusted quiet contributors answer urgent executive questions on pivots, proofs of concept, and sensitive research.

Practical guidance covers energy-aware calendaring, meeting preparation, venue familiarization, exit strategies, deep versus wide networking, leading other introverts, and career accelerators—a career care group, an external portfolio, stakeholder influence matrices, and showing vulnerability to unlock creativity—closing with Cain’s advice to match work to natural concentration and the work that matters.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Krzysztof Dębski - Collaborate with Agents: Build Your First Multi-Agent System
talks.teaser: Walks through LangGraph4j multi-agent systems on the JVM, covering graph design, demos, and pitfalls like infinite loops.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting early rule-based chat bots—such as a Polish moderation agent backed by tens of thousands of regex lines—with today’s LLM-driven agents. The speaker argues that real processes like know-your-customer checks branch, cycle, and cross borders in ways that resist simple linear code, and that multi-agent setups can orchestrate flexible flows while sharing state and remaining observable.

After sketching supervisor, swarm, and graph-style architectures, the talk surveys young frameworks including AutoGen, CrewAI, Google’s agent kit, and LangGraph, then centers on LangGraph4j for JVM developers. It explains nodes, edges, conditional routing, shared graph state, checkpoints for chat memory, reducers, and patterns such as supervised routing and graphs exposed as tools. A compiled demo graph uses a supervisor to dispatch researcher and coder agents; a arithmetic prompt succeeds, while a question about city populations triggers a non-terminating supervisor loop.

The closing section catalogs practical failures: fast-moving and inconsistent APIs, concurrency quirks in state merging, strict ordering between AI and tool messages, tool calls that retry forever on empty results, ever-growing message state, and latency far above typical microservice expectations—including timeouts on event-driven cloud triggers. Audience questions touch on splitting responsibilities across agents, prior marketplace chat automation, actor-style modeling, and when integration-oriented workflow tools suit teams that are not full-time coders.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Michał Gwarzynski - The Art of Trade-off
talks.teaser: Explores pragmatic architecture trade-offs while evolving a near-real-time marketing automation platform through production experiments.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames software engineering as a daily balancing act among scalability, simplicity, consistency, availability, and delivery speed. Using a marketing automation platform at Allegro as the backdrop, the speaker walks through how abandoned-cart style scenarios force product and technical choices about channels, personalization, and when not to notify users.

The first major arc is a greenfield shift from batch Spark processing to near-real-time behavior via a bridge module on the legacy stack, a modular monolith, Kotlin with MongoDB, and a walking-skeleton launch that traded polish for fast feedback. A core aggregates module then drove write-heavy workloads, naive versus grouped document modeling tested in production, discovery of MongoDB replication locking, a Cassandra migration validated through shadow deployment, and relief from data skew by blacklisting outlier merchants.

Organizational pressure later reversed the Cassandra bet after improved MongoDB replication and platform team support. Closing guidance stresses multidimensional context, partnering with business to soften requirements, learning tools deeply while questioning their assumptions, and frequent reality checks through tests, scripts, and production deployments.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Marton Kodok - AI Agents with Gemini 2.0: Beyond the Chatbot
talks.teaser: Walks through Google's Gemini models, developer tools and the Agent Development Kit, then builds agents live.
talks.summary:
The session starts with the Gemini product landscape, separating consumer apps, research tools, open local models such as Gemma, and the developer and enterprise routes through AI Studio and Google Cloud's Vertex AI. It explains that a single SDK can switch between those endpoints, and covers capabilities such as long context windows, adjustable thinking budgets and built-in tools like Google Search. Function calling is shown as a loop where the application, not the model, executes the requested function and returns the result.

The middle moves to the Agent Development Kit, an open-source framework where the model decides how to route work between agents, with connectors for OpenAPI tools, MCP servers and the agent-to-agent protocol. A live demo builds a web-reading agent with a BigQuery toolset to load conference agenda data into a table, but table creation hit a missing dataset error. A second case covers a wine-bottle catalogue, where large images initially returned no usable text until resolution settings and segmentation masks were used to crop the labels.

The closing advice is to start with prompts before writing orchestration code, and to read a PDF book on agent behaviour. The speaker points to a trading-simulator tutorial and a codelab covering ADK, A2A and MCP on Google Cloud as hands-on follow-ups. On maintenance, the argument is that agents rest on APIs and business logic, so swapping a protocol should be a prompt-driven change rather than a rewrite.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Vadzim Prudnikau - Wrong and Useless Models built by using Domain-Driven Design
talks.teaser: Shows how tactical domain-driven design keeps models small, useful, and aligned with business rules instead of reality.
talks.summary:
The session opens by separating domain knowledge from models: a domain is a broad sphere of knowledge, while a model is a simplified representation aimed at one problem. The speaker cites fraud detection in banking and navigation as examples where the same domain admits different models, and uses a hiking story to show that tools like map apps work in some contexts but fail in others. The familiar line that all models are wrong but some are useful anchorss the rest of the talk.

A large share of the material covers tactical domain-driven design after a brief strategic prelude. Value objects are immutable and defined by their values; entities have identity and lifecycle; aggregates form consistency boundaries around invariants, with business logic living on the aggregate root and a single repository per aggregate. The speaker warns against starting with renaming data access objects to repositories, recommends event storming before coding, and critiques monolithic schemas with hundreds of tables. Practical guidance includes not mirroring full reality in the schema, allowing simple CRUD where rules are thin, avoiding bidirectional associations, discarding early drafts, and aligning class names with ubiquitous language.

Closing sections address implementation and persistence. Behavior and tests should drive fields rather than private lists chosen by habit. Persistence advice favors pragmatism over early table obsession, mentions snapshot-style mapping when relational schemas fight graph-shaped models, and limits repositories to loading whole aggregates for domain operations rather than open-ended query surfaces or reporting. Tactical patterns are presented as a toolbox applied after strategic work, with off-the-shelf solutions acceptable outside the core business.

talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Maciej Krzysica - Why should we be careful with AI?
talks.teaser: Shows how AI-made images, fake shops and text detectors create fraud and misinformation risks for everyday users.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI brings real risks alongside its productivity gains. It opens with a comparison of human and artificial brains, then moves to deception. Examples include an AI-generated photo of a politician in a military uniform, a real G7 photo that viewers might doubt, and a video built from a former US president's voice samples. Detection tricks such as checking light reflections in the eyes help, but they are imperfect.

Fraud and accuracy come next. Fake online shops use generated product images and disappear quickly, leaving buyers with the wrong goods. A job candidate on LinkedIn hid behind a generated face while answering questions with an AI tool. Nearly a quarter of surveyed respondents reported inaccuracy problems from AI adoption. Text is hard to check too: one detector rated the US Declaration of Independence as nearly 98% likely AI-written, and words such as intricate and meticulous have spread in scientific publishing.

The closing advice is practical: check every AI output, get approval before using AI, and disclose its use. Copyright and legal rules remain unsettled, and AI has no concept of truth, so people carry responsibility for accuracy. In the Q&A, the speaker expected AI to change jobs rather than replace them and warned that learning and focus may suffer when students and workers lean on it too much.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Jarek Ratajski - The Story of BASIC
talks.teaser: A narrative tour traces how BASIC shaped home computing, Microsoft's founding, and why mainstream languages eventually fade.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by noting the talk is deliberately impractical yet interesting: BASIC once saturated schools, engineering benches, and early microcomputers, then largely vanished from professional software culture. He polls the room on Java tenure as a parallel for long-lived mainstream languages, then walks from Dartmouth’s design goals through General Electric hardware, punch-card delays, and the choice of a simple interpreted language aimed at non-specialists.

The middle follows Bill Gates and Paul Allen writing 8080 BASIC for the Altair without physical hardware—emulator, manual, bootstrap loader on switches, and brutal memory tricks such as marking string terminators with the high bit. Steve Wozniak’s paper-coded Integer BASIC, Commodore ROM deals, software copying debates, and dialect fragmentation on PET, Apple, and IBM PC show how Microsoft BASIC became the de facto platform layer. A short Commodore 64 demo illustrates POKE, GOTO-heavy style, and tape-era workflows.

He closes on why BASIC faded: perceived slowness, incompatible dialects, Dijkstra-era disdain for GOTO, and replacement by spreadsheets, shells, Python, and web tools for tasks users once coded themselves. Practitioners gain a concrete lineage from hobbyist affordance to licensing wars and a lens for asking whether today’s default languages might age the same way—not because the tech failed, but because casual users no longer need to program to get results.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Erik Dörnenburg - A Developer's Perspective On Greener Future: GreenOps in practice
talks.teaser: Connects carbon efficiency, grid-aware workload shifts, and GreenOps metrics to concrete changes in how teams build and run software.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames sustainability of IT—making software itself less carbon-intensive—as a meaningful share of global electricity use, even when individual teams feel their footprint is tiny. He walks through carbon efficiency concepts such as CO2 equivalent, power usage effectiveness in data centers, embodied emissions from hardware manufacturing, idle server draw, and research comparing language runtime energy use, while noting when simplifications break down.

Carbon awareness comes next: grid mix changes by time and region, so deferrable jobs can run when electricity is cleaner. Examples include enterprise cloud workloads, large GPU training runs, and public data about regional carbon intensity. Measurement is often estimation; the Etsy migration story and the open Cloud Carbon Footprint approach show how billing APIs, SPEC power curves, PUE, and grid factors combine, with Kepler cited for attribution in Kubernetes when hardware telemetry exists.

GreenOps parallels FinOps, and practitioners are urged to treat carbon like an architecture concern. Tactics include cloud elasticity, shifting regions, scheduling CI farms to working hours, separating storage and compute where it avoids wasted capacity, and weather-informed batch scheduling as in a Microsoft and UBS case study. Machine learning guidance favors foundation models, efficient accelerators, smarter hyperparameter search, and time-or-region-aware training, with cloud sustainability checklists as review aids.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Jan Martiška - Developing AI applications in Java with Quarkus and Langchain4j
talks.teaser: Shows how Quarkus and LangChain4j let Java developers build LLM chat, retrieval and tool-calling features with little setup.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces LangChain4j, a Java library that offers common abstractions for chat models, chat memory, embedding stores and AI services, and explains why pairing it with Quarkus makes it easier to use. The speaker outlines the benefits Quarkus adds: CDI injection, one configuration file, build-time setup, native image support, out-of-the-box metrics and tracing, and a development UI for trying models from one place.

The demos start small: a JBang script of about a dozen lines that exposes an HTTP endpoint returning jokes from an OpenAI model, and an AI service interface for a hotel booking bot whose response maps directly onto a Java class. For retrieval-augmented generation, an easy-RAG sample ingests a folder of mixed-format documents at startup into an in-memory store, and the same setup is then pointed at a Neo4j store. A second approach skips embeddings: a query transformer rewrites a follow-up question, the model generates SQL against a PostgreSQL movie table, and the results are passed back to the model as JSON context. The speaker also shows a tool that lets the model send an email, with the resulting traces and metrics appearing in the observability tools.

The talk closes with a reminder that LLM-generated SQL needs guarding against misuse, so the SQL approach is presented as an experiment rather than production advice. Local models through Ollama are mentioned as an option for in-house deployments. Developers come away with a sense of how much plumbing Quarkus removes when building LLM features in Java.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Vadym Kazulkin - High performance Serverless Java on AWS
talks.teaser: Shows how to cut Java Lambda cold starts on AWS with SnapStart, priming, JVM tuning and GraalVM native images.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why Java functions on AWS Lambda suffer from long cold starts, which the speaker argues has slowed Java adoption for serverless work. A cold start occurs when Lambda builds a new execution environment, such as after a deployment or a container recycle, and it covers runtime startup, class loading and static initializers. In a demo with API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB at 1 GB of memory, default settings gave P90 cold starts of about 3.3 seconds.

Each optimization was then measured against that baseline. Moving clients into static initializers and priming the code with a fake DynamoDB call moved framework setup out of the first real request. SnapStart, combined with priming, brought the P90 cold start down to a little over one second. Smaller deployment packages, a JIT setting that stops at level one, and the AWS CRT HTTP client also helped, with around 1 GB of memory as the sweet spot. GraalVM native images on a custom runtime reduced cold starts further, but they need Linux builds, substantial build resources and reflection configuration.

The main takeaway is to start with SnapStart where the code can be primed, since it is a managed checkbox, and to consider native images for latency-critical services that can absorb the extra build work. The speaker also flagged SnapStart limits: managed Java runtimes only, x86 only, about 2.5 minutes of added deployment time, and snapshots removed after 14 days without invocations.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Rafał Legiędź - XR Demystified Separating Facts from Fiction in 2024
talks.teaser: The session charts a decade of mainstream XR hardware and clears common myths about cost, sickness, isolation, and enterprise adoption.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by arguing that peers underestimate how far augmented and virtual reality have come, then proposes extended reality as a single umbrella with only two experiences: augmented reality overlays on the real world and virtual reality’s full immersion. He frames 2014 as a market inflection after Google Glass, then walks year by year through mainstream business-relevant hardware—from HoloLens and PlayStation VR through ARKit, ARCore, standalone Meta Quest lines, Magic Leap, and Apple Vision Pro—with pricing, tracking advances, and practical trade-offs such as weight, batteries, and enterprise fit.

Industrial examples anchor the middle: shipyard piping measurement on Magic Leap 2 and HoloLens-guided laser welding training, countering the idea that XR is only gaming or entertainment. He then tackles recurring misconceptions—motion sickness tied to software quality rather than hardware alone, AR versus VR distinctions, isolation eased by mixed-reality passthrough, and claims that the field has peaked—using headset design constraints and growing mainstream adoption as counterevidence.

The close recommends entry points by budget and role: Meta Quest 3 for value, iPhones and iPads for mobile AR tracking, Magic Leap 2 for optical see-through enterprise work, and Vision Pro where Apple’s ecosystem matters. Getting started means free Unity, AR Foundation for cross-device APIs, and Microsoft’s Mixed Reality Toolkit for head-worn UI, with brief Q&A on older Oculus hardware, AI-assisted authoring, accessibility uses, and camera glasses paired with assistants.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Tomasz Kowalczewski - Using vectors in Java [...]
talks.teaser: Connects dark silicon and Java's Vector API through live cosine-similarity benchmarks and the memory-layout constraints SIMD rewards.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting decades of for-loop performance with why transistor growth no longer yields free speedups: Dennard scaling has faded, leaving dark silicon that cannot all be powered at once, which helps explain heterogeneous chips with performance and efficient cores plus specialized blocks.

From there it introduces Java's Vector API—species, shapes, loading from arrays or memory segments, lane-wise math, fused multiply-add, and horizontal reduction—using cosine similarity on float embeddings as the worked example. A JMH run on roughly ten million elements reports scalar code in the low microsecond range versus a vectorized path roughly twenty times faster when the JVM keeps the hot path optimized to tight load-add style assembly.

The closing emphasis is practical limits: domain objects and row-oriented data force costly gathers and copies, columnar packed layouts suit vector loads better, and compression fights in-register use; masking, shuffles, and latency versus throughput matter for scheduling. Vector code optimizes well until it falls off a cliff into heap allocations, so the speaker treats the API as preview material best explored outside production until value types mature.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Rafal Foltynski
talks.teaser: Surveys why IT teams chase velocity, then shows Java micro-optimizations, Spring Boot startup cuts, and process changes that compound.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that customers, support, product owners, and developers all care about speed, then traces how calculation throughput grew from mechanical looms and punch-card machines through MIPS benchmarks to today's assumption that computers are instantly fast. The speaker contends that virtualization, containers, cloud growth, AI hype, extreme layering, and résumé-driven stacks often hide regressions behind buzzwords and premature “legacy” labels.

The technical core centers on Java: JMH-style benchmarks comparing for-loops, foreach, and cached sizes on ArrayList versus arrays; a custom Spring Boot autoconfiguration inclusion filter that reportedly trims startup from about 1.1–1.2 seconds toward roughly 900–950 milliseconds; precomputed hash codes versus Lombok-generated equals and hashCode in hash collections; and GC Viewer analysis of a Netty-based file sender that allocated tens of gigabytes in minutes until a fork cut heap churn. Each improvement took on the order of two to four hours, illustrating compounding small gains.

The closing sections shift to organizational speed: measure rather than guess, test enough to change code safely, shrink planning meetings, pair program, collaborate across teams, trim unused features, and mix methodologies pragmatically. The takeaway is to favor simple, fast, testable systems over fashionable complexity, contribute fixes upstream when possible, and verify performance in realistic environments.
