talks.title: GeeCON 2025: Baruch Sadogursky, Leonid Igolnik - Back to the Future of Software
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2025: Baruch Sadogursky, Leonid Igolnik - Back to the Future of Software.
talks.summary:
Baruch Sadogursky and Leonid Igolnik present the "intent integrity chain," a methodology for safely leveraging AI-generated code by constraining Large Language Models (LLMs) through structured validation at each stage of development. The keynote addresses widespread fears that AI will replace programmers, noting that while companies report 30% AI-generated code adoption, LLMs are fundamentally stochastic systems producing incorrect code 60% of the time. Cited studies show GitHub Copilot, Amazon CodeWhisperer, and ChatGPT have error rates of 62%, 46%, and 31% respectively. Beyond incorrect output, LLMs hallucinate confidently—inventing non-existent libraries and introducing security vulnerabilities in 40% of generated code. Unlike previous technology fears (cloud, Java bytecode, SaaS) that proved unfounded after maturation, LLMs are inherently different because they generate wrong code by design due to their stochastic nature.

The core problem is expressing intent clearly to non-deterministic systems. The speakers introduce the "curse of knowledge"—domain experts unconsciously omit obvious details when describing systems, while LLMs have no context and execute instructions literally. Example: when asked to speed up a JSON parser, an LLM removed validation logic and then deleted the tests that caught this mistake.

The solution is the "intent integrity chain," a multi-stage validation process: (1) Humans write free-form prompts; (2) AI generates structured specifications in readable format (Gherkin); (3) Humans review and approve specs; (4) Deterministic systems generate tests from specs without variability; (5) AI generates code; (6) Tests are locked (immutable) so LLMs cannot modify them. Each stage is validated either by humans or deterministic machines, building "executable shared understanding"—documentation that is both human-readable and machine-executable.

Three foundational pillars enable this approach: deep domain expertise (understanding business and technical domains), structural imagination (envisioning failure modes), and guardrails (constraints preventing undesired shortcuts). Test-Driven Development becomes critical not as an aspirational practice (only 5% of developers use it daily) but as a guardrail automatically enforced by AI agents.

The speakers demonstrated the concept using IntelliJ, generating a to-do application. The system automatically created system architecture documentation, technical assumptions, test scenarios in plain English, formalized them into Gherkin specifications, and generated tests—all reviewed and approved before code generation. The process iterated when missing features were discovered, regenerating components while maintaining version control with high-quality commit messages. After multiple iterations, all tests passed and functional code was generated.

The speakers emphasize that mastery matters more than ever. Previous abstraction layers (cloud, Java, DevOps) triggered similar fears but created new roles—system administrators evolved into platform engineers. Similarly, developers will guide AI agents rather than write all code themselves. Smaller, simpler tasks yield better LLM results, aligning with microservices architecture. They also describe a "reverse intent integrity chain" for extracting specifications from existing code, enabling documentation of legacy systems.

Throughout, the speakers stress that domain expertise is not replaced but amplified by AI. Without expertise, using these tools becomes harmful. The rapidly evolving ecosystem (Cursor, Windsurf, Claude, GitHub Copilot, IntelliJ) increasingly supports configurable guardrails and guidelines. The speakers conclude that every industry abstraction started with panic but ultimately enabled building more complex systems, and this pattern continues with LLMs—provided developers master both the tools and their domains.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Ted Neward - Why the Next Five Years Will Be About Languages
talks.teaser: Explores how virtualization, better compilers, and service boundaries could spark a programming language renaissance.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by rejecting the idea that artificial intelligence is the only future-facing topic developers must chase, framing the real anxiety as staying employable amid relentless complexity. He recounts decades of web stacks swinging between thick clients, server rendering, single-page applications, and server-side rendering again, arguing that languages exist mainly to hide physical details and raise abstraction, as C, C++, and Java did in earlier eras.

Much of the talk diagnoses a long-standing gap between practitioners who need shipping software and academics who prototype novel paradigms, using functional programming’s decades-long path to database access as an example. He describes four converging enablers—virtual machines, language construction tools, renewed interest in linguistic ideas from Haskell and Lisp, and microservice boundaries over HTTP—that let designers target JVM or CLR ecosystems without rebuilding everything. Examples include aspect-oriented tooling, Java streams and iterators, reactive user-interface patterns, and brief showcases of Jolie for services, Wing for cloud-shaped local testing, and Inform for literate, naturalistic game code.

He closes on concurrency after the “free lunch” ended, pain in pure object models for transactional work, and bloated framework bootstraps. Adoption hurdles—skeptical managers, senior engineers guarding expertise, and fear of picking losers—mirror framework bets. He urges audiences to monitor emerging and legacy languages alike, involve teams when shaping domain-specific approaches, and remember that languages should serve people rather than dictate how they work.

talks.title: GeeCON 2024: Natan Silnitsky - Scaling Horizons Effective Strategies for Wix's Scaling challenges
talks.teaser: A infrastructure lead walks through five horizontal scaling patterns Wix applies to Kafka, web traffic, and databases at massive scale.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Wix’s scale—thousands of microservices, billions of daily HTTP requests, tens of billions of Kafka events, and petabytes of transactional data—and frames scaling as a choice between vertical growth and distributing work across more nodes. A recent Redis CPU saturation incident illustrates why vertical limits and cost eventually force horizontal answers, and why both the application layer (HTTP balancing, event consumers, database sharding) and the routing key strategy matter.

Five real patterns span from fixed partitioning to dynamic hashing. Kafka consumer proxies are split per cluster to cut managed-consumer cost and avoid a single failure stopping all event processing. Webhook delivery uses separate quality-of-service fleets so slow endpoints do not delay critical tenants like restaurant orders, with manual moves between pools when alerts or complaints appear. Site traffic splits editor and public segments via host-based rules behind load balancers. A high-throughput reactions service combines Kafka partition parallelism with DynamoDB’s partition behavior, including awareness of per-partition capacity and hot keys. For enterprise GDPR-style locality, ProxySQL routes MySQL traffic using query hints to geographic or dedicated clusters while supporting broader sharding goals.

The closing guidance favors vertical scaling while machines stay cheap, then horizontal approaches with eyes open to operational complexity. Prefer fixed shards when tenant groups stay small; use predetermined rules when domain knowledge exists (hosts, regions, SLAs); fall back to consistent hashing when routing cannot be predefined. nginx, Kafka, DynamoDB where autoscaling justifies cost, and MySQL behind ProxySQL for economical control appear as the core toolkit, with room to combine fixed segments and dynamic routing inside them.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Štěpán Šindelář - GraalVM Scripting Languages as Maven Dependencies
talks.teaser: Explains how GraalVM Truffle languages ship on Maven Central and embed Python in Java apps with polyglot APIs.
talks.summary:
GraalVM is more than native image: the talk centers on Truffle-based scripting languages and JVM integration. The speaker contrasts JIT, native image, and polyglot compilation, then reviews GraalVM for JDK 21 changes that retire the gu updater and split JDK distributions from language packs via the Truffle Unchained effort.

Languages such as GraalPy, GraalJS, Ruby, LLVM, and WebAssembly can be consumed as standalone runtimes or as Maven Central artifacts on JDK 21 and newer Oracle or OpenJDK builds. The polyglot API drives live demos: isolated contexts, host-access rules for Java arrays, performance with and without the Graal compiler, native image packaging, and a Micronaut UI that evaluates user-supplied Python filters against in-memory book data.

Practitioners learn concrete dependency coordinates, backward-compatibility plans through Java 25, warnings when JIT is unavailable, sandboxing via native image isolation, GraalPy compatibility and Jython migration notes, and planned Maven plugins for Python dependencies. Q&A covers debugging, licensing, resource cost, Django and Flask fit, Gradle support, and ML native-extension limits.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023 Prague: Ignasi Marimon-Clos i Sunyol - The Emperor Has No Docs
talks.teaser: A developer maps documentation to testing practice and shares habits, triggers, and stakeholder arguments for writing docs first.
talks.summary:
The session opens by dramatizing how dense, passive prose loses readers, then restarts with a proper conference frame: audience, expectations, and a promised arc from personal change through tricks, habits, and business impact. The presenter describes years of spec skimming, coding, and deploying without tests or docs, then a shock after joining an open-source team that needed heavy public documentation right after a release.

The middle ties documentation to familiar engineering craft. Layered models (context through code), clarity properties, and Diátaxis-style doc types set structure; parallels to test-first work cover blank pages, expert paradox, naming, and even drafting behavior in Scala before implementation. Triggers use idle time and pull-request workflow; culture tips favor low friction, discoverable in-place docs, and answers that point to written sources instead of chat.

The close stages a debate with common objections—maintenance, detail level, stability, storage—answered with empathy, “some docs beat none,” and API examples where manuals change outcomes. Stakeholder themes cover onboarding, bus factor, and conventions. It ends with an emperor’s-new-clothes fable beat and a board-game rules demo showing how official text often goes unread when interfaces look alike but rules differ.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Paweł Marks - The origin of the feature
talks.teaser: A structured walkthrough explains how language features are born, judged, and sometimes redesigned, with Scala as the central case study.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by framing what actually distinguishes programming languages beyond Turing completeness: how much boilerplate a task takes, how invariants are enforced, how the language guides newcomers, and how all of that feeds maintainability. He walks through concrete illustrations—Java before and after records, Rust’s safety model, Scala dependent types that stop cross-user event mix-ups, and refinement-driven GraphQL clients that get IDE completion without schema downloads or codegen.

The middle of the session turns criteria for a “good” language feature: real improvement, simplicity and its costs (Rust lifetimes versus Java GC), false simplicity, uniqueness of mechanism and naming, discoverability of syntax, composability with existing features, and consistent tooling support. Scala 2’s overloaded implicit keyword serves as a cautionary design; Scala 3’s given, using, and extension keywords show a sound idea reimplemented more clearly for separating inputs from environment.

He closes by arguing that neat scorecards rarely suffice—intuitiveness depends on audience, type-system choices trade structural versus nominal strengths, and languages converge on ideas independently while rarely inventing wholly new theory. A brief note on AI assistants suggests boilerplate may matter less while compile-time safety and guidance matter more. Q&A touches on reasons to adopt Scala in 2023 and Java ergonomics around immutability.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Vojtěch Juránek - Feeding the ML model with data from the database
talks.teaser: Change data capture streams database writes to Flink and TensorFlow so models learn and score in real time with less SQL load.
talks.summary:
The talk opens on a slice of MLOps: moving data from operational databases into machine learning models without drowning the database in queries, losing rows, or breaking consistency when everything must run in real time. The speaker contrasts one-off SQL loaders and custom dual-write services with change data capture as the piece that belongs in that pipeline.

Change data capture watches the database transaction log and emits insert, update, delete, and schema events as a stream. He presents Debezium as an open source CDC platform—often deployed as a Kafka Connect source, though it can target other brokers and sinks—and mentions snapshots before streaming, broad database support, and operational extras such as a UI and a Kubernetes operator. For machine learning he walks through Debezium into Kafka with Apache Flink, including built-in Debezium support that can avoid Kafka, and a short online clustering example using Flink’s ML libraries. With TensorFlow he notes that Kafka records may arrive as strings, and shows how Debezium single message transforms can reshape payloads—for example to CSV—so a small parse step restores numeric tensors.

Practitioners should treat CDC as the bridge from OLTP stores to live models and online learning, lean on prepared integration examples where available, and keep SMTs in mind when downstream frameworks expect a different wire format.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Szymon Sadowski - The art of investigating problems in software
talks.teaser: Case studies cover problem isolation, Wireshark on npm auth, Maven remote debugging, and strace around container kill rules.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that productive debugging starts with attitude: treating long sessions as learning time rather than wasted effort, and staying willing to inspect systems layer by layer. It introduces problem isolation as the core habit—pinpointing where a failure appears before chasing fixes—and illustrates that pattern with mis-encoded non-Latin text moving through a multi-tier encyclopedia stack, substitution tricks to exclude components, and a network troubleshooting walk aligned with layering from physical links upward.

Four worked examples carry most of the technical depth. Unauthorized errors while wiring Lerna to a private npm registry yield nothing useful in HTTP authorization until packet capture shows the issue is really version-range behavior in the tool itself. A duplicate-project failure in a huge Maven reactor lacks location hints in the error, so the speaker downloads Maven sources, attaches a debugger via the debug goal, uses an exception breakpoint and drop-frame replay, and surfaces two conflicting module import paths in the default project builder. A Kaniko build breaks after adding a drop-kill security context; syscall tracing reveals a Dockerfile pattern where a shell-spawned daemon keeps a different effective user ID than the parent process.

Closing guidance is deliberately simple: enthusiasm to keep going and courage to open third-party code or unfamiliar tracers when high-level messages stop helping. A brief audience question on reactive WebFlux debugging is deferred because it sits outside the speaker’s day-to-day stack.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Piotr Przybył - Integration tests are needed and simple
talks.teaser: Live demos contrast part-level unit tests with real integration checks, then show how Testcontainers runs Java services in Docker.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a physical metaphor: a homemade gas alarm whose LEDs, speaker, and sensor were each unit-tested, yet nobody would mount it in a kitchen. A commercial detector’s “push to test” button only fakes danger; sealing it with real carbon monoxide proves whether the whole system works. That sets up the software question—why teams still ship like the DIY box when one containerized end-to-end test can matter more.

The middle builds a demo carbon-monoxide service in Java: an HTTP server that ingests particles, checks every second, and prints an alarm above 400 particles per million. Integration tests spin a generic Testcontainers image, copy the JAR, map ports, and assert startup within four seconds, periodic “checking” logs, and alarm output after sending 1,000 oxygen posts and one CO post. Failures trace to waiting strategies (port open before logs say “started”), divide-by-zero in ratio math, and integer BigDecimal division—each fixed in front of the room.

The close positions Testcontainers across Java, .NET, Python, Node, and Rust atop Docker, with modules for databases, Kafka, Redis, and Toxic Proxy, plus optional cloud offload instead of local CPU. Practitioners should treat integration tests as foundation, not a replacement for focused unit tests on parts you control, and avoid hard-coded hosts or ports when talking to containers.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Jorge Franco - Microservices or not? A dependency management decision
talks.teaser: Shows how a Java modular application can keep microservices as a later, optional deployment choice.
talks.summary:
The speaker's company, Magnolia, sells a large, old Java monolith with many coupled modules in three models: on-premises, managed cloud and SaaS. The lab team needed to decouple it, and they started from the view that microservices need a concrete reason, not a default answer.

The approach separates each module into an API module holding only domain interfaces and simple records, with no logic and no external libraries. A shared test suite, modelled on a compatibility kit, defines what any implementation must do, and an implementation module runs those tests. Applications depend only on the API and inject the implementation. To make a module remote, the team adds an endpoints module written against standard Jakarta REST, an HTTP client that implements the same interface, and a packaged service. The application then changes only its dependency to use the remote version. The talk also lists drawbacks, including more code and the conversions needed between separate DTO and domain classes.

The takeaways are to keep modules simple, put a domain interface in front of external libraries, provide testing tooling for module consumers, and test in production-like environments rather than local mocks. In the Q&A, the speaker said generated OpenAPI clients add HTTP coupling to a module, which is why the team kept its own separation, and noted that the approach demands strong team discipline.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Daniel Pokusa - Linux terminal for java developers - boost your efficiency!
talks.teaser: A live terminal walkthrough shows Java developers how to navigate faster, search smarter, and automate daily shell workflows.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a distinction between accumulating technical knowledge and building day-to-day proficiency, then reframes the shell as an RPG-style tutorial where small habits compound into saved time for harder problems. Most of the delivery happens live in the terminal: moving between projects with stacks and fuzzy directory jumpers, locating files with find, fzf, tree, and broot, and searching content with grep, ripgrep, and bat instead of raw cat and tail on huge files.

The middle covers “inventory” concepts—passive helpers such as a rich prompt, git status cues, and SDKMAN switching Java (and related) versions when entering project folders, versus active tools like tldr, Ctrl-R history search, editor toggles, lazygit, and kubectl piped through awk. A Fallout-themed demo ties the pieces together: polling an HTTP status on an interval, tailing logs, piping through an interactive plumber, and extracting a path with jq before running a retrieved script—while stressing that pasted scripts deserve a read first.

The close turns to crafting: aliases, suffix opens, small bash scripts, expect for non-interactive input, and bashly for generating CLI scaffolding. A public GitHub repository mirrors the demo material, and Q&A covers zsh setups on Linux, WSL, and macOS, Terminator, plugin sprawl, and roughly thirty-minute machine bootstrap via personal dotfiles and Ansible.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Guy Royse - So You Think You Know Redis!
talks.teaser: A game-show session quizzes the room on Redis strings, bitfields, eviction policies, modules, lists, sorted sets, and persistence settings.
talks.summary:
The session frames Redis literacy as a live game show: the presenter poses multiple-choice puzzles while the audience answers through Slido, with candy prizes for correct responses. Early rounds focus on how Redis treats string values as opaque byte blobs rather than encoded text, including emoji storage, CLI escape output, piping binary via redis-cli -x, and a demo that round-trips a JPEG through GET/SET.

Middle segments dig into lesser-known commands and operations. BITFIELD extracts and mutates arbitrary bit ranges across string bytes, including cross-byte reads and increments that visibly alter stored text. Memory management covers maxmemory limits, volatile versus persistent keys, TTL semantics, and eviction policies such as volatile-lru when memory is exhausted, plus a “never full” LRU cache pattern. A trick question highlights that vanilla open-source Redis ships without loadable modules, contrasting Redis Stack extensions (JSON, search, time series, Bloom filters, functions) and the one-way risk of unloading modules that introduced custom types.

Later questions clarify list push ordering, sorted-set intersections and score aggregation, and persistence: save directive thresholds versus blocking SAVE, background RDB snapshots, and append-only file tuning with fsync tradeoffs. The closing message stresses treating Redis as a configurable, memory-first database with replication and clustering options—not only a cache—and points listeners to command references, Stack, Insight, and community channels for follow-up.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Bartłomiej Kuczyński - ID, EGO and Super EGO of your entity
talks.teaser: Compares sequences, UUIDs, ULIDs, and custom generators for entity IDs across JVM internals, databases, and distributed apps.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames entity identifiers beyond JPA alone—anything persisted in relational, NoSQL, or cloud stores—and uses Freud’s id, ego, and super-ego as a metaphor. The “id” layer covers how the JVM recognizes objects in memory through ordinary object pointers, mark words (identity hash codes, lock bits, GC metadata), and class pointers, plus when layout matters for monitors, cache lines, or embedded JVMs.

The “ego” section walks through technical identifier strategies: database sequences, in-process atomic counters, UUIDs, ULIDs, Snowflake-style IDs, and a compact base-58 generator inspired by short public URLs. Each option is judged on uniqueness, speed, ease of use, sortability, gap-free numbering, multi-node coordination, and index behavior—with demos and benchmarks on Ubuntu, OpenJDK 20, and concurrent hash maps showing collision rates when many threads each own a generator.

The “super-ego” layer covers natural and business identifiers: email, national IDs, invoice numbers, order references across contexts, GDPR sensitivity, and customer-facing usability. Practitioners should match identifier shape to aggregate roots in domain-driven design, prefer index-friendly randomness over naive UUID storage in some databases, and reserve gap-free sequences for domains that truly require continuous numbering.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Rustam Mehmandarov - 5 quick tips to make your Java apps more awesome
talks.teaser: Five Jakarta EE and MicroProfile tips deliver fault tolerance, probes, metrics, toggles, and automation for cloud-ready Java.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames “awesome” Java applications as services that stay usable when dependencies fail, report their own condition, and ship without manual environment clicks. He uses Jakarta EE Core Profile and MicroProfile as concrete examples, noting the rename from Java EE and that vendors implement the same specifications.

Five capabilities drive the walkthrough. Fault tolerance covers timeouts, retries, fallbacks, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and async handling, with a dice-based flaky HTTP service failing over to a backup endpoint so users still get a degraded response. Health checks separate liveness, readiness, and startup probes for orchestrators such as Kubernetes. Metrics expose built-in and custom counters via a standard scrape endpoint. Feature toggling, demonstrated with Unleash, flips behavior without redeploying and supports gradual rollout and hiding incomplete work. Environment and infrastructure treatment stresses configuration libraries, Terraform or Pulumi-style automation, and choosing platforms—including when Kubernetes may be oversized.

Live demos tie toggles and failover together in a multi-container setup documented in the project readme. The closing note is to keep documentation aligned with what production actually runs.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Rustam Mehmandarov, Mads Opheim - Modern Java App Development in the Cloud
talks.teaser: Follows a simple Java app from local run to serverless cloud deployment using MicroProfile and Quarkus.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a tiny Java program that prints two random words and asks what it takes to make that program available to users over HTTP in the cloud. The speakers argue that the answer has changed a lot over the past couple of decades. They pick Jakarta EE and MicroProfile as their framework, explaining that MicroProfile is a specification aimed at microservices running in containers on Kubernetes. They highlight features such as health checks used as Kubernetes probes, externalised configuration, a REST client, and fault tolerance, which save developers from writing the same HTTP and error-handling code repeatedly.

Next they containerise the application with a Dockerfile, pointing out how layer caching and multi-stage builds reduce build time and keep the final image small. Builds are automated on every push rather than deployed by hand. For hosting, they move the service to Cloud Run, a serverless platform that scales instances up and down, and they stress that new instances must start quickly. They present Quarkus as a runtime that moves most startup work into the build step, and they show native compilation with GraalVM through a live demo, comparing a cold start in JVM mode with a native binary.

The main takeaway is that deploying modern Java depends on choices about framework, runtime and platform, and that startup time and state handling should be considered early. According to the speakers, moving between MicroProfile implementations is mostly a matter of configuration files rather than rewriting code.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Michael Feathers
talks.teaser: Surveys IDE completion, comment, and chat modes for coders, along with temperature, vague prompts, and tests as executable constraints.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames a late-2023 view of how programmers use generative models in daily work. He groups tooling into completion, comment-driven generation, and chat, then argues that temperature trades determinism against creativity—the same knob that enables hallucinations when teams need correct code and refactorings.

He walks through friction between precise programming habits and loose natural-language prompts, comparing completions to copying snippets from forums. Chat mode shines for explaining unfamiliar code, planning extractions, and spotting cohesion; session state and context limits push work toward smaller chunks. Generated boilerplate should stay separated from hand-written logic, and availability bias can narrow design choices when generation feels effortless.

He introduces prompt hoisting—writing executable tests first and asking the model to satisfy them—and the broader “generate from constraints” pattern with external checkers. He closes on human-in-the-loop review, liability for wrong output, limits on novel structural reasoning, and where ideation beats blind compilation into production systems.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: David Matejcek - Fighting the Technical Debt of GlassFish
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2023: David Matejcek - Fighting the Technical Debt of GlassFish.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Juarez Junior -Unleash the power of your applications with Micronaut and GraalVM
talks.teaser: Shows how Micronaut paired with GraalVM native images trims startup time and memory, using an Oracle database example.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Micronaut, a Java framework built from scratch in 2017 and supported by Oracle, aimed at cloud-native and serverless workloads. Dependency injection, AOP and configuration are resolved at compile time, so the framework avoids reflection, runtime proxies and classpath scanning. Version 4 requires Java 17 and supports virtual threads by default.

The middle section covers GraalVM, which compiles Java ahead of time into native executables. The speaker argues this gives faster startup, lower memory use, compact deployment artifacts and a smaller attack surface, since unused code is left out of the final binary. He also reviews Oracle database connectivity options, including the JDBC driver's virtual thread support, the Universal Connection Pool, and R2DBC for reactive data access.

A live demo runs a Micronaut application against an Oracle Autonomous Database deployed with Terraform. The application first runs on the JVM, with startup around 14 seconds, and then as a precompiled native executable that starts noticeably faster. The takeaway is that pairing Micronaut with GraalVM can reduce startup time, memory use and infrastructure cost for cloud workloads.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Wojtek Ptak
talks.teaser: Shows how a fintech engineering leader keeps fast-growing banking systems simple by deferring costly architecture decisions.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a system design interview scenario for a global payments system. The speaker walks through how a simple card payment flow gains services, queues, caches and specialised databases as the imagined scale grows from one country to five continents. The result is a globally distributed ledger that relies on atomic clocks and GPS, which he presents as a clear example of how a system becomes complicated rather than complex.

Using a systems-thinking model, the speaker separates randomness from complexity and names three sources of complication: too many tools, inconsistent processes between teams, and uneven skills. He then describes the architecture used at Revolut, which relies on plain Java services, Python for machine learning, Kubernetes, and Postgres for much of the data work. He also notes a small infrastructure team of about 15 people, no dedicated QA function, and a design review step where senior engineers challenge proposals. He contrasts this with domain-driven design, banking pattern catalogues, and deliberate use of bounded contexts for organised complexity.

The closing argument is to keep simple things simple, defer irreversible decisions until they are truly painful, and deliver business value quickly, because change outside an organisation can outpace its internal speed. In the Q&A, he explained that splitting a large legacy monolith made sense once team communication and release dependencies slowed delivery.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Nicolas Fränkel - Data Residency: the fun of storing data worldwide
talks.teaser: Maps data residency laws to a double-routing design using API gateways and country-based database sharding.
talks.summary:
The session opens on data residency: digital data still sits in a physical place, and many countries require citizens’ or companies’ data to stay in territory. Operating in one market is simple; crossing borders brings jurisdictional friction, such as an EU firm using a US-owned cloud whose parent may face US disclosure demands. When local cloud capacity does not exist, the practical path is software that routes each record to the right region.

The speaker contrasts placement of country-routing logic in the client, application, proxy, or API gateway, noting latency and wrong-lane redirects when the decision happens too early or too late. The proposed pattern mirrors duplicate client and server validation: the gateway routes from metadata, then the application recomputes near the database and corrects mismatches. A Docker Compose demo uses Apache APISIX and ShardingSphere with separate US and Europe app and database lanes, HTTP headers, and sharding rules keyed on owner country.

Takeaways for architects include accepting added complexity to keep rules authoritative at the data tier, leaning on gateways for topology awareness, and leaving legal choices to counsel rather than engineering alone. Demo materials are shared publicly, with extended Q&A on documentation gaps, caching, and organizational pushback.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Otavio Santana - Mastering Java Persistence: Best Practices for Cloud-Native...
talks.teaser: GeeCON Prague 2023: Otavio Santana - Mastering Java Persistence: Best Practices for Cloud-Native...
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from GeeCON Prague 2023, Otavio Santana explores the critical role of data persistence architectures in software engineering, with a focus on cloud-native Java applications. He highlights that software and persistence decisions are fundamentally governed by trade-offs, where understanding the "why" is more essential than the "how." Emphasizing the importance of domain isolation, data modeling, and performance, Santana details the concept of polyglot persistence across relational and various NoSQL paradigms, as well as the fundamental impedance mismatch between object-oriented programming (OOP) and database storage models.

### Key Topics
Santana explains how databases serve as the stateful foundation for otherwise stateless microservices and business opportunities. Rather than treating all data storage needs with a single relational mindset, systems should embrace polyglot persistence by matching requirements with database models:
- **Key-Value Stores (e.g., Redis, Amazon S3):** Modeled similarly to hash maps and suited for session management, caching, real-time analytics, and pub/sub. They prioritize horizontal scalability but offer low query flexibility beyond primary keys.
- **Wide-Column Databases (e.g., Apache Cassandra):** Feature flexible columns per row, time-to-live (TTL) options, and masterless multi-datacenter replication. Denormalization is favored because write operations are typically cheaper than reads.
- **Document Stores (e.g., MongoDB):** Utilize tree structures such as JSON or BSON, supporting embedded documents and secondary indexing for catalogs, content management, and mobile apps.
- **Graph Databases (e.g., Neo4j):** Embrace directional, property-rich relationships connecting nodes or vertices, making them suitable for social networks, fraud detection, and recommendation engines.

### Technical Details
The presentation delves into the "civil war" and impedance mismatch between application code and database storage. While OOP leverages inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation, storage layers rely on specific schemas or structural models, often spending significant performance overhead converting between the two. Santana contrasts data-oriented programming (which separates schema from generic data representation) with OOP/clean code principles (which encapsulate data behind behavior).

To bridge this gap, Santana outlines six core persistence patterns ordered by proximity to the database versus the application domain:
1. **Driver (e.g., JDBC):** Sits closest to the database, providing raw access and high flexibility at the expense of heavy boilerplate and risk of bugs.
2. **Data Mapper (e.g., JPA annotations, JdbcTemplate mapping):** Centralizes object-relational mapping logic to convert database structures into domain entities.
3. **Data Access Object (DAO):** Centralizes imperative data access operations (`insert`, `update`, `delete`) in a structured layer.
4. **Active Record:** Combines domain entity logic and database persistence operations within the entity itself (popularized in frameworks like Quarkus Panache), trading single-responsibility separation for simplicity.
5. **Repository (e.g., Jakarta Data, Spring Data):** Sits closest to the application domain, offering declarative persistence (such as generic `save` semantics) while abstracting lower-level storage mechanisms away from the domain model.
6. **Data Transfer Object (DTO):** Facilitates schema versioning, API exposure, and separation of read/write representations when implementing patterns like CQRS.

### Takeaways
- Every persistence choice involves trade-offs between horizontal scalability, operational complexity, and query flexibility.
- NoSQL databases must not be treated like relational databases; operations like complex joins should be avoided in favor of access-pattern-driven modeling and denormalization.
- Technology isolation is essential: database-specific exceptions or constraints should not leak into business domain logic or user interfaces.
- Choosing persistence patterns requires balancing domain abstraction against database proximity, code complexity, and mapping overhead.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Jarosław Pałka
talks.teaser: Shows how Java's foreign memory and linker APIs let code allocate off-heap memory and call C libraries directly.
talks.summary:
The talk takes aim at the trade-off made by managed runtimes such as the JVM: they give safety but take away low-level control. The speaker argues that Java's old workaround, the internal Unsafe API, is a shaky route for databases and message brokers that need speed, and that the JDK is now adding official APIs to get closer to the hardware.

The bulk is a live walkthrough of the Foreign Memory API, which was in preview in Java 20. Off-heap memory is held in memory segments tied to scopes such as global, automatic, confined and shared arenas, with bounds checks that throw exceptions instead of crashing the JVM. Memory layouts describe the bytes, so offsets and struct fields can be reached through var handles and method handles, and misaligned access fails. For native calls, the Linker performs a downcall that invokes getpid from the default lookup, and an upcall registers a Java static method as a Linux signal handler, which the talk triggers from outside the process. A small SDL-based game then shows generating Java bindings from C headers with jextract.

The closing takeaway is that these APIs let Java call native libraries without hand-written JNI wrappers, which may help drivers, big data, machine learning and I/O work. The speaker notes that the APIs were still changing, the first version targeted C libraries on 64-bit platforms, and memory allocated off-heap still carries a cost when it is freed.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: David Vlijmincx - Introduction and pitfalls of virtual threads
talks.teaser: Explores Java 21 virtual threads, carrier scheduling, pinning pitfalls, and structured concurrency for large numbers of lightweight tasks.
talks.summary:
The session opens on traditional Java concurrency: platform threads wrap operating-system threads, roughly a megabyte of memory each, and familiar patterns such as one thread per task or fixed executor pools. Those pools reuse workers but still waste capacity when threads block on I/O, and they expose pitfalls like thread-local leakage and hard-to-debug async styles.

Java 21’s virtual threads are presented as heap-backed alternatives scheduled on carrier platform threads. Demos compare memory when scaling to tens or hundreds of thousands of tasks—platform threads exhaust memory while virtual threads stay near a few hundred megabytes—and explain unmounting when calls block. Pitfalls include pinning from synchronized blocks, JNI, and some I/O, detection via JVM diagnostics, avoiding pools and CPU-bound work, and favoring blocking I/O workloads such as REST or database waits.

Structured concurrency closes the loop for managing many short-lived virtual threads. Preview APIs such as StructuredTaskScope illustrate shutdown-on-success and shutdown-on-failure, deadlines, and a custom scope that cancels sibling tasks once a criterion is met. Practitioners should treat virtual threads as cheap, blocking-friendly workers paired with explicit lifetime rules instead of ad hoc thread cleanup.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Stanisław Tokarski - From a rebellious individualist reinventing the wheel...
talks.teaser: Delivers mentoring guidance as mentee, new mentor, and daily practice, beyond corporate one-size-fits-all development paths.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with a shortage of senior software engineers and argues that teams should grow juniors faster when hiring cannot close the gap. Mentoring is framed as the main lever, introduced through three lived angles: receiving a corporate mentoring program as a student, stepping into the mentor role, and mentoring younger developers day to day.

As a mentee, imposed development paths from management are contrasted with real mentoring as agreed direction and guidance, not a fixed curriculum. Choosing a mentor, trusting that relationship, and bringing a mentee-owned agenda are emphasized, along with mentors helping prioritize when enthusiasm outpaces capacity. When becoming a mentor, the talk notes sparse formal training, everyday mentoring in onboarding and code review, and the gap between pure technical coaching and broader career and communication support.

From hands-on mentoring, the speaker highlights time cost, delayed visible payoff, listening over quick fixes, actionable feedback, and when to let mentees struggle. Closing themes treat mentors as guides rather than classroom teachers, seniority as soft skills as well as code skill, lifelong menteeship, and reciprocal growth for mentors—including leadership preparation and satisfaction.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Christophe Breheret-Girardin - Let's adopt the `clean archigonal`
talks.teaser: Compares hexagonal and clean architecture, showing how isolating business logic keeps code flexible and testable.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the problem of tangled "spaghetti" codebases, where business rules, persistence models and user interface code depend on each other so that a change in one place breaks another. It shows how layered designs, microservices and a test pyramid each helped only partly, because the same data model kept leaking into every layer and the domain stayed hard to change.

The middle section covers hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters. The domain sits inside interfaces, and adapters such as web controllers, batch jobs or database implementations plug into those ports, so one port can have several adapters. It then contrasts clean architecture, which uses concentric circles of entities and use cases, with presenters for output and dependencies pointing inward. The talk argues that both share the same goal and differ mainly in how much guidance they give about modelling.

The closing argument is that neither pattern suits every project. Simple data-centric applications may do better with transaction scripts, and logic held mostly in the database may need neither. The speaker recommends learning the fundamentals first, then combining the best parts of each approach to fit the situation, and keeping the business domain separate from technology.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2023: Jaroslav Tulach - Turn your Java library into low-code/no-code system
talks.teaser: Shows how the Enso language and IDE expose Java libraries to spreadsheet-oriented users through dual visual and textual programming.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with spreadsheets as a widespread form of visual, formula-driven computation and notes where that model stops short of full programming. It frames a recurring industry goal: tools that stay approachable for non-programmers yet scale for power users, with live feedback and interoperability rather than isolated silos.

The core subject is Enso: a dynamic language with value-oriented typing, functional style, and both spreadsheet-like nodes and readable text. Live demos walk through string processing in the IDE, generated source, debugging on the JVM, filtering rocket-launch data from Excel, and calling Python via foreign blocks. For Java audiences, the emphasis is GraalVM-style integration—polyglot Java import for JDK and custom JAR types, plus a prototype path to wire Random and stream APIs directly in the visual editor with refresh-driven recomputation.

Practitioners should take away that a Java library can be surfaced to business-facing pipelines without a full rewrite: thin wrappers or direct class use inside Enso, Truffle execution on recent JDK releases, and optional cloud batch execution. The project is open source; embedding the IDE in existing UIs is presented as a follow-on discussion topic.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Jarek Ratajski
talks.teaser: A case against sprint rituals, velocity games, and time-centric estimates urges weighing developer energy over clock time.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the familiar monkey-and-ladder parable as a stand-in for workplace habits nobody questions, then turns to why software task estimates behave like random variables: teams guess from partial context on work that never repeats the way construction does. The speaker contrasts house-building stability with constantly shifting codebases, cites long-running public megaprojects, and argues that most sprint-level numbers change little when wrong.

The middle of the talk targets scrum mechanics: planning poker over trivial differences, velocity Tetris to avoid management attention, developers coding through planning meetings, story points collapsing to disguised time, burn-down charts mainly policing morale, and a scrum master refusing a specialist for fear of hurting velocity. Alternatives include labeling work trivial, boring, or risky to surface real disagreement, asking product owners whether quick-and-dirty delivery is acceptable, and separating fixed-price budgeting from day-to-day story sizing.

The close revisits waterfall as a manufactured enemy, notes how extreme programming contributed practices without its KPI circus, and encourages process experiments. The speaker's closing thesis is that calendars poorly capture human capacity: meetings can drain energy without filling the day, and methodologies obsessed with time may miss what actually limits useful output. Audience questions extend the no-estimates stance, junior voices, priorities over sprints, and who invented velocity pressure.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Guy Royse - Tracking Aircraft
talks.teaser: Shows how a cheap software-defined radio dongle can decode live aircraft positions and plot them on a Redis-backed map.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a hobbyist's introduction to software-defined radio. A small USB receiver passes raw signal data to software instead of decoding it in hardware, so one cheap device can cover shortwave, ham bands, FM stations and even satellite signals. The speaker points out that much of the interesting traffic is data rather than audio, including amateur packet position reports and packets picked up from the International Space Station.

The main demo tracks aircraft. A decoder tool called dump1090 turns the 1090 MHz transponder signals from nearby planes into readable messages, and the speaker shows that a vertically oriented antenna picks up noticeably more of them than a horizontal one. The decoder publishes the data on a local port in a CSV format called SBS1. A small JavaScript ingester writes each message into a Redis stream, a consumer forwards updates over a websocket, and a web app plots the coordinates on a map. Indoors the signal was weak, and not every message carries a position, so the live map filled in slowly.

To close, the speaker covers practical advice. A starter dongle and a cheap antenna are enough to begin, an up-converter helps with shortwave reception, and listening rules differ from country to country. He also describes carrying the gear through airport security, with the antenna packed separately. The takeaway is that inexpensive parts and open tools are enough to follow aircraft and other radio traffic.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Michał Ostruszka - Things I wish I knew before I started with event sourcing
talks.teaser: Delivers event sourcing for one service: command replay, aggregates, read-side projection, and eventual consistency.
talks.summary:
The presentation narrows event sourcing to the scope of one service or neighboring services, contrasting with a prior session on the wider landscape. It walks through command handling: commands arrive at a handler, current state is reconstituted by replaying facts from an event store, business rules run, and new events are appended. A read side projects those events into UI models, notifications, and integrations.

The speaker frames event sourcing as a state-management choice rather than a whole-system architecture, comparing it to CRUD on complexity and fit. Benefits include audit trails, analytics on the full history, and CQRS-style scaling of reads versus writes. Trade-offs cover harder debugging, tooling to inspect streams, and embracing eventual consistency—with email uniqueness handled via pending accounts and compensating events on the read model.

Domain modeling with aggregates and bounded contexts receives heavy emphasis, including splitting a monolithic account stream into smaller aggregates when streams grow. Versioning (often with protobuf), refactoring via replay, framework coupling versus isolated domain tests, snapshots, in-memory aggregates under a single-writer rule, and keeping side effects off command handlers in favor of read-side processors round out the guidance. The close urges trying event sourcing on one aggregate where history and scale matter, not everywhere.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Konrad Szałkowski - How to make your electrons do more in Java
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2023: Konrad Szałkowski - How to make your electrons do more in Java.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2023 presentation, Konrad Szałkowski explores how Java developers can achieve maximum hardware performance by taking advantage of SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) CPU operations and offloading parallel computing workloads to GPUs and FPGAs. Historically, Java lacked low-level primitives to directly access specialized hardware acceleration, relying primarily on C2 compiler auto-vectorization (superword optimization) or JVM intrinsics. The talk examines modern alternatives that bring direct hardware execution to the JVM: the Java Vector API introduced in Java 16 and the TornadoVM framework developed at the University of Manchester.

### Key Topics
- **SIMD Architecture and History**: Overview of vector instructions executing a single operation over multiple data points (e.g., additions, multiplications, vector reductions). Historical context traces hardware vectorization from the Intel Pentium MMX (1997) through SSE, AVX, and ARM Neon/SVE, highlighting use cases across gaming, 3D graphics, physics simulations, image processing, and artificial intelligence.
- **Java Vector API**: Introduced in Java 16, the Vector API provides an explicit, high-level programming model that compiles down directly to platform-native SIMD instructions without bytecode execution overhead.
- **GPU Programming Challenges in Java**: Hardware architecture differences between CPUs and GPUs, such as massive parallelism across thousands of cores, distinct memory spaces (host RAM vs. GPU VRAM over PCIe), lack of garbage collection on GPUs, and differing mental models for data and thread mapping.
- **Historical and Modern JVM GPU Frameworks**: Previous attempts to bridge Java and GPUs (JCuda, JOCL, Oracle's Project Sumatra, Project Rootbeer, and FPGA frameworks like MaxJ), contrasting them with TornadoVM.
- **TornadoVM**: An open-source plug-in leveraging GraalVM to compile Java code (particularly static methods annotated for parallel loop execution) to execute seamlessly on SIMD CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs.

### Technical Details
- **Vector API Mechanics**: Uses `VectorSpecies` as an abstraction representing element type and vector bit-width (e.g., a 128-bit species holding four 32-bit integers). Demonstrates loading batches via `VectorSpecies.fromArray()`, stepping with loop offsets based on species length, and manually handling the tail/remaining elements that do not fit into full vector widths.
- **Vector API Benchmarks**: The speaker shows naive benchmark comparisons on large arrays: summing 100 million integers completed in 26 ms with scalar Java versus 20 ms with the Vector API; max search dropped from 36 ms to 20 ms; and quadratic equation solving demonstrated substantial speedups.
- **TornadoVM Architecture and Ray Tracer Demo**: TornadoVM constructs an execution plan via a `TaskGraph`, managing explicit data transfers to and from device memory and dispatching computational tasks. A live 3D Ray Tracer demo running on a CPU executed at roughly 1.5 FPS, reached 3 FPS using CPU parallel streams (ForkJoinPool), and maintained smooth high-framerate real-time rendering when executed on the GPU.
- **Dynamic Reconfiguration**: TornadoVM features dynamic reconfiguration, assessing at runtime whether data transfer latency across the PCIe bus negates GPU execution advantages; if so, it automatically falls back to CPU execution.

### Takeaways
While the Vector API gives Java developers explicit control over SIMD processing with measurable latency improvements, it requires manual handling of tail iterations and extra boilerplate. For massively parallel tasks, TornadoVM abstracts driver initialization, memory allocation, and kernel dispatch across heterogeneous hardware (CPUs, GPUs, integrated graphics, and FPGAs) using GraalVM. Developers can leverage these tools on local hardware or cloud GPU instances (e.g., AWS EC2) to accelerate computationally heavy workloads in Java.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Adam Warski - Effects: to be or not to be?
talks.teaser: Compares Java checked exceptions, futures, and functional effect libraries on one example and explicit trade-off criteria.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames effect systems as an extension of the same trade-off that static typing already makes: extra structure and compiler constraints in exchange for documentation, safer refactors, and fewer bugs. It defines effects as observable changes to system behavior beyond returning a value, distinguishes effect-free and pure functions, and argues that remote calls should not be modeled like local calls because latency and failure modes differ.

Using a recurring rocket-launch scenario, it scores several approaches against criteria such as location precision, syntax overhead, type safety, referential transparency, concurrency support, failure handling, and resource safety. Checked exceptions in Java score low on pinpointing where effects occur and draw criticism for swallowing errors, coupling, and weak polymorphism with lambdas. Scala Futures improve location precision but impose flatMap sequencing and custom control flow. ZIO treats computations as lazy descriptions interpreted at runtime, improving referential transparency and resource safety at the cost of pervasive flatMap composition; ZIO Direct partially restores familiar syntax. Unison abilities use bang-forced lazy blocks with medium syntactic cost, and a imagined Loom-plus-capabilities design keeps direct style while hiding capability tokens.

The closing message is that no option delivers high location precision, low syntax overhead, and full referential transparency together; practitioners must decide which constraints matter for their codebase and what lessons to take from Java’s checked-exception experience.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Tannaz N. Roshandel - Machine Intelligence
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2023: Tannaz N. Roshandel - Machine Intelligence With Humans in Mind.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, the speaker discusses the pervasive role of artificial intelligence and machine intelligence across modern life, ranging from entertainment recommendations and chatbots to healthcare, transportation, and education. Despite the substantial benefits in automation and decision-making, widespread AI deployment introduces significant ethical risks and real-world harms. The presentation explores the nature of ethics, the risks inherent to algorithmic black boxes and data aggregation, and the social responsibility developers and individuals carry to build fair, transparent, and accountable technology.

### Key Topics
- **Ethical Challenges and Real-World Harms**: Highlighting algorithmic failures, including self-driving car accidents, HR systems that screen out qualified women, misidentifications by facial/security systems, unfair mortgage denials for minorities, and AI avatars generating misleading diversity representations.
- **The Nature of Ethics vs. Algorithms**: Defining ethics as a human process of discovering, questioning, and defending core values. While technology operates through mathematical models without innate morality, human creators must take responsibility for ethical outcomes.
- **Data Tracking and Filter Bubbles**: How smartphones and wearable devices continuously collect telemetry—noting that individuals generate roughly two megabytes of data per second—which services combine to exploit vulnerabilities, predetermine choices, and isolate users within narrow filter bubbles that impair critical thinking.
- **Individual and Corporate Responsibility**: Referencing Milton Friedman's 1970 observation that businesses cannot have responsibilities independent of the individuals operating them, emphasizing that engineers, users, and diverse organizations must actively shape ethical norms.

### Technical Details
- **Black Box Processing**: Modern AI functions mimic neural structures via mathematical models trained on vast historic datasets. Because algorithms learn and iterate autonomously, the underlying operations frequently function as opaque black boxes, making results difficult to anticipate or explain without explicit explainability features.
- **Explainable, Trusted, and Responsible AI**: The speaker underscores the necessity for frameworks such as Explainable AI (XAI) to inspect why systems make particular decisions (e.g., auditing HR models to identify which specific input features disqualified candidates).
- **Data Aggregation Risks**: The core privacy concern is often not a single service capturing data in isolation, but the cross-service compilation and correlation of multiple datasets to model user behaviors.

### Takeaways
- AI is an assistive tool to augment productivity and decision-making, not an autonomous replacement for human judgment, empathy, or moral reasoning.
- Mitigating bias requires building diverse engineering and leadership teams that incorporate a broad spectrum of perspectives, backgrounds, and life experiences.
- Individuals and technologists must continuously practice critical thinking—observing, analyzing, and evaluating consequences—while advocating for transparency, open communication, and fair AI practices.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Daniel Kec - Helidon Nima
talks.teaser: The presentation explains how Helidon replaces its reactive web server with Nima using Java virtual threads for imperative code.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by positioning Helidon as a lightweight Java microservice stack built for Kubernetes, with flavors from reactive Helidon SE on Netty to imperative Helidon MP with CDI and JAX-RS. The speaker frames the core server problem as cheap concurrency: platform threads cost memory and context switches, which pushed years of reactive streams, steep learning curves, and fragile debugging when handlers block event loops.

The middle revisits Project Loom virtual threads in Java 21, contrasting a reactive Helidon SE endpoint with the same flow written imperatively on Nima. Blocking on I/O yields the carrier thread while keeping throughput. Helidon 4 alpha moves MP onto Nima, removes the reactive web server, and benchmarks Nima close to raw Netty despite fuller HTTP handling. An older MP comparison on Nima reportedly showed about a fourfold gain after dropping the reactive layer.

Practitioners hear cautions on pinning from synchronized sections with I/O, CPU-heavy work that holds carriers, and large ThreadLocal payloads. Development notes cover unlearning reactive habits, garbage collection outperforming manual buffer reuse in tests, and simpler HTTP/2 with a thread per stream. Q&A covers scope values versus Helidon context, preferring reentrant locks over synchronized, Java 21 as the Helidon 4 baseline, and Loom-oriented debugging with jcmd and flight recorder.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Robert Piwowarek - What is animation engineering?
talks.teaser: Maps skeletal pipelines, blending, root motion, procedural IK, and runtime trade-offs across modern game engines.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames animation engineering as the software side of 3D skeletal animation in games. It walks through artist-driven groundwork—meshes, joint hierarchies, skinning, and rigs—then sketches a minimal runtime: animation clips as pose sequences, loading data, updating the skeleton, and driving playback from code.

From there it explores interpolation between keyframes, blend spaces keyed on speed, and why mismatched clips produce bad transitions. It shows locomotion animation graphs in Unreal’s Lyra sample, contrasts capsule-based movement with mesh motion, and explains root motion extraction. The middle covers code-driven versus animation-driven locomotion, foot sliding, mixed approaches, and motion warping (delta correction) to stretch traversal clips to arbitrary targets. Inverse kinematics, including a FABRIK-style solver, is introduced for terrain-aware grounding before a section on Switch-oriented scale compression, culling, streaming, distance-based update rates, synchronized playback, and GPU-oriented instancing tricks.

The talk closes with a brief “iceberg” of advanced topics—motion matching, retargeting, facial animation—and pointers to GDC talks and books. Audience questions touch on animation-engineering roles, virtual bones for weapons, FPS blending, debugging graphs, and why automated animation tests remain rare.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Emilia Lendzion-Barszcz - Performance Testing is not only API
talks.teaser: Walks through building unit-level performance checks in Java, from tool selection to nightly deviation tracking and the setbacks met.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a QA architect with only theoretical performance testing experience, was asked whether a client's logic could be load tested at the unit level without network effects. After agreeing shared definitions of shift-left and performance testing, they surveyed the client's Java, Spring Boot, JUnit and WireMock stack and chose an open-source harness on license and community grounds. Requirements were low effort, a reusable pipeline template and response-time monitoring.

Test selection targeted unit and component tests that ran frequently or had high complexity, skipping serialization already covered by widely used libraries. Each performance test maps an existing test to a method, with settings for threads, warm-up, run count and reporting. A nightly run compares results against a baseline to flag deviations. Setup exposed problems: date-time values were too coarse, so nano time replaced them; JUnit 4 configuration clashed with JUnit 5 teams; parallel classes ran sequentially; a shared Spring context broke repeated runs; and reports duplicated results.

Of the teams considered, none needed the tests, since the client's service only mapped data, so the work became a proof that the implementation was feasible. Advice from the Q&A: run performance tests in a separate pipeline so regular builds stay fast. Customizing the library with JUnit 5 took about 80 hours, and a good implementation was estimated at roughly one week.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: David Vlijmincx - Introduction and pitfalls of Java's new concurrency model
talks.teaser: Walks through Java virtual threads and structured concurrency, from platform-thread costs to pitfalls, demos, and scoped shutdown policies.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting familiar platform threads, which wrap costly operating-system resources, with the thread-per-task style many developers still use. It explains why executor services and pools reuse threads but introduce problems such as thread-local leakage and idle platform threads blocked on I/O, and why callback-heavy async code is harder to write and debug.

The middle focuses on Project Loom virtual threads as a JVM-managed alternative: cheap creation at large scale, heap-resident stacks, carrier platform threads, and work-stealing scheduling with mount and unmount when tasks block. Live examples use startVirtualThread, builders, and the virtual-thread-per-task executor, including spinning up on the order of a hundred thousand sleeping tasks without running out of memory. The speaker stresses that virtual threads and structured concurrency are not mainstream until Java 21, and warns about pinning on synchronized blocks, JNI, file I/O, CPU-bound work that never yields, avoiding pools, and using semaphores or locks instead of pools to cap database connections.

Structured concurrency is presented as lifetime management for many virtual tasks: implicit cleanup when parents fail, StructuredTaskScope with shutdown-on-success and shutdown-on-failure, and a custom scope that keeps forking until a price criterion is met. The close emphasizes that only startVirtualThread and newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor are required to begin, while structured concurrency is optional sugar for clearer shutdown behavior.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Rafal Foltynski, Nick Palmer - Determinedly deterministic and how it can help you
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2023: Rafal Foltynski, Nick Palmer - Determinedly deterministic and how it can help you.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2023 presentation, Rafal Foltynski (Raf) and Nick Palmer from financial exchange LMAX present the architecture, design principles, and performance benefits of deterministic systems. Given the high-throughput, low-latency requirements of institutional financial trading—operating with sustained rates of hundreds of thousands of orders per second and strict price-time priority execution—handling shared state across concurrent threads or distributed microservices introduces severe complexity and latency jitter. The speakers explain how isolating business logic into single-threaded, deterministic execution pipelines backed by ring buffers, journaling, and snapshotting delivers predictability, fault tolerance, and extreme performance.

### Key Topics
- **Definition of Determinism**: A deterministic system is one where a given initial state and input sequence will always yield the exact same result with zero randomness, enabling reliable replayability.
- **Architectural Antipatterns**: In standard microservice architectures (e.g., separate gateway, user service, and matching engine), state is smeared across services and updated asynchronously, breaking deterministic replay and complicating ordering.
- **Core Requirements for Determinism**: Three fundamental rules must be followed: record all incoming inputs, update state using only a single writer, and produce no non-reproducible side effects.
- **Ring Buffers & The Disruptor**: Using ring buffers (such as the LMAX Disruptor) enforces strict event ordering and sequencing, permitting efficient inter-thread communication and fast replay.
- **Journaling & Snapshots**: Events are journaled to disk before execution ("if it didn't journal, it didn't happen"). Snapshotting in-memory state and buffer sequence positions avoids replaying history from the beginning of time during recovery.
- **Verification via Binary Comparison**: Determinism can be formally verified by taking a base snapshot, replaying recorded journals, taking a subsequent snapshot, and comparing them for binary equivalence.

### Technical Details & Pitfalls
- **Common Determinism Breakers**:
  - *Wall-clock time*: Calling `System.currentTimeMillis()` introduces nondeterminism. Instead, events must be timestamped once upon entry into the ingress ring buffer, using that timestamp as the single source of truth.
  - *Unordered collections*: Iterating over structures like `HashMap` produces non-deterministic iteration order across snapshot reloads.
  - *Side effects & blocking I/O*: Direct database queries, RPC calls, HTTP requests, or JMX manipulation pollute the core processing path. Any persistence or database storage must be pushed downstream to asynchronous, idempotent consumers.
- **Single-Writer Performance Optimization**:
  - Lock-free single-writer execution eliminates lock contention and synchronization overhead (contrasting multi-threaded locks or atomic constructs verified via JCStress).
  - Isolating CPUs and pinning the single application thread via tools like `hwloc` (`lstopo`), `cset`, or `tuned` prevents kernel rescheduling and reduces latency jitter, crucial for sub-80-microsecond responses.
  - Ring buffers provide natural back-pressure when thread capacity is saturated.
- **Replication & Scaling**:
  - Replicated state machines clone the sequenced input events to backup replicas before processing, allowing live replicas to run concurrently without duplicate external outputs.
  - When a single thread reaches CPU capacity, systems scale through state partitioning (sharding) along low-cardinality discriminators (e.g., independent order books per currency pair).
  - Backward compatibility in event schemas is maintained using protocol versioning (e.g., Protobuf or custom versioned serializers) while retaining old deserializers.

### Takeaways
Designing core stateful services as deterministic, single-writer state machines significantly reduces architectural complexity by eliminating locks and concurrency bugs. Decoupling I/O and persistence to downstream consumers allows single threads pinned to dedicated cores to process massive workloads with minimal jitter. Furthermore, combining sequenced journaling with periodic snapshots provides seamless fault tolerance, active-passive replication, and the ability to reproduce and debug exact production issues locally.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Mike Wojtyna
talks.teaser: Shows how running quick experiments on a domain model in code helps developers learn business rules faster.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that developers often build software without understanding why, and that the business behind a product should be learned as quickly as possible. The speaker presents Domain Experiments, a way to run cheap experiments directly on a domain model instead of building costly prototypes. The approach moves from broad knowledge crunching to extracting key business processes, then splitting those processes into concrete examples with example mapping.

To illustrate, the speaker works through an example platform for passive investments, focusing on the requirement that a borrower can start fundraising for a project. Starting from a failing test, the model grows step by step. A borrower starts a project, an underage borrower is refused, and this leads to a new registration case where only adult borrowers can register. Later examples add a criminal-record check and a rule that projects of 10,000 or more must be verified. Each iteration produces questions for domain experts, and the model is kept free of databases, Kafka or other infrastructure.

The closing message is that the model should be checked with domain experts through short feedback loops, and that architecture decisions can follow from what is learned. The speaker uses the board game Gloomhaven as an analogy: clear rulebook text still leads to different interpretations, and the code becomes the source of truth. The takeaway is to minimise the gap between the rules as described and the rules as implemented. The question session covers mob programming, criminal-record checks and applying behaviour-driven development to the domain.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Tomer Gabel - What Scala Taught Me About Software Engineering
talks.teaser: A veteran Scala developer distills lessons on declarative style, compile-time safety, and expressive typing for everyday engineering.
talks.summary:
The presenter looks back on using Scala professionally since 2011, mainly at Wix, and on a later stretch working in other languages. That gap led him to articulate what Scala changed about how he writes software, and he frames three lessons for the audience.

First, he contrasts imperative Java-style filtering with stream-style code and argues Scala pushes engineers to state what they want rather than micromanage how. That shift cuts accidental complexity and leaves room for libraries and runtimes to optimize. Second, he treats heavy reflection in common Java stacks—naming Spring, Jackson, and Hibernate—as a runtime tax paid in startup, memory, fragility, and extra tests; he points to code generation, macros, and type classes as compile- or build-time alternatives Scala popularized. Third, he makes the case for strong static typing for autocomplete, refactor safety, and clearer errors, and traces ideas like lambdas, optionals, pattern-matching switches, and sealed types from Scala’s influence on Java and other ecosystems.

He closes with two principles: expressiveness supports efficiency, while type and build-time safety make teams more effective. He credits Scala with shaping Kotlin, TypeScript’s typing culture, Python’s gradual typing, and Rust features, encourages experimentation even when Scala is not the day job, and invites disagreement in Q&A.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Sebastian Rabiej
talks.teaser: Explores how software teams stumble on hype, legacy rewrites, rigid agile, and folklore that nobody verifies.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting software’s freedom of abstractions with industries bound by physics, then frames several recurring weaknesses—"kryptonite"—that shape why projects diverge and why some organizations outperform others. The first theme is enthusiasm for new tools and architecture labels: layered, hexagonal, ports and adapters, and similar patterns are often rebrands of the same ideas, and conference narratives tend to highlight happy paths until failures surface years later. Practitioners are urged to read internals, map problems to familiar patterns, and reject stack choices that do not fit—GraphQL is offered as an example where power can backfire on heavy queries.

A long middle section ties legacy work to the unfinished Sagrada Família: replacements and migrations can produce technological inconsistency, functional bugs when semantics drift, and conceptual mismatch across teams and time. The speaker describes a "life cycle of decisions" where later generations inherit consequences without context, and recommends architectural decision records, blameless reviews after incidents, and project glossaries so knowledge survives turnover. Graceful legacy is presented as a goal worth pursuing rather than ridiculing past choices.

Later segments critique rigid, metric-obsessed Scrum implementations, warn against decontextualized quotes and misapplied research such as the Dunning–Kruger curve, and note confirmation bias in how the industry shares lore. The close argues that no single flaw defines every career: the field is young, practices are still forming, and teams improve by naming their weaknesses and adapting process to real context. A brief Q&A touches accepting partial architectural inconsistency versus costly rewrites.
