talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Nicolas Frankel - Chopping the monolith
talks.teaser: Questions microservices fashion and shows peeling volatile pricing off a monolith behind an API gateway.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by challenging the assumption that microservices are always the right choice, using Martin Fowler’s criteria to show how few teams actually meet what “microservices” properly implies. Much of the gap is organizational: Conway’s law, product versus project funding, and the need for autonomous “two pizza” teams—changes that depend on middle managers even when the target architecture has little room for them.

The speaker walks through common rationales for splitting systems—strong module boundaries, technology diversity, and faster deployment—and argues that boundaries and diversity are often better served without distributed services, while deployment speed is an older problem with other mitigations (release trains, rules engines for volatile business logic). Drawing on Chris Richardson’s strangler pattern, the talk advocates chopping only the fast-changing portions while keeping stable code in the monolith.

A live shop demo illustrates the idea: Apache APISIX fronts a Dockerized monolith, pricing is exposed as its own route, then traffic for that route is forwarded to a separate implementation (including a serverless option) via gateway configuration alone, without redeploying the core application. The closing message is to resist resume-driven microservice migrations and prefer minimal, targeted extraction.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Patrycja Wegrzynowicz - The Hacker’s Guide to Kubernetes
talks.teaser: Shows live attacks on a vulnerable Kubernetes cluster, from exposed kubelet APIs to reverse shells and hijacked sessions.
talks.summary:
The talk is a live Kubernetes hacking session built around two demos that hijack user accounts in a deliberately vulnerable web application. The speaker first reviews the control plane and worker node architecture, where the API server and kubelet expose HTTP interfaces, and then walks through the OWASP top ten risks for Kubernetes.

In the first demo, the speaker scans a private subnet with kubeletctl to find an exposed kubelet API, lists pods, and runs commands in a container that runs as root. From a reverse shell, the writable filesystem and open egress let them install tcpdump, which captures a session token that is then replayed to log in as a victim. The second demo starts with remote code execution in a separate app in the same cluster, which gives a shell. A port scan then reveals an unauthenticated Redis store holding JSON web tokens, and removing a token from that store and reusing it shows how a token denylist fails when the store is open.

The takeaways are secure kubelet defaults, including disabling anonymous access, avoiding root and read-only root filesystems, trimming tools from images, segregating workloads with network policies, encrypting internal traffic, and requiring authentication on data stores. The speaker stresses layered defense, using the Swiss cheese model, and continuous learning, since no single control is enough.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Marcin Chrost - Enums on steroids - let's look at sealed classes!
talks.teaser: A lightning walkthrough refactors a simplified loan engine from Java enums to sealed types, records, and pattern-matched switches.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a small loan-evaluation scenario with three mutually exclusive outcomes: approval, refusal, or suspension with extra requirements. That domain model first uses a classic enum for the response type, combined with a modern switch that labels each branch without break statements.

The speaker then shows why a single response class accumulating every field and factory method becomes a code smell. The design moves to a response interface with separate record types per outcome, which cleans up construction but leaves awkward instanceof checks in the main flow. Pattern matching in switch expressions removes explicit casts, yet a default branch remains because the compiler cannot prove the interface has only those three implementers.

Sealed interfaces with a permits clause close the hierarchy so the switch can stay exhaustive without a default branch. The talk closes by contrasting tests against the enum blob versus the typed hierarchy, pointing to sample code listeners can run locally, and briefly discussing polymorphism versus external handling in Q&A.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Fawaz Ghali - Building High Performance Real-time Stream Processing Microservices
talks.teaser: Shows how to build real-time stream processing microservices that join live events with historical data for alerts and trends.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at building microservices that process data in real time at high performance. The speaker, a principal data science architect at Hazelcast, starts by pointing out that a simple design hides real problems: packaging, deployment, handling spikes instead of averages, balancing load, recovering when a node fails, and monitoring running jobs. He notes that "real time" depends on the use case, and that live events gain value when they are combined with historical data for context.

Data flows from sources such as Kafka or Pulsar through a set of small microservices, which can be reused and written in different languages, and ends in alerts or downstream services. Because latency targets can be tight, compute and data should sit close together and scale at both levels. A study the speaker cited reported 1 billion transactions per second at 99% accuracy, with 30 milliseconds latency, across 45 nodes, scaling linearly. In the demo, log entries are stored as key-value pairs in maps, a score threshold raises alerts, and a linear regression trend predicts whether the next message will be an error.

The closing section shows running the platform locally from a jar file or serverless on Hazelcast Viridian, with the Management Center used to inspect clients, jobs and maps. The main takeaways are to combine live and historical data in one platform, choose a serialization format based on speed or analysis needs, apply eviction policies, and protect sensitive log content.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Otavio Santana - How to Become a Top-Performing Software Engineer through Open Source..
talks.teaser: Explores how open source practices in documentation, testing, and communication help engineers grow influence and career options.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that open source is not merely a philosophy of sharing code but a dominant model in modern software, citing industry scale, Red Hat’s acquisition, and widespread dependency on open components in phones, servers, and enterprise stacks. He links mature open source projects to evolutionary architecture, global collaboration, and practices such as code review, CI/CD, and test automation that enterprises increasingly mirror through inner source.

The core of the talk is a staged playbook for engineers who want leverage from open source participation. Step one is articulating why before how, aligned with architectural thinking in foundations like Eclipse. Step two stresses documentation and testing as non-negotiable quality habits: README rationale, changelogs, API specs, C4 and technology maps, ADRs, meaningful coverage plus mutation testing, layered tests including integration, and UI checks. Step three covers communication through writing, talks, and internal advocacy so influence—not only technical skill—shapes job choice and staff-plus pathways. He closes with a reminder to pursue simplicity in design rather than applying patterns blindly.

Practitioners should treat open source norms as a career accelerator: justify work clearly, document and test like a public project, communicate proposals inside and outside the company, and favor simpler designs. The Q&A briefly invites contributors to Jakarta Data via its public mailing list.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Tomer Gabel - How shit works: Databases
talks.teaser: Explains B-trees and LSM trees so teams can match database engines to real write and read access patterns.
talks.summary:
The session frames database choice as a product engineering problem: many stores exist, and “it depends” only becomes useful once you know what problem each engine optimizes. It defines a DBMS around modeling, storing, and querying data, then narrows the on-disk story to key-value thinking and two dominant index structures.

B-trees are presented as wide, self-balancing trees tuned for disk pages, with splits and merges to keep height low and reads fast—at the cost of read-before-write lookups and write amplification when updates are frequent. A social “like” example illustrates mismatch when events are appended constantly but rarely looked up individually. Log-structured merge (LSM) trees invert the tradeoff: writes land in a memory table and flush to immutable sorted tables, with compaction merging levels so append-heavy workloads avoid tree rebalancing, accepting slower or multi-table reads.

Closing guidance orders decisions by operational capacity, then read/write access patterns, then scale—often favoring familiar tools early. The practical takeaway is that most familiar SQL and NoSQL products lean on B-tree or LSM variants; knowing which path your workload stresses makes later migrations less arbitrary.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Patrick Viry - A parallel programming language extension for Java
talks.teaser: Adds compositional parallel operators to Java, expressing concurrency, data parallelism and distribution without raw threads.
talks.summary:
Patrick Viry opens with a recurring problem: small domain-specific languages start simple, then grow into large, poorly maintained systems. The alternative presented is to start from a general-purpose language like Java and add only what a domain needs. The project covered, pH, extends Java for parallel programming.

The talk surveys parallelism models, including raw threads, task launching, message passing from scientific computing, OpenMP-style annotations on C and process algebras. The core idea is a compositional parallel operator: combining two statements yields a new statement that ends when both branches end. Examples included a parallel loop over matrix elements, a recursive Fibonacci with parallel calls, and speculative sorting where the first returned result wins and other branches are discarded. Channels with send and receive handled message passing, and a choice construct took whichever value arrived first. Matrix multiplication ran at speed close to hand-written threads while making alternative layouts easy to try. Annotations could place a branch on another machine or on a GPU through OpenCL.

On correctness, the speaker argued that compositional constructs let each parallel composition be checked locally, instead of requiring thread safety across a whole program, which can partly be automated. The implementation converts extended Java to standard Java source so existing tools keep working. Open problems were developer reluctance to adopt a new language, heavy editor and debugger work, and no general fix for clashes between language extensions. Lightweight fibers in Java would help scale. The project is no longer maintained, though code samples are on GitHub.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Monica Beckwith - The `-ilities` of Software Engineering - How Qualities...
talks.teaser: Maps performance and scalability requirements to garbage collector design, cloud measurement, and Java engineering tradeoffs.
talks.summary:
The session frames software engineering as balancing functional requirements with non-functional “-ilities” that customers expect. Performance is treated as something to define explicitly through SLAs, footprint, response time, throughput, capacity, and utilization, rather than vague goals like “fast.” The speaker contrasts responsiveness with throughput using pause-heavy timelines, then walks the audience through designing two garbage collectors from first principles: one optimized for throughput with parallel stop-the-world work and fallback handling, and one optimized for low latency using regions, concurrent and incremental collection, and graceful degradation. Those designs are mapped to real OpenJDK collectors such as Parallel GC, G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah.

Scalability is separated into scale-up versus scale-out tradeoffs, then grounded in measured Azure VM experiments across core counts. Charts illustrate nonlinear capacity curves, scaling-factor drops at certain core counts, and when multiple JVM processes outperform a single JVM on older hardware generations. Projections are contrasted with Amdahl’s law and Neil Gunther’s Universal Scalability Law, emphasizing measurement over guessing.

Shorter sections tie portability to OpenJDK porting work, usability to collector tuning complexity and language improvements, and customer experience to reliability and capability. The closing Q&A reinforces G1 as the common default, upstream-aligned JDK variants, when to experiment with throughput versus latency collectors, and Java Flight Recorder as the primary observability path for JVM and GC behavior.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Asaf Mesika - OpenTelemetry Metrics: observability’s holy grail
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2023: Asaf Mesika - OpenTelemetry Metrics: observability’s holy grail.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2023 presentation, Asaf Mesika, Principal Engineer at StreamNative, provides an in-depth evaluation of OpenTelemetry Metrics, awarding it a top score compared to traditional libraries. Mesika shares his background in observability at Kotendo, Akamai, and Logz.io, leading up to his work on Apache Pulsar at StreamNative. Pulsar's architecture enables rapid horizontal scaling, geo-replication, tiered storage, and support for up to one million topics. However, monitoring one million topics can create an unmanageable volume of unique time series (up to 100 million). Addressing this high-cardinality monitoring challenge required consolidating Pulsar’s legacy metrics implementations into a modern, unified metrics library, prompting an evaluation of Dropwizard Metrics, Prometheus Java Client, Micrometer, and OpenTelemetry.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Legacy Metric Libraries:** Dropwizard lacks label/attribute support; Prometheus Java Client is tightly coupled to Prometheus protocol and faces performance bottlenecks under high time-series loads; Micrometer failed to achieve widespread vendor-neutral standard adoption.
- **OpenTelemetry Project Architecture:** Comprises four core components across metrics, logs, and traces: API (interfaces for defining and recording telemetry), SDK (implementation including transformations, exports, and auto-instrumentation), OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol using Protobuf/gRPC or HTTP/JSON), and the OpenTelemetry Collector (lightweight proxy for receiving, transforming, and exporting data).
- **OpenTelemetry Metrics API Concepts:** Core API concepts include Instruments (virtual recording objects), Measurements (recorded numerical values), Attributes (key-value contextual metadata), Meters (named and versioned factories for instruments), and Meter Providers (factory for meters and SDK configuration point).
- **Instrument Types:** Core instrument primitives include Counters (monotonic, incrementing only), UpDownCounters (can increment or decrement), Gauges (asynchronous, callback-based values representing independent non-additive measurements such as temperature), and Histograms (recording values like latency to produce statistical bucket distributions).

### Technical Details
- **SDK Aggregations and Decoupling:** In OpenTelemetry, instruments act as generic input mechanisms whose values flow into distinct aggregation interfaces (e.g., Sum for counters, Explicit Bucket Histogram for histograms). Buckets and aggregations are decoupled from initial instrument declarations.
- **The Power of Views:** Views allow SDK users to customize how instrument data is processed without modifying underlying application or third-party library source code. With Views, operators can:
  - Override default aggregations (e.g., replacing expensive explicit bucket configurations with cheaper bucket boundaries).
  - Filter attributes to dramatically reduce memory consumption and cardinality (e.g., dropping source IP addresses from an HTTP latency instrument while preserving HTTP status codes).
  - Clone instrument data into multiple views with different aggregations simultaneously.
  - Apply wildcard matching to uniformly reconfigure bucket layouts across all matching instruments (e.g., targeting any instrument ending with `latency`).
- **Reading and Exporting Data:** Metric Readers (such as the Prometheus HTTP Server or PeriodicMetricReader) interface with a MetricProducer to pull aggregated metrics from memory. PeriodicMetricReader forwards metrics to MetricExporters (such as OTLP gRPC or OTLP HTTP exporters) on a schedule.
- **Advanced SDK Features:** The SDK incorporates Semantic Conventions (standardized attribute naming across logs, traces, and metrics to streamline cross-telemetry correlation) and Temporal Aggregation (enabling Cumulative or Delta aggregation, the latter particularly beneficial for search engines like Elasticsearch/OpenSearch).

### Takeaways
- OpenTelemetry Metrics provides a unified, cross-language specification backed by the CNCF and broad multi-vendor support, positioning it as the future standard that will likely deprecate single-vendor or legacy metric frameworks.
- The Views mechanism offers unprecedented control over third-party library metrics, allowing operators to prevent out-of-memory errors and curb metric ingestion costs directly at the client side.
- Recent performance optimizations driven by low-latency workloads (like Apache Pulsar) have significantly reduced memory allocations, making OpenTelemetry Metrics increasingly viable for high-throughput, latency-critical systems.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Ron Veen - Modern Java: This is not your father's Java anymore
talks.teaser: Surveys language and JVM changes from Java 11 through 17 and previews virtual threads in Java 19 for practitioners.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how Java moved from multi-year, waterfall-style releases to a six-month train, including shorter LTS cycles and why staying current matters for stacks such as Spring Boot 3, which baseline on Java 17. The speaker polls the room on production versions and ties adoption to framework baselines.

The core walkthrough covers language features shipped between the Java 11 and Java 17 LTS lines: switch expressions and yield, text blocks for SQL and markup, records as concise immutable carriers with constructor-only construction, sealed types with permits and non-sealed subclasses, and pattern matching in instanceof checks and switch, including guarded cases and record deconstruction. These pieces are framed as data-oriented programming, with an example refactoring asynchronous results using sealed hierarchies, records, and exhaustive switches.

The close introduces Java 19 preview capabilities: platform versus virtual threads, carrier scheduling when I/O blocks, starting virtual threads and replacing pooled executors, cautions around synchronized pinning, and pointers that structured concurrency and production readiness target a later LTS. Audience questions extend records versus deserialization, ThreadLocal cost at scale, LTS policy, and interoperability limits versus other JVM languages.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Jakub Marchwicki - Frameworks Unplugged: Building Distributed Systems in Pure Java
talks.teaser: Builds pure Java literacy for replicating session keys, covering discovery, serialization, concurrency, CAP, and clocks.
talks.summary:
The session starts from a narrow question: what can fail before a client receives acknowledgment that data was written successfully. Using a toy goal—replicating a simple session key across nodes—the speaker builds a mental model of distributed systems using only JDK facilities, not third-party databases or frameworks, and stresses that the goal is architectural literacy rather than shipping a homemade cluster.

The middle walks step by step through an HTTP listener and client, TCP messaging between members, and ways nodes find each other, from static lists through Kubernetes or ECS APIs to multicast gossip. It compares star, ring, and full-mesh topologies, uses inboxes and outboxes with background workers, and discusses why Java’s built-in object serialization is often a poor wire format compared with schema-driven approaches. Serialization choices and schema evolution set up the harder problem of concurrent updates across an all-to-all cluster.

The close ties design to the CAP tradeoff: strong consistency clashes with availability when any node may accept writes. Wall-clock and NTP timing are unreliable for ordering; logical clocks, vector clocks, and conflict handling via CRDTs and last-write-wins appear in real stores such as Voldemort, Riak, and Cassandra. A short Q&A clarifies limits of Lamport clocks versus vector clocks and dotted version vectors as a follow-on study path.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Marton Kodok - Discover BigQuery ML, build your own CREATE MODEL stmt
talks.teaser: Shows how developers train, evaluate, and score models in BigQuery with CREATE MODEL and related SQL workflows for everyday data problems.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a common developer problem: rich e-commerce and engagement data that must be stored at full granularity, then analyzed without standing up heavy ML infrastructure. It introduces BigQuery as a managed warehouse, including scale examples, partitioning and clustering, streaming ingest, and joins to operational SQL or Sheets before turning to BigQuery ML.

Most of the session is hands-on SQL. A logistic regression CREATE MODEL predicts whether a site visitor will transact, followed by evaluation on held-out data and ML.PREDICT with probabilities. Further demos cover k-means for segmentation and outlier-style data errors, matrix factorization for recommending products to a limited audience (with warnings about query cost without filters), brief ARIMA Plus forecasting, object tables over Cloud Storage, imported TensorFlow models under size limits, and remote functions that wrap Places and geocoding APIs—illustrated by mapping charging-station applicants from company names alone.

Practitioners should treat BigQuery ML as fast, warehouse-native experimentation for conversion, recommendation, and maintenance forecasting, not millisecond online inference. Batch scores belong beside the app in cache layers; cost control leans on partitioned tables, materialized views, and scoped WHERE clauses. Q&A reinforces append-only sync from operational databases, encoding for categoricals, encryption and column masking for sensitive fields, and MySQL export-to-file loads into BigQuery.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Alina Yurenko - Supercharge your Native Image applications
talks.teaser: Covers GraalVM Native Image for production Java: build plugins, native testing, reflection agents, and cloud deployment tradeoffs.
talks.summary:
The session positions GraalVM as both a drop-in JDK with an alternate optimizing compiler and as an ahead-of-time toolchain that turns Java programs into standalone native binaries. The presenter contrasts JVM warmup and memory overhead with native image startup, pre-initialized heap state, and leaner scaling—especially where cloud bill depends on footprint.

Hands-on segments walk through Maven and Gradle native build plugins, running JUnit in native mode, and integration testing with Micronaut test resources and Testcontainers against MySQL. Reflection under the closed-world model is demonstrated with a tracing agent that emits reachability config, plus automatic discovery from a community metadata repository that fixed an H2 dependency demo. Profile-guided optimization, garbage collector choices, JFR and VisualVM monitoring, UPX compression, and static versus mostly static container images extend the production story.

Practitioners should treat native builds as a late pipeline step, lean on framework-native testing helpers, and combine agents or shared library metadata when dynamic features appear. The closing security notes highlight reduced runtime code injection surfaces and absence of JIT-time attack paths, while Q&A covers quick-build flags, Spring Boot native support, versioning in the central config repo, and large-scale adopters such as Alibaba and Disney streaming on AWS Lambda.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Sebastian Gebski - Unicorn's baby steps: what should you know as a 1st-time startup CTO
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2023: Sebastian Gebski - Unicorn's baby steps: what should you know as a 1st-time startup CTO.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2023 presentation, Sebastian Gebski—Principal Architect at AWS and former CTO/VP of Engineering—breaks down the essential realities, mental models, and challenges faced by first-time startup CTOs and aspiring technical leaders. The talk addresses how technical leadership differs fundamentally from hands-on software development, particularly within high-ambiguity, growth-oriented startup environments where organizations must operate rapidly with low inertia. Gebski traces the technical leadership lifecycle across four distinct stages of growth, highlights practical leadership trade-offs, and addresses controversial realities regarding pressure, technical debt, and company culture.

### Key Topics
- **CTO Archetypes & Roles:** Gebski distinguishes three common CTO profiles: the Architect (owning the core technical vision, algorithms, or framework), the Head of Delivery (managing systems, processes, and engineering execution), and the Advocate (serving as a technical spokesperson and liaison, similar to Werner Vogels at Amazon). He also differentiates the "leader" hat (influencing people) from the "manager" hat (managing systems), noting that while a CTO does not need to excel at every hat personally, those responsibilities must be actively delegated.
- **The Four Startup Stages:** 
  1. *Envisioning:* Focusing on understanding user problems, unique value propositions, and validating assumptions with data (both hard data and anecdotal fieldwork) before writing code.
  2. *Product-Market Fit:* Determining what to prove with limited runway and deciding what to build first. Gebski illustrates this using Midjourney, which focused purely on generative image quality and launched as a Discord bot rather than building web or mobile apps.
  3. *Operating with Real Users:* Addressing explicit and implicit customer promises, uptime implications, and business-metric monitoring. Gebski recounts an outage in a beauty/wellness SaaS platform that revealed salons could not operate without seeing scheduled appointments, prompting the implementation of graceful degradation (minimal read-only access).
  4. *Organizational Scaling:* Transitioning from single codebases to parallel, multi-site engineering teams, managing component ownership, and formalizing architecture around non-functional requirements ("-ilities").
- **Decision-Making Frameworks:** Adopting formal mechanisms such as Amazon's classification of one-way door (irreversible, high-risk, requiring deep research and "disagree and commit") versus two-way door decisions (easily reversible) to avoid CTO bottlenecks.
- **Agility and Development Friction ("Boiling Frogs"):** Maintaining development velocity by recognizing gradual slowdowns like sluggish builds, untracked breaking builds, manual approval gates, and over-engineering.
- **The Social Contract, Pressure, and Skin in the Game:** Managing startups requires sustained push and pressure from leadership. Gebski advocates establishing an upfront, explicit "social contract" regarding working hours, compensation, and risk tolerance, coupled with "skin in the game" (such as equity sharing) so contributors share in both success and loss.

### Technical Details & Common Pitfalls
Gebski challenges standard engineering dogmas by emphasizing that technical debt is not bad engineering; rather, it is a strategic tool traded consciously for speed and runway. He highlights architectures "designed for rewrite," where services bounded by stable business contracts allow underlying components to expire and be replaced easily. Additionally, he warns against critical mistakes:
- Pursuing engineering perfectionism and clean code over business pragmatism.
- The fallacy of "technical success" where developers build the requested software successfully but the product ultimately fails commercially.
- Misjudging the build vs. buy dilemma by underestimating ongoing maintenance costs when choosing to custom-build infrastructure instead of leveraging existing cloud services.

### Takeaways
A startup CTO's core responsibility is driving business outcomes rather than pursuing technical perfection. To succeed, technical leaders must establish clear decision-making frameworks, measure operational and business metrics early, communicate expectations transparently via social contracts, and prioritize focus over trying to build everything.

talks.title: GeeCON 2023: Daniel Oh - Event-driven autoscaling for Serverless Java
talks.teaser: Compares HPA, KEDA and Knative for scaling a Quarkus Java app on Kubernetes using Kafka event load.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to scale Java workloads on Kubernetes when demand comes from external event sources such as Kafka, rather than from CPU or memory use alone. The built-in horizontal pod autoscaler only reacts to resource metrics, and a namespace can typically enable only one metric adapter at a time, which makes per-service scaling on external events awkward. The speaker uses a Quarkus application that consumes messages from a Kafka topic while a large batch of generated records is produced.

The first demo relies on the standard autoscaler with a CPU target, and the speaker shows that it responds slowly to a growing message backlog. The next demo adds KEDA, a CNCF project that reads external metrics, creates the scaling object, and hands control to the autoscaler for scaling beyond one replica. In that run KEDA scaled out noticeably faster and reached the configured maximum of 10 replicas. For serverless behaviour the talk moves to Knative, which can scale to zero and back, but it requires rewriting Kubernetes resources and using CloudEvents, and in the demo it scaled to a single instance.

The closing demo combines KEDA and Knative through a sandbox integration, where a Kafka source drives scaling with configured minimum and maximum replica counts. The application scaled from zero up to several instances and back down as the workload changed. The main takeaway is to use KEDA for non-serverless event-driven workloads, Knative for serverless cases with limited scale, and the combined integration when both scale-to-zero and high concurrency are needed.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Kelly Jille - Be ‘Mr. Miyagi’ or find one! A talk about the power of mentoring
talks.teaser: Mentorship practices and workforce data show how guided apprenticeship can grow juniors and counter rising IT talent shortages.
talks.summary:
Opening with the Karate Kid’s Mr. Miyagi, the speaker traces how strong mentors shaped karate training, legal apprenticeship, and a later pivot into software engineering. After entering IT as a lateral hire, she found onboarding mostly certificates and conflicting answers until a director-led move to Ordina paired her with a tech lead who supplied the contextual guidance documentation alone could not.

The middle defines mentorship as mutual, trust-based learning and centers on apprenticeship: masters training future masters. Mentors challenge, advise, integrate newcomers into culture, and share past failures, while poor matches can harm people. She lists ten practices—voluntary pairing, mentor training, style matching, confidentiality, shared agendas, avoiding cloning the mentee, empathy, protected time, structured programs, and separating mentor support from performance ownership—and cites Robert Greene on tacit knowledge gained after formal school.

She closes on industry data: rising experience demands, reported skill shortages, and projected multi-hundred-billion dollar costs from delays and quality slips. Mentoring, she argues, improves retention, engagement, and knowledge transfer at scale. The Q&A mentions online mentor platforms and regular relationship reviews. The call to action is to institutionalize mentorship so finding a “Mr. Miyagi” is normal, not luck.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Thomas Sundberg
talks.teaser: Shows how ports and adapters let one test suite run fast in-memory and against a real database.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a testable architecture built from three ideas: ports and adapters (also called hexagonal architecture), executable specifications written in Gherkin, and reusing the same test examples across several implementations. The running example is a to-do list whose core domain depends only on a persistence port, so the aim is to keep confidence high while feedback stays fast and cheap.

The speaker starts with an in-memory task repository, which is quick to change and fast to run. He then writes a shared abstract repository test that runs against both the in-memory stub and an SQL implementation backed by an H2 database. Setting up the H2 database took about five seconds in the example, compared with roughly 20 milliseconds for the in-memory version, so most unit tests use the stub while the adapter tests confirm the real store behaves the same. He argues for a reusable stub over mocks when the same fake is needed in many test classes, pointing to about 70 classes in his own project, and recommends passing domain objects rather than raw strings through the core.

The talk closes by showing that the mixed approach gives fast feedback and confidence together. The speaker reports about 1,800 unit tests finishing in roughly 12 seconds on his machine, and says the team deploys on every passing build. The practical takeaways are to keep most tests on fast in-memory adapters, keep a small set of slow adapter tests, and limit end-to-end browser scenarios, since 11 Selenium scenarios were flaky.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Fawaz Ghali - Real-time Fraud Detection: Challenges and Solutions
talks.teaser: Explores sub-millisecond fraud detection challenges, combining stream processing, caching, and composite scoring at banking scale.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing how “real time” differs by audience, then narrows fraud work to speeds humans cannot follow—roughly tens of thousands of payment events per second and decision windows measured in fractions of a second. High-throughput payment rails and fraud rules must coexist; most stacks optimize one side or the other, which drives false declines and lost revenue.

The middle walks payment authorization, clearing, and multi-channel flows (cards, ATMs, mobile, FX), emphasizing the tiny latency budget where software can still act. An operational data store backed by in-memory caching sits beside stream ingestion from Kafka and other feeds, with composite scores from several algorithms that can be swapped without downtime. Scaling examples cite on the order of one billion events with roughly thirty milliseconds latency across dozens of nodes, plus a bank case where fraud losses and fees dropped materially after scaling the detection tier.

Two demos illustrate geo-impossible card use using airport coordinates and travel-time math, and trend-based scoring that labels the next transaction as likely legitimate or suspicious. The close stresses marrying historical account data with live streams, autoscaling for seasonal spikes, and treating fraud as an always-on pipeline rather than batch files.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: David Vlijmincx - Introduction and pitfalls of Java's new concurrency model
talks.teaser: Surveys Java 19 virtual threads and structured concurrency, with pitfalls like pinning, heap stacks, and unbounded external calls.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting expensive platform threads with familiar mitigations: fixed thread pools, callback-heavy async code, and the operational headaches those patterns create, including thread-local leakage and orphaned worker threads when parents fail.

It then walks through Project Loom preview APIs in Java 19: virtual threads as heap-backed, JVM-managed tasks scheduled on a small set of carrier platform threads via a fork-join style work-stealing model. Blocking I/O unmounts a virtual thread from its carrier, but synchronized blocks, object wait, and some JNI paths can pin threads and waste carriers. The speaker demonstrates Thread.startVirtualThread, thread builders, per-task virtual executors, and adapting older executor services with a virtual thread factory.

Structured concurrency with StructuredTaskScope is presented as a way to bind child thread lifetimes to a scope, with shutdown-on-failure and shutdown-on-success policies, deadlines, and result handling that avoids classic fork-join races. Pitfalls include avoiding pooled virtual threads, using semaphores when cheap threads can flood remote systems, legacy libraries tuned for scarce threads, and heavier garbage-collection pressure from heap-resident stacks. The closing Q&A addresses pinning limits, carrier sizing, fibers naming, and nesting scopes.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Erik Dörnenburg
talks.teaser: A consultant ties cloud-native delivery, fitness functions, and self-service platforms to the business agility enterprises actually want.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a common gap between business leaders asking for customer focus and market responsiveness and IT leaders asking for faster, more efficient delivery. It argues that unpredictable markets push most software work into the complex domain, where cause and effect are clear only in hindsight, so shortening delivery cycles matters more than exhaustive upfront analysis.

The middle connects familiar modernization themes—cloud native versus lift-and-shift, microservices, high deployment frequency, evolutionary architecture, and fitness functions that govern trade-offs without prescribing designs. Examples span production telemetry for app launch time and pipeline checks for dependency drift, alongside shift-left security ideas such as secrets management, policy as code, scanners in CI, and supply-chain risk from lagging framework versions.

The close centers on platform engineering: small stream-aligned teams need a compelling internal product of APIs, templates, and self-service tooling, with Backstage cited for larger estates. Practitioner takeaways include measuring developer satisfaction, avoiding ticket-driven platforms, investing in test automation and true continuous integration before fancy platforms, and using pair programming where four-eyes review is needed—so platforms reduce cognitive load while governance stays automated.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Andrzej Dębski - How to avoid common mistakes and misconceptions when working...
talks.teaser: Covers JVM Lambda cold starts, cost trade-offs against Fargate, and pitfalls of in-memory caching on short-lived function instances.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames AWS Lambda as a choice that brings JVM-specific latency traps, pricing surprises, and caching models that differ from long-lived servers. It walks through the function lifecycle, separating init-phase cold starts from JVM warmup where classes load lazily and JIT optimization only accelerates code after repeated executions. Measured examples show init durations near two seconds on a trivial handler, container recycling after idle periods, and latency spikes when traffic hits a less-common code path that loads new libraries.

Mitigation options include provisioned concurrency (with alias routing and CloudWatch spillover metrics), legacy keep-warm traffic, alternative runtimes or GraalVM, and constructor-time dummy execution of code paths when instances are provisioned. A cost section compares on-demand versus provisioned Lambda against Fargate using the AWS Pricing Calculator, including hello-world load, matched CPU/RAM scenarios, and a high-traffic estimate inspired by published Stack Exchange statistics. It notes free tier limits, gigabyte-second billing, when provisioned concurrency can beat on-demand at sustained throughput, and total cost of ownership beyond line-item price.

Caching advice stresses that in-process L1 caches see poor hit rates because instances are recycled quickly, background threads freeze between invocations, and routing cannot stick clients to one instance. External caches such as Redis, optional Lambda extensions, and realistic local/CI testing workflows round out what teams should validate before committing to Lambda for latency-sensitive or cache-heavy APIs.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Marit van Dijk - Keep your dependencies in check
talks.teaser: Covers dependency selection, vulnerability discovery, SCA dashboards, JVM update bots, and migration tooling for maintainable codebases.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why open-source dependencies are ubiquitous on the JVM and what can go wrong: transitive bloat, version clashes, and security flaws, illustrated by Log4j and Spring4Shell-style incident response. It contrasts teams that avoid libraries entirely with those that adopt every fashionable package, then walks through criteria for choosing dependencies—fit, size, duplication, maintainer activity, community tone, documentation, and how deeply a library embeds in the codebase.

Research sources include Maven Repository, GitHub signals, and JetBrains Package Search in the browser or IntelliJ, including Package Checker links to known CVEs. Maintenance starts with local `dependency:tree`, update listings, and unused-dependency analysis in Maven and Gradle, then scales to organization-wide software composition analysis. Automated options on GitHub—Dependabot, Renovate, and Snyk Open Source—are compared on alerts, pull requests, scheduling, and PR metadata.

When upgrades break builds, the talk points to IntelliJ migrations, Error Prone with Refaster, Picnic’s open rules, and Open Rewrite recipes for framework and test migrations. The closing message favors periodic re-evaluation, automation where possible, and steady updates over panic-driven firefighting; Q&A touches exploitability versus mere linkage, Spring Boot BOM versions, and convincing product owners to budget maintenance time.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Grzegorz Piwowarek - CompletableFuture and its Quirks
talks.teaser: Surveys CompletableFuture sharp edges in cancellation, allOf, anyOf, and default executors for Java teams.
talks.summary:
The session targets developers who already use Java futures and want to avoid learning CompletableFuture’s sharp edges only after something breaks in production. It contrasts the older Future model with CompletableFuture’s decoupling from a single worker thread, then focuses on APIs and defaults that look intuitive but behave differently.

Cancellation via the standard Future interface does not interrupt work tied to a CompletableFuture pipeline the way many expect. Methods such as allOf wait for every input future to finish even when one fails immediately, which can add pointless delays unless teams implement short-circuiting themselves. anyOf and applyToEither can surface exceptional completions ahead of successful ones, contrary to common assumptions about “first result wins.”

SupplyAsync and chained stages often run on the JVM’s shared ForkJoin common pool unless an executor is supplied explicitly; mixing blocking work there can slow parallel streams and crowd CPU-oriented pools. Synchronous stages may execute on the calling thread when a future is already complete, so blocking code can run inline despite an async-looking API. The speaker illustrates these pitfalls with live demos, notes seeing similar bugs in production and open source, and closes with brief guidance on join versus get, Project Reactor for heavier reactive needs, and using dedicated executors for blocking tasks.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Mary Gryglewski - Event Streaming for the Best of All Worlds
talks.teaser: Explores event streaming and Apache Pulsar as a cloud-native option beside Kafka for real-time pipelines and tenancy.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames computing events as time-bound occurrences and walks through stream processing, complex event processing, and how event-driven pub/sub differs from point-to-point message-driven designs. Batch processing remains valid for clearing, ML training, and large offline jobs, but streaming targets immediate reaction to high-volume feeds such as IoT telemetry.

Apache Pulsar is introduced as an Apache top-level project born at Yahoo, pairing stateless brokers with Apache BookKeeper for log storage and ZooKeeper for coordination. The architecture separates compute from persistence to ease horizontal scaling and rebalancing compared with tightly coupled Kafka deployments. Subscription modes (exclusive, failover, shared, key-shared) unify queue and topic semantics; tiered storage, geo-replication, multi-tenancy, and pluggable auth are highlighted for regulated, multi-region use.

Selection guidance contrasts Kafka and Pulsar on planning partitions, latency, and managed versus self-hosted offerings. A short console walkthrough shows creating streaming tenants, topics, tokens, and sample Java producer and consumer setup on a hosted platform. Audience Q&A notes on-prem microservices suitability, production maturity, ecosystem overlap with Flink and Spark, and operational cost of rebalancing.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Bartłomiej Żyliński - The tale of math and scalability
talks.teaser: A story-driven tour explains contention and coherency delay, then applies Amdahl's and Gunther's laws to size nodes and costs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames scalability as a recurring crisis for a profitable but stateful system whose traffic spikes first overwhelm vertical scaling. The engineers discover contention—competition for shared resources—and use Amdahl's law to explain why adding CPUs and memory yields diminishing returns when part of the work stays effectively single-threaded.

After optimizations buy headroom, marketing growth pushes them toward horizontal scaling, which for stateful designs demands architectural and infrastructure change. Adding many nodes paradoxically slows the system; consistency ordering and coherency delay emerge as the culprits. Gunther's universal scalability law extends Amdahl's view with a coherency term, plots realistic curves including performance cliffs, and supports choosing an optimal node count plus upfront resource and cloud cost estimates before launch day.

The closing argument is that mathematics can predict scalability in principle because the laws are architecture-agnostic, yet parameters such as the serial fraction and coherency overhead must be measured experimentally—there are no universal cookbook values. Queuing theory is noted as a related path left for another session. Practitioners should treat contention and coherency as inevitable constraints and use these models to bound expectations before scaling bets go live.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Szymon Stepniak - It's an HTTP client. It feels like Spring Data...
talks.teaser: Micronaut's declarative HTTP client proxies a users API live, fixes event-loop blocking, and adds circuit breakers with SQS fallbacks.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a Spring Data analogy for developers who only know Spring Boot, then sets four goals: explore Micronaut basics through live coding, show benefits of declarative HTTP clients, warn about painful traps, and briefly mention reusing the same client outside Micronaut. The demo application accepts client requests, forwards them to a separate users API with an API key, and supports listing and creating users with validation on name and email.

Implementation walks through a `@Client` interface, configuration properties for the key, and controllers that delegate to the client. The talk shows how `HttpResponse` wrappers expose headers such as target host, named services in configuration, and the event-loop deadlock risk when the default Netty group serves both inbound requests and blocking outbound calls. Mitigations include dedicated event loop groups, `@ExecuteOn` for the IO pool, and reactive `Publisher` return types; Siege load tests illustrate roughly 100 versus about 1,500 requests per second on the demo setup. Consul-based service discovery replaces a fixed URL, and built-in circuit breakers with a fallback client return empty results when instances are down.

For failed user creation, fallback logic enqueues requests to Amazon SQS via Micronaut Worker; a scheduled job and a listener on circuit-closed events retry creates when the users API recovers. The speaker skips the promised Spring Boot bonus for lack of time and closes with Maven compatibility notes and a pointer to bite-sized Micronaut tips on social media.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Yan Khonski
talks.teaser: Explains PostgreSQL transaction isolation, MVCC, vacuum behavior, and scaling trade-offs for large production databases.
talks.summary:
The session frames why concurrent readers and writers need explicit isolation guarantees, then walks through the SQL standard levels from read committed through serializable and the anomalies each level allows or prevents, including dirty reads, phantom reads, write skew, and lost updates. Postgres-specific behavior is spelled out, including how read committed remains the default compromise and when repeatable read or serializable forces retry logic and affects replicas.

The middle of the talk compares optimistic and pessimistic concurrency control, two-phase locking with SELECT FOR UPDATE, and a production anecdote where long transactions plus in-process caching collided with shared locks on MS SQL Server. It then explains multiversion concurrency control: tuple xmin and xmax fields, snapshots, visibility rules, 32-bit transaction ID wraparound, freezing, and why updates create new row versions that bloat tables and indexes.

Vacuum and autovacuum are described step by step—visibility map, heap and index scans, heap reclaim, and why VACUUM FULL needs an exclusive lock—along with latency spikes, circuit breakers, read replicas, partitioning, and sharding to limit blast radius. The closing message is that teams building global SaaS products should understand these internals before committing to a datastore, because migration cost grows sharply once millions of users depend on production behavior.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Magda Stożek - Say goodbye to implicits - contextual abstractions in Scala 3
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2022: Magda Stożek - Say goodbye to implicits - contextual abstractions in Scala 3.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At GeeCON 2022, Magda Stożek discusses the overhaul of contextual abstractions in Scala 3, focusing on the elimination of the overloaded `implicit` keyword. Reflecting on her five years of experience as a Scala developer, Stożek highlights how implicits in Scala 2 caused confusion due to a single keyword serving multiple disparate roles, sneaky implicit conversions, and cryptic compiler errors. Scala 3 redesigns this system by replacing `implicit` with dedicated, purpose-built language constructs designed to improve readability and developer experience.

### Key Topics
The talk contrasts Scala 2 and Scala 3 across seven concrete use cases:
- **Providing Context**: Replacing implicit parameters and values with the `using` and `given` keywords.
- **Adding Functionality**: Replacing implicit classes with explicit `extension` methods.
- **Type Classes**: Implementing ad-hoc polymorphism using `given` definitions and resolving instances via `summon` instead of `implicitly`.
- **Conversions**: Replacing implicit methods with implementations of the dedicated `scala.Conversion` class.
- **Imports**: Introducing separate import syntax (`import module.given`) to distinguish contextual givens from normal wildcard imports (`import module.*`).
- **Unused Names**: Allowing anonymous givens to avoid naming variables required only by the compiler.
- **Compiler Errors**: Improved compiler messages that clearly identify where and why contextual parameters are missing, including import suggestions.

### Technical Details
- **Contextual Parameters**: In Scala 2, context (such as an `ExecutionContext` for `Future`) relied on `implicit val` and an `(implicit ec: ExecutionContext)` parameter list. In Scala 3, this is defined using `(using ec: ExecutionContext)` and supplied via `given`.
- **Extensions**: Instead of wrapping types in `implicit class Qualifies(book: Book)` to add methods to closed types, Scala 3 directly declares `extension (b: Book) def qualifiesForChallenge: Boolean`.
- **Type Classes & Summoning**: Type class instances are declared via `given Scorable[Book] with ...`. When using context bounds (`[T: Scorable]`), Scala 3 replaces `implicitly[Scorable[T]]` with the `summon[Scorable[T]]` method.
- **Conversions**: Rather than defining `implicit def bookToItem(b: Book): Item`, Scala 3 requires defining a `given Conversion[Book, Item]` with an `apply` method, preventing ambiguous conversion definitions.
- **Scoped Imports**: In Scala 2, wildcard imports imported both normal members and implicits. In Scala 3, `.*` imports explicit members only, while `.given` must be used to bring `given` instances into scope.
- **Migration and Interoperability**: Scala 3 allows gradual migration; in Scala 3.0 and 3.1, `given` definitions and `implicit` definitions can interoperate via compiler flags before deprecation warnings and errors are introduced in later versions.

### Takeaways
Scala 3 splits the overloaded responsibilities of the `implicit` keyword into distinct mechanisms (`given`, `using`, `extension`, and `Conversion`). This shift aligns with functional programming principles by clearly expressing intent rather than implementation mechanics. Teams can adopt Scala 3 incrementally without rewriting all contextual code at once.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Jakub Nabrdalik - Malevolent Architect: only bad decisions
talks.teaser: A satirical tour of architectural and operational choices that look prudent yet amplify outages, obscure logs, and prolong burnout.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames software leadership as a dark game: cause lasting harm through decisions that still earn praise or promotion. It opens on production incidents, arguing that an immediate all-hands rush to patch often triggers shotgun debugging, stacked fixes, and worse customer impact than a disciplined approach of listing hypotheses, cheap checks first, and only then deeper verification.

The middle skewers common friction: blocking production access behind slow deploy pipelines, unusable debug environments, weak or noisy logging, and log platforms that split errors and traces so investigations miss failures. A personal medical story parallels arrogant first guesses versus careful diagnosis. Antipatterns extend to toxic burnout advice and to ignoring emotions; neuroscience examples illustrate how unconscious processes drive choices before conscious narrative kicks in.

The close ties engineering habits to wellbeing: make local reproduction and clear logs normal, reject heroics, and treat sadness or mismatch as signals—journal, rest, connection—rather than quitting blindly. Recommended reading on brain and behavior backs monitoring inner state the way teams monitor systems.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Jan Lahoda - Source code models in the JDK and their use
talks.teaser: The session maps JDK APIs for modeling Java source and shows compile-time validators, generators, and in-memory compiler tests.
talks.summary:
An Oracle engineer who works on javac introduces the JDK facilities for representing Java source during compilation. The talk separates standard pieces—the language model for declarations and types, the annotation processing hook, and the javax.tools API to run the compiler programmatically—from javac-specific public APIs that expose AST nodes and finer-grained compiler behavior.

Live examples walk through enforcing team rules at compile time. One checker uses the Element API and ElementKind to reject public fields that are not final by traversing the declaration tree. A second uses TypeMirror and recursive checks on generic type arguments to flag methods that return arrays, including nested cases such as collections of arrays. The speaker then wires validators into AbstractProcessor implementations, explains annotation processing rounds, Messager reporting, and service-loader registration, and demonstrates generating localized message bundles and accessor code from annotations so broken resource keys fail during compilation rather than in production.

The closing segment covers testing processors entirely in memory with getTask, custom file objects, diagnostic listeners, and -proc:only. A TreeScanner-based validator on the AST catches calls to String.toLowerCase() without an explicit Locale where the element model cannot see method bodies. Question answers cover processor classpath setup, templating for codegen, and the limits of bytecode AST access.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: David Vlijmincx - Introduction and pitfalls of Java's new concurrency model
talks.teaser: Surveys Project Loom virtual threads and structured concurrency in Java 19, highlighting pinning risks and resource pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with how traditional Java platform threads work: creating a thread triggers an operating-system kernel thread and allocates on the order of one to two megabytes of stack, which makes spawning huge numbers of threads impractical and nudges teams toward thread pools, async callbacks, and familiar pain points such as thread-local leakage, blocked pool threads, and orphaned child work when a parent fails.

The core material explains Project Loom virtual threads as cheap JVM concepts scheduled on carrier platform threads, including unmounting on blocking I/O, preview APIs such as starting virtual threads directly or via a per-task virtual executor, and pinning when synchronized blocks, Object.wait, or some native calls keep a virtual thread on its carrier. The speaker warns against pooling virtual threads, describes connection storms when a fixed external limit is replaced by unbounded virtual concurrency, and notes that older libraries may assume expensive threads or use blocking primitives that defeat unmounting.

Structured concurrency is shown through structured task scopes with shutdown-on-failure and shutdown-on-success, join with deadlines, and safe result access after join. The close stresses preview instability, extra heap use from virtual stack frames, and Q&A on carriers, fiber naming, synchronized support, and mixing virtual threads with existing executors via thread factories.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Jakub Marchwicki - They say testing triangle but you are doing microservices. Now what?
talks.teaser: Explains how to split testing for microservices across unit, integration, contract and black-box layers under a fast time budget.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the classic testing triangle of unit, integration and UI end-to-end tests and argues it breaks down once a system becomes independently deployed microservices. Monolithic suites grow slow and brittle, and running every service on a laptop is impractical. The speaker sets out to decide which kind of test belongs in which place, so each layer answers a specific question about whether a service starts, deploys and runs.

Unit tests stay fast but miss framework wiring. Integration tests with the real Spring context check configuration, JSON mapping and cache behaviour, at a cost of about a second per test. Contract tests, in consumer-driven and Spring Cloud Contract styles, along with Swagger or gRPC compatibility checks, catch breaking API changes. Real databases, brokers and caches come in through embedded or container instances. The speaker warns that Testcontainers restarts a container for each test unless reuse is set up, while Spring reuses its test context. At the far end, black-box tests run the packaged service with production-like configuration, health probes and metrics.

The main takeaway is the time budget. Feedback under about 100 milliseconds feels instant, but past roughly 10 seconds developers drift to other tasks, so slow suites should be trimmed and layered. Once a fast, reliable pipeline exists, the speaker suggests teams can experiment in production with feature toggles and staged releases. In audience questions, he said real databases suit mapping and query checks, while mocks are reasonable for service logic once that layer is verified.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Dominik Moštěk - From objects to functions
talks.teaser: Explains how object-oriented design pairs with functional implementation to lower change cost in Java systems.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by noting how modern “object-oriented” practice often emphasizes classes, inheritance, and language features rather than the messaging, local state, and loose coupling Alan Kay described. He contrasts textbook OOP vocabulary with those original principles and uses the Internet as an example of message-based design at scale.

Walking through registration and notification examples, he argues that polymorphism is one implementation choice among many, not messaging itself. He covers local retention pitfalls when code assumes a shared JVM, and a graduated scale for loose binding—from direct calls through event buses—matched to expected change. For behavior, he reframes classes as partially applied functions, separates pure computation from plumbing, and shows composition, caching, and testing benefits via a portfolio-style example and a line-filtering pipeline.

He closes with four “quadrants” (design, functions, plumbing, types), each with different quality goals, and recommends DDD and clean code alongside OO design plus functional implementation. Q&A covers hiring for functional Java, exceptions, performance, debugging, and libraries such as Cactus.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Ionut Balosin - Techniques for a faster JVM start-up
talks.teaser: Surveys Hotspot dynamic CDS, OpenJ9 shared class cache, and GraalVM native image to cut cold JVM startup for serverless-style workloads.
talks.summary:
Cold JVM startup dominates latency and cost for short-lived and serverless workloads, so the session centers on call startup rather than warming the interpreter or resuming a steady state. It argues that default class-data sharing in modern JDKs helps only marginally unless teams invest in application-specific archives.

The first segment walks through Hotspot dynamic CDS: how archives layer on default system-class caches, how metaspace and heap regions map at fixed addresses, and a Spring Pet Clinic demo that measures HTTP readiness instead of Boot log lines. Roughly one second or up to twenty to thirty percent faster cold starts appear possible without code changes, alongside strict limits on JDK version, platform, unchanged JARs, and stable class paths.

OpenJ9’s shared class cache is contrasted as a single-run, more flexible workflow that can also retain ahead-of-time compiled code, yielding larger gains in the same demo. GraalVM native image via Spring Native is presented as the strongest startup option, with trade-offs around closed-world compilation, reflection, and framework-specific preparation. Closing questions cover default versus dynamic CDS, baking archives into Docker CI/CD, and leaning on native binaries for AWS Lambda.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Tomasz Skowroński - Are immortal libraries ready for immutable classes?
talks.teaser: A Java session compares mutable habits with immutable modeling across Spring, JPA, and Jackson, and what library support looks like today.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with a playful contrast between easy mutable classes and the hidden complexity that grows as objects gain lifecycle and ordering constraints. Mutable enterprise patterns—getters, setters, encapsulation, and Lombok—are portrayed as familiar and fast to write, while genuinely immutable types need more than final modifiers and can surprise teams when static analyzers score “immutable” annotations.

The middle of the talk explains why Java codebases still mutate: team habits, framework conventions, and persistence models that expect accessors. Examples walk through constructor-based Spring injection, immutable query-parameter DTOs, and cases where immutable JPA entities make sense for events or legally fixed invoices. Serialization receives heavy focus: Jackson can bind JSON into immutable types via per-field annotations, constructor properties, or compiler-retained parameter names. Complex state changes are shown as staged immutable types rather than in-place mutation, echoing builder flows such as Spring’s response-entity pattern. Testing notes cover Mockito configuration for final classes and questioning whether mocks are needed at all.

The closing call to action is design-first: when creating a class, consider whether immutability models the domain better rather than banning mutable entities wholesale. A brief Q&A mentions MapStruct’s builder-oriented path for immutable mappings and trade-offs when mixing JVM languages for DTOs.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Andrii Rodionov - Implementing Raft protocol
talks.teaser: Walks through a Raft implementation using Java Project Loom virtual threads for RPC, elections, and log replication.
talks.summary:
The session opens by motivating consensus in distributed clusters: replicated state machines must apply the same commands in the same order while tolerating node failures, and Raft has largely replaced Paxos for practical adoption in systems such as Hazelcast, etcd, Consul, MongoDB, Redis, and Kafka. The speaker outlines Raft roles, leader election, append-only log replication, heartbeats, and term handling, illustrating behavior with an interactive Raft visualization.

The core of the talk maps those concerns onto Java concurrency pain points—many blocking network calls, retries, and complex follower–candidate–leader state changes—and argues that Project Loom virtual threads and structured concurrency fit this workload better than callback-heavy reactive styles for imperative business logic. Implementation topics include Spring Boot servlets patched for virtual-thread executors, an event-loop style state machine on virtual threads, parallel vote gathering with timeouts, scheduled heartbeats, and hierarchical cancellation via try-with-resources scope patterns demonstrated in live code.

A multi-node demo shows election when nodes join, log consistency across followers, failover when the leader stops, and catch-up replication when a late node starts. The closing Q&A contrasts Loom with reactive streaming, notes evolving thread-local semantics for virtual threads, and sketches how Hazelcast might eventually reduce thread counts and simplify async code once Loom reaches a stable JDK release.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Robert Piwowarek - Gamedev through the eyes of a backend engineer
talks.teaser: A former backend developer surveys Perforce, CI, Steam betas, and Unreal C++ patterns that shape day-to-day work in commercial game studios.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from the perspective of someone who moved from Scala backend work into gameplay programming at a Polish studio behind narrative-heavy titles. The speaker frames game development as creative, cross-disciplinary work, then focuses on programmer tooling rather than art packages: IDEs, engines, issue trackers, and the rising adoption of JetBrains Rider in the space.

The middle section walks through version control and delivery mechanics that differ sharply from typical IT practice. Perforce is default because of centralized truth and binary file locking, with trade-offs for code review. Jenkins automates multi-target builds and tests; Unreal Game Sync coordinates Perforce syncs with compatible editor binaries to avoid broken editor launches. Steam branch betas distribute internal builds. Console dev kits, remote testing tools, and pandemic-era remote workflows appear as practical constraints.

The closing half covers programming inside Unreal Engine: assisted C++ without the standard library, Unreal Build Tool, property specifiers and garbage collection, Blueprint and specialized graph systems, C++ and visual debugging aids, and cautious automated testing after prototyping. The speaker notes sparse public documentation and heavy studio-specific tribal knowledge, then answers audience questions on platforms, JVM use, Git LFS, and multi-platform shipping pain.

talks.title: GeeCON 2022: Mohammed Aboullaite - What the hell is service mesh anyway!?
talks.teaser: A walkthrough clarifies what service meshes add beyond orchestrators, with live Istio canary routing and fault injection on a sock shop app.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with an analogy between telephone switchboards and how backend architecture evolved from monoliths through enterprise service buses to microservices. That history frames why east-west traffic inside clusters needs tooling beyond containers and API gateways, and why client libraries hit language and maintenance limits.

The core argument defines a service mesh as infrastructure-layer sidecars plus a control plane that handles observability, security policies, mutual TLS, and resiliency without baking those concerns into application code. Examples include cascading failure when an unhealthy downstream slows callers, Peter Deutsch’s fallacies of distributed systems, and contrasts with message brokers, ESBs, gateways, and Netflix-style libraries. The Istio demo on Kubernetes exercises sock-shop traffic splitting, canary weights, header-based routing, deliberate delays, and fault injection, alongside discussion of Consul, Linkerd, and overhead benchmarks.

Closing guidance urges skepticism: meshes carry CPU, memory, latency, lock-in, and learning-curve costs. They may still help large service estates, monolith modernization, release confidence, debugging distributed calls, and chaos experiments—but only after a concrete use case justifies the complexity.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Ondro Mihályi - Afraid of Java cold starts in Serverless? Fear not, Java is fast
talks.teaser: Shows how Java cold starts on AWS Lambda compare across app servers, lightweight frameworks and JVM tweaks.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether Java is too slow for AWS Lambda, beginning with how a Lambda function is initialized before it handles an event. The speaker explains that a cold start covers preparing the environment and running static initialization, and that custom runtimes shift that setup time onto the bill. Cold starts matter most for user-facing calls, and much less for background jobs that run occasionally.

Measurements compare a servlet application across several stacks, timing from JVM start to the first response. GlassFish 7 took about six seconds, embedded GlassFish under four, and Spring Boot about two and a half. A plain Java program with no HTTP listener started in roughly 70 milliseconds. Quarkus and a Piranha-based setup landed near half a second. Quarkus does much of its dependency injection and configuration at build time and can produce GraalVM native binaries, while Piranha is a modular servlet container built from only the parts an application needs. Among JVM tweaks, turning off the second-level JIT compiler gave around 10 percent, and class data sharing cut a more complex app from about 800 to 600 milliseconds.

The speaker also covers more memory and CPU, boosted startup, pre-warmed instances, custom trimmed JVMs, and CRaC checkpoint and restore, which was still emerging. The takeaway is that framework and JVM choices can bring Java cold starts close to half a second, but how much that matters depends on how often the function runs and who is waiting for it.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2022: Péter Ábel Nagy - Blockchain technology can be a powerful tool
talks.teaser: Gives a broad overview of blockchain basics, proof of work versus proof of stake, use cases, and how to start a career in it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a quick poll on cryptocurrency ownership and losses, then argues that blockchain development is a growing career path, citing a reported 500 percent rise in open positions over the last year. The speaker presents blockchain as a tool with possible uses in healthcare record sharing, real estate ownership records, IoT interaction logs and supply chain tracking, while judging voting and social media to be less realistic fits.

The middle section explains the mechanics. Each block stores its own hash and the previous block's hash, which links the blocks so they cannot be reordered easily. Proof of work makes rewriting history costly through mining, while proof of stake picks validators according to the coins they stake. The talk compares public, private and consortium ledgers, weighing cost, reward risk and trust between participants, and mentions projects that aim to replace certificate authorities with distributed validation.

The closing part covers getting started. Core blockchain engineers design protocols and networks, while blockchain software developers build applications that use the technology. Suggested first steps include reading Bitcoin's white paper, learning smart contracts and studying Solidity for Ethereum. Several languages and Java libraries are named as options. The talk ends with a question round on energy use, quantum resistance and example projects.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Ewelina Wilkosz - Jenkins Configuration as Code -Automate your automation Server
talks.teaser: Covers Jenkins Configuration as Code for versioned YAML master settings, Docker-based demos, and open-source contribution paths.

The talk opens with the limits of managing Jenkins only through its web UI: sprawling Manage Jenkins pages, no undo, and operators hoarding screenshots before each tweak. It introduces Jenkins Configuration as Code as a plugin-driven alternative—declarative YAML for core server, security, credentials, and tools—contrasted with Job DSL, Jenkinsfiles, init Groovy, and XML exports.

The middle section follows how Pragma and CloudBees contributors aligned on a single community solution, relying on plugin data-binding conventions instead of per-plugin glue code, with generated docs and schema validation tied to each live instance. A Docker Compose walkthrough disables the setup wizard, installs plugins from a pinned list, mounts config repos, sets CASC_JENKINS_CONFIG, and reloads via the UI or CLI, including dry-run checks and YAML export from an existing master.

The closing emphasis is operational payoff—faster rebuilds, git blame, cloning identical controllers—and honest limits such as update-center plugin management. It also encourages newcomers to fork, build with Maven, open small plugin compliance pull requests, and use good-first-issue labels or project chat.
