talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Andrzej Grzesik
talks.teaser: Shows how to read GC logs, analyze heap dumps and cut allocations in Java apps before reaching for GC tuning.
talks.summary:
Java developers often meet memory trouble through errors such as Java heap space and GC overhead limit exceeded. The speaker argues that the garbage collector's role is to clear unneeded objects, so reducing garbage in the code often beats tuning collector settings. Throughput, the share of time spent on application work rather than collection, is presented as the key measure. Enabling GC logging in production and development is recommended, with different flag syntax on JDK 8 and on JDK 9 and later. Printing the final JVM flags to verify what is actually set, and dumping the heap on an out of memory error, were also covered.

The middle part covered tools for analysing the output. GCeasy was shown for uploading GC logs, and a commercial analyser was demonstrated for summary metrics such as total allocated bytes. For heap dumps, Eclipse Memory Analyzer, VisualVM and the newer Hippo project were mentioned as options. Two common culprits were discussed: String objects on Java 8, where character arrays add memory overhead and string deduplication under G1 can help at a speed cost, and boxed Long values in ArrayList, where specialised primitive collections reduced allocations significantly in one case. Escape analysis, inspected with JIT Watch, and allocation profiling in VisualVM were presented as later-stage steps.

The closing advice was to benchmark every change on an isolated machine with GC logs running, since results depend on the workload. Binary formats were suggested over JSON where a schema is practical, and tuning was described as a fallback once code changes are exhausted.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: M.Salatino - From Java Monolith to K8s:Lessons learned in an Open Source project
talks.teaser: Walks through deploying a Java app to Kubernetes with Jenkins X, then splitting it into services with orchestration.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a conference-management Spring Boot application as it moves from a single monolith to a set of services running on Kubernetes. The speaker starts by importing the monolith into Jenkins X, which generates Dockerfiles and Helm charts, builds and releases each change, and opens a pull request against an environment repository so the cluster state is kept in git. The same import approach is then applied to each part of the application, and releases are promoted to staging or production from there.

Once the application is split into a front end and separate call-for-proposals, agenda and email services, requests are routed through a gateway built with Spring Cloud Gateway. The speaker then shows how a proposal decision flow buried in service-to-service calls becomes hard to change, monitor and recover when failures happen. Moving that flow into a workflow model run by an orchestration engine keeps the logic visible and makes its state queryable in Elasticsearch. Services can register workers for pending jobs, so a job waiting on a service that is not yet deployed runs once that service comes up.

The main takeaways are that many of these Kubernetes tools are open source and worth reading to learn how complex platforms are built, and that a team needs a shared framework for deciding which problems to solve itself and which to integrate. Practitioners should weigh the added data, dependency and resilience concerns before splitting a monolith into microservices.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Adam Dubiel - Back to basics: threads
talks.teaser: Maps JVM threads to Linux scheduling and memory, then shows how unbounded Spring pools and Docker limits break production apps.
talks.summary:
The session steps back from abstractions to what actually runs a typical Spring Boot service on Linux. Starting a sample Undertow application creates dozens of threads within seconds and well over a hundred once traffic arrives, so the speaker graphs creation timing and asks what those threads cost.

On Linux, each JVM thread is a real pthread. Process listings show them beside the Java PID, and native memory tracking reports about one megabyte of stack per thread. That arithmetic matters in containers: cgroup memory limits include off-heap thread stacks, and exceeding the cap kills the process without the slack VMs often allowed. The talk also contrasts virtual address space with resident set size when stress-spawning threads, and links many blocked platform threads on few CPU cores to expensive context switches that evict cache working sets.

Back in application code, default Spring @Async spins a fresh thread per task instead of reusing a pool. The speaker walks through ThreadPoolExecutor with bounded queues and rejection policies rather than JDK factory defaults with unbounded queues, plus optional prestarting core threads. Closing advice ties Linux ps and jstack together via hexadecimal native thread IDs, favors Java 11 name propagation into ps, and recommends metrics on pool and queue utilization rather than fixed sizes left unchanged for years.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Maciek Próchniak - Being transactional in 2019 - what does it actually mean?
talks.teaser: Traces how transactional guarantees shifted across relational databases, NoSQL, and Kafka, and what practitioners must verify themselves.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with a painful early project built on event sourcing, sagas, and immature NoSQL, then contrasts it with calmer Spring work until SIM-card reservations exposed how little `@Transactional` defaults really promise across database vendors. He walks through ANSI isolation levels, snapshot isolation pitfalls such as the joint bank-account example, optimistic locking, and Martin Kleppmann’s Hermitage project as a reality check on vendor behavior.

The middle connects that history to 2019’s landscape: MongoDB multi-document transactions, misunderstood CAP formulations versus Brewer’s partition and availability assumptions, weaker session models like causal consistency, and the cost of two-phase commit when sharded MongoDB finally spanned shards. He contrasts microservice-style sagas and idempotence with homogeneous distributed stores, sketching Spanner’s Paxos writes and TrueTime, Calvin’s declarative batching, and why enterprise XA rarely scales.

The close shifts to Kafka’s log-based transactions: coordinator topics, commit markers, atomic multi-partition produces, and patterns for exactly-once between topics, databases, and offsets. The takeaway is to read vendor docs skeptically, map marketing claims to formal definitions, and revisit trade-offs as hardware and products evolve, with Hermitage and Daniel Abadi’s writing as practical references.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Martin Štefanko - A different flavor of the distributed transaction
talks.teaser: Maps saga compensations onto MicroProfile long-running actions with a live Quarkus demo across coordinating microservices.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting everyday transaction volume with cryptocurrency traffic, then revisits ACID using a business-trip booking scenario spanning flight, hotel, and car rental. Two-phase commit is walked through as the dominant production consensus approach, including prepare and commit phases, locking, and the failure mode where a coordinator outage leaves resources locked and services unresponsive—at odds with reactive, always-responsive design goals.

The speaker introduces the saga pattern from its 1987 origins, emphasizing compensating actions that semantically undo prior steps when later steps fail, and contrasts ACID isolation and consistency with BASE availability and eventual consistency under CAP constraints. Choreography versus orchestrated coordination are outlined before the talk shifts to Eclipse MicroProfile Long Running Actions as a Java annotation model for sagas, with Red Hat Narayana as one implementation.

A live Quarkus build adds the LRA extension, runs a Narayana coordinator, and wires JAX-RS resources with @LRA, @Compensate, cancel-on status codes, context headers, propagation to a second service, end=false semantics, @AfterLRA callbacks, coordinator states, and explicit close endpoints. Practitioners leave with a concrete picture of when sagas beat two-phase commit in microservices and how to experiment via the open MicroProfile LRA project on GitHub.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: E.Demčenko - Extending Cloud/Desktop IDEs, providing a new choice for developers
talks.teaser: GeeCON Prague 2019: E.Demčenko - Extending Cloud/Desktop IDEs, providing a new choice for developers.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON Prague 2019 presentation, speaker E. Demčenko from Broadcom discusses the motivation and technical architecture behind modernizing developer environments for mission-critical systems, specifically z/OS mainframe environments. Mainframes continue to handle high-stakes workloads such as global financial transactions and power management, representing decades of established infrastructure. However, a major generational shift in the workforce is taking place: veteran mainframe developers are retiring, and incoming engineers accustomed to modern developer tooling (such as Git, GitHub, and VS Code) often balk at traditional 3270 green-screen terminal interfaces. Rather than embarking on high-risk, expensive migrations of millions of lines of mission-critical production code to distributed systems, Broadcom and the open-source community are bridging the gap by bringing modern cloud and desktop IDE standards to mainframe development.

### Key Topics
- **Generational Shift and Mainframe Relevance:** Mission-critical mainframe systems remain actively developed and essential. Modernizing the developer experience avoids rewriting massive production codebases while making mainframe development accessible to new generations of developers.
- **Eclipse Che vs. Eclipse Thea:** The evolving roles of cloud development tools. Eclipse Che has evolved into a containerized workspace manager rather than a standalone IDE, while Eclipse Thea acts as an extensible, multi-language IDE framework built with TypeScript, Node.js, and Electron that runs both in desktop and browser environments.
- **Open Industry Protocols:** The adoption of community-driven standards—namely the Language Server Protocol (LSP) and the Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP)—to decouple editors/IDEs from specific programming languages and debuggers.
- **Tooling Integrations:** Demonstrations of Eclipse Che on Red Hat OpenShift, Gitpod integration for instant workspace provisioning directly from GitHub, and Broadcom's Che4z project targeting mainframe languages.

### Technical Details
- **Eclipse Che Architecture (v7.1):** Che serves as a workspace controller orchestrating user runtimes in container pods across Kubernetes or OpenShift clusters. Each plugin and user runtime runs in its own pod with persisted state in a database. It supports single-user or multi-user configurations, with multi-user setups relying on OpenID and PostgreSQL.
- **Eclipse Thea Framework:** Designed as an extensible alternative to proprietary IDE architectures. It uses JSON-RPC for communication, shares architecture similarities with VS Code, but offers open-source friendly licensing and deeper framework extensibility beyond standard VS Code extensions.
- **Language Server Protocol (LSP) & Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP):** Defined via JSON-RPC microservice architectures, separating client-side UI from language processing (syntax checks, semantics coloring, intelligent code completion) and debugging logic. The speaker references implementations such as LSP4J, Xtext (by TypeFox) for language parsers, and custom language servers implemented for COBOL and Assembler (developed in C++ by Charles University students). Debuggers for mainframes execute remotely (e.g., debugging CICS/kicks transaction regions) while exposing standard DAP interfaces to the IDE frontend.

### Takeaways
- Standard protocols like LSP and DAP prevent vendor lock-in and enable cross-compatibility across VS Code, Eclipse Thea, Eclipse, and IntelliJ.
- Adopting standardized cloud-based workspace managers (Eclipse Che) and extensible IDE frameworks (Eclipse Thea) allows organizations to provide turn-key development stacks for diverse, legacy, or specialized languages.
- For mission-critical and mainframe environments, bringing modern developer ergonomics and Git-centric workflows bridges the skills gap for incoming developers without abandoning proven production systems.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: M.Fusco/M.Swiderski - How we turned our Java projects into serverless components
talks.teaser: Shows how the Drools and jBPM Java projects were refactored to run as GraalVM native images and serverless cloud services.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who lead the Drools rule engine and jBPM process automation projects, explain that their long-established Java codebases relied on reflection and dynamic class loading, which GraalVM's closed-world assumption does not permit in native images. They introduce Kogito, a project that aims to turn business rules, decisions and processes into cloud-ready services without hand-written glue code, while still requiring a clear understanding of the business domain.

To show the result, they start three native-compiled services that make up an onboarding application: one process-driven service and two decision-driven services for payroll and HR. The native builds start in about seven milliseconds and use around 22 MB of memory, where the same services on the JVM would commonly need 100 MB or more. The core of the work was replacing reflective constraint evaluation with generated Java lambdas and a pure Java model of the rules, moving process parsing and XML handling to compile time, and swapping name-based class loading for constant class references. An early proof of concept showed a native build running a small rule set in sub-millisecond time, compared with about 730 milliseconds on the JVM.

The talk then covers Quarkus, which runs the same code in JVM mode or as a native image and suits short-lived function workloads. The speakers built a Quarkus extension so that DRL and BPMN files trigger code generation and live reload in dev mode, and a customer benchmark showed the native build keeping a flat execution profile where the JIT-compiled JVM version eventually performed better. Their takeaway is to plan for ahead-of-time compilation early, expect refactoring, and treat framework restrictions as a prompt to clean up code.

talks.teaser: The presentation covers intermediate Kotlin topics such as Arrow, sequences, delegates, inlining, and DSL construction.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames the session as Kotlin 102: beyond introductory syntax, not a deep language dive. He assumes the audience already reads higher-order functions and collection pipelines, then surveys features in a practical order.

Much of the middle focuses on functional style with the Arrow library—Either, Validated, Try, Option, composition, and partial application—contrasted with hand-rolled sealed result types and standard-library limits. He compares eager collections with lazy sequences and generateSequence for large or infinite data, then walks built-in property delegates, custom delegates, type aliases for API deprecation, and experimental APIs with compiler flags.

Inlining, non-local versus labeled returns, noinline, crossinline, and reified type parameters lead into inline classes, experimental contracts, trim margin, Duration as an inline class, and kotlinx immutable collections. The close demonstrates building a DSL with lambda-with-receiver and invoke, inviting questions afterward.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Dmitry Vyazelenko - What Lies Beneath
talks.teaser: Delivers a bytecode-to-CPU tour: constant pool, template interpreter, JIT tiers, and cache misses, via javap and JMH microbenchmarks.
talks.summary:
The session follows a deliberately small Java program—constants such as cafe babe and dead beef, division, and a private add method—to show what the platform does after compilation. Using javap, the speaker walks through the constant pool, operand stack, and local variables, then executes the bytecodes step by step until the stack holds 255 (0xFF).

The talk then opens the template interpreter: integer division becomes lengthy x86-64 with checks for Integer.MIN_VALUE divided by -1. A naive billion-iteration timing loop is shown to be meaningless because the JIT folds the work away; JMH comparisons with the JIT disabled illustrate interpreter cost, while disabling inlining exposes call overhead and strength-reduced division. With full optimization, the benchmark collapses to returning 255, illustrating inlining, constant propagation, and tiered C1/C2 compilation.

The second half shifts to the machine: caches, prefetch, and memory latency dominate modern chips. Microbenchmarks contrast linked lists, dense int arrays, and ArrayList, explaining L1/L2/L3 misses, pointer chasing, and overlapping cache-line loads. The close recommends primitive-friendly libraries, JITWatch for compilation logs, and caution about code-cache exhaustion, profiling probes, and breakpoints forcing interpreted execution—with brief Q&A on NUMA counters, inlining limits, and historical JIT bugs.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Andrey Adamovich - Yamlware and the state machine
talks.teaser: A practitioner surveys YAML pain points and how provisioning tools behave as state machines when applying infrastructure code.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames widespread infrastructure-as-code configuration as “yamlware,” then splits into two acts. The first half argues that YAML’s popularity outpaced its fitness: unsafe deserialization in some parsers, duplicate keys interpreted differently across tools, colon-related gotchas in Docker Compose, unreadable anchor graphs, loose boolean typing, and files that remain valid when truncated—all of which create opaque production failures.

The second half treats Terraform, Ansible, Kubernetes, and peers as state machines that reconcile declared intent with reality. A fictional solar-system engine illustrates surprises practitioners recognize: deleted manifest lines that leave orphan resources, dependent objects that clean up correctly while standalone ones do not, and attribute edits that trigger full recreation instead of in-place updates. Real anecdotes tie those patterns to cluster rebuilds and nearly catastrophic pipeline applies.

The closing synthesis covers idempotence, dependency graphs, parallel applies, write-once fields, dry-run planning, and deployment-time versus continuous reconciliation. A comparative maturity matrix contrasts Ansible, Kubernetes, and Terraform across language ergonomics, world querying, execution features, and whether removed code deletes remote objects. The practical takeaway is to match tool and language to complexity, dry-run before apply, and reach for templating or real programming languages when declarative data files become the logic.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Karolina Garbacz
talks.teaser: The session shows how chatbots rely on NLP stacks, corpus design, and retrieval and why bad training data breaks assistants.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by defining chatbots as programs that converse in natural language, contrasted with older command-and-interface models. It walks through familiar consumer examples—virtual assistants on phones, messenger bots, and cases where assistants resolve ambiguous questions or fail on simple prompts—and cites Microsoft’s 2016 Twitter bot as a cautionary lesson about learning from unfiltered public input.

The middle section frames business value: messaging apps outgrew social networks in active users, so bots can cover customer service, scheduling, ecommerce, and data gathering around the clock. It distinguishes AI-driven bots that learn from conversation history from simpler FAQ-style flows built on fixed scenarios, and stresses that useful NLP needs large, carefully chosen text corpora, with speech handled as speech-to-text and text-to-speech around the same core.

The closing material decomposes enabling techniques—information retrieval, extraction, text mining—and an NLP pipeline from tokenization through syntax, semantics, discourse, and pragmatics. Named entities, sentiment, translation, and question answering are tied to how production assistants behave, with the takeaway that front-end chat layers depend on disciplined language processing and curated knowledge underneath.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Konrad Kamiński
talks.teaser: Shows Kotlin/Native's worker-based concurrency and frozen-object memory model, with C interop for native binaries.
talks.summary:
Konrad Kamiński explains what Kotlin/Native is and how it differs from Kotlin on the JVM. The compiler turns Kotlin front-end output into LLVM IR instead of JVM bytecode, so binaries can target platforms such as iOS, Linux, embedded devices and WebAssembly. Native platform APIs like POSIX and Win32 are reachable directly, and C libraries can be used through generated bindings.

The core of the talk is the concurrency and memory model. Rather than sharing mutable objects freely between threads, Kotlin/Native runs jobs on workers, actor-like queues that return futures. Live demos show that returning a mutable object is rejected while other references to it exist, that freezing is permanent and covers everything the object references, and that top-level variables need shared immutable or thread-local annotations. Detached object graphs let a mutable object change hands between threads.

The memory model also explains the garbage collector, which can clean memory per thread without global stop-the-world pauses, using reference counting with cycle detection. The final demos cover C interop: native memory is allocated in an arena and released with memScoped when the scope ends, while reading a file line by line with fgets. The speaker closes by pointing to the official documentation and the compiler repository, and stresses that immutable objects make concurrent code safer.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Gerrit Grunwald - Not dead yet
talks.teaser: Surveys Java desktop UI toolkits from AWT to JavaFX, weighing their drawbacks and strengths and showing a browser-rendered demo.
talks.summary:
Gerrit Grunwald opens by questioning the claim that desktop software is dead, pointing out how many native applications still sit on a typical machine. He then walks through the Java GUI toolkits still in use: AWT, SWT, Swing, JavaFX, and OpenJFX, the open-source continuation of JavaFX that has not shipped with the JDK since Java 11. Each toolkit is placed by its age, its portability and whether it wraps native controls.

The middle of the talk weighs the strengths and weaknesses of Java on the desktop. The weaknesses he lists include few third-party controls, a hard-to-customise table view, weaker UI design tools than older Swing options, a perceived lack of Oracle interest, and heavy memory and CPU use. The strengths include one platform across Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and embedded, CSS styling in JavaFX, a stable API with long application lifecycles, and shared libraries and IDE between server and client. He illustrates these with examples such as a NASA trajectory explorer, an open-source Airbus wing-simulation viewer, and a Zeiss application, and notes that many companies keep their desktop Java use quiet.

He closes with a requirements-first approach: score criteria such as licence cost in a weighted matrix before choosing web or desktop technology. A live demo then runs one dashboard application natively and in a browser through JPro, using the same code.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Brian Vermeer - Live exploiting your open source dependencies
talks.teaser: Demos live exploits in common open source dependencies and explains how to scan and fix them across the development lifecycle.
talks.summary:
Brian Vermeer argues that developers ship far more third-party code than they write, and that security is often added too late. He points to the Equifax breach, which came through an outdated Apache Struts dependency, and shows how small starter projects pull in dozens or hundreds of transitive dependencies and hundreds of thousands of lines of code. He also cites survey and vulnerability figures showing how slowly known flaws get fixed in legacy applications and how many issues sit in base Docker images.

Using a deliberately vulnerable to-do app, he runs several demos. A path traversal in a static file library is reached by URL-encoding dot-dot-slash sequences until the request lands in the root directory. A regular expression denial-of-service makes a crafted input hang a Node process through backtracking. A malformed content-type header triggers OGNL expression injection in Struts, which runs shell commands on a Heroku-hosted instance. Finally, a zip slip archive writes a file outside its target folder and overwrites a JDK tool. He stresses that these issues usually form a chain, such as a service running as root.

For remediation he covers culture, process and tooling, arguing that developers, security, operations and management need aligned goals. He recommends running dependency checks early, through local IDE plugins, on the main branch, on pull requests and on release snapshots, and using static analysis alongside them. Developers should also follow secure coding cheat sheets for their language.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Sander Mak - Coding Your Way to Java 13
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn on preview flags and use Java 13 features such as text blocks, switch expressions, HttpClient, JShell, var, and modules.
talks.summary:
The session opens by noting how many teams still run older Java in production while the platform ships feature releases on a six-month rhythm, and argues for learning new capabilities through hands-on experimentation rather than release notes alone.

The core walkthrough covers language and library highlights around Java 13 and nearby releases: multi-line text blocks and preview switch expressions that return values, enabling preview features in the compiler and build, the standardized HttpClient with synchronous and asynchronous requests plus CompletableFuture callbacks, and JShell as an interactive way to probe APIs. Live coding also demonstrates local variable type inference with var, including cases where inference picks surprising types, and factory methods that yield immutable collections.

The close ties preview usage to modular applications: module-info exports and requires, replacing classpath coupling with explicit module boundaries, and a small multi-module text-analysis demo that fails fast when dependencies are not declared correctly. Migration guidance touches jlink for slimmer runtimes, aligning JDK vendor choices with support needs, and planning moves from Java 8 without assuming every dormant language feature must be adopted immediately.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Ondro Mihalyi - Reactive features of MicroProfile you need to learn
talks.teaser: Explores reactive application concepts and MicroProfile APIs for streams, messaging, and fault-tolerant microservices in Java.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing reactive applications around user experience, elasticity, and failure handling rather than chasing heroic efficiency alone. It contrasts blocking, one-thread-per-request server models with non-blocking work that releases threads during I/O and chains completion stages or callbacks, using diagrams to show how fewer threads can still serve parallel requests.

The middle surveys the Java ecosystem: CompletionStage, Reactive Streams and the Java 9 Flow API, RxJava, Spring Reactor, and limitations of Java Streams for true reactive pipelines. MicroProfile is introduced as an Eclipse Foundation effort to standardize reactive operators and messaging so teams can bridge libraries via Reactive Streams, reuse stream-like naming familiar from Java Streams, and separate subscribing from running pipelines with methods such as onError, onComplete, and run.

The close covers MicroProfile Reactive Messaging for bridging publishers and subscribers across brokers with incoming and outgoing channels, automatic versus manual message acknowledgement, and MicroProfile Fault Tolerance interceptors that retry when methods return CompletionStage. Practitioners gain a learning path from core concepts through inter-JVM messaging without needing to master every operator in a single reactive library.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Michal Petřík - How to survive as a Team leader
talks.teaser: Practical commandments help developer leads balance coding skill, meetings, trust, and agile delivery without burning out.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting deep technical GeeCON topics with everyday operational leadership at the bottom of a large org chart, where Scrum has no formal team-leader role yet someone must still drive decisions like cloud migrations and broken integrations. He argues the job blends strong engineering with people work: domain knowledge, transparent communication, and handling the awkward shift when friends become reports.

Most of the session walks through ten leadership habits framed as commandments. Natural authority comes from responsibility and trust, not positional threats. Effective work means refusing pointless meetings, applying urgency-importance prioritization, delegating, and reacting fast when plans collapse because of illness, student schedules, or tight hiring markets. He stresses honest communication—including not hoarding shifted deadlines—management by wandering around, lightweight planning, conscious competence over know-it-all posturing, structured feedback for conflicts, and arriving with options when reporting delays.

He closes with anti-patterns such as email forwarding, blame shifting, decorative reporting, indecision, and giant cross-department workshops, plus reminders to shelter the team, mentor, and quit the role if it makes you miserable. Recommended reading includes classic software project management books for human interaction, not tools alone.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: T. Roshandel / R.Mehmandarov - IoT Edge to the rescue
talks.teaser: Shows how a low-power edge AI device can count people privately, comparing CPU and TPU speed and sharing build lessons.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a simple brief: build a system that counts people entering and leaving a room or passing down a corridor, without recording who they are, responds in real time and stays cheap to run. The speakers argue that small connected devices can handle this if processing happens on the device rather than in the cloud. They separate plain IoT sensors, IoT edge devices and cloud, and describe fog as the networking layer between them. Local processing lowers latency and the amount of data sent, which helps privacy, but a single edge device has no redundancy and can be attacked more easily.

The team compared edge AI hardware, including an Nvidia Jetson, a USB accelerator stick and a Google Edge TPU board, with a CPU-only Raspberry Pi 3. They explained the difference between classification, detection and tracking, and why keeping identities consistent across video frames is harder than detecting people in one image. Their pipeline captured frames, resized them for the model, ran inference and displayed the results. A live comparison of CPU and TPU running the same algorithm showed a large speed gap, and the speakers noted that model choice and even a few print statements changed frame rates considerably.

The practical lessons were mostly about immature tooling. Compiling a large C++ tracking library on the device made the system swap and stall, and building it on a Raspberry Pi with the same hardware worked after hours. A workaround that changed package sources and forced upgrades worked, but the speakers said it should not be repeated. The talk ended with a short live demo of a camera pointed at people, and the speakers noted that the model was not tuned for the bright lighting in the room.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Hadi Hariri - Welcome to the Machine
talks.teaser: Traces how ads, social platforms and personal data collection shape what people believe and how much privacy they keep.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with Neil Postman's warning that television could entertain people into passivity, set against the visions of Orwell and Huxley. The speaker argues that the internet has delivered both futures at once. He walks through how advertising has moved from banners to native sponsored content and micro-targeted campaigns that reach narrow groups without appearing in public feeds.

The middle of the talk covers sharing and data. Platforms reward engagement, people often share without reading past headlines, and misinformation spreads faster than corrections. Public shaming over a single tweet shows how quickly a reputation can collapse. The speaker also covers app and device data collection, default privacy settings that are hard to change, data-broker sites that compile personal profiles, algorithmic bias in hiring and policing, and state projects such as China's citizen ranking.

The close argues that the problem is less about technology than about how people produce and consume information. The speaker urges the audience to verify sources, question their own confirmation bias, review privacy settings, favor interfaces that protect privacy, and think about consequences before sharing. Technologists, the speaker says, carry the greatest responsibility.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2019: Jakub Nabrdalik - Common mistakes when moving to microservices
talks.teaser: Covers common organizational and architectural mistakes teams make when moving to microservices and public clouds.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at recurring mistakes organizations make when they move to microservices and public cloud platforms. The speaker argues that architecture is often described only at the infrastructure level, with Kubernetes and managed cloud services, while domain design gets little attention. Enterprise architects are frequently handed responsibility for software architecture, and architecture guilds are formed without the practices and culture they need to work.

Further problems concern testing, release control and event-driven design. QA teams may still expect end-to-end tests to be feasible, and managers may want to sign off and control every deployment. Pipelines and processes imposed on developers can stop them from becoming devops practitioners, because the culture does not change with the tooling. Developers often default to REST everywhere, and Kafka is sometimes used as a plain message queue without streaming, read models or persistence. Managed cloud services are often assumed to be cheaper and safer than self-hosted open source, even when they are immature. Teams created without repository ownership produce error-prone setups, and business pivots are often left out of system design.

The closing sections cover organisational structure versus architecture, clashes of culture, and security, including vertical slices in microservices and how developers can get around security checks. The talk ends with proposed solutions and a look at an architecture guild after its first year.

talks.teaser: GeeCON Prague 2019: Dmitry Kornilov - Building cloud-native microservices with project Helidon.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Bartłomiej Kuczyński - Monolith? Microservices? Who cares?
talks.teaser: Argues that modular, well-tested code matters more than the monolith or microservices label, and shows how to keep options open.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking what "architecture" means in an IT organisation, separating enterprise, infrastructure, system and application levels. The speaker then examines when a team should settle on a design: at the start of a greenfield project, at the end of a short one, in the middle of a long one, or never, when someone else chooses it. Technology limits, business fashion and buzzwords are presented as pressures that often drive the choice, and architecture is described as something that must change as a product and its legal obligations evolve.

The core argument is that a codebase with clear module boundaries can move from a monolith to microservices without much pain, because the deployment shape matters less than the modularity of the code. The speaker uses Lego bricks as an analogy, points to module systems in several languages, and discusses the cost of writing tests that encode design rules, weighed against return on investment. Architectural rules should be checked automatically in the code rather than assumed, and teams should ask what happens when the system must handle 10 times the load.

The closing part separates deployment architecture from the system itself, treating the application as an artifact that the deployment process has to accept. Teams should therefore agree early on the format their deployment platform expects, so the design is valid input for it. The main takeaway is that disciplined modular code keeps the monolith-versus-microservices decision reversible.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Ted Neward
talks.teaser: A keynote links outsourcing and automation to iconoclasm, urging developers to stay valuable via perception and communication.
talks.summary:
The session opens with anxiety about global outsourcing, cheaper engineering labor, and tools that raise abstraction until much of traditional coding feels replaceable. Rather than offering a playbook to defeat automation outright, it argues that machines tend to win repetitive contests and that practitioners must evolve.

The middle weaves folk and tech parables—John Henry, Kasparov versus Deep Blue, Steve Jobs on the iPod, glass artist Dale Chihuly, Florence Nightingale’s hygiene campaign, the Dixie Chicks’ political stance, Ellsberg’s ambiguity aversion, and the Challenger O-ring disaster framed as groupthink—into a model of the iconoclast who perceives patterns others miss. Optical illusions illustrate how experience shapes judgment; a universal “box, arrow, cylinder” sketch frames decades of system designs.

The close distills three traits: see the world differently, accept the social fear of bucking consensus, and communicate ideas through familiarity and reputation built at conferences or through sustained open-source contribution. The practical takeaway for builders is to specialize in unconventional insight and credibility so employers cannot commoditize the role.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Ted Neward - Busy Architect’s Guide to the Cloud Offerings
talks.teaser: Explains cloud terms, deployment models and the trade-offs developers face when moving applications off their own hardware.
talks.summary:
Ted Neward opens by arguing that "cloud" is a vague term, so he sets out the vocabulary he wants the audience to share before discussing it. He explains the economics behind cloud, including economies of scale and the appeal of provisioning capacity in minutes instead of months. He then goes through the deployment models (public, community, private, virtual private, hybrid, colocation and vendor platforms) and the service layers of platform, infrastructure and software as a service.

The middle of the talk turns to practical concerns. Physical location, or "dirt", determines which data laws apply, which matters for customers with residency requirements. Multi-tenancy and the number of running instances change which architectures still work, since in-memory caches must be propagated across instances. Neward recounts an anecdote about a startup that ran 10,000 micro instances for a load test and received a bill of about two million dollars. He also notes that distance between regions adds latency, that a provider's availability commitments must line up with what a business promises its own customers, and that testing, debugging and capital versus operational spending all become harder in the cloud.

He closes with a survey of the major providers, Amazon, Microsoft and Google, plus smaller platforms such as Salesforce, Heroku, App Harbor, Meteor and Parse. His takeaway is that developers should first decide what they actually need from the cloud, then plan early for cost controls, failure modes and the trade-offs involved.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Valentin Deleplace - MADPIG: Measure and deepen performance in Go
talks.teaser: Walks through measuring Go code with benchmarks, pprof, flame graphs and execution traces to find and fix real bottlenecks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why slowness matters: users run out of patience during waits, so developers should measure rather than guess where time goes. It separates service time from response time, since queuing and network trips add to what a user actually experiences. It also warns that the bottleneck can sit outside the Go service, for example in how a page loads its assets.

A sample Go program that searches downloaded Wikipedia articles for keywords is then tuned step by step. Traces and CPU profiles, shown as graphs and flame graphs, showed the suspected network cost was tiny: about 97% of time went to reading and seeking in files, and only 1% to downloads. Moving the file opening out of the inner loop gave almost a fourfold gain, and loading the whole file into memory gave a 6 times speed gain. Downloading each article once instead of once per keyword gave a 4x speed-up, and standard library byte functions brought version 7 to about 300 times faster than version 0. Some edits made no measurable difference, so every change was checked by measuring again.

The main takeaways are to focus on real bottlenecks and ignore one-off scripts or background jobs nobody waits for. Strong automated tests keep refactoring safe, and concurrency can help I/O-bound code even on a single core, though it is harder to write correctly. Wait groups and the race detector help keep such code manageable, and tools like pprof, traces and escape analysis belong in everyday work.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Dmitry Kandalov
talks.teaser: The session walks through coroutine models in Lua, JavaScript, and Scheme, from cooperative threads to async/await and call/cc.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that coroutines are widely used in industry yet poorly understood, and frames the session as a language-spanning overview of what they mean at a fundamental level. A condensed history runs from early academic work through the thread-heavy 2000s to renewed support in Python, C#, JavaScript, Kotlin, and C++20, with Java on the horizon.

Three implementation flavors drive the middle of the talk. Lua illustrates stackful coroutines that mimic thread handoffs, status, and value passing across yield and resume. JavaScript generators and async/await show yield-based lazy iteration and promise-linked suspension, including how transpilers lower generators to finite state machines. Scheme call/cc demonstrates continuations as captured “rest of the program,” tying coroutine behavior to continuation-passing style.

The closing sections compare coroutines to promises for flattening callback-heavy code, note limits of promise-only sequential and retry logic, and list practical caveats: mangled stack traces, awkward debugging across asynchronous gaps, and thread-safety around shared mutable state. Practitioners gain a mental model for choosing coroutines versus threads or promises, and for reading how modern languages implement the feature underneath familiar syntax.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Leonid Igolnik
talks.teaser: Coverage of GeeCON 2019: Leonid Igolnik from the conference program.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2019 presentation, Leonid Igolnik (Head of Engineering at SignalFx, with co-author Baruch Sadogursky of JFrog) frames the journey of adopting and scaling DevOps as a classic four-act Greek tragedy. Using the hypothetical payment-processing startup "Pentagon Inc.", Igolnik illustrates how organizational, procedural, and technological challenges evolve as an engineering organization grows. Rather than treating DevOps as a simple intersection of development and operations, the talk positions it at the intersection of technology, processes, and people across distinct maturity stages.

### Key Topics
- **DevOps Definition**: Moving beyond Dev, Ops, QA, or DevSecOps to view DevOps as the evolving intersection of technology, processes, and people.
- **The Four Maturity Stages**:
  1. *Act 1: The Fire Brigade (Reactive Operations)*: Characterized by early-stage startup assumptions, microservices, containerization, serverless/"NoOps" ideals, minimal process (Kanban), and ad-hoc troubleshooting during outages.
  2. *Act 2: Smoke Alarm Installers (Reactive Improvement)*: Initiated after Series A growth and hiring, introducing basic Scrum, on-call rotations, root cause analyses (RCAs), postmortems, and monitoring tools.
  3. *Act 3: Scaling Challenges & Impasse*: Growth to around 100 engineers introduces specialized enablement roles, compliance requirements, non-functional backlogs, and multi-team coordination issues that cause failures if handled without proactive validation.
  4. *Act 4: Fire Prevention (Proactive Improvement)*: Transitioning to data-driven decision-making, automated dependency scanning, non-functional definitions of done, and systematic load testing.
- **Blameless Incident Management & Transparency**: Examining high-profile outage responses (such as GitLab's database incident) and incident reporting structures to foster customer trust and process reliability.

### Technical Details
- **Incident Investigation & Dependencies**: Early startup mistakes highlight operational blind spots, such as uncoordinated server time zones across cloud regions in AWS CloudWatch logs and broken CI/CD pipelines caused by transitive dependency failures (e.g., the NPM `left-pad` incident).
- **Monitoring & Alerting Evolution**: The talk traces the progression of monitoring tooling from basic remote ping checks (Pingdom) to centralized logging, metric collection, and Application Performance Monitoring (APM) systems (such as SignalFx) capable of tracing millions of spans per minute.
- **Incident Reports**: Key structural elements of effective incident reports include affected environments, duration, detailed timeline of events (captured via Slack or Zoom virtual rooms), symptoms, interpretation, determined root cause, and concrete action items.
- **Tooling and Infrastructure Scaling**: Toolchains shift across maturity stages: starting with AWS Elastic Beanstalk, GitHub, Travis CI, and Jira; moving to Artifactory, Confluence, and UTC timestamp standardization; and later adopting configuration management (ZooKeeper), architectural scaling frameworks (SAFe, LeSS), and dependency vulnerability/license scanners (JFrog X-ray).
- **Data-Driven Analysis**: Real-world examples demonstrate using ticket resolution data in spreadsheets to identify systemic operational problems. In one referenced case, 52.3% of high-severity support tickets were resolved via "information provided" rather than code fixes, proving that cross-training support teams solved the issue more effectively than refactoring code.

### Takeaways
- **Maturity Stages Cannot Be Skipped**: Organizations must progress through reactive firefighting and reactive improvement before successfully executing proactive fire prevention.
- **Role of Centralized DevOps and Quality Engineering**: Dedicated DevOps and QA teams should act as knowledge hubs and tooling enablers rather than siloed departments throwing work over the wall.
- **Non-Functional Definition of Done**: Production services require standard baselines driven by architecture, including standard logging formats, health checks, metrics emission, and tracing instrumentation.
- **Transparency Preserves Trust**: Being honest, detailed, and blameless about outages and recovery plans builds lasting trust with enterprise customers.
- **"Pain is Instructional"**: Painful operational failures should directly guide engineering practices, logging fidelity, and observability investments.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Andrzej Grzesik - What do I do with 1000 cores
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from running Java simulations on many-core machines, covering NUMA effects, cloud variance and benchmark pitfalls.
talks.summary:
Andrzej Grzesik looks at what changes when a simulation can use hundreds or a thousand cores and wall clock time is the metric that matters. His focus is agent-based modelling, where many interacting objects are simulated repeatedly with varied parameters. Cited hardware ranges from a 2010 Top500 entry with 1,280 cores to large cloud instances, though access to such machines typically requires a direct request to the provider.

Measurements showed uneven results. Cloud runs of one workload were spread widely, with about half taking more than 1.3 times the shortest run, which the speaker linked to noisy neighbours on hypervisors. A concurrent counter benchmark ranked differently on a laptop and a server because of NUMA memory layout, and binding processes to one node with numactl was one workaround. Some AMD Threadripper dies without direct memory access showed similar effects. On Linux, clock readings may not be monotonic across cores, so the speaker suggested managing simulation time explicitly. Sending a 1 KB message from every agent in a UK-sized population produces about 76 GB of traffic, which a 1 Gbit link handles poorly.

Practical advice included getting algorithm basics right, using event sourcing so events can be reordered and placed to suit the hardware, splitting problems with divide and conquer, and testing guesses by making reverse changes rather than trusting profilers blindly. Keep a representative local machine for experiments, since cloud measurements can mislead.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Marharyta Nedzelska - Rediscovering gRPC
talks.teaser: Explores gRPC over HTTP/2 and Kotlin coroutine libraries that replace callback-heavy Java client code in microservices.
talks.summary:
Microservice teams often default to HTTP/1 and REST, yet network calls dominate cost and complexity when scale grows. The speaker frames gRPC as a Remote Procedure Call stack on HTTP/2: one connection per client, bidirectional streaming, binary Protocol Buffers payloads, and built-in flow control for slow clients.

A Star Wars–themed “Death Star” demo walks through `.proto` definitions, generated Java stubs, and a streaming `destroy` RPC. The Java path stacks nested callbacks; futures help only partly because bidirectional streams still need stream observers. The talk then “rediscovers” the same service with gRPC-Kotlin channels and coroutines, and again with Kroto-plus, where request/response channels remove extra `launch` boilerplate so business logic reads linearly. Flow control in Java needs explicit ready handlers; Kotlin channel iteration enables it by default.

Practitioners hear that gRPC fits polyglot shops (Java, Scala, Node, Python, Kotlin), that protobuf’s optional fields ease schema evolution, and that community libraries—grpc-kotlin, Kroto-plus, Salesforce grpc-java-contrib—are maturing but not all at 1.0 yet. Takeaways: consider gRPC for efficient service-to-service calls, prefer coroutine wrappers to callback hell when on Kotlin, and contribute to stabilize ecosystem gaps.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Jonatan Kazmierczak - Secrets of top performance in Java revealed
talks.teaser: Benchmarks word-count pipelines across Java library versions and compares optimized runs against C++ on large text.
talks.summary:
The session opens by challenging the idea that C or C++ is always the fastest choice, using competitive programming leaderboards where slower algorithms in the same language finish far behind better designs. The speaker argues that solution quality is the first universal performance secret, then shifts to Java and the HotSpot JVM, including tiered JIT compilation from C1 through C2 and optional GraalVM paths.

A fixed Bible-scale text file becomes the benchmark: roughly 4.3 million characters and more than 825,000 words. Four Java implementations share one interface—extract words, count frequencies, return the top fifteen—while varying standard libraries from Java 2 through Java 8, including parallel streams. Timings show Scanner-based word parsing hurts badly, naive parallel streams can lose before JIT warmup, and repeated runs shrink latency as C2 optimizes hot methods. The same workload is compared to a C++ version in the public repository.

After warmup, optimized Java 2 code can match or beat C++ overall on this task, though C++ still wins some sorting steps. The closing guidance is to profile real steps with a stopwatch, treat library complexity as a performance risk in short-lived apps, and validate GraalVM native-image ahead-of-time builds instead of assuming they always help.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Łukasz Gajowy - what do I gain?
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2019: Łukasz Gajowy - Apache Beam - what do I gain?.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Sergei Egorov - Don’t be Homer Simpson with your Reactor!
talks.teaser: Explains Reactor debug tooling, BlockHound blocking detection, and parallel-scheduler pitfalls for production reactive Java.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting hype around reactive programming with painful first steps: chains defined at assembly time do nothing until something subscribes, and production behavior diverges sharply from what looked fine locally. A central theme is unreadable stack traces when failures occur on worker threads far from application code.

The middle walks through mitigations the speaker helped build. Runtime operator-debug hooks capture call sites but are too slow for production. Manual checkpoints are fast but tedious and error-prone. The reactor-debug-agent instruments bytecode similarly to APM tools, auto-inserting checkpoints with modest overhead. A live demo shows parallel-scheduler starvation when blocking work occupies all threads. BlockHound, a JVM agent, flags blocking native calls on non-blocking threads and integrates with tests. The talk also warns that Kafka’s asynchronous send can still block on metadata for up to 60 seconds.

Practitioners should treat reactive pipelines like controlled fire: use debug agents or checkpoints for traceability, run unavoidable blocking I/O on dedicated schedulers, add BlockHound to catch sneaky blocks before deploy, and verify “async” APIs in code—not only docs. Recent reactor hooks help propagate tracing and logging context across scheduled threads.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Serban Iordache - The Java Module System in practice
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of modularizing Java code with Gradle and Maven, from module paths and plugins through jlink runtimes and platform installers.
talks.summary:
The presentation begins with lessons from modularizing an open-source workflow engine while keeping Java 8 compatibility, including adding module descriptors across several libraries and discovering that early Gradle builds needed heavy manual work. It explains how Java 9 split the JDK into modules and how code can break on Java 11 even without modularizing, illustrated with a small XML serialization example that fails until a standalone JAXB dependency is added.

The middle section covers module descriptors, encapsulation, classpath versus module path, automatic modules, unnamed modules, and split packages, then walks through running, testing, and distributing a modular Gradle app before and after the Java modularity Gradle plugin. Further use cases include mixed-release jars for Java 8–compatible modular libraries, building trimmed runtimes with jlink for a Vert.x service that mostly lacks module metadata (via ModiTect per-artifact modularization or a merged “badass” module), and packaging a JavaFX demo with jpackage—including a path to custom runtimes for apps that stay non-modular.

Practitioners should expect classpath and module path to coexist for years, lean on current Gradle and Maven plugins to automate repetitive wiring, and treat full modularization of large frameworks like Spring Boot as possible but awkward. The speaker closes by fielding questions on Spring Pet Clinic experiments and version switching scripts.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Raam Rosh Hai - From notebooks to production - bringing devops to scientists
talks.teaser: Describes a library-led path from Python notebooks to Kubernetes production, with queues, CI/CD, and scientist-owned debugging.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a familiar pipeline pain: a scientist prototypes in a notebook, wraps code as a model, then waits on engineers and DevOps while interest and usefulness fade before launch. The alternative argued is giving scientists full control and responsibility over turning ideas into deployed services, while sharing frustrations like waiting, context switching, and misaligned priorities between engineering and data science.

The middle introduces a simple model-serving platform built around a single library import that exposes any function as a high-performance server. Infrastructure runs on Kubernetes with centralized services, caching, collectors, and connectors over RabbitMQ request and response queues. The design favors message-passing concurrency, tracing and monitoring on the collector, and what the speaker calls Darwinian production—live usage exposes gaps and justifies deeper investment. A live demo serves movie recommendations from a trained model with scikit-learn or Surprise via one start call.

Closing topics cover CI/CD where scientists push to GitHub, Drone runs their tests, and platform changes propagate without engineers repeating glue work. Boilerplate covers Python layout, Docker, build, and deploy files with bounded cross-team knowledge. A production anecdote shows a slow NLP service improved after adoption proved value; Q&A contrasts the stack with TensorFlow Serving and discusses back-pressure on slow predictors.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Tomasz Kowalczewski - Is writing performant code too expensive?
talks.teaser: Balances shipping features against optimization cost, then shows JVM benchmarks for NUMA layout, memory bandwidth, and branch prediction.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting the urge to polish microservices with the pressure to ship user-facing work, especially in startups. A costly internal analytics initiative—heavy JVM and Linux tuning on huge per-user datasets—failed in the market, which pushed the team toward faster validation patterns such as short design sprints instead of building production pipelines too early.

The middle of the talk frames economics: senior engineering time versus renting very large cloud instances, the cultural appeal of the “10×” optimizer versus a disciplined “0.1×” minimizer, and lessons from database and distributed-streaming literature where hand-tuned or single-threaded approaches dramatically beat expensive clusters when datasets still fit reasonable hardware. The message is that scalability papers often hide coordination overhead, and intuition about machine limits should come before heroic engineering.

The closing section turns that intuition into measurements on modern many-core hardware using Java microbenchmarks. Cross-socket NUMA placement changes thread signaling latency by several times; sequential RAM reads reach tens of gigabytes per second per core while random access collapses throughput; and branch-heavy loops on hundreds of megabytes of integers swing between tens and hundreds of milliseconds depending on predictor friendliness, with branchless mask tricks helping when mispredictions dominate. The takeaway is to wear both hats: default to product validation and restraint, but when hardware headroom is real, measure layout, memory access patterns, and control flow before buying more metal.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Dmitry Vinnik - Modern Web Testing: Going Beyond Selenium
talks.teaser: The session compares test-pyramid shapes for web apps and weighs JavaScript tooling from Selenium through Cypress for team adoption.
talks.summary:
Dmitry Vinnik frames web quality work as infrastructure design rather than a single-tool tutorial. He revisits the classic test pyramid—many unit tests, fewer integration checks, and a thin cap of end-to-end cases—and contrasts it with common real-world inversions such as ice-cream cones, hourglasses, and cupcakes, where heavy UI automation and manual regression dominate.

He argues that context drives choices: blended engineering roles, shared ubiquitous language from domain-driven design, and aligning test code with the web stack, often JavaScript and Node on the client. Using a simple todo demo, he walks unit testing with Jasmine, integration and snapshot regression with Jest, and end-to-end flows that emphasize user tasks and screenplay-style abstractions instead of brittle element-by-element scripts. Selenium WebDriver and webdriver.js remain the baseline; Protractor suits Angular’s lifecycle hooks, while TestCafe and Cypress attack flakiness, waiting, parallel runs, and fast feedback—each with trade-offs such as browser support and team skills.

Closing guidance stresses evaluating whether change is needed at all, matching tools to the application shape (API-first teams may lean on REST testing), unifying strategy across developers and testers, running proofs of concept before commitment, and pruning bloated UI suites in favor of fewer high-confidence scenarios.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Kamil Owczarek - Data Streaming: Which horse to bet on?
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2019: Kamil Owczarek - Data Streaming: Which horse to bet on?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from GeeCON 2019, Kamil Owczarek examines the landscape of stream processing engines, addressing why organizations migrate toward data streaming and how to choose the right framework for specific use cases. Drawing from consulting experience as head of a Big Data practice, the speaker explores core streaming mechanics—including time handling, windowing types, joins, aggregations, and failure recovery—and compares four prominent technologies: Akka Streams, Kafka Streams, Apache Flink, and Apache Spark Streaming (Structured Streaming), with brief commentary on Apache Beam.

### Key Topics
- **Drivers for Streaming**: Real-time connected cars, financial and trade analytics, IoT telemetry, and user interaction/clickstream analysis (including fraud prevention and targeted advertising).
- **Processing Paradigms**: Pure event-by-event streaming versus micro-batching (used by Spark), where intervals are kept minimal but latency remains higher than true streaming.
- **Notions of Time & Windowing**: Processing time, event time (embedded in records to handle out-of-order data), and ingestion time. Windowing models covered include tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping, useful for anomaly detection and trends), and session windows (gap-based activity tracking).
- **Stream Operations**: Stream-to-stream joins (which require explicit time boundaries to prevent unbounded memory growth) and windowed aggregations.
- **Evaluation Metrics & Reliability Features**: Latency versus throughput trade-offs, lateness handling (watermarking), checkpointing (local filesystem vs. distributed storage/external persistence), savepoints (Flink), and third-party data integration capabilities.

### Technical Details
- **Akka Streams**: Operates on the Akka actor model (Scala/Java), offering massive concurrency, reactive backpressure, granular low-level I/O control, and extensive connectivity via the Alpakka project. It lacks native out-of-the-box watermarking and native checkpointing, and lacks explicit built-in session windows, but provides very low per-record latency.
- **Kafka Streams**: Tailored specifically for reading and writing to Apache Kafka. It runs lightweight embedded instances on the JVM, supports watermarking, local checkpointing, and session windows, but lacks native connectors to outside datastores without integrating auxiliary tooling like Kafka Connect.
- **Apache Flink**: True event-driven cluster processing platform with support for watermarking, local and distributed checkpoints, user-triggered savepoints (enabling seamless cluster upgrades and maintenance), and native session windows. It balances low latency (approaching Kafka Streams) with scalable throughput.
- **Apache Spark Streaming (Structured Streaming)**: Micro-batch architecture that sacrifices ultra-low latency (typically around one second minimum, up to multiple tens of seconds for complex computations) in exchange for massive throughput, cluster-wide caching, and unified integration with Spark ML and graph modules. It supports distributed checkpoints and watermarking, but lacks explicit session window constructs.
- **Apache Beam**: Serves as an abstraction layer over engines like Spark and Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow, but does not target lightweight JVM frameworks like Akka Streams or Kafka Streams, and suffers from inconsistent cross-engine feature parity.

### Takeaways
Owczarek emphasizes that there is no universal "silver bullet" in streaming architectures:
1. **Ultra-Low Latency / IoT**: Akka Streams (especially via protocols like MQTT or raw TCP) or Kafka Streams are preferred when immediate reaction times are critical and records arrive individually.
2. **Extensive Data Integration**: Apache Flink or Apache Spark are optimal when out-of-the-box connectors to multiple diverse databases, message queues, and distributed file systems are required.
3. **User Behavior & Clickstreams**: Kafka Streams is ideal due to native session window support, fast processing, and built-in state management.
4. **Complex Iterative Analytics & Machine Learning**: Apache Spark Streaming excels when massive aggregation, distributed caching, and built-in ML libraries outweigh sub-second latency requirements.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Dmitry Vinnik - Stress Driven Development, and How to Avoid It
talks.teaser: Looks at the causes of long-term stress in developers and offers habits for sleep, fitness, nutrition and work to avoid it.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that stress is not uniformly bad: short-term stress, such as a sauna session or a fight-or-flight response, can be useful, while long-term stress harms health. The speaker illustrates the problem with examples from the games industry, including a widely shared letter from the spouse of an Electronic Arts employee about overtime, contractors working on Rockstar projects who said overwork affected their families, and a recent layoff at Telltale. He also recounts his own panic attack, which he says pushed him to change his routine.

It then covers four areas: sleep, nutrition, fitness and work. On sleep, it stresses consistent hours, waking at the same time each day and reducing light and noise. On food, it warns against strict diet dogma and recommends cutting processed sugar and eating within a set window, such as intermittent fasting. Fitness covers regular exercise, varied activity and mental practices such as meditation and time alone. Habits are framed as a cue, routine and reward loop, and the speaker suggests starting with a keystone habit, such as running, that spreads positive effects to other areas.

For work, the speaker favours quieter or remote settings over open-plan offices, asynchronous communication instead of instant replies, and turning off phone notifications. The closing message is to change habits gradually, set goals, find a supportive community and keep long-term stress in check.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Adam Warski - From annotations to code: describing HTTP endpoints
talks.teaser: Replaces annotation-based HTTP endpoint mappings with plain Scala values that can be served and documented.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that annotation-driven Java frameworks, such as Spring, have pushed a limited metadata language too far. Annotations bring fast startup but reduce type safety, control and code navigability, because much of the wiring happens at runtime through classpath scanning. The speaker proposes describing endpoint metadata with ordinary code instead, keeping it separate from business logic while still allowing it to be inspected and reused.

Live in Scala, the session builds endpoint descriptions for a small book-listing service. One endpoint filters books by publishing year with an optional limit, and another fetches a single book by identifier. Shared parts are pulled into a base endpoint, a custom codec maps a year wrapper type from the query string, and the query parameters are combined into a named filter class checked at compile time. The same immutable description is then interpreted in several ways: as a running HTTP server through Akka HTTP, and as an OpenAPI document shown in Swagger UI, where an example value is added to the documentation.

The takeaway is that endpoint mappings written as code can be explored with standard IDE features such as go to definition and find usages, just like business logic. The speaker also explains that functional programming is mainly about functions and immutable values, and that separating a description from its interpreters gives flexibility. The approach aims to keep the declarative nature of annotations while adding type safety and composition. The project is open source.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Jakub Marchwicki - The time relativity principle
talks.teaser: Explains how time zones, epochs and shifting daylight saving rules trip up software, and how to keep timing data minimal.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how software mishandles time and time zones, starting from a small XML fragment in a bus timetable message. The speaker compares the epochs that different platforms use, from the Unix 1970 start to a 2000-based database, and notes that a misused Java date constructor can produce a 1899 value. An audience quiz on converting a timestamp to local time shows how easily the offset gets applied in the wrong way.

Next, the speaker argues that time zone rules are not stable. European offsets and daylight saving practice have changed over the decades, Libya dropped daylight saving with only two weeks' notice, and a Pacific nation moved from UTC minus 11 to UTC plus 12, skipping a date. Changes like these should be expected rather than treated as rare edge cases.

For the practical takeaway, the speaker recommends keeping only the timing information a system actually needs. Bus timetables can run past midnight into service days of 25 to 27 hours, so storing seconds since midnight on the schedule's start day works better than storing local clock time. Unneeded fields such as the year should be dropped. The talk closed with a short Q&A, where the speaker said the right handling depends on context.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Sergei Egorov - Testcontainers: a year-in-review
talks.teaser: A co-maintainer surveys Testcontainers' first year: Docker-based integration testing, new modules, and faster reusable containers.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that integration tests catch real issues unit tests miss, yet they traditionally required heavy VMs, local database installs, or declarative Docker Compose setups that fight imperative test code and break across Mac, Windows, and Linux environments. Testcontainers is introduced as a JVM library on top of Docker Java that discovers the local Docker setup, starts real service images, waits until they are actually ready, and tears containers down after tests—with modules and a generic container abstraction for anything in a registry.

A Spring Boot demo runs PostgreSQL, Redis, and MockServer together using JDBC URLs with a TC prefix, singleton containers for speed, and container IP addresses instead of localhost. A year-in-review covers Kafka, Cassandra, Couchbase, Pulsar, and ClickHouse modules; Ryuk sidecar cleanup; Maven BOM; OkHttp transport replacing Netty; Windows and credential-helper fixes; host port exposing for Selenium; chaos-style network fault injection; and JUnit 5 support. PostgreSQL tmpfs tuning and dependency trimming are noted as quiet performance wins.

The close shares roadmap items—a simpler DSL for Kotlin and Scala, GraalVM polyglot use, extracting container core from JUnit—and debuts reusable containers that hash configuration and restart in under 200 milliseconds for local test-driven work while staying off by default on CI. Practitioners should treat the library as the default way to run real dependencies in code, avoid localhost assumptions, and enable reuse only when test isolation allows.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Krzysztof Dębski - When your boss decides to have an architecture team…
talks.teaser: Why architect roles appear, how hiring and frameworks fail, and what credible architects deliver beside active delivery teams.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by questioning why organizations create architect roles when developers rarely want someone else to design systems they must build. Drawing on nine years under titles such as enterprise, solution, and software architect, he links the gap between vague corporate strategy and daily engineering work to frameworks like TOGAF and SAFe that assign architects to connect the two. He skewers unrealistic strategic goals, contradictory job ads mixing microservices with legacy certification demands, and abstract definitions that ask one person to own performance, scalability, and deep code review at once.

The middle of the talk reframes architecture as costly decisions and trade-offs rather than universal standards. He favors simple diagrams over heavy UML, collaborative techniques such as event storming and user story mapping, and C4-style layered views with legends and shared language. Apollo 13’s improvised CO₂ filter illustrates when strict standardization misses the point; technical debt arises mainly from non-functional requirements that nobody can fully satisfy at once. He warns against proof-of-concept theater, local optimization when entering new markets, ivory-tower design far from implementation, and architects who rarely talk to teams.

He closes by comparing failed team models—external support groups, architects who only code, lone firefighters, and large teams without a shared product goal—with patterns he prefers: coding architects, T-shaped depth in at least one domain, evolutionary design a sprint or two ahead, and tight coupling between architecture choices and actual technology. A short Q&A covers UML, detached global architecture teams, and whether architects can sit outside delivery teams while still staying credible.
