talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Tomasz Borowiec - The Slower the Stronger: A Story of Password Hash Migration
talks.teaser: Walks through a real customer password hash migration to slow algorithms, with the pitfalls met along the way.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that slow hashing algorithms protect stored passwords if a database of hashes is ever leaked, because each guess an attacker makes is deliberately costly. It contrasts fast general-purpose hashes such as MD5 and SHA-1 with bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2 and Argon2, and explains salts and cost parameters. A live timing demo shows how far apart the speeds are.

The main case study is an online shop with about 700,000 customers. Its bcrypt hashes used cost 8, and older accounts still carried MD5-derived values. Benchmarks suggested cost 12 added only a fraction of a second per login. An application security team then provided a password hashing wrapper built on a vetted cryptography library, storing a hash vector that chains MD5, bcrypt and PBKDF2 with SHA-256. The migration ran as background jobs that translated legacy hashes, upgraded them to the latest step, and finally removed the old values once the new code was verified. Keeping the old hashes until release allowed rollback.

Problems included roughly a month of continuous CPU work, handled by a spare application node kept off the load balancer during the run. Testing also exposed orphaned password rows left by a smoke-test routine that never deleted them; these were moved to a cloned table before removal. The project took over a year, partly due to a pause for a performance investigation. The speaker's takeaways were to re-check hashing time as hardware improves, test migrations thoroughly, and clean up old hashes. Q&A advised against combining algorithms and suggested rate limiting against denial-of-service risk.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Ben Vinod - Leveraging Emerging Technologies in Travel for Competitive Advantage
talks.teaser: Surveys how a travel software company applies machine learning, big data and blockchain to industry problems.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that travel companies, like firms in other industries, need emerging technologies to stay competitive. The speaker, who works in product strategy at a travel software company, describes rising air traffic, a shopping system that handled 170 billion shops in 2018, and ancillary sales of 93 billion dollars that make bundling harder. He explains a three-tier data approach over internal and external sources exceeding 15 petabytes, with Hadoop on commodity hardware making storage practical.

Several machine learning cases follow. To handle passports from countries that are not ICAO compliant, the team labelled about 500 names and trained recurrent neural networks, reaching roughly 85 percent accuracy on about 100,000 names so check-in could continue. Pattern recognition was used to flag robotic shopping, which the speaker put at about 23 percent of shops. Persona segmentation paired unsupervised learning with a recommendation model, while chatbots and natural language processing of contract terms covered other needs.

The closing section uses the Gartner hype cycle to place technologies such as democratized AI, blockchain and quantum computing. Blockchain prototypes for airline revenue settlement could cut a three-month process to about one day, whereas quantum computers were judged not yet ready for optimization problems. The takeaway is that developers should learn accessible AI tools and test them against concrete business problems.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Maciej Lasyk - 8ms/99th write percentile latency - is it fast?
talks.teaser: A developer-led shop explains how it scaled SRE, error budgets, and Cassandra automation to stay fast at huge request volume.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why classical “learn every mistake” mastery fails for reliability, then grounds the narrative in DevOps and site reliability ideas: user-perceived uptime, error budgets, SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs. The speaker describes joining a no-ops company on AWS that averages hundreds of thousands of requests per second, where developers maintain Cassandra, custom databases, and in-house monitoring without a separate operations org.

The middle covers adapting Google-style SRE to a mid-sized firm: cross-team reliability meetings, prioritizing sleep over heroics, blameless postmortems when customers are hurt, a service catalog, and SLOs tied to business-defined user journeys. Monitoring shifts toward Datadog while Hyperion/Nemo remain relevant; operational work consolidates in Rundeck with audited, cloud-agnostic automation instead of ad hoc scripts. Cassandra receives extended treatment—partition design, replication, consistency tradeoffs—and hard-won operability fixes, drills, and game-like outage exercises.

The close ties metrics to outcomes: high write and read percentiles in the millisecond range, dashboards for rights and latency, and reduced night-time pages. Takeaways emphasize treating reliability as the top feature, automating toil deliberately, making data stores operable before developers casually self-host them, and preparing upgrades and failures with procedures people trust.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Michał Kordas - Taming Code Quality in the Worst Language I Know: Bash
talks.teaser: Outlines bash pitfalls, strict modes, style guides, and ShellCheck so shell glue scripts fail fast instead of silently.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames bash as the worst language he knows—not universally, but worse than the JVM stacks he usually trains on—and argues it still appears everywhere as unavoidable glue. Early war stories include a feed-download script pointed at a home directory and famous tales of undefined variables expanding empty under `rm -rf`, which motivate overriding bash defaults rather than trusting them.

The middle of the talk tours splitting, globbing, arrays, carriage returns, and quoting, citing Stack Overflow and the Greycat wiki on why every variable expansion should be quoted. He contrasts bash with POSIX sh, recommends `/usr/bin/env bash` shebangs, surveys Google’s shell style guide and common lint rules, and demos ShellCheck plus IntelliJ/bash-support formatting and inspections, including quirks like `[[ false ]]` evaluating true without spaces.

He closes with `set -euo pipefail`, limits of errexit with `local`, debugging via `set -nx`, and testing advice: prefer integration tests in containers over unit tests except for rare bash libraries, keep scripts short, and reach for Python or similar when logic grows.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Ensar Basri Kahveci - java.util.concurrent for Distributed Coordination
talks.teaser: The session maps JDK concurrency primitives onto strongly consistent distributed coordination in Hazelcast via Raft-backed CP APIs.
talks.summary:
Distributed applications need leader election, locks, barriers, and shared metadata without baking fragile custom coordination into business logic. The speaker contrasts Chubby, ZooKeeper, and etcd: each exposes a strongly consistent key-value layer, yet developers often still assemble recipes or client libraries to get usable primitives.

The core proposal reuses familiar `java.util.concurrent` types—atomic references, countdown latches, semaphores, and locks—as linearizable cluster-wide APIs in Hazelcast’s CP subsystem, implemented on Raft rather than earlier eventually consistent variants. Demos walk through pet-photo pub/sub with atomic reference plus latch, leader election with FencedLock, and session TTL trade-offs between safety and liveness, including fencing tokens so stale leaders cannot keep acting after failover.

Practitioners should treat coordination as infrastructure: prefer hardened libraries, document failure semantics, and validate with tools like Jepsen. CP members can run on a subset of a large cluster; dynamic membership and separate CP groups address availability and throughput.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Heinz Kabutz - Enough java.lang.String to Hang Ourselves ...
talks.teaser: A JDK-by-JDK tour of java.lang.String covers memory layout, concatenation, hash collisions, and HashMap denial-of-service risks.
talks.summary:
The session begins with audience polls on string idioms such as valueOf versus concatenation and on different append strategies for building web output. It then traces java.lang.String from Java 1.0 through later releases: early char-array layouts with offset and count, sampled hashCode on long strings, shared backing arrays between String and StringBuffer, and substring behavior that could retain huge buffers.

Hashing changes drive much of the narrative. Moving from sampled to full-character hashCode made large-string hashing linear and upset tests that assumed stable codes. The speaker brute-forces seven-letter strings with hashCode zero, shows that combinations stay at zero, and demos a “string dos” program where doubling entries in a HashMap roughly doubles lookup time on Java 6. Java 7’s alternate hashing helps only when explicitly enabled; Java 8 treeifies crowded buckets when keys are Comparable, restoring roughly logarithmic worst cases without extra flags.

Later topics include StringBuilder versus synchronized StringBuffer, compressed and compact byte-backed strings, G1 deduplication versus intern trade-offs, jcmd visibility into the string table, invokedynamic concatenation from Java 9 onward, and JVM intrinsics for equals. Takeaways for practitioners: use plus for simple string mixes where benchmarks now favor it, keep StringBuilder inside tight loops, avoid assuming immutability in edge cases such as shared char arrays, and treat hash-heavy maps and intern tables as potential performance and abuse surfaces.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Lieven Doclo - Automating your development experience
talks.teaser: Explains how TypeScript delivery machines replace scattered CI YAML when organizations run hundreds of microservices.
talks.summary:
Organizations adopting cloud-native architectures face explosive growth in services, deployment targets, and pipeline definitions. Copying YAML between projects works for a handful of repos but breaks at hundreds or thousands of services, so a single request such as organization-wide CVE scanning or centralized test coverage forces mass edits across fragmented Jenkins, Travis, or Azure DevOps configs.

The presentation frames CI/CD as a repeatable blueprint—build, test, containerize, deploy—and shows how Atomist captures metadata from source control, issue trackers, existing build systems, and operational tools without sending application source to a cloud service. A software delivery machine runs in the organization's infrastructure as testable TypeScript instead of declarative YAML logic or bash wrappers. Live demos walk through push rules, auto-fixes, Maven builds, timestamped Docker versions, and Kubernetes deployment via Slack chat ops, including opinionated “Rug” defaults that infer manifests from project structure.

Practitioners should treat delivery policy as code: correlate commits to builds and incidents, enforce standards across repos, and query the estate for drift such as inconsistent base images or missing governance files. The closing argument favors real programming languages for delivery logic and points toward simpler manifests while keeping integration, correlation, automation, and policy as core pillars.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Tomer Gabel - How shit works: TCP/IP
talks.teaser: A narrative-driven tour explains TCP connections, reliability, sliding windows, retransmission, and clean teardown for practitioners.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting an idealized text chat with a chaotic, overloaded exchange that lacks ordering, reliability, and clear session boundaries, even though cellular routing and radio layers still deliver bits successfully. That gap motivates the end-to-end principle: the network moves packets but cannot enforce sensible application-level conversations, so endpoints need their own protocol.

The core of the session designs TCP incrementally on top of IP as a point-to-point, connection-oriented transport. It walks through the three-way handshake and round-trip timing, then reliability via sequence numbers, cumulative acknowledgments, retransmission timers, and fast retransmission after duplicate ACKs. Flow control appears through receiver-advertised sliding windows, with brief coverage of MSS, dynamic window sizing, and RTT-driven timeout tuning.

The close covers polite shutdown with FIN and ACK exchanges, impolite RST behavior familiar from “connection reset by peer,” and why TIME_WAIT exists to discard delayed duplicates. The speaker stresses simplification over specialist depth but argues that knowing what TCP guarantees—and what it does not—helps everyday engineering and debugging.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Charlie Gracie - Create your own Interpreter with a JIT in 1 hour
talks.teaser: Shows how Eclipse OMR’s JIT and interpreter builders let one bytecode implementation serve both interpretation and native JIT compilation.
talks.summary:
Charlie Gracie frames a common runtime roadmap: ship a simple interpreter first, add performance later with a JIT. He argues for writing bytecode logic once and sharing it between interpreter and compiler paths, using IBM’s open, dual-licensed Eclipse OMR toolkit and its portability, GC, tracing, and compiler pieces.

He introduces the teaching stack VM “EL,” its bytecode shape, and a classic dispatch loop, then explains JIT Builder (startup APIs, MethodBuilder subclasses, IL expression trees) and his Interpreter Builder prototype, which registers per-opcode handlers. Live coding wires push, add, return, print, jump, and call bytecodes; a compile path reuses the same handlers after a threshold, yielding large speedups on iterative Fibonacci versus pure interpretation.

He outlines follow-on work—inlining, async compile threads, profiling hooks, a register VM example, and bindings beyond C++—and answers questions on OMR platform support, parser generators versus runtime tooling, interpreter/JIT transitions, and forthcoming C bindings. Demo sources live on the OMR conf-2019 branch and the EL GitHub project.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Thomas Sundberg
talks.teaser: Shows how adapter factories let one Gherkin scenario run against model, REST, and Selenium web seams.
talks.summary:
Thomas Sundberg frames test automation around “seams”: places where automated checks can attach to a system, from the fast in-memory model up through REST and slow browser UI paths. He argues one executable specification should stay valid no matter which seam is used, while acknowledging that deeper layers give speed and outer layers give user-facing confidence.

Using a Cucumber scenario about remembering to buy cat food for impatient stakeholders, he live-refactors step glue into a delegator backed by an adapter factory. The factory reads a seam setting (model, rest, or web) and returns the matching implementation—direct model access, a Dropwizard REST client, or Selenium driving fields and task lists in a browser. He ties the layout to hexagonal (ports and adapters) architecture, adds database and browser switches, and runs a script suited to CI that exercises in-memory and SQL storage plus headless Firefox and Chrome.

The closing emphasis is practical: keep refactors on a green bar, centralize how tests reach the application, fail loudly on unknown seams, and default to the model seam during tight feedback loops while reserving full cross-seam runs for broader assurance. Reference implementation code is offered for download and experimentation.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Maurice Naftalin - What Lies Beneath
talks.teaser: A tiny Java program is traced from bytecode and interpreter assembly through JIT inlining to CPU caches and measured misses.
talks.summary:
The session opens with an intentionally minimal Java class using familiar hex constants, then walks through what happens when it runs. Starting from javap output, it explains the constant pool, local variable table, and stack-based JVM execution for a compute method that divides one supplied value by another and passes the result to a small add helper.

Execution is followed into the template interpreter’s generated x86, including why integer division needs extra checks around Integer.MIN_VALUE and divisor −1 despite Java not trapping overflow. JMH benchmarks contrast interpreted code, disabling JIT inlining, and full optimization, where scores drop from about 178 to about 3. The narrative then shifts to hardware: modern CPUs spend much time waiting on memory, so cache hierarchy and misses matter more than raw instruction counts.

Stride prefetching helps regular access patterns but struggles with pointer-heavy object layouts. Linked-list versus primitive-array iteration under JMH and perf shows rising L1 misses as list size grows, with per-operation cost scaling roughly fourfold while instruction counts stay flat. The closing message is to look below source code with tools such as JMH, perf, and hsdis rather than treat the runtime as magic.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Jean-Philippe Bempel
talks.teaser: Walks through how low-latency JVM garbage collectors like C4, Shenandoah and ZGC use concurrent marking and load barriers.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem of garbage collection pauses in latency-sensitive Java systems, such as trading applications that must respond in under 100 microseconds. It assumes the audience already knows the basic mark, sweep and compact phases and focuses on what low-latency collectors add. Concurrent marking comes first, explained with the tri-color abstraction, and the speaker shows how a reference overwritten during marking can make a live object look like garbage. Two remedies are compared: snapshot-at-the-beginning, which relies on a pre-write barrier the JIT inserts into compiled code, and incremental update.

The middle section covers three collectors. Shenandoah is a non-generational, region-based collector that adds concurrent compaction using a Brooks forwarding pointer and write barriers that keep writes going to the to-space. Azul's C4 is generational and uses a load barrier, a self-healing step, and memory protection traps with virtual memory remapping. ZGC, which the speaker says closely resembles C4, stores state in colored pointers and uses multi-mapping so one physical page can be reached through several virtual addresses. The speaker also describes a Hadoop NameNode with a 580 GB heap that moved from G1 to C4 and had no GC issues from October 2017 onward.

The closing advice is to choose C4 if you need a mature, battle-tested low-latency collector that also limits JVM pauses. Shenandoah is available in OpenJDK, including JDK 12, but not in Oracle's builds, so it suits teams that want to avoid a commercial JVM. ZGC was still in experimental mode at the time. The speaker ends with references on the algorithms and implementations.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: A.Mahdy AbdelAziz
talks.teaser: Shows how the browser Payment Request API replaces hand-built checkout forms, with a Java demo and the remaining gaps.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a travel anecdote about trying to buy a bus ticket and sign up inside a native app, which shows how slow sign-up and payment forms frustrate both users and developers. It frames the problem as lost purchases on the web and presents progressive web apps as a way to let the browser handle much of the repetitive work.

The middle section focuses on the Payment Request API. The speaker explains how the autocomplete attribute already helped forms fill faster, then shows how the API hands the payment sheet to the browser, which displays saved cards and addresses. The developer supplies the accepted payment methods, the display items and the total label, but the API does not calculate totals or process payments; the backend does that. A live demo runs a Java wrapper around a web component in a Jetty server, where a saved card is selected, paid and the resulting data is received by the server.

The closing part lists open gaps: the CVC code still has to be typed, third-party payment vendors and multi-factor authentication are not well covered, and button labels, native wallets, coupons and real card validation remain unsolved. The API also requires HTTPS. The takeaway is that a standard, one-tap checkout could reduce abandonment, while developers should still plan for the parts the browser does not yet handle.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Bruce Eckel
talks.teaser: Surveys Kotlin, Julia and WebAssembly, explaining the design philosophy behind each language and why its decisions matter.
talks.summary:
The session opens with logistics and the speaker's side projects, including a flat software development organization and nonviolent communication. It then turns to three languages, framed by the design philosophy behind each. Kotlin is presented as a language built for seamless Java interoperability that adopts proven features from other languages rather than inventing new ones. Examples include C++ stack versus heap allocation, the dropped new keyword, type inference, extension functions, and null handling with the Elvis operator.

The middle section covers Julia, aimed at scientific and numerical programmers who want Python-like syntax with native speed. The speaker explains its compile-on-first-call approach using LLVM, its built-in support for concurrency and parallelism, and the two-language problem it tries to solve, where prototypes written in Python or R had to be rewritten in C or Fortran. A Fibonacci function is shown in recursive and iterative forms. WebAssembly is then discussed as a way to get beyond JavaScript, letting modules written in languages such as C, C++, Rust and Go run in the browser alongside existing JavaScript, and possibly serve as a portable binary format outside it. Elm and Pony are briefly introduced.

The closing question-and-answer segment covers Scala versus Kotlin, whether Kotlin will displace Java, Groovy in Gradle builds, and whether WebAssembly will repeat the fate of Java applets. The main takeaway is that understanding a language's design philosophy explains its trade-offs and helps practitioners choose the right tool.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Grzegorz Piwowarek
talks.teaser: Explains persistent data structures and how immutable collections trade copying cost for structural sharing in Java.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a method that looks like it takes a list and returns a list, but in practice it mutates its input and changes shared state in several hidden ways. The speaker argues that mutable APIs make code hard to reason about, while immutable designs reduce the number of invalid states and allow values to be shared and cached. He also notes that immutability depends on the abstraction layer: a Java string looks immutable to its users even though its internals are not, and immutable objects are not always thread safe.

The middle of the talk covers persistent data structures, which keep earlier versions intact by sharing structure instead of copying everything. Examples include a singly linked list where prepending reuses the old list, a binary search tree that copies only the path to a changed node, and queues built from two reversed lists, which give amortized rather than worst-case constant time. The speaker then walks through hash array mapped tries, which approach hash-map performance with a high branching factor, and finger trees. He also warns that sublists and Guava transformers are live views over mutable data, which can break tests that assume copies.

The closing part addresses concurrency. Sharing one immutable collection across threads still requires external synchronization, and compare-and-swap retries waste work and create garbage. The takeaway is to weigh correctness against performance, keep immutability where it pays off, and measure before optimizing. Persistent collection libraries for Java are suggested for experimentation.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Heinz Kabutz - Thread Safety with Phaser, StampedLock and VarHandle
talks.teaser: Compares Phaser, StampedLock, and VarHandle for Java thread coordination using live coding and nanosecond benchmarks.
talks.summary:
The session centers on three Java synchronizers for correct, efficient multithreading: Phaser, StampedLock, and VarHandle. The speaker frames thread coordination as easy to get wrong and promises substantial live coding, with audience questions routed through a second laptop.

For Phaser, the talk contrasts it with CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier, notes dynamic party registration and fork/join pool integration, and benchmarks several “joiner” strategies to start worker threads at nearly the same instant. Implementations range from no coordination and volatile spinning through wait/notify and CountDownLatch; Phaser’s arrive-and-awaitAdvance pattern yields the tightest start skew (on the order of ten microseconds worst case in the demo) and far less accumulated wait time than the alternatives. StampedLock coverage explains optimistic versus pessimistic reads, stamp-based unlock from other threads, and upgrade paths unlike ReentrantReadWriteLock. A position class moving diagonally without exposing invalid (x,y) pairs—illustrated with a colorful anecdote—shows write locks for updates and optimistic reads with validation and retry for distance calculations, with timing comparisons against synchronized methods.

VarHandle closes the arc as the Java 9-facing alternative to sun.misc.Unsafe, covering access modes from volatile through plain and compare-and-set on a consolidated coordinate array. Refactoring the position example with compare-and-set for moves and volatile reads for distance improves measured throughput over StampedLock and synchronized baselines. Takeaways include when each API fits, careful interrupt handling in await paths, and choosing lighter-weight coordination when microseconds and CPU waste matter.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Rafał Foltyński - Why you (don't) want to write you own memory buffer recycler?
talks.teaser: Walks through pooling byte buffers in a Java Elasticsearch logging plugin to cut garbage collection pauses and memory churn.
talks.summary:
The speaker maintains an open-source Log4j appender plugin that batches log events into bulk requests sent directly to an Elasticsearch cluster. Serializing each event allocated many strings and short-lived objects, which under heavy load caused frequent garbage collection, long stop-the-world pauses and eventually out-of-memory errors. To reduce this, the plugin pools byte buffers, borrowing one for serialization and returning it once the HTTP request completes. The talk covers borrowing and reference-counting recycling styles, allocation triggers such as allocating when the pool is empty or preemptively at a load factor, and resize strategies.

Before writing a pool, the speaker compared the option with Netty's composite byte buffer, which already resizes dynamically, and considered the complexity of building a buffer from scratch. The custom pool was given a reusable API, automatic growth and shrinking, and an on-empty allocation strategy. In the benchmarks, pooled runs kept garbage collection activity flatter as load rose. With 200-byte messages, freed memory over the measured period fell from 80 GB to 11 GB, while average pause time rose only slightly. With 1 KB messages, accumulated pause time dropped sharply, and a run of 100 million logs at 5,000 messages per second took about five and a half hours.

The takeaway is that pooling pays off when allocation volume is very high, but a hand-written memory manager brings the risk of leaks and mismatched buffers. The speaker noted the library was already running on client servers, and that shipping a working version mattered more than squeezing out further gains.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Jaroslav Tulach - Forget Go. Go, Java, go!
talks.teaser: Contrasts Go and Java deployment trade-offs, demos GraalVM Native Image compact binaries and faster JNI native access.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing why Go wins mindshare for cloud and container workflows: one self-contained binary, quick startup, and modest runtime overhead, while Docker’s Go codebase reinforced that story. A fair prime-number benchmark on the same algorithm shows plain JVM Java finishing around twice as fast as Go on raw compute, which sets up the real friction—shipping and running Java, not peak speed on long-lived servers.

The middle centers on GraalVM, especially Native Image, as a way to keep familiar JVM languages while matching Go-like deployment. After contrasting classic JDK weight, slow cold starts, and heavy metadata with Native Image ahead-of-time compilation, live demos build the benchmark into a sub–3 megabyte executable that starts immediately, uses less memory, and trades roughly 10% peak performance for operability. Limitations appear clearly: platform-specific binaries, restricted reflection and dynamic loading, and adaptation work for some libraries.

The closing segment tackles the JNI boundary with a GNU Scientific Library matrix demo. Crossing between HotSpot and native code millions of times makes trivial JNI take on the order of five seconds, while compiling appropriately shrinks that to about 70 milliseconds. Alternatives span JNA comfort versus speed, native-image shared libraries with C entry points, and annotating C structures for direct access—giving practitioners concrete patterns for cloud-ready Java and less painful native interop.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Mary Grygleski - Reactive for the Impatient - A Gentle Intro to Reactive Java
talks.teaser: A gentle tour of reactive programming principles, patterns, and popular JVM libraries for developers new to non-blocking systems.
talks.summary:
The session frames why reactive approaches gained traction alongside multicore hardware, virtualization, cloud deployments, and demand for responsive user experiences. It introduces the Reactive Manifesto and walks through responsiveness, elasticity, resilience, and message-driven design, separating reactive programming, functional reactive programming, and reactive systems architecture. Event-driven versus message-driven communication is clarified with observables, streams, marble diagrams, and operators such as map and subscribe, contrasted with imperative blocking code.

A noodle-shop analogy illustrates matching orders with seat availability through observables, and the middle section surveys design patterns including circuit breakers, back pressure, CAP trade-offs, and the Reactive Streams specification. Reactive programming inside microservices is distinguished from reactive coordination between services, with brief coverage of Lagom and related ecosystem pieces.

The closing portion compares RxJava, Spring WebFlux and Project Reactor, Akka’s actor model, and Eclipse Vert.x through hello-world style examples and Spring MVC versus reactive flux behavior. Takeaways stress patience while learning the paradigm, elegance of declarative pipelines, and the reality that fully reactive stacks still hit blocking layers such as many relational databases, with R2DBC addressing only part of the gap.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Hrvoje Crnjak - Developer's guide to selling your soul
talks.teaser: A team lead delivers eleven opinionated management rules for developers promoted into people leadership roles.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames the session as a deliberately informal counterpoint to technical conference talks, with a upfront disclaimer that everything reflects personal opinion. He argues that working with people is unavoidable and offers eleven lessons on leading teams.

Early lessons cover culture and fit: avoid tolerating toxic behavior, recognize the Peter Principle when strong engineers become weak managers, and remember that a lead is not smarter than the room—only accountable for smooth execution. Middle sections stress that bosses own outcomes even when others fail, that leadership is not democracy though input still matters, and that meetings must end in actionable decisions even when the choice is to wait or do nothing.

Later lessons address expectations (what, how, and especially why), treating mistakes as improvement opportunities, frequent behavioral feedback, and transparency about priorities and status versus tribal knowledge. He closes by noting that teams mirror a leader’s tone and standards, including during crises, and briefly answers a question that flat structures still need someone on the hook for responsibility.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Tomasz Nurkiewicz - CharBusters
talks.teaser: Walks through common Unicode pitfalls in Java, from code points and surrogate pairs to normalization and whitespace handling.
talks.summary:
Nurkiewicz argues that character encoding is often assumed to be a solved problem, and frames the talk as ten common mistakes developers make when handling Unicode. He opens with a lighter detour through estimation failures in computing history, including IPv4 address exhaustion, the Y2K date bug, and a routing table size limit that caused a 2014 internet outage, to show how limits get underestimated.

The core section explains why one byte or one Java char does not equal one character. Legacy encodings for Polish letters conflicted with each other, and Unicode code points must be stored as UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32. In Java, characters beyond 16 bits become surrogate pairs, so a substring can split a musical symbol and a naive string reversal can break it. Flags built from letter pairs, skin-tone modifiers and zero-width-joined family emoji show that one visible character can span many code points. Length, whitespace definitions across trim, regex and Character methods, and default-charset getBytes calls all behave differently. Decomposed and precomposed letters compare unequal until normalized, and Turkish-locale case conversion mangles the letter I, which broke certificate and XML parsing in several JDK paths.

He closes with a real case from Turkey, where a dropped dot in a text message changed its meaning and contributed to a deadly argument. His practical advice is to use UTF-8 explicitly, normalize input, count graphemes rather than relying on length, and keep a pangram string in unit tests to catch garbled data.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Jorrit van der Ven / Riccardo Lippolis - Kotlin is for hipsters
talks.teaser: Developers hear six months of Kotlin lessons on null safety, data classes, Spring plugins, coroutines, and collections versus Java streams.
talks.summary:
Two Netherlands-based developers describe adopting Kotlin after roughly six months on a Port of Rotterdam logistics project: a React front end, Kotlin microservices, and Neo4j for container routing similar to a maps product for shippers. They position themselves as experienced Java engineers, not Kotlin experts, and structure the session as pros and cons across the language, libraries and frameworks, and tooling.

On language features they highlight compile-time null safety versus legacy Java interop, data classes with Jackson and Hibernate caveats (including lazy collections in hash codes), extension functions and properties for geographic coordinates, collection operators versus Java streams and sequences, and coroutines with async and await-all style patterns. Framework coverage centers on Spring Kotlin support, the open-class plugin, and surprises when beans come from external configuration; testing touches Mockito's when keyword and the Kotlin Mockito plugin.

They close with lessons: they prefer not to return to Java, recommend prior functional programming exposure, start small rather than rewriting entire enterprises, use IntelliJ EduTools for practice, and note IDE refactoring slowness and Gradle Kotlin DSL performance versus Groovy. Q&A contrasts lazy sequences with eager collections, Java-to-Kotlin conversion in IntelliJ, and chained collection costs.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Janet Yu/A.Mukherji - Survivability of Observability: Taking your DIY system to success
talks.teaser: Operators learn how to mature in-house observability stacks beyond early wins in complex cloud and microservice environments.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that containers, Kubernetes, and microservices accelerated delivery but made production behavior far harder to understand than in monolith days, so homegrown observability becomes essential—and initially popular—until growth exposes gaps. Success without ongoing investment leads to failure: more users, richer demands, outages, and expectations that telemetry supports capacity planning, A/B tests, incident response, and executive-level service health—not just host CPU alerts.

They structure maturity around practical pillars: combined metrics, traces, and logs; integration programs that track constantly changing stacks; a unified collection pipeline for compliance, backend swaps, and ML experiments; pre-aggregation and time rollups for population-level queries; rich mutable metadata; and analytics for SLOs, dynamic thresholds, and fast drill-down. A second segment covers survivability in production: per-user quotas against noisy neighbors, relief queues, data retention, expert-curated templates for casual users, alert runbooks, naming standards, LDAP or SSO, RBAC, backups, audit logs, and APIs or Terraform for monitoring-as-code.

The closing message treats observability as an organizational program—not a one-time tool—that must evolve with the business, user roles, and compliance needs so adoption and trust endure.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Dan Lebrero
talks.teaser: Practical habits cut interruptions, automate repetitive work, and shorten feedback loops for software teams.
talks.summary:
The presentation distinguishes efficiency from effectiveness, arguing that coding quickly only pays off when choices do not create future drag. It cites research on interruption cost—often quoted as 10 to 15 minutes, with a much longer reload into task context—and urges minimizing distractions by turning off notifications, batching email, and thinking before pinging colleagues.

Habits covered include single-tasking, deep knowledge of the IDE, scripting repetitive work (with live bash pipelines over JSON news data), time-boxing automation attempts, favoring composable CLIs over GUIs, automated tests (including reproducing bugs before fixes), one-command setups via Docker Compose, test-first development, and exploratory REPL sessions instead of one-off tools like Postman. Pair programming appears as a way to absorb interruptions and share tooling tricks.

The close advocates continuous, small code reviews—often through side-by-side pairing—so feedback arrives while changes stay tiny. The closing message is to pause, reflect on how you work, and keep learning your craft.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Jarek Ratajski - Another year, another language
talks.teaser: Surveying history from analytical engines to Kotlin, the session shows why churn persists and how side projects repay Java veterans.
talks.summary:
The talk opens on developer fatigue: Polish community threads each summer ask why yet another framework or niche language appears and whether learning ever ends. The speaker frames that complaint against a fast-paced history of computing, from Babbage’s planned analytical engine and relay machines through machine code, assembly, Fortran, COBOL, Lisp, Algol, C, BASIC, Pascal, C++, Java, and JavaScript, with hardware shifts—from mercury delay lines to transistors and multi-core CPUs—driving each wave.

Each milestone is tied to recurring motives for inventing languages: automating tedious machine coding, targeting scientists or business users, experimenting with ideas like functional programming, preventing errors, or shipping a free platform. Stories include Algol 68’s operator overload, null’s introduction in Algol W, Dijkstra’s goto debate, and how placement in browsers or microcomputers made some languages ubiquitous. For a JVM-focused audience, Kotlin and Scala illustrate how richer type systems and syntax shrink boilerplate, tame nulls, and can model safer reactive or event-sourcing designs than idiomatic Java alone.

The close rejects a single “ultimate” language: new hardware and ideas reset the cycle of ceremony versus simplicity. Practitioners with families need not chase every fad in production, but prototypes, trainings, and open source remain low-risk places to learn. The speaker argues that even partial fluency in a second language often sharpens skill in the first—before the familiar one starts to feel limiting.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Marcin Zajączkowski - How to save money on long-term support for Java 11?
talks.teaser: Outlines options for reducing Java 11 long-term support spend while staying current across Linux and Windows deployments.
talks.summary:
The session centers on the cost and logistics of long-term support for Java 11, framed against vendor-led models and the pressure to keep runtimes patched on multiple operating systems. Fragments of the discussion point to Oracle as the familiar commercial authority behind Java versioning and updates, and to the puzzle of matching authority, release dates, and platform coverage when teams cannot rely on a single default path.

Much of the audible material contrasts how different organizations source support: commercial customer support channels, open initiatives, and in-house or community-facing approaches. Linux and Windows—including references to Fedora and older Windows generations—appear alongside JVM-related wording such as hotspot and virtual machine, underscoring that support savings hinge on which distribution and build teams standardize on, not only on license price.

The close returns to practical judgment: comparing what peers and vendors actually provide, weighing software update mechanics, and deciding whether an open or alternate supplier can cover the same platforms without sacrificing continuity. Listeners are left with a checklist mindset—vendor contract, target OS fleet, and update pipeline—before committing spend on extended Java 11 support.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Dmitry Kandalov - Test && commit || revert
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of test-commit-revert explains its state machine, rationale, and a live Kotlin FizzBuzz exercise using a custom IDE plugin.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces test-commit-revert, abbreviated TCR, a workflow Kent Beck popularized after a workshop participant proposed symmetry: revert when tests fail if you commit when they pass. A diagram compares it to test-driven development as state machines. TDD alternates green cleanup, red failing tests, green implementation, and further cleanup, whereas TCR stays green throughout—cleanup, then test plus implementation together, with failed attempts returning to the prior green snapshot rather than leaving red builds behind.

The speaker argues TCR pushes microscopic changes, discourages wasted work on reverted edits, may sharpen problem-solving, and could scale toward continuous delivery when many developers ship tiny passing steps. An arcade-game analogy treats failure as respawn to the last safe state. A Kotlin demo in IntelliJ uses a custom Limited Work-in-Progress plugin on a FizzBuzz-style exercise: commits require passing tests, failing runs wipe changes, and incremental steps cover divisibility rules, refactoring to when expressions, and harder combinations. Reverts surface copy-paste typos and ordering mistakes; larger refactors demand smaller steps because lost code cannot be debugged in place.

Quirks include awkward stack-trace navigation after revert, friction with classical red-then-green TDD, unsettled policy on reverting failing tests alone, and open questions about commit messages, squashing, and whether to push automatically. The close invites practitioners to try TCR via Maven, Git reset, or the plugin.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Ken Sipe

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Aiko Klostermann
talks.teaser: Argues that developers should write names, commit messages and tests for the people who will read them later.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces what the speaker calls consumer driven software development, a way of making everyday coding decisions by asking who will read the result and what they need to know. Drawing on years of pair programming across consulting projects, the speaker argues that naming, commit messages and tests are small products with consumers, most often other developers, including one's future self. The speaker starts with user stories, which already frame work from a user's point of view, and notes that this perspective passes along when a product owner writes the story for a developer.

The middle of the talk gives concrete cases. A commit message that only says a function was moved leaves a reader unable to tell where it went or why, so the speaker asks for the reason behind each change to be recorded in the body. A test failure reporting only that a response should return 200 gives no context, and borrowing the given-when-then structure from behaviour driven development lets a test name state the condition it covers. The speaker then compares Python's two string representation methods, where one serves end users and the other serves developers by giving an unambiguous form that can be pasted back as code.

The closing takeaway is practical: before naming or documenting something, identify the consumer and write for them. The speaker is comfortable with long, descriptive method names on modern wide screens, and suggests keeping commit subject lines to about 70 characters while using the body for the reasoning.

talks.title: GeeCON 2019: Fred George - Chaos Development: Removing software as the inhibitor of Agile
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2019: Fred George - Chaos Development: Removing software as the inhibitor of Agile.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Fred George discusses "Chaos Development"—an approach to designing software processes and architectures that accept and accommodate constant requirement changes rather than trying to control or suppress them. Drawing parallels to chaos engineering, where production systems are built to withstand and recover from unpredictable infrastructure failures and attacks, chaos development focuses on eliminating software development practices that inhibit agility. George explains that development environments have shifted drastically from the 1970s mainframe era of small codebases and isolated machines to massive enterprise codebases with shifting requirements and distributed integrations. Using the Cynefin framework, he differentiates between traditional (simple/complicated) problems and fuzzy (complex/chaotic) problems, presenting distinct development and architectural paradigms for each.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Systems and Fallibility of Testing**: From small IBM 1130 programs of 4,000 lines to 100-million-line codebases, modern systems inevitably suffer from bugs—both internal and external (such as failing third-party APIs). Acceptance testing is increasingly superseded by active production monitoring and resilience engineering.
- **Traditional vs. Fuzzy Problems (Cynefin Framework)**: Traditional/complicated problems have cause-and-effect relationships where domain experts and story-driven Agile workflows excel. Fuzzy/complex problems (such as recommendation engines, Google advertising, and financial markets) lack predictable cause-and-effect; in this domain, no true experts exist, making rapid experimentation essential.
- **Extreme OO and Agile for Traditional Systems**: For traditional systems, agile productivity comes from manufacturing-style flow, minimizing work-in-progress, and writing code engineered for rapid change using Smalltalk-inspired object-oriented design.
- **Asynchronous Microservices for Fuzzy Systems**: For fuzzy domains, tiny, decoupled microservices connected via an asynchronous event bus enable continuous deployment, rapid experimentation, and graceful degradation.

### Technical Details
- **Smalltalk-Style Object-Oriented Design Rules**:
  - Keep methods extremely short (averaging ~2.3 lines per method at Nationwide, and ~1.5–1.6 in Kotlin).
  - Minimize class sizes (averaging around 25 lines of code) and avoid "God classes" or classes ending in `-er` / `-or` (e.g., Managers, Calculators).
  - Strictly enforce encapsulation: eliminate public variables, getters, and setters.
  - Eliminate conditional complexity: avoid `switch`/`case` statements, `else` branches, enums, and non-guard `if` statements, replacing them with patterns such as State or Strategy.
  - Avoid primitives representing behavior: eliminate raw booleans, unstructured maps, naked numbers, and raw strings from core domain models.
- **Microservices & Event Bus Architecture for Fuzzy Systems**:
  - Built as very small units (often 30–40 lines of code) developed by single individuals ("team size of one").
  - Implement the **Need Pattern** over an event bus: a service publishes a need (e.g., deciding whether to issue a loan or serve a promotional ad), and independent, decoupled services publish offers or evaluations asynchronously.
  - Tolerate eventual and delayed consistency (even days out of date) and lack of strict transactions.
  - Rely on graceful degradation: if an individual service or external feed fails, the broader choreography still yields answers.
  - Support ultra-high deployment velocity: George describes a London startup running ~300 microservices where 53 developers made 652 production deployments in a week (a release every 3.5 minutes on average).

### Takeaways
- Organizations must match their engineering processes to the nature of the problem: traditional/complicated problems benefit from disciplined Agile, Smalltalk-style design, and domain stories, whereas fuzzy problems require discarding traditional ceremonies in favor of autonomous developers experimenting directly.
- In fuzzy domains, competitive advantage belongs to whoever can try out ideas fastest; experimentation drives innovation.
- Investing directly in developer skills through continuous pair programming and eliminating organizational fears (e.g., fear of failure, fear of inaccurate estimates) yields far greater productivity gains than management tooling alone.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Tomer Gabel - The Folly of TDD
talks.teaser: A keynote dissects claimed TDD benefits, where test-first fails, and why dogma outruns evidence in hiring and practice.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens a deliberately provocative keynote by clarifying that test-driven development is neither evil nor a panacea, then polls the room on who practices and enjoys TDD. He walks through Wikipedia’s red-green-refactor definition and the long list of benefits advocates cite online, noting that even experts rarely agree on the purpose beyond vague ideas like coding with less fear.

The middle of the talk stresses when test-first breaks down: the solution must be known, understood, stable, and finite. Social feeds, search quality, recommendations, exploration-heavy designs, external dependencies, and machine-learning style problems often cannot be specified in advance as unit tests. He then challenges the axioms of lower bug density, fewer regressions, and higher quality—arguing that test code needs maintenance, tests can lie, and many regressions are performance, security, or integration issues outside unit TDD. Surveyed academia offers guarded, contradictory results over tiny samples; code coverage percentages are criticized as misleading, including a trivial example that reaches full coverage without real assurance.

He closes by contrasting TDD with BDD, design by contract, property-based testing, and formal methods such as TLA+ used at large cloud vendors, plus research suggesting overall testing time matters more than test-first ordering. Even favorable views leave performance, security, and capacity untested. The practical takeaway is to treat TDD as a limited tool, combine it with other techniques, experiment locally, and resist dogma—including interview norms that treat abstaining from TDD as unprofessional without evidence.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Thomas Sundberg
talks.teaser: GeeCON Prague 2018: Thomas Sundberg - A testable architecture.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from GeeCON Prague 2018, Thomas Sundberg, an independent developer from Stockholm, addresses the challenge of building a testable software architecture while ensuring developers first understand what problem they need to solve. Sundberg defines done as working software in production and argues that an effective test suite must balance three properties: confidence that the software works, high speed (short feedback loops), and low maintenance cost. He demonstrates how Behavior-Driven Development (BDD), collaborative specification techniques, and architectural patterns like hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters) allow teams to use a single business-readable specification across multiple testing layers.

### Key Topics
- **Bridging the Communication Gap**: Teams frequently fail to deliver correct software due to miscommunication. Collaborative discovery practices, such as the "Three Amigos" (developers, testers, and product owners/business analysts), help surface knowledge across different quadrants, especially uncovering the "danger zone" of unknown unknowns.
- **Example Mapping and Concrete Examples**: Abstract requirements are difficult to parse; concrete examples written using techniques like example mapping allow teams to validate rules and questions before formulating them into living documentation.
- **Living Documentation with Gherkin**: Writing scenarios in Gherkin (`Given`, `When`, `Then`) allows product owners, testers, and developers to review and criticize acceptance criteria, avoiding unreadable raw unit test code.
- **The Agile Testing Pyramid and Testing Iceberg**: Testing through the user interface provides confidence but suffers from slow execution, high costs, and poor diagnosis precision. Unit and model-level tests offer high execution speed and precise diagnostics. Teams should strive to push tests down to faster layers while maintaining confidence.
- **Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)**: Proposed by Alistair Cockburn, this architectural style keeps domain models free from external infrastructure and transport concerns (such as web frameworks or databases), making it possible to execute business scenarios through multiple entry points.

### Technical Details
Sundberg walks through an implementation using Java, Gradle, Cucumber, and Selenium WebDriver for a simple note-taking application. 
- **Step Definitions as Simple Translators**: Step definitions map Gherkin steps to code and should act strictly as thin translators (one or two lines) that delegate directly to helper abstractions rather than hardcoding UI automation or domain calls.
- **Abstraction Layer via Helper Classes**: Sundberg introduces a helper interface with two implementations: `InMemoryNoteHelper` and `BrowserNoteHelper`. A system property (e.g., `-Dbrowser=true`) decides at runtime which helper executes the scenario.
- **Dual Execution Profiles**: In-memory execution connects directly to domain repositories, running in under one second. The Selenium browser-driven test starts the embedded server (e.g., using Spark framework on port 4567) and opens a real browser to exercise the UI and background JavaScript, taking around 4–5 seconds. While too slow for every local build, the UI test verifies server startup and wiring in CI pipelines.

### Takeaways
Automated testing without a proper understanding of the core problem is wasted effort. Adopting BDD enables teams to specify behavior collaboratively using concrete examples. By decoupling core business logic via hexagonal architecture and maintaining thin translation layers in test suites, developers can execute identical acceptance criteria both in memory for fast local feedback and via full-stack browser automation for end-to-end confidence.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Peter Van de Voorde - Working Remotely: Dream vs Reality
talks.teaser: A developer advocate contrasts remote-work dreams with real schedules, time zones, and family trade-offs, then shares team habits that help.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with how he joined Atlassian as a fully remote developer advocate, including a first in-person meeting with his manager at an event in Prague. He frames “remote” as always working away from a central office—not occasional work-from-home—and describes a globally scattered team spanning many time zones.

He walks through dream versus reality: working from beaches, resorts, and trains sounds glamorous, but most days happen in a simple home office, often around forty hours a week, with late-evening meetings to align with the US and Australia. Upsides include no commute, flexible scheduling, control over workspace, and fewer office interruptions; downsides include loneliness, work–family blur, visibility and trust issues, fear of missing hallway news, and home distractions. He describes concrete coping strategies: remote-first meeting etiquette, remote ShipIt hackathons, puzzle-style remote social events, co-working spaces, meetups and conferences, and tooling for video, chat, issue tracking, wikis, and calendars with blocked personal time.

He closes by arguing remote suits experienced teams with clear ownership, and wraps Atlassian values into remote practice—open communication, teamwork, sustainable balance, driving change, and treating teammates and family as the real “customers.” Q&A covers boundaries with young children, productivity comparisons, async versus sync communication, and when face-to-face still pays off.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Michael Nygard
talks.teaser: Coverage of GeeCON Prague 2018: Michael Nygard from the conference program.
talks.summary:
Michael Nygard explores coupling in software systems and strategies for deliberate decoupling to improve system maintainability and flexibility. He opens with a metaphor contrasting well-organized modular structures (buckyballs) with tensegrity structures that hold themselves together through tension and compression. Software systems often evolve from modular buckyballs into tensegrity-like blobs where moving one piece affects distant, seemingly unrelated parts—a consequence of uncontrolled coupling spreading throughout the codebase.

Nygard defines five types of coupling: operational coupling (runtime dependencies preventing execution without the provider), development coupling (requiring coordinated code changes), semantic coupling (shared concepts requiring synchronized changes across systems), functional coupling (shared implementation requiring parallel modifications), and incidental coupling (unnecessary dependencies). He illustrates these through real-world examples: email systems with SMTP and Exchange (strong semantic and operational coupling, weak development coupling due to protocol standardization); direct database access (strong operational, development, and semantic coupling); REST interfaces (moderately reduced operational coupling, improved failover transparency); and message-oriented architectures (weak operational and development coupling, though strong semantic coupling remains).

Nygard warns of two significant pitfalls. 'Semantic polymers' occur when concepts spread throughout an enterprise as shared data feeds, making any individual concept difficult to change—illustrated by a retail system where SKU concepts required organization-wide modifications when introducing price points. 'Long arrows' represent interfaces that appear simple in architecture diagrams but actually involve many sequential steps, accumulating the worst performance and availability characteristics of each component rather than the best.

The primary solution framework comes from David Parnas's 1972 paper on system decomposition. Parnas demonstrates how restructuring the same system with information-hiding (later termed decision-hiding) interfaces can encapsulate specific concerns—character encoding, memory management, storage mechanisms—allowing changes to localize to single modules. This approach introduces more components but paradoxically increases simplicity through reduced coupling. Nygard emphasizes orthogonality and separation of concerns: decisions about different system aspects should be independent, with each module hiding decisions behind clean interfaces.

A key insight is that composability—the ability to flexibly combine components—is inversely proportional to the number of distinct interfaces and data types. Modern microservices often increase coupling by creating unique APIs and data types for each service, whereas standardizing on fewer interfaces and data types improves composability and reduces coupling across all dimensions.

Nygard recommends: explicitly identify which coupling types matter most for specific systems; prefer libraries over services to avoid trading recurring runtime costs for development efficiency; standardize on fewer interfaces and data types across services; use all available structural tools (modules, components, abstractions); and always make decisions explicit rather than implicit. Coupling is necessary to accomplish coordinated effects, but uncontrolled diffusion makes systems brittle and expensive to modify.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Dmitry Vinnik - Stress Driven Development, and How to Avoid It
talks.teaser: Explores sleep, nutrition, fitness and workplace stress, and offers habit-based ways to tackle them.
talks.summary:
Dmitry Vinnik opens by arguing that stress is not uniformly harmful. Short bursts, such as a cold shower or a sauna, can get the body going, while long-term stressors drain energy and affect health. He shares a health scare from his early twenties as an example of how a warning can motivate change, and points to published cases of overworked game developers as evidence the problem persists. He then splits the topic into four areas: sleep, nutrition, fitness and work.

For sleep, he recommends limiting blue light and noise, protecting uninterrupted eight-hour sleep and keeping a consistent wake time. On nutrition he argues against strict diets in favour of consistency and experimentation, and describes intermittent fasting with a 16/8 eating window as one option. Fitness covers physical and mental training: gamifying workouts, scheduling movement into the workday, and mindfulness, solitude and guided meditation. To change routines, he explains the habit loop of cue, routine and reward, and suggests keeping the reward while changing the routine, and building on keystone habits that ripple into other areas.

For work, he covers open offices, asynchronous communication, phone notifications and do-not-disturb modes, noise control, and quiet-room norms, along with scope creep and unrealistic expectations. He closes with warnings against rigid dogma and skipping gradual training, and urges listeners to find a purpose, a supportive community and a trusted specialist, starting with small changes.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Ansgar Brauner - Introduce girls to programming and reduce the gender gap
talks.teaser: Covers STEM stereotypes, gendered children's games, and a reusable model for all-girls programming days with mentors and hardware.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by acknowledging that a male colleague is delivering a talk normally shared with his co-speaker Laura, then frames STEAM as science, technology, engineering, arts, and math. OECD-style findings show European boys are far more likely than girls to expect careers in engineering or computer science, which the speakers tie to lost societal talent when paths are chosen from stereotypes rather than interest.

The middle of the talk walks through reinforcing influences: early computer access often through male relatives, gendered toy and game marketing (including stark differences between generic and “girls” listings on mobile app stores and boy-heavy STEM game packaging on retail sites), and internalized stereotypes illustrated through the “run like a girl” campaign contrast between adults and children. Estimates that the gender pay gap may take decades or centuries to close motivate deliberate acceleration, including girls-only outreach before primary-school ages when norms harden.

The close is operational. At a large German food-retail digital hub, internal hackathons precede “HEK days for girls” that host dozens of girls aged seven to seventeen for Scratch warm-ups, outdoor breaks, and Calliope microcontroller projects ending in demos for parents. Practitioners receive staffing ratios, mentor diversity goals, hardware choices (Raspberry Pi, Calliope, BBC micro:bit), parent communication, outdoor activities, registrations, GDPR-aware photo consent, and planned open documentation—aimed at enabling similar events in companies or Java user groups.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Martin Hochel - Ultimate React Component Patterns with TypeScript
talks.teaser: Live coding delivers TypeScript patterns for controlled and uncontrolled React components, render props, and HOC enhancement.
talks.summary:
The session opens by setting expectations: it will not re-teach all of React or TypeScript from scratch, but instead focus on component patterns that scale into full applications, with one-way data flow from parent to child. Through live coding in an editor beside a running browser, the presenter builds up from simple function and class components with typed props, default props, and optional fields inferred from implementation rather than duplicated in types.

The middle of the talk adds stateless and stateful examples—a typed button with literal color tokens and callbacks, then a counter with internal state and safer refactoring by deriving state types from constants. Controlled versus uncontrolled counting follows, including optional change callbacks, a getState helper, and a small factory for increment and decrement handlers. Render props expose count and handlers so consumers can customize markup (for example red styling) without forking core logic. A higher-order component then injects counter behavior into a thin presentational piece, using conditional mapped types to extract render-prop argument types and subtract injected props from the wrapped component’s public API, plus an optional max-count cap demonstrated in the UI.

Practitioners should leave with concrete patterns—controlled/uncontrolled, children-as-function, and HOC enhancement—that TypeScript can keep consistent through inference and lookup types, reducing duplicate annotations and compile-time mistakes during refactors.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Oleh Dokuka - Refactor to Reactive with Spring 5 and Reactor 3
talks.teaser: A staged walkthrough migrates a blocking Spring 4 chat demo to Spring 5, WebFlux, Reactor, server push, and non-blocking I/O.
talks.summary:
The presentation starts from a familiar Spring Boot chat dashboard that polls Gitter, aggregates chat statistics in MongoDB, and blocks threads on external calls and database access. The speaker shows how polling and synchronous I/O waste threads, degrade under load, and surface harsh errors when MongoDB stops, motivating a move toward reactive characteristics from the Reactive Manifesto.

The middle of the talk walks through concrete migration steps: Spring Boot 2 and Spring 5, then server-sent events with Reactor types such as Mono, Flux, and ReplayProcessor to push updates instead of client polling. The flow continues with reactive repositories, WebClient for Gitter, Gitter streaming instead of polling, and optional Netty as the server engine for higher throughput, with brief mentions of RSocket and R2DBC for later exploration.

Practitioners should leave with a phased refactor playbook—when to swap blocking types for Mono or Flux, how to wire push APIs and retries, and trade-offs including learning curve, rewrites on large codebases, and testing with Project Reactor test support. The live demo emphasizes resilience: the UI stays usable during outages and recovers when dependencies return.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Nitsan Wakart - Allocation
talks.teaser: Explains how Java object allocation creates garbage collection cost, and how to profile and reduce it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the other side of garbage collection: how application code creates the garbage the collector later has to clean up. It covers thread-local allocation buffers, why allocation stays cheap until caches and main memory become involved, and how generational collection can suffer when dead old objects keep young ones alive. This effect, called nepotism, can drag whole linked queues or tree structures into the old generation.

The speaker shows how to observe allocation, using GC logs, visual GC tools, and profilers such as Java Flight Recorder and async-profiler. Flame graphs are presented alongside their collapsed-stack text format, which makes it easy to write small scripts that filter and summarise allocation samples. A JMH demonstration shows that escape analysis removes a short-lived object but not a short-lived array, and a second experiment shows that allocation throughput drops sharply even when only a small fraction of objects survive.

For reducing garbage, the speaker recommends profiling first and then targeting hotspots. Suggestions include replacing iterators in hot loops with counted loops, avoiding varargs and string-based protocols, returning shared empty collections, lazily allocating maps and lists, and reusing buffers or pooling objects where that is justified. Object layout also matters, since headers, alignment and small objects add overhead, and bit flags can be more compact than boolean arrays. The takeaway is to measure allocation hotspots first and reduce indirection and footprint where it pays off.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Jarosław Ratajski - Another year, another language
talks.teaser: Traces programming language history from assembly and Fortran to C, Java and Scala, and why new languages keep appearing.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a recurring thread on a Polish developer forum asking why programmers keep chasing new languages. The speaker answers through history, starting with an audience poll on first and favourite languages.

He traces the line from Babbage's unbuilt analytical engine and Ada Lovelace's notes through lambda calculus and assembly. Each step addressed a pain point: Fortran eased scientific programming, COBOL targeted business, and Lisp offered a functional style too slow for machines of the day. Algol 68 showed the risks of design by committee, while C, C++, Java and JavaScript each tackled problems left by their predecessors.

Later sections weigh static against dynamic typing, show how Scala's type inference reduces ceremony, and note that Haskell's pure functions suit multi-core systems. The speaker's central idea is a loop in which new hardware enables new ideas, which bring new bugs and restrictions. He ends by encouraging developers to learn new languages through prototypes or hackathons, since the habits they build carry back into everyday code.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: D.Lebrero-REPL Driven Development: immediate feedback for your server side code
talks.teaser: Shows how a REPL attached to a running JVM application gives instant feedback while exploring data and writing server-side code.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that slow build and startup cycles break developer focus. Starting a small Tomcat application took around 30 seconds, and an interruption can cost many minutes to regain context. Mocked tests only approximate real systems, so he proposes a REPL that runs inside the live application instead.

He demonstrates a Clojure REPL embedded in a Java web application on Tomcat, connected from the IDE over a socket and used to evaluate code in the running JVM. He adds the Postgres driver at runtime, queries database metadata to find transaction tables, and inspects sample rows. After spotting two currencies, he calls an exchange-rate HTTP endpoint and parses its response. The explored results become realistic test data, and a watcher reruns only the tests affected by each saved change. He also shows keeping application state across reloads, inspecting and changing it, and adding a Swagger-documented endpoint whose controller simply delegates to the tested logic.

The closing section covers trade-offs. A REPL left open in staging or production is powerful but dangerous, and he cites NASA changing the running code of a distant spacecraft as a precedent for extreme care. Practitioners should expect REPL features to vary by language, and the same approach applies to Android, iOS, desktop applications and big data tools.
