talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Simon Belak
talks.teaser: Sketch algorithms compress huge datasets so practitioners estimate percentiles and ranks with bounded memory.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames analytics where row counts swing from hundreds on tiny servers to hundreds of billions in warehouses, and where streaming makes it hard to keep raw data for later questions. Sketch algorithms answer by summarizing observations into compact structures that can be updated incrementally, merged in parallel, and stored instead of replaying entire pipelines.

The core walkthrough is a histogram: fixed bucket count, merge of adjacent buckets when capacity is exceeded, MapReduce-friendly combination, and weighted interpolation for means, variance, and percentiles. The speaker extends that to time-sliced histograms for drift during experiments, sampling from a histogram for downstream jobs, segmented targets, and count-min sketches with pairwise-independent hashes to estimate heavy-hitters when cardinality is enormous. Examples come from Metabase and Clojure, including Anscombe-style cases where summary statistics hide different shapes.

Practitioners are urged to treat persisted sketches as first-class artifacts, reason in distributions rather than lone averages, watch metrics change over time, and accept approximate answers when latency and organizational use matter more than exact counts.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Martin Osovský - Beyond thermostats: Distributed Applications living on the Edge
talks.teaser: Shows layered edge architecture with local compute, offline autonomy, data lifecycle design, and conflict handling beyond IoT hype.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames edge computing as a logical evolution beyond cloud-only designs, using Y Soft’s print-management domain as a case study in large, geographically distributed deployments. It opens with why pushing computation toward devices matters, contrasting consumer examples such as Apple’s on-device processing with cloud-centric models, and recounts a European banking customer that needed hundreds of branch locations to keep working when WAN links or headquarters connectivity failed.

The speaker maps their hybrid SafeQ architecture onto familiar edge patterns: horizontally scalable layers, site-local application services, declarative device twins from Azure IoT Edge and AWS, and limited autonomy when central systems drop. Operational pressures include bandwidth (25 terabytes of print data staying local versus hundreds of gigabytes crossing headquarters), latency-sensitive authentication, and sudden growth such as hundreds of new nodes in India.

Later sections stress data design as the hard part: lifecycle-aware caching, avoiding distributed sessions and cross-layer transactions, and replacing a fragile print-document state machine with CRDT-style merging. Practitioners should treat edge as layered, loosely coupled scale-out architecture with computation near data origin, not merely IoT gadgets, and plan explicitly for offline tolerance and configuration conflict handling.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Cyrille Martraire - DDD beyond the infamous repository pattern
talks.teaser: Clarifies the core building blocks of Domain-Driven Design, beyond repositories, and shows how to model a business domain.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Domain-Driven Design is often reduced to its tactical patterns, with repositories treated as little more than data access objects. The speaker moves attention back to the business domain, to modeling it directly in code, and to the idea of Bounded Contexts. Tactical building blocks such as entities and value objects are covered, along with an example of writing a repository against an interface first, using an in-memory implementation before a persistence layer is connected behind it.

The second part turns to strategic design. Examples from fraud detection and an e-commerce setting show how one word, such as customer or product, can mean different things in different parts of a system. The speaker presents splitting the model into separate contexts, with shipping, billing and catalogue views as examples, as the way to keep each model coherent.

The takeaway for practitioners is to start from the business language, express it in code, and use Bounded Contexts to decide where one model ends and another begins. The talk is pitched at junior and senior developers who are starting with DDD.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Hugh McKee - 7 Reasons why your microservices should use Event Sourcing & CQRS
talks.teaser: Shows how event sourcing and CQRS decouple microservice data, survive outages and scale, trading off eventual consistency.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that microservices should split their persistence as well as their code, and presents event sourcing and CQRS as a way to do that. The speaker outlines the basic model: a command is validated, the resulting event is appended to an event log that is never updated or deleted, and separate read-side stores are built from those events to serve queries.

Seven reasons follow. Event storming gives teams a smooth path from domain design into implementation. Pull-based consumption of events reduces coupling, so a failing service does not cascade into others. Consumers pulling by offset provide at-least-once delivery that survives outages, and separating reads from writes eases database bottlenecks and traffic spikes at the cost of eventual consistency. Each service can keep its own copy of the data it needs, and the approach can reduce the approvals needed to get new databases or topics. The speaker also contrasts simple REST calls, which may drop messages, with stronger messaging semantics.

The closing message is that this is a trade-off rather than a universal fix. Teams should ask what will go wrong in each failure scenario and test whether eventual consistency is truly intolerable before rejecting it. In the Q&A, the speaker notes that consumers must handle duplicate messages and that hard real-time requirements may not fit the model.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Bartłomiej Kuczyński - How to build flexible applications with JLupin
talks.teaser: A live demo shows how JLupin decomposes Spring Boot into remoted services you can run and redeploy on a laptop with minimal platform glue.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames a customer story: a small Spring Boot shop API that worked until hiring slowed onboarding and merge conflicts grew. Familiar code-level practices and Maven modules helped only partly, because API layers still pulled in concrete implementations and runtime sprawl made even shrinking deployments painful compared with spinning up full cloud stacks locally.

He traces the same tradeoffs from EJB 2.1 remote versus local beans through modern service buses and discovery, then introduces JLupin as a microservice runtime that bundles orchestration pieces developers otherwise stitch from Spring Cloud, Mesos, Marathon, and similar tools. A shortened GeeCON demo adds REST, storage, and customer services via an IntelliJ plugin, wires interfaces without hard implementation dependencies, and uses delegators for binary in-process calls with built-in balancing. He starts the platform node, Maven deploys services, sketches servlet versus native JVM (and optional polyglot) services, and walks blue-green style restarts, nginx fronting, and a web console for uploads and node metrics.

Practitioners hear that configuration—not business code—carries most JLupin-specific structure, that hot redeploy can continue load tests during swaps when setup is right, and that Polish banks reportedly run large JLupin estates. The closing message is to develop and stress the full platform on a single PC before leaning on remote Kubernetes-scale tooling.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Andrey Adamovich
talks.teaser: Shows why Java functions on serverless platforms face cold-start delays, with a live load test and mitigation options.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that serverless is a misleading name, since servers still exist somewhere. It presents the idea instead as a billing model where you pay only for the resources you use and leave infrastructure to the provider. Functions still depend on databases, storage and messaging bought from a cloud provider, and Java support has lagged behind other languages on several platforms.

A middle section follows a community automation project moved from local scripts to AWS Lambda, with API Gateway, S3 storage and a Slack command. Limits surfaced quickly: gateway timeouts, Slack's three-second reply window, image generation taking around a minute, and JVM cold starts of two to three seconds. A routing function that hands work to another function asynchronously helped, and scheduled warm-up events reduced cold starts, though parallel requests still launched new instances. A live load test of a newly deployed Java function showed a median near 400 milliseconds and a maximum around two and a half seconds, improving once warm.

A later project, a searchable database of developer videos, handled around 40,000 users in one day without capacity work, at low cost. For Java, the talk covered mitigations such as class data sharing in Java 10, ahead-of-time compilation and GraalVM native images, where one experiment roughly cut cold start time threefold. The takeaway: Java suits functions without strict latency needs, while provider runtimes and tooling are still catching up.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Andrea Provaglio
talks.teaser: Shows how listening, curiosity and courage can shift leadership in agile organizations, through metaphors and a client case.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an agile enterprise coach who moved from writing code to working with people, opens with a metaphor: an organization that does not want to change cannot be transformed by an outsider. Visible practices rest on deeper paradigms, and he defines leadership as the deliberate force that moves a group from here to there. He contrasts top-down hierarchies with networks of teams, where two-way communication matters most.

A client case follows. An IT department of about 50 people, serving product managers across roughly 30 nations, was swamped by uncoordinated requests, while a cafeteria screen ranking top sellers fuelled competition among those managers. He explains the pressure with the tragedy of the commons, comparing two fishermen who each overfish one lake; in software, demands for ever more features drain the team. He also covers listening levels, from downloading to generative listening, with judgment, cynicism and fear as blockers and curiosity, empathy and courage as enablers.

He notes that Scrum and Extreme Programming both list courage, respect and openness among their values, yet teams often keep only the process. Based on his own impression rather than measured data, he suggests roughly 95% of companies seeking agile coaching really want consultancy that fixes them without touching power structures. His advice: pay attention to how you listen, practise with a colleague, and lead by example, because you can change yourself but not other people.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Mark West - A Practical-ish Introduction to Data Science
talks.teaser: Maps data science workflow and roles, covers regression, trees, and clustering, and builds a Titanic classifier in scikit-learn.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing data science as interdisciplinary work that blends domain knowledge, software skills, and statistics, then contrasts it with traditional business intelligence and separates machine learning from the broader AI hype. The speaker outlines an iterative hypothesis-driven workflow—from gathering data through exploration, modeling, interpretation, and stakeholder communication—and stresses that production deployment and supporting roles such as data engineering, visualization, and process ownership sit outside the lone scientist stereotype.

The middle segment explains supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning at a high level, then dives into practical algorithm families: linear regression and least squares, decision trees with overfitting and random forests, and k-means clustering with elbow plots. Generalization versus memorization is illustrated with intuitive model-quality examples before each technique’s strengths, weaknesses, and data pitfalls are discussed.

The close is a Jupyter notebook walkthrough on the classic Titanic dataset: exploratory stats, honorific-based age imputation, encoding categorical fields, visual checks against class and gender hypotheses, train-test splitting, default and depth-limited decision trees, accuracy and confusion matrices, and a brief note on free tooling such as scikit-learn and Anaconda. Takeaways emphasize starting with simple algorithms, investing in feature engineering and domain sense, and tuning hyperparameters only when the underlying method is understood.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Edson Yanaga
talks.teaser: Walks through Effective Java's third edition advice with live coding on factories, equality, lambdas and enums.
talks.summary:
The session revisits the third edition of Joshua Bloch's Effective Java, picking out favourite items and newer additions from the book and working through them with live coding. It starts with object creation, arguing for static factory methods over constructors. Factories can have descriptive names, return cached instances, return subtypes behind an interface, and validate arguments early so invalid objects never get created.

The middle of the talk covers value objects. For an immutable class, the speaker writes equals and hashCode by hand and points out the cost of boxing primitive fields and of varargs array allocation in Objects.hash. Caching the hash code is suggested when the object cannot change. toString is framed as a debugging aid, while a Formattable implementation handles user-facing output, and getters should be added only when data is exposed on purpose. Comparable is implemented with comparator chains, moved into a reusable constant.

The Java 8 section looks at when to declare a @FunctionalInterface, why the standard java.util.function types cover most needs, and how method references can replace many lambdas, unless the reference becomes longer than the lambda. A template method is refactored into a strategy using suppliers. Enums are shown carrying operations through a function field and a separate class, and as the simplest safe singleton. The speaker closes by noting where he differs from the book and that generated-code libraries such as Lombok are a matter of taste.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Alex Soto
talks.teaser: The session maps isolation, data, resilience, and delivery patterns from microservices onto well-structured Java monoliths.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames the talk around industry fatigue with microservices and argues that many of their benefits can be reproduced inside a single deployable application when the codebase is structured deliberately. He walks through module boundaries using API versus implementation splits, enforcement with ArchUnit or Java 9 modules, per-module database schemas with Flyway migrations, and parallel data loading with RxJava when cross-schema joins are forbidden.

Network-oriented resilience appears next: circuit breakers on database or remote calls, demonstrated with a sample games catalog project and Resilience4j rather than heavier libraries. The middle and closing sections shift to delivery culture and infrastructure—Docker images, Kubernetes replicas, replicated SQL, in-memory grids instead of sticky sessions, and blue-green, canary, or dark-launch release tactics applied to monoliths.

The closing argument is operational: master frequent, safe monolith releases and modular discipline first; only then consider splitting services. Stack Overflow is cited as a high-traffic monolith with very frequent deployments, underscoring that architecture style alone does not determine release cadence.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2018: Anton Arhipov - Kotlin DSL in under an hour
talks.teaser: A live-coded path turns Java builder APIs into nested Kotlin internal DSLs using lambdas, receivers, apply, and scope-safe markers.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting external DSLs, which need custom grammars and parsers, with internal DSLs that reuse a host language’s syntax and tooling. A rapid tour of real Kotlin libraries—including HTML generation, Android layouts, Gradle scripts, database access, routing, Kubernetes configs, and CI configuration—highlights the shared pattern of nested blocks and task-specific vocabulary.

The core demo starts from unchanged Java model classes and builder calls, then migrates to Kotlin via IDE conversion, extension properties for pretty printing, and a factory built around lambdas, lambda-with-receiver, and apply. Nested twitter and company sections illustrate how extension functions shape readable configuration, while @DslMarker-backed wrapper types stop calls from leaking across the wrong nested scope. A shorter second example uses infix extensions on integers and dates to make timestamps more readable than raw java.time calls.

Practitioners should treat DSL sugar as worthwhile when the same structured configuration repeats across projects and can ship as a library, not for one-off syntax sugar. Compiler-checked receivers reduce whole classes of nesting mistakes, and the Q&A touches contracts, gradual adoption from Java, interoperability, and why markers trade some initialization flexibility for safety.

talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: X. Rene-Corail / I. Balosin - Building evolutionary architectures in agile environments.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Charles Oliver Nutter - Keep Moving Forward: How Open Source Changed Java Forever
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Charles Oliver Nutter - Keep Moving Forward: How Open Source Changed Java Forever.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Milen Dyankov
talks.teaser: Explains how to split a Java application into modules and services, comparing layouts through a live cleaning-business analogy.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to break a large Java application into smaller, well-bounded parts. Rather than naming the approach with one buzzword, the speaker walks through a running analogy about a small house-cleaning business that grows step by step. Each stage is compiled and run live, showing what goes wrong. A flat layout lets any component reach any other, and hiding internal packages alone still leaves shared assets exposed to callers.

The next stages move toward a company-style structure, where internal processes sit behind a published use-case interface. Java 9's module system enforces those boundaries at compile time, but it requires knowing which modules to load up front, and one failing component can stop the whole service. Using the service loader lets a backup provider be swapped in. The OSGi approach, shown on Java 8, allows bundles to be installed and started at runtime, and package versioning rules, checked during the build, flag interface changes that would break existing consumers.

The closing point is that arguing over architecture labels distracts from the consequences of design choices. The speaker suggests that a practitioner should focus on clear boundaries, explicit contracts and semantic versioning, and keep the codebase tidy over time, much as one would teach a child to keep a room clean.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Tobi Ajila - The future of Java

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Bruno Bossola - Are you using an OS library? There's a good chance you are vulnerable
talks.teaser: Explores famous breach cases tied to open-source libraries and walks through a Jackson databind exploit plus dependency scanning defenses.
talks.summary:
Modern applications lean heavily on open-source libraries, yet teams often audit only code they wrote while direct and transitive dependencies age in production. The presentation opens with three well-known incidents: San Francisco’s MTA weekend shutdown after ransomware encrypted 2,112 systems via Java deserialization and Apache Commons Collections on WebLogic; a Canada Revenue Agency compromise linked to Apache Struts 2 multipart header remote code execution; and Equifax’s theft of roughly 143 million U.S. and 44 million U.K. records when Struts 2 was not patched months after a public fix.

The middle section explains Maven dependency trees, hidden transitive flaws, and screenshots of vulnerable Vert.x, Struts, and Spring Boot stacks. A live demo targets Jackson databind polymorphic type handling: malicious JSON instantiates an Xalan TemplatesImpl payload (or JDK classes on older releases), achieving code execution on a small Spark Java product API. The speaker notes such an end-to-end exploit took only about two hours to prepare once the weakness was understood.

Preventive guidance centers on continuous dependency scanning in CI/CD using tools such as OWASP Dependency-Check or commercial analyzers, illustrated with a scan flagging Jackson issues and recommending upgrades. The close rebuts common management excuses—that unused APIs, input validation, or routine penetration tests are enough—because one enabled mapper line or a missed transitive jar can bypass those controls. The practical takeaway is to update production libraries now and automate checks on every build.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Jurgen Appelo
talks.teaser: Shows how to make workplace change stick by celebrating experiments and using game mechanics like scarcity and social pressure.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by observing that speakers at conferences try to persuade audiences to change, yet ideas rarely stick. Jurgen Appelo uses a ship's bell rung beside a coffee machine to celebrate team wins, then argues that teams should also celebrate well-run experiments that fail, not only successes. He presents a grid that sorts good and bad practices against success and failure.

The middle of the talk covers practices he tried with a remote team. Members drew personal mind maps that colleagues then questioned, and a video-call 360-degree feedback round asked each person for two compliments and one suggestion, with a puppet held to soften criticism. A values workshop failed because nobody remembered the values afterwards. He contrasts slow, rule-based change programmes with the fast uptake of Pokémon Go, and walks through an eight-part gamification model covering accomplishment, scarcity, unpredictability, ownership, and social influence. Examples include a limited supply of recognition cards, a Friday selfie wall, a bottle spun to pick the next participant, and a cake limit on a Kanban board.

He closes with advice for people working in rigid organisations: be a square on the outside by complying with forms and Gantt charts, while running agile practices as a circle inside. He describes filling in appraisal forms over dinner with his team, which built trust with his CEO. Listeners are urged to think about how to make their ideas engaging before presenting them to colleagues.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Chris Thalinger - Twitter's quest for a wholly Graal runtime
talks.teaser: Walks through enabling Graal on JDK 10, benchmarking against C2, and lessons from months of Twitter production use.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that the Graal just-in-time compiler is production-ready for large Java and Scala workloads, separate from the broader GraalVM distribution. It motivates adoption with Twitter’s need for a mature alternative to HotSpot’s C2, including months of datacenter use without operational incidents, while steering cost-savings depth to other recordings.

Most of the session answers where to obtain Graal via OpenJDK 9 and 10, JVMCI in chapter 43, and the jdk.internal.vm.compiler module, then demonstrates flags on a freshly provisioned Linux cloud host: unlock experimental JVMCI, select the JVMCI compiler, tune heap sizes for fair comparison with C2, and interpret lazy initialization and tiered compilation. The speaker contrasts C2’s C++ native compiler graphs with Graal compiling on the Java heap, explains bootstrap and meta-circular warmup using spare cores, and walks through GC logging on benchmarks. Production-oriented numbers include roughly two and a half percent fewer GC cycles and about eleven percent less CPU on a Scala tweet microservice, plus a factory benchmark where Graal roughly halves GCs and runs notably faster.

Practitioners should treat micro-benchmarks skeptically, expect Scala-friendly inlining and partial escape analysis wins, and plan heap headroom for rare large compilations during startup before traffic arrives. JDK 9 or 10 ahead-of-time compilation of Graal can remove bootstrap pain; otherwise enabling the documented flags and warming services like ordinary deployments matches Twitter’s approach.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Marc Struberg - The cool and the cruel of MicroService
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Marc Struberg - The cool and the cruel of MicroService.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Dmitry Ornatsky - Demystifying AI-chatbots: just add CUI to your business apps
talks.teaser: Explains where chatbots help retail businesses and how a conversational search assistant was built with off-the-shelf tools.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at chatbots and conversational user interfaces from a business perspective rather than an AI research one. The speaker, who works at a professional services firm, argues that text and voice interfaces make sense because people already message more than they call, and because natural language can help users reach features that menus bury. The talk also places the current hype on an analyst-style curve, using an early Microsoft Twitter bot that turned offensive within a day as a cautionary example.

The main case is retail conversational search. When a catalogue search returns nothing, an assistant can suggest a close alternative, such as the same dress in another colour or a slightly longer style, or narrow a query that spans unrelated product categories. One architecture places channel adapters in front of a shared core of language understanding and a dialogue manager, connected to back-end business systems. The example system combined Google's Dialogflow with MongoDB for conversation history and a search tagger. The speaker stressed that shopping vocabulary differs from everyday English, so systems need synonyms, typo tolerance, brand recognition and checks for mis-attributed products.

Toolkits, both hosted dialogue services and a modular research platform, can be specialised with sample requests mapped to intents, so people without deep AI expertise can build useful, narrowly focused bots. Success can be measured by business conversion and by precision and recall on intent classification. The closing questions covered human-likeness and deception, and the speaker's view was that narrowly scoped assistants are the practical goal.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Julian Warszawski - Models vs Reality: Quest for the Roots of Complexity
talks.teaser: Shows how misfit models drive complexity and why domain language aligns business intent with engineering better than tools.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with an audience sketch of a car to show that a model can be adequate for one purpose and misleading for another. He contrasts schematics, concept art, wireframes, and mockups, then ties the idea to model-dependent realism: several models can be equally valid within their bounded context, including whimsical examples that describe behavior without matching physical reality.

He argues that most software constructs are abstractions for communication, layered on operating systems and languages, and warns that teams often pile mass on good foundations without extending abstractions thoughtfully. The middle of the talk maps the hardware–software–business stack, where physicality and formality fade and miscommunication thrives at the business boundary. He compares informal metaphors, semi-formal product artifacts, and domain-specific languages such as SQL and GraphQL, noting cases where non-programmers queried APIs directly. Complexity metrics such as cyclomatic and cognitive complexity help at method scale but struggle at system scale; structure tools and dependency thinking address architecture yet miss whether the business idea itself is wrong.

The close ranks wrong code, wrong specification, and wrong idea, urging engineers to break organizational walls, enable experiments and deployments that test ideas, and use practices like event storming and domain-driven design. His takeaway is that complexity often lies in how teams choose to speak about systems; codifying a language for the business can matter more than handing off another tool.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Jakub Kubrynski
talks.teaser: Explores quantified architecture metrics, safe-to-fail design, and observability stacks that turn vague quality goals into measurable KPIs.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by contrasting stereotypical architects who live in diagrams and vague qualities with an engineering mindset that treats architecture as measurable structure. He argues that goals like scalability, security, and testability mean nothing until they are written down with scales, initial values, and credibility estimates, and that designs must remain implementable by real teams.

He walks through war stories and organizational patterns: production code-coverage experiments showing most lines never run, a Hibernate cache misconfiguration fixed only after measurement, explicit definitions of testability, and the shift from fail-safe testing armies to safe-to-fail designs using feature flags and fast rollback. He describes matrices used in his company—zero schema migration or cross-service contract surprises, sub-hour time to fix, backup windows, portability between cloud vendors—and tools such as Flyway, contract tests, infrastructure-as-code, and enforced naming conventions that make violations fail builds.

The closing section ties decisions to dashboards: Prometheus, alerting, and business-visible KPIs such as onboarding duration. Practitioners should inventory requirements as scales in roughly a day, baseline current values, instrument applications quickly, and weigh every architectural change against those numbers so refactoring and reliability work earns budget in terms leaders already track.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Cliff Click - A Crash Course in Modern Hardware
talks.teaser: Explains why CPU speed stopped scaling and how caches, speculative execution and coherency now dominate performance.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a brief history of CPU performance. It contrasts early machines, where instruction counts and page faults drove speed, with the later era of rising clock rates. Clock scaling stalled about a decade ago because of a power limit on heat, and memory latency stayed bound by the distance to off-chip DRAM, so chipmakers added cores instead of raw speed.

The middle covers how processors hide memory latency. Pipelining overlaps instruction stages, while branch prediction, speculative execution, register renaming and multiple issue keep work moving during a cache miss. A dispatch example shows two overlapping misses dominating runtime. A Java singleton without volatile shows how caches and coherency can produce a real data race that returns stale data. Spectre and Meltdown are then explained: speculation leaves changes in cache state, which an attacker reads back with timing measurements to leak secrets.

The closing advice is practical. Cache misses are hard to see in ordinary profilers, so hardware performance counters are needed to confirm them. Repeatedly converting data between formats often costs more than the work itself, so keeping data in raw form and reducing conversions can yield large speedups. Immutable data suits parallel reads, and hyper-threading helps less when shared floating-point units are already saturated.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Miro Cupak - Clean code with Java 9
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Miro Cupak - Clean code with Java 9.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2018 presentation, Miro Cupak discusses how Java 9 introduces several small APIs, convenience methods, and enhancements that improve the ability to write clean, maintainable, and readable code. Drawing inspiration from software design principles and books such as *Clean Code* and *Effective Java*, the talk demonstrates practical improvements using JShell (Java's REPL tool) across collection creation, resource management, interface design, stream processing, optionals, stack traces, and HTTP networking.

### Key Topics
- **JShell (REPL):** A tool for evaluating code snippets and commands interactively, useful for prototyping, quick testing, and exploring APIs.
- **Convenience Factory Methods for Collections:** Static factory methods (`List.of`, `Set.of`, `Map.of`, `Map.ofEntries`) that provide concise syntax for creating truly immutable collections.
- **Try-with-Resources Enhancements:** Allowing final or effectively final variables to be managed directly by try-with-resources blocks without creating redundant local references.
- **Private Methods in Interfaces:** Enabling helper methods to encapsulate common logic between interface default methods without exposing them to the public API.
- **Diamond Operator Improvements:** Extending diamond operator type inference to anonymous inner classes.
- **Stream API Extensions:** Introduction of `takeWhile`, `dropWhile`, improved `iterate` with predicates, and `Stream.ofNullable`.
- **Optional Enhancements:** Additions including `ifPresentOrElse`, `or`, and the `stream()` method for cleaner chained operations.
- **StackWalker API:** A modern, lazy, stream-friendly replacement for `Throwable.getStackTrace()`.
- **Incubator HTTP/2 Client:** A cleaner, feature-rich replacement for `HttpURLConnection` supporting HTTP/2, WebSockets, TLS, and asynchronous calls.

### Technical Details
- **Immutable Collections:** Methods like `List.of(...)` and `Set.of(...)` offer 0–10 fixed-parameter overloads alongside a varargs variant to optimize performance and prevent array allocation overhead. `Map.ofEntries(...)` handles heterogeneous key-value mapping concisely. Returned collections are strictly immutable rather than just unmodifiable views.
- **I/O & Try-with-Resources:** Java 9 eliminates the need to assign resources to fresh variables inside the `try (...)` parentheses. Additionally, `InputStream.transferTo(OutputStream)` provides a single convenience method for streaming bytes between input and output.
- **Stream Control:** `takeWhile` acts like a predicate-based `limit`, and `dropWhile` acts like a predicate-based `skip`. `Stream.iterate` now accepts a predicate condition functioning like a standard `for` loop, mitigating infinite stream bugs. `Stream.ofNullable` creates an empty stream if passed `null`, removing unnecessary ternary or null check boilerplate.
- **Optional Integration:** `Optional.ifPresentOrElse(Consumer, Runnable)` removes conditional branching, `Optional.or(Supplier<Optional>)` enables fluent fallback options, and `Optional.stream()` simplifies flattening streams of optionals via `flatMap(Optional::stream)`.
- **Stack Inspection:** `StackWalker` traverses JVM stack frames lazily via streams, avoiding the heavy performance cost of eagerly capturing entire stack traces. It can retain class references directly and permits filtering or limiting stack depth.
- **HTTP/2 Client:** Split cleanly into `HttpClient`, `HttpRequest`, and `HttpResponse` using the builder pattern and supporting asynchronous flows with `sendAsync(...)` returning a `CompletableFuture`. In Java 9 and 10, it is distributed as an incubator module.

### Takeaways
Developers can significantly clean up Java codebases by replacing verbose patterns and external boilerplate libraries with native JDK 9 capabilities. Defaulting to immutable collections, leveraging stream and optional convenience methods, adopting `StackWalker`, and utilizing modern try-with-resources semantics eliminate defensive copying, null checks, and legacy side-effect-heavy APIs.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Rafał Łojek - What do Software Developers have common with Motorcycle Drivers?
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Rafał Łojek - What do Software Developers have common with Motorcycle Drivers?.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Charlie Gracie - Deep dive into the Eclipse OpenJ9 GC technologies
talks.teaser: Walks through OpenJ9's garbage collection policies and their trade-offs in pauses, throughput and memory footprint.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Eclipse OpenJ9, an open-source Java virtual machine that IBM has run internally for about 17 years, and explains why garbage collection can leave a process using more memory than its heap setting and can cause unpredictable pauses. The speaker also covers the read and write barriers a collector may insert into object accesses, which add hidden runtime cost.

The main part walks through OpenJ9's collector policies. The default generational concurrent policy splits the heap into a nursery and a tenured space, copies live nursery objects between survivor spaces, and runs a concurrent mark-sweep collection for the old space, with application threads doing part of that marking work. The metronome policy is an incremental collector with no compaction. Its default pause goal is three milliseconds, and it guarantees the application about 70 percent of each timing window. The balanced policy is region-based and uses partial collections plus a global mark phase, aimed at very large heaps and NUMA machines.

The closing section compares the trade-offs. The default collector gives the best throughput for most applications, balanced becomes worthwhile for heaps over 20 gigabytes, and metronome suits workloads that cannot tolerate pauses but accept lower throughput. The speaker encourages developers to try alternative collectors, since they can change both throughput and pause times.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Michael Plöd - Reducing Chattiness: Communication Strategies for Microservices
talks.teaser: Explains how to pick communication styles between microservices, from bounded contexts and REST to messaging and event-driven designs.
talks.summary:
Michael Plöd opens by noting that teams often adopt microservices by default, and that splitting a monolith exposes dependencies that were previously hidden inside it. Each new boundary can become a remote call, so the communication load grows quickly. He stresses that distributed systems are hard and that a monolith may be the better choice for some teams.

Next he covers integration beyond technology: team communication, coupling at the business-model level, and explicit quality criteria such as consistency and scalability. Using domain-driven design, he explains bounded contexts and a context map, with relationships such as upstream and downstream, conformist, anti-corruption layer, shared kernel, published language and separate ways, and links them to Conway's law. Technically, he compares synchronous REST, which needs service discovery, resilience patterns such as bulkheads and circuit breakers, and load balancing. He then covers messaging, where latency is the main concern, and event-driven designs, where he advises against embedding mutable REST endpoints in events. Orchestration versus choreography is presented as a macro-architecture decision.

He also presents HTTP Atom feeds as a way to reach eventual consistency without running a message broker, and warns against using event sourcing as a global pattern. He closes by urging teams to decouple business models, make quality criteria first-class, and agree on a few macro-architecture rules instead of trying to master every option.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Sven Decker - Building lightning-fast sites for the mobile web
talks.teaser: A lead engineer explains how mobile traffic dominance reshapes e-commerce conversion and which frontend techniques cut load times.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with traffic patterns at a large German online marketplace, where smartphone share dominates desktop and tablet yet conversion still lags until pages feel instant. The speaker ties revenue to perceived speed, citing multi-second load thresholds and poor connectivity as blockers, especially on mobile networks.

The middle walks through architectural responses: bundling assets, limiting parallel requests, inlining critical CSS, lazy-loading images, and leaning on Google’s accelerated mobile pages and cache-oriented delivery so first paint arrives before heavy scripts. A live-style demo contrasts an older storefront against a trimmed page with fewer round trips, faster hero content, and a visible purchase path.

The close covers greenfield rollout, conversion flags on key funnels, and measured gains—often more than double on mobile versus legacy desktop-first stacks. The takeaway for practitioners is to treat mobile performance as a product requirement, instrument it, and align design, frontend, and caching so checkout stays usable on slow links.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Volker Simonis - Class Data Sharing in the HotSpot VM
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Volker Simonis - Class Data Sharing in the HotSpot VM.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Marc Philip - JUnit 5 Extensions: From Conditional Test Execution to Test Templates
talks.teaser: Walks through JUnit 5 Jupiter extension points from conditional execution to custom test templates and parameterized sources.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with JUnit 5’s release history and its split architecture: the platform for discovery and reporting, the Vintage engine for older tests, and Jupiter as the modern programming and extension model. Registration paths are outlined—`@ExtendWith`, field-based registration, and global hooks via the service loader—along with composed meta-annotations.

Working examples show how extension points solve everyday testing problems. An execution condition skips methods unless a system property matches allowed deployment stages, with global auto-detection and a property to deactivate conditions. A Docker-backed fixture uses before/after callbacks, the extension store for container IDs and shared clients, and a parameter resolver that injects dynamic port bindings for parallel runs. Built-in parameterized sources lead to a custom JSON arguments provider, and a test-template provider repeats invocations to illustrate simple property-style checks with assumptions.

The close emphasizes combining extension interfaces, upstream support utilities, growing third-party extensions, and where to find guides, sample projects, and Javadoc. Practitioners gain patterns for environment-aware integration tests, reusable fixtures, custom data sources, and multi-invocation templates without forking the framework.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Hanno Embregts - QWERTY or DVORAK? Debunking the Keyboard Layout Myths
talks.teaser: Traces QWERTY’s real history, weighs common layout myths, and outlines what a Dvorak switch costs in time, speed, and RSI relief.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why the speaker considered leaving QWERTY after years of touch typing and ongoing repetitive strain issues, stressing that speed was never the main driver. Audience polls show almost everyone still uses QWERTY and captures guesses about why the keys are arranged that way.

The core walk-through reviews four popular explanations: slowing typists, slowing telegraph traffic, preventing mechanical jams, and typing “typewriter” on the top row. Historical timing, typewriter mechanics, and iterative layout changes—driven partly by telegraph operators correcting Morse-style input—argue against several myths while leaving jam prevention partly open. The talk concludes that QWERTY reflects obsolete constraints.

Dvorak’s home-row letter distribution is compared to QWERTY with simple frequency stats. The speaker describes a year-long learning path, dual-layout friction (passwords, Citrix, punctuation, shell commands), and charts showing Dvorak still below prior QWERTY speed. Practitioners hear a blunt takeaway: switch only for ergonomics and patience, not guaranteed velocity.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Michał Płachta - Building testable APIs using functions & meshes
talks.teaser: Demonstrates functional APIs, server-free HTTP route tests, and mesh routing for isolated production trials via a Pac-Man game server.
talks.summary:
The speaker challenges the traditional test pyramid and argues that the foundation should be fast, stable tests that exercise real behavior with far less mocking. He walks through a Pac-Man game engine in Scala built on immutable game state and pure state-to-state functions, with small readable tests for movement, rotation, walls, and dots; the entire engine suite completes in under a second.

He then extends the same style to HTTP APIs. Game routes are factory functions that accept narrow function dependencies instead of embedding state, separating JSON handling from domain logic. Akka HTTP routes are tested against production code without starting a server, using simple fakes and single-function stubs. A thin integration layer ties concurrent state storage, the engine, and a test scheduler while still asserting through HTTP.

For distributed setups he turns to service mesh sidecars and control planes for discovery, resilience, and observability. On minikube he deploys backend and frontend pods, then applies route rules so only his requests hit a new grid version while everyone else sees stable production. He closes by wiring mesh-level metrics and describing isolated production experiments as the pyramid’s hard top, with a public repository for the sample project.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Marcus Fihlon - Kotlin EE: Boost your Productivity
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Marcus Fihlon - Kotlin EE: Boost your Productivity.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2018 presentation, Marcus Fihlon explores how combining the Kotlin programming language with Jakarta EE (formerly Java EE) and Docker containers can create lightweight, productive microservices. Addressing common criticisms that Java EE is inherently bloated, Fihlon argues that modern enterprise APIs combined with containerization offer a streamlined development model that delegates transitive dependency management to server runtimes while leveraging Kotlin's concise, modern syntax.

### Key Topics
- **Kotlin Language Features**: Statically typed, interoperable with Java bytecode, transpiles to JavaScript, and compiles to native code (supporting Android and iOS). Kotlin reduces Java boilerplate via features like immutability (`val` vs. `var`), null-safety types, data classes, string templates, built-in singletons (`object`), and co-routines.
- **Jakarta EE and Dependency Management**: Rather than managing complex dependency trees and transitive version conflicts (e.g., conflicting Guava versions) in Maven or Gradle, Jakarta EE offers "library management as a service." Standard APIs (JAX-RS, JPA, CDI, Bean Validation) are provided by the runtime application server (e.g., Payara Micro).
- **Thin Docker Images**: By separating application logic into a tiny `.war` file layered over pre-configured vendor application server images, developers maintain minimal Docker build times and small deployment artifacts.
- **Kotlin & Enterprise Runtime Pitfalls**: Standard Java EE application servers rely on proxies and reflection, requiring non-final classes and zero-argument constructors. Because Kotlin classes are final by default and generate parameterized constructors, builds must configure compiler plugins: `kotlin-allopen` and `kotlin-noarg`.

### Technical Details
Fihlon demonstrates a live implementation of two microservices using Gradle and JAX-RS running inside Payara Micro Docker images:
- **Time Service**: An internal REST endpoint that outputs plain-text timestamps using `java.time.LocalDateTime.now()`. It is mapped to the internal Docker network and not exposed externally.
- **Hello Service**: An externally accessible REST endpoint accepting dynamic path parameters via `@PathParam("name")`. It uses the JAX-RS `ClientBuilder` to query the internal `time-service` using Docker's built-in DNS service discovery and round-robin load balancing (`http://time-service:8080/api/time`).
- **Container Orchestration with Docker Swarm**: Using `docker-machine` with VirtualBox drivers, Fihlon provisions a local four-node Swarm cluster (one manager and three worker nodes). He creates an overlay network (`geekcon`), deploys the visualizer tool to track nodes, launches services using `docker service create`, and scales both services across the cluster to three replicas using `docker service update --replicas 3`.

### Takeaways
- Combining Kotlin with Jakarta EE avoids verbose enterprise boilerplate while keeping business logic clean and expressive.
- Utilizing build-time compiler plugins (`allopen` and `noarg`) seamlessly resolves reflection and proxying constraints imposed by EE application servers.
- Packaging enterprise applications into thin Docker layers deployed on container orchestration tools like Docker Swarm provides reproducible, easily scalable, and testable microservice architectures.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Alexander Tarlinder - Using Developer Testing to Boost the Quality of Your Code
talks.teaser: Lays out practical developer testing techniques, from test design and test doubles to legacy code, to improve code quality.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames developer testing as the deliberate and systematic use of testing tools and techniques during development. Faster delivery cycles, from sprints to continuous delivery, make manual regression checks impossible, so developers need to build quality in. He also points to harder problems, such as software calling APIs at high speed and many partner integrations.

The talk revisits unit test basics: a naming scheme that states the subject and expected outcome, keeping the arrange, act and assert stages separate, and separating semantic from syntactic assertions. Test design techniques follow, including equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables and state transition testing. Testability is broken down into controllability, observability and smallness, with dependency-breaking patterns for legacy code. Test doubles are distinguished: stubs and dummies cannot fail a test, while mocks verify interactions and are often overused. Parameterized, theory and generative tests are presented as ways to scale input coverage.

Test-driven development is treated as a design technique, with fake-it, obvious implementation and triangulation as ways to get from red to green, and negative cases written last. Higher-level tests are described as more complex, less stable and slower to diagnose. The closing advice is to pick competencies based on the system profile, such as a greenfield project or legacy code, and apply them deliberately.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Norbert Wójtowicz - Datalog: Biting the Silver Bullet
talks.teaser: A step-by-step GitHub example shows how Datalog and entity-attribute-value facts model joins, graphs, updates, and client pull queries.
talks.summary:
Norbert opens by positioning Datalog as a declarative way to model information systems when data arrives unpredictably and must be stored, combined, and returned. He argues that entity, attribute, and value triples are enough to represent a domain, then walks through a GitHub-shaped example: users, emails, organizations, repositories, owners, forks, languages, and stars, all as append-only facts without upfront schema tables.

The middle of the talk builds query power in small steps: pattern matching, variables, joins, rules with OR semantics, recursion for graph questions, multi-valued attributes, aggregations such as star counts, and host-language predicates including Lucene full-text search. He explains how EAV indexing can mimic key-value, row, column, document, and graph access patterns, then addresses updates through transactions with assertion and retraction flags, metadata on attributes and transactions, and time-travel APIs such as as-of, since, history, filtering for redacted client views, and hypothetical what-if queries. A pull API sketches GraphQL-shaped data retrieval for clients.

Practitioners leave with concrete patterns for flexible domain modeling, safer evolution than rigid SQL schemas, event-sourcing-friendly raw storage, and production paths via Datomic and DataScript, including scaling reads and a cloud deployment sketch. A linked gist points to deeper workshop material.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Michał Matłoka
talks.teaser: Maps the big data landscape, from storage trade-offs and MapReduce to stream processing guarantees and resource managers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a quick tour of the big data landscape, noting how many tools and papers exist and how the hype has moved from big data to machine learning and blockchain. It defines big data through volume, velocity and variety, and warns that clusters add complexity, so a single node is often faster until the data truly outgrows it.

Using a hypothetical air-pollution network of thousands of sensors, the talk starts with storage. It explains why relational databases lose features when spread across clusters, tying this to the CAP theorem and the ACID versus BASE trade-offs, and surveys NoSQL models such as key-value, columnar, document and graph stores. One cited benchmark found a single CockroachDB node two to seven times slower than a single Postgres node. Batch processing with MapReduce and stream processing follow, covering event time, windows, watermarks, delivery guarantees, and the Lambda and Kappa architectures.

The closing section looks at querying across several databases with Presto, which exposes SQL and JDBC access over MySQL and Cassandra, and at resource managers such as YARN, Mesos and Kubernetes for placing services on shared machines. Attendees are pointed to open datasets and reading material. The main takeaway is to choose the simplest tool that fits the problem and to match delivery guarantees to what the use case can tolerate.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Tomer Gabel - Slaying Sacred Cows: Deconstructing Dependency Injection
talks.teaser: Questions whether inversion of control containers really help, arguing that manual wiring keeps code easier to navigate and test.
talks.summary:
The talk sets out to answer a simple question: is dependency injection a good thing? The speaker first separates the terms. The D in SOLID refers to dependency inversion, not injection, and the framework-driven approach many developers have in mind is really an inversion of control container. Dependency injection itself only asks that a component receive its dependencies instead of creating them, and it needs no framework or container.

The middle of the talk compares manual wiring of a small service's object graph with an equivalent container-based module, and finds about the same amount of code in each. The speaker argues that automatic wiring hides what an application is made of, pushes configuration mistakes to runtime, and complicates testing, because tests must rebuild and mock a large graph instead of only the unit under test. Containers also make dependencies proliferate, since adding a constructor parameter is effortless. Dynamic reconfiguration at runtime is dismissed as rare in practice, and aspect-oriented programming is set aside as a separate debate.

The closing argument is that containers trade coherence for convenience. They let less experienced developers become productive quickly, but large systems built on them become hard to navigate and maintain. The practical takeaway is to keep wiring explicit and to build smaller systems with fewer hidden dependencies.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Mauricio Salatino - From Java EE to Spring Cloud
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from moving an open source project from Java EE to Spring Cloud and onto Kubernetes.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts an open source team's move away from Java EE toward cloud native applications built with Spring Cloud, and what that shift demanded in practice. The speaker starts with the team's situation: a large existing monolith with around 60 services, from which they chose a first set of six core services to rebuild as separate, bounded projects. He explains early decisions about shared dependency management, optional infrastructure such as databases and message brokers, running that infrastructure locally with Docker Compose, and using multi-stage Docker builds to keep images small.

The middle section covers the trade-offs of Spring Cloud's abstraction layers. Choosing a service registry or tracing tool means each service picks up that implementation's dependencies, and the footprint grows with every option supported. Moving to Kubernetes changes the picture, because its built-in service discovery and configuration maps make some Spring Cloud components unnecessary. The speaker then demonstrates Jenkins X, importing a sample Spring Boot service, generating its pipeline, and promoting it through staging environments.

The takeaway is to adopt cloud native patterns gradually rather than rewriting everything at once, to understand how the platform and its tools work instead of inventing your own, and to rely on established community practices for pipelines, environments and service bindings.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Andrei Solntsev - Selenide: fall in love after 15 slides
talks.teaser: Shows how the Java library Selenide makes browser UI tests concise and stable, sparing testers from timing and Ajax issues.
talks.summary:
The session starts from a common problem: developers often skip UI tests because they are tricky and tedious, yet an web application needs checks that keep passing after many changes. The speaker presents Selenide as a free, open-source Java library for writing short, readable browser tests that can serve as executable documentation of how the application should behave.

The middle of the talk is a live demonstration. The speaker opens a browser, locates elements, clicks buttons, fills in fields and checks texts, then walks through a short Google search test. Selenide handles waiting for elements, so testers do not need to write their own timeouts for Ajax calls or slow page updates. The speaker also shows how elements can be found by their text or by their parent and child relationships when exact locators are not available, and mentions screenshots and custom conditions as ways to extend checks.

The closing part is a quick overview rather than a deep dive. The main takeaway for practitioners is that a Selenide test can stay focused on business logic instead of browser timing quirks, which makes UI coverage easier to maintain as the application changes.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Adam Dubiel - Back to basics: threads
talks.teaser: Examines how JVM threads map to Linux natives, traces startup thread bursts, and explains thread pool pitfalls in Spring defaults.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by asking when anyone last ran a truly single-threaded JVM application in production, arguing that frameworks hide where threads come from and how many exist. On a simple Spring Boot service with HTTP and MongoDB, he charts roughly twenty-five seconds of startup: an initial burst of about twenty JVM threads, more near six or seven seconds for a total near thirty-five, then roughly one hundred additional threads when traffic arrives.

He explains that a Linux process is a shared-memory collection of threads, and that JVM threads are native pthreads observable via ps, top, /proc, and jstack. Matching hot threads to Java stacks requires converting the native ID from ps to hex and finding it in jstack; from Java 9 onward, set thread names can surface in ps (fifteen characters). Native memory tracking illustrates on the order of one megabyte per thread stack by default, while virtual versus resident size shows lazy stack growth and the risk of evening load spikes. Ubuntu’s max user processes limit (around eight thousand) and context-switch cache effects motivate keeping thread counts closer to CPU cores.

Spring’s default SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor spawns unbounded new threads per @Async work; fixed pools use unbounded queues unless configured via ThreadPoolExecutor. Pools start lazily, so many HTTP worker threads appear only after traffic; prestartAllCoreThreads can warm them. Unified JVM logging (Java 9+) can log every thread birth. The closing advice is to treat JVM threads as OS threads for troubleshooting, limit thread count where it hurts CPU-bound work, and audit library defaults for pools and executors.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Jarek Ratajski - Walking in Code
talks.teaser: Shows how PMD violation data becomes a walkable 3D code galaxy in the browser using A-Frame, Three.js, and a Scala JSON server.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with human–computer interaction frustrations familiar to developers: cramped flat screens, keyboard-bound typing, and long hours in a chair. Gaming-grade VR convinced the speaker that immersion could change how people relate to software, but the goal is not another game—it is a way to wander through real project code instead of drowning in flat reports.

On legacy Java engagements the speaker leans on static analysis such as PMD and Sonar, with red and green cues for hotspots. The demo maps PMD XML through a Scala cache server into JSON consumed by an A-Frame scene in the browser: classes appear as colored blocks, import relationships as lines, and related types cluster like a galaxy. Volunteers try HTC Vive navigation while the room watches; the speaker compares Unity and Unreal with A-Frame and vanilla JavaScript, notes shaky VR controller support, and explains a force-based layout that uses springs and dispersion over hundreds of simulation steps before positions stabilize.

Practitioners should expect strong passive exploration but weak text editing and blurry glyphs at Vive resolution; dictation and Web Speech API clashed with Firefox, the browser that worked best for WebVR at the time. The takeaway is that browser VR plus existing analysis output can make codebase tours memorable and fast to prototype, while headset ecosystems and layout stability after refactors remain open problems before the approach suits daily professional use.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Jakub Kubrynski - Infrastructure as a code simplified by conventions
talks.teaser: Shows how strict naming conventions cut complexity when rolling out infrastructure as code with Jenkins, Terraform, and Ansible.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing infrastructure as code broadly: everything from hypervisors and virtual machines through operating system setup, build pipelines, deployment scripts, and application configuration. Manual operations make disaster recovery slow and error-prone, while per-machine configuration complicates backups and migrations. Code in version control instead makes architecture visible, enforces consistency, and preserves an audit trail tied to issues and authors.

The middle section contrasts configuration with conventions treated as functions that derive deployment values from a few inputs, such as matching application name, repository name, and artifact name. A Jenkins Job DSL example replaces repetitive per-plugin job definitions with a single plugin-name parameter and shared naming rules. The same pattern extends to a Groovy DSL that emits Terraform for Azure—resource groups, networks, subnets, VPN components, and virtual machines link automatically because naming conventions imply relationships without hand-wiring every reference.

The close applies the idea to Ansible host configuration, parameterizing users and service names from the application name so one playbook serves many components. The practical takeaway is to start with the noisiest manual work, codify simple conventions first, then grow automation; without conventions, scripts balloon and teams abandon the effort.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Thomas Enebo - Static vs Dynamic Typing: red &&|| blue pill
talks.teaser: Compares compile-time and runtime type checking through audience polls, syntax puzzles, and decades of multi-language experience.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by lowering expectations and promising few firm conclusions, then polls the room on preference for static typing, dynamic typing, or neither. A quick game with Java, Ruby, Groovy, Crystal, and Haskell shows that syntax alone does not reveal whether a language is static or dynamic.

The core dispute is framed with standard definitions: static languages check types before execution, while dynamic languages check at runtime. Advocates of static typing treat compiler errors as free debugging; dynamic advocates lean on testing and often argue that relying on the type checker for correctness signals deeper process problems. The talk walks through test-driven development friction, code length versus clarity, Rust ownership benefits versus ceremony, Java wrapper boilerplate versus Ruby duck typing, IDE navigation versus grep and ctags, and REPL workflows.

Performance comparisons cover ahead-of-time optimization using type information versus JVM JIT profiling in dynamic languages, with the speaker arguing that raw loop speed rarely drives project outcomes. Closing themes emphasize ecosystem size, hiring, compiler quality, and fit for concurrency over typing alone; questions cover Rails metaprogramming, TypeScript gradual typing, and F# compile-time logic checking.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Spencer Gibb
talks.teaser: Shows how Spring Cloud Gateway can front a monolith and route traffic to new services with filters, fallbacks and rate limiting.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through splitting a single Spring Boot application that serves fortunes into smaller services, with Spring Cloud Gateway placed in front of it. The speaker first proxies all traffic to the existing monolith using a Java route builder that matches on path. Static front-end assets are then routed to a separate UI service, first to a hard-coded address and then through Eureka service discovery with load-balanced lookup, so several instances can share the traffic.

Next, the greeting logic is moved into its own service. A custom gateway filter rewrites a query parameter into a path segment before the request goes downstream, and the speaker notes that built-in filters such as rewrite path and set path cover similar cases. A circuit breaker is then added around the monolith's fortune route, with a fallback implemented as a local controller that returns a default fortune when the monolith is down, so the UI keeps responding.

For a new versioned fortune endpoint, the talk adds a request rate limiter backed by Redis and the token bucket algorithm, keyed on a request header. A quick test shows alternating 429 responses once the limit is exceeded. The speaker closes by arguing that the gateway suits cross-cutting concerns such as blocking actuator endpoints, disabling a faulty route quickly, and centralizing rate limits, and that the monolith can be retired once clients have moved to the new versions. Questions at the end covered registering monoliths that are not Eureka clients, such as VM-hosted applications.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Oleksandra Dmytrenko - Playing programming with kids and BB-8
talks.teaser: Shows how to run memorable programming lessons for kids with BB-8, block apps, and themed games when robots are optional.
talks.summary:
A Java developer who trains young programmers explains how to introduce coding to children from about age eight, when sustained focus becomes more realistic. She frames goals as showing a possible future path and a hobby beyond endless computer games, not replacing school curriculum. Lessons work best when they feel special: greeting learners as friends, sitting at their level, using gentle humorous consequences instead of blaming the child, mixing visual and physical activities, and changing pace roughly every twenty minutes for eight- and nine-year-olds.

Past sessions wrapped Sphero-style block programming inside pirate and Harry Potter stories. Tasks covered robot movement, sensors, collisions, lights, cycles, variables, and team challenges such as Quidditch-themed hot-potato play with the droid. For older kids she moves from visual blocks toward JavaScript, discussing blocking versus asynchronous behavior and building programs on a board before phones drive the robot.

On stage she splits volunteers into teams that assemble a car simulation on BB-8: color, rolling motion, engine start and drive sounds with continuation blocks, and if-then logic on a variable to switch colors. She notes cheaper Sphero options and that Scratch alone can suffice; unpredictability from students is normal, and memorable themes matter more than perfect plans.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Tomer Gabel - Non-deterministic Software for the Rest of Us
talks.teaser: Explores why passing tests miss product quality in search and scraping, and how user metrics guide engineering.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting “correct” software that runs reliably with “good” software that actually satisfies users. Green unit and integration tests are not enough when outcomes are subjective, inputs are unbounded, or behavior depends on scarce resources—search ranking, social feeds, and ride-matching are the framing examples.

Two production case studies carry the argument. A social-graph search startup shipped quickly with strong test discipline yet delivered poor results, showing that acceptance testing cannot capture relevance. Later, a social-listening platform scraped review sites at scale; customers demanded completeness, correctness, and near-real-time updates while targets changed markup, throttled crawlers, and fingerprinted traffic. The team answered with daily re-harvest comparisons, similarity scoring, trend charts, and simple anomaly alerts, plus cost models that traded polling frequency against proxy spend and fed tiered product offerings.

Practitioners are urged to pair every feature with explicit success criteria and measurable signals—especially user actions such as clicks, paging, and query refinement. Experimentation infrastructure, continuous dashboards, and iteration on trends rather than version labels matter more than intuition or manual QA opinions. Line-of-business systems with fixed specs stay deterministic; many modern web, optimization, and machine-learning products do not.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Adam Warski - What have the annotations done to us?
talks.teaser: Shows how annotation convenience costs type safety and explorable code, offering plain-Java wiring and mapping alternatives.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how Java annotations, added in 2004 to reduce large amounts of XML configuration, became the foundation of popular frameworks such as Spring and Java EE. The speaker groups their uses into three areas: mapping Java classes to external models such as SQL, JSON or XML; expressing cross-cutting concerns such as transactions or security checks; and wiring the whole application together through dependency injection.

He argues that annotations form a small interpreted language glued onto Java, with little type checking, and that containers only read them at runtime. Using an example from the Spring pet clinic project, he shows the same wiring written as plain Java, with manual dependency injection and an explicit startup sequence in the main method. He questions classpath scanning, because it makes startup behaviour hard for a reader to trace. For endpoint mapping, he notes that annotation combinations are checked only at startup and that string parameters go unverified until used, so he proposes describing endpoints and JPA-style mappings as ordinary Java values built with a fluent API.

To show this is not just theory, he points to Spark Java, jOOQ and the functional web framework in Spring 5, which all rely on plain Java instead of annotations. He closes by advising readers to favour code that is easy to explore over code that is short to write. He is not arguing against Spring, which he regards as strong for business applications because of its integrations.
