talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Jarek Ratajski - Beauty and the beast
talks.teaser: Explains how the ETA compiler runs Haskell on the JVM, with live code, tail-call fixes and Java interop.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces ETA, a Haskell compiler that targets the JVM, and asks why a Java developer would want pure functional code on a platform already used in production. The speaker first reviews the existing workarounds: writing Haskell-style code with Java's flatMap chains, imitating Haskell with Scala libraries, and transpiling Haskell to Scala.

Live coding builds a quicksort in Haskell and compiles it with the ETA toolchain into a runnable jar. The talk explains that ETA follows GHC closely by going through an intermediate STG stage before emitting bytecode, and that its Cabal-like build tool works in a similar way. Hackage packages that rely on C imports need small patches that switch them to Java equivalents. A Fibonacci example exposed a tail-call bug in the compiler, which the speaker fixed with help from the maintainer. Tail-call optimization and trampolines then let deep recursion run on the JVM. Naive benchmarks put plain Java ahead of ETA, though the speaker stresses that those measurements were not rigorous.

The talk closes with three ways to mix Haskell and Java: deploying Haskell as a servlet, calling Java objects from Haskell through foreign imports, and driving a Haskell game of life from a Java controller. The speaker says ETA is still pre-production, so it suits experiments for Haskell developers who want to reuse code and for Java developers who want to learn functional style.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Cliff Click - A War of Words: Self-Awareness for Introverts
talks.teaser: Offers introverted programmers practical ways to handle verbal attacks, recover emotionally, and prepare for salary talks.
talks.summary:
Cliff Click opens this non-technical talk aimed at introverts and anyone who has been caught off guard by a sudden verbal attack. He explains that he cannot process words and emotions at the same time, so an outburst during a coding session left him replaying the exchange for hours. His approach is to prepare a few stock phrases in advance, walk away from abuse, and burn off adrenaline through physical activity so anger does not turn inward.

The middle of the talk covers relationships and workplace dynamics. He sorts people into green, yellow and red groups, staying close to trusted friends, keeping neutral with acquaintances, and distancing himself from people who drain him. He applies the same ideas to his personal life, such as telling a partner ahead of time when he will stop talking during intimacy. In group brainstorms he suggests acknowledging quieter members so they feel safe to speak. He also describes warrior, farmer and wizard temperaments, and argues that salary negotiation is a civil fight that needs rehearsal as well as preparation.

He closes with negotiation advice: know your walk-away point before the meeting, practice the conversation with a partner, and turn questions about your current pay back on the employer. The talk ends with the point that self-awareness is a lifelong process, that people cannot be forced to change, and that asking for help is a strength. In the Q&A he notes that his observations come from smaller talks and may apply to many introverts.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Kamil Szymański
talks.teaser: Live coding walks through blocking MVC, async servlets, and Project Reactor while measuring throughput, streaming, and backpressure.
talks.summary:
The session opens on why reactive streams libraries exist: concurrency control, better resource use, and backpressure. The presenter drops slides for live examples on Spring Boot and Project Reactor, arguing the ideas transfer to other reactive stacks.

Starting from a classic blocking endpoint with one-second I/O, benchmarks with siege show how servlet thread limits cap transactions per second even when latency stays at one second. Async servlet handling and then WebFlux illustrate moving work off request threads, event-loop pitfalls when blocking Netty, and using schedulers such as subscribeOn with bounded pools. A Flux that emits large documents highlights waiting for full JSON arrays, heap blowups, and fixing time-to-first-byte with application/stream+json.

Backpressure is demonstrated through subscription request sizing, custom subscribers, and operators like buffer and parallelize. JPA list-to-Flux loading is contrasted with Hibernate streaming and a teaching JDBC Flux that maps result sets row by row. The close emphasizes resilient, readable threading control, plus trade-offs: harder debugging, thread-local pitfalls, and JDBC’s blocking roots.

talks.title: GeeCON: Marek Chmiel - Securing your applications front to back at scale
talks.teaser: Walks through OAuth grants, JWT validation, and Keycloak demos for securing web APIs and mobile clients across growing estates.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story many teams recognize: one web app with form login, a second app reusing the same data layer, an internal REST API left unprotected, basic authentication for direct API use, and mobile clients that finally force a shared authorization server. From that path the presenter distills OAuth-style rules—avoid keeping user passwords in applications, limit what tokens can reach, and treat third-party clients as untrusted—and positions Keycloak as an off-the-shelf authorization server backed by Red Hat.

The core walkthrough maps actors (users, clients, authorization server, resource APIs) and contrasts grant types. Redirect flows keep credentials off the client; direct flows such as resource-owner password credentials exchange username and password at the token endpoint. Live demos use a Node console client and a React web app with John Snow, then explain why access tokens behave like short-lived secrets, how refresh tokens renew access (and why implicit public clients do not get them), and how JWT payloads carry expiry, audience, roles, and custom claims so APIs can verify signatures locally instead of hammering the authorization server on every call. Client credentials unify machine-to-machine auth; authorization code plus client secret is recommended over implicit or password grants for production browsers.

Demos add a Spring Boot product API with Keycloak dependencies, role mapping for product viewing, and front-end UI gated on decoded token roles. The close shows themed login, Kibana views on Keycloak audit events integrated with Elastic Stack, and tracing user actions across apps via session and token metadata.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Peter Palaga - srcdeps - stop letting dependencies dictate your life!
talks.teaser: Describes how srcdeps lets Maven and Gradle builds pin dependencies to Git commits instead of published artifacts.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces srcdeps, a Maven and Gradle extension for declaring dependencies by Git revision rather than fixed release coordinates. The presenter walks through a srcdeps.yaml mapping from Maven group and artifact patterns to repository URLs, then explains the runtime flow: intercepting local repository resolution, checking out the matching source tree, aligning its version with the requested revision, building, and installing so the main project consumes the result like any other dependency.

A live Maven demo forks JUnit to add a custom greeting assertion, wires the dependent project to that commit, and shows a failing test until the application code matches the new behavior. The speaker outlines branch-based rebuilds, tag pins, test and plugin dependencies, tuning options such as verbosity and timeouts, and disabling srcdeps for release profiles. Limitations include Git-only support, fragile remote history, imperfect binary reproducibility, and clashes when two projects build the same revision with different profiles.

The closing compares srcdeps to Maven snapshots, JitPack, and Gradle composite builds. Snapshots and remote snapshots are criticized for ambiguity; JitPack is noted as more constrained and centrally built. The takeaway is that dependent-project maintainers regain control over when and from which commit dependencies are built, while published artifacts that rely on srcdeps should not be shipped to public repositories.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Marcin Moskała
talks.teaser: Shows how Kotlin coroutines simplify asynchronous code on both front-end and back-end, and how the compiler makes them work.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a common front-end problem: fetching data from an API and updating the screen without freezing the main thread. The speaker compares callbacks, which become hard to read and do not run requests in parallel, with RxJava, which works but is verbose. Coroutines are presented as a flatter alternative, where a function suspends while it waits and frees its thread, and parallel requests can be grouped with deferred values and awaited together.

For back ends, the speaker argues that a thread per request is expensive, using a demo that starts 100,000 threads and runs out of memory, while the equivalent coroutines finish almost instantly. He then explains what happens under the hood: each suspending function gets an extra continuation parameter and is compiled into a state machine that resumes at the saved label after a delay. The talk also covers how the same mechanism enables sequence generators and channels, and how coroutines can be used to build other concurrency models.

The closing part gives practical basics: coroutine builders such as launch, runBlocking and async, the role of the coroutine context and dispatchers, cancelling jobs (important on Android before leaving an activity), and support in Retrofit, testing with a mocking library, and sharing presenter code across platforms in a multiplatform project. Attendees leave with a starting point for using the kotlinx.coroutines library.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Peter Hilton - Beautiful code: typography and visual programming
talks.teaser: Explores how monospace fonts, ligatures, and layout habits limit code readability—and imagines poster-style and visual alternatives.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that maintainability hinges on reading code, yet tools and habits still optimize for writing. It traces how line printers and IBM Selectric compromises produced Courier and Courier New, how Windows 3.1 locked those choices into editors, and how syntax highlighting and fonts such as Consolas and Fira Code added color and ligatures without changing the basic typewriter model.

The middle section treats layout as neglected typography: multi-column and newspaper-style views of huge Java classes, themed “poster” presentations of the fast inverse square root snippet, and a satirical annual-report style for corporate code. The speaker rejects tabs-versus-spaces as a false dichotomy, likening both to typewriter-era layout, and sketches having designers turn important code into wall posters for teams that already invest in marketing design.

The close contrasts mainstream text-file programming with Scratch, BPMN, and Kraków’s Luna visual language, which pairs diagrams with a Haskell-inspired textual notation and live debugging. Punch cards frame text files as a transitional medium. The takeaway is to question whether the next generation will accept today’s paradigms, watch for visual tools built outside traditional developer culture, and prioritize readability innovations rather than language fashion alone.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Vladimir Dejanovic
talks.teaser: Compares traditional REST APIs with GraphQL by building a sample blog API in Spring Boot and weighing their trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking what REST really means, since its formal definition from a doctoral dissertation is often misunderstood. The speaker outlines its core constraints, including client-server separation, statelessness, cacheability, layering, optional code on demand and a uniform interface. Most developers, the speaker notes, actually mean traditional CRUD-style APIs that pass database data straight to the front end. To illustrate, the speaker builds a small blog with authors, posts and comments in Spring Boot and MongoDB, exposing a set of REST endpoints.

GraphQL is then introduced as a specification rather than a product, so behaviour depends on the chosen implementation. Using a Java library, the same data is exposed through a schema and a single endpoint, and a built-in playground shows autocomplete and lets clients pick fields. Adding a link from posts to authors takes one extra resolver, and linking comments as well turns the model into a graph. Mutations are shown for writing data, while subscriptions are described but not demonstrated. The talk also covers risks such as cyclic queries that can overload a server, and protections like timeouts, maximum query depth, complexity scoring and throttling.

The closing section weighs trade-offs. Clients gain flexibility, but servers lose control over how their data is requested, and caching, pagination, authorisation and versioning must be handled by the implementation or the team. Tooling and client-side support are less mature than for REST, and retrofitting an existing system can be costly. GraphQL is therefore not a silver bullet, though many familiar REST techniques, such as adding a service layer for caching, still apply.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Maxim Novak - The Joy of Scala
talks.teaser: Shows how Scala cuts Java boilerplate and why its immutability, pattern matching and DSL features boost developer productivity.
talks.summary:
This talk introduces Scala to Java developers, arguing that the JVM language removes much of the ceremony Java requires. The speaker starts with a small Java 7 checkout class and converts it step by step: public is the default, semicolons and return statements become optional, and parameters are immutable by default. Case classes replace the getters, setters, equals and hashCode code that Java needs, and type inference keeps signatures short while the compiler still checks types.

The middle section covers features that change how code is organised. Option replaces null checks, and map, getOrElse and for-comprehensions handle nested lookups without repeated checks. Pattern matching works on values, types, guards and case-class extractors, and custom extractors can label URL schemes. Default and named parameters remove telescoping constructors and builders, while string interpolation with triple quotes handles text and JSON. Implicit classes and infix notation let the specs2 testing library read almost like prose.

The closing part addresses adoption. Scala runs on existing JVM tooling and interoperates with Java, so teams can start by writing tests in Scala, convert classes one at a time, and use collection conversion helpers. A two-commit rename keeps file history intact. The speaker also lists caveats: the language's freedom can produce hard-to-read code, compilation is slower on large projects, IntelliJ support lags behind Java, and experienced Scala developers are harder to hire.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Pete Larson - Is disruption an imperative or an illusion?
talks.teaser: Links Gartner-style hype, whole-solution delivery, and trust in distributed teams so innovation matures instead of stalling on buzzwords.
talks.summary:
The speaker asks whether relentless “disruption” is a real mandate or largely illusion for people who ship technology. He argues smartphones, app stores, and open networks inverted innovation: startups and individuals now set the pace while large firms scramble to match capabilities that once required massive R&D.

Using the Gartner hype cycle, he describes how triggers and inflated expectations push ideas into a long trough of disillusionment. Developers and architects, he contends, must flatten that curve by guiding employers and customers—blockchain is the running example—past “we need one” demands toward layered solutions spanning presentation, cloud scale, cybersecurity, and data protection, and toward integrations such as IoT and telematics that connect existing products rather than inventing entirely new categories.

The closing arc ties delivery to people: support work exposes user unpredictability and internal team friction; stories from the 2004 Boston Red Sox and Google’s team-performance research emphasize trust, bonding, and psychological safety over credentials alone. Remote collaboration tools help but each step away from face-to-face contact erodes connection, so he urges honest tool choices, small human habits in Slack and meetings, and high-performing teams as the way to break the hype cycle and bring mature tech to market faster.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Thorben Janssen - The Hibernate Universe
talks.teaser: Shows how Hibernate handles multi-tenancy, audit logging and full-text search beyond basic object-relational mapping.
talks.summary:
The talk goes beyond Hibernate's usual mapping role to cover three features modern applications often need: multi-tenancy, audit logging and full-text search. For multi-tenancy, the speaker compares a database per tenant, a schema per tenant, and shared tables with a discriminator column. Hibernate handles the first two through connection selection, while the shared-table approach would require changing every query. The demo implements two interfaces, one that resolves the current tenant and one that supplies its connection, and shows that the rest of the application code stays unchanged.

Audit logging records inserts, updates and deletes. Audited entities get a revision table and a history table per entity, with a code marking each operation type. The speaker stresses that only changes made through entity lifecycle operations are captured, not direct database writes or bulk queries. The history can be read per record over time or as a snapshot at a chosen point in time. Adding the user who made each change requires a custom revision entity and listener, because authentication sits outside Hibernate.

Full-text search uses Hibernate Search with Lucene or Elasticsearch, keeping the index in step with database writes. Indexed fields must be chosen up front, since adding fields later means rebuilding the index. Queries return matching IDs, and entities are then loaded from the relational database. A custom analyzer with lowercase filtering and stemming lets variants such as validate and validation match. The extra lookup adds some latency, which is usually acceptable at normal scale.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Nicolas Fränkel - Starting with Ethereum, a developer approach
talks.teaser: Guides developers through Solidity in Remix, a voting-token referendum demo, Rinkeby deployment, and Truffle-based local testing.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a developer’s view of blockchain as an immutable, distributed ledger, contrasting speculative cryptocurrencies with Ethereum’s appeal as a platform where code can be deployed and called from outside the chain. The presenter maps the Ethereum virtual machine to a replicated database with externally owned accounts and smart contracts, explains transactions and gas in accessible terms, and introduces Solidity as the main route to bytecode.

The middle of the talk is hands-on in Remix: simple arithmetic contracts, pure versus state-changing functions, named and tuple return values, then a richer example pairing a fungible voting token with a referendum contract where casting a vote burns tokens. A live segment deploys a minimal math contract to the Rinkeby test network using a desktop wallet and faucets for test ether, stressing that writes cost gas while reads can execute locally.

The closing portion addresses the lack of built-in testing familiar from mainstream stacks and walks through Truffle for project layout, migration tracking, a private develop chain, and Mocha-style JavaScript tests. A failed run against Rinkeby shows why accounts need ether for state-changing operations. Questions cover faucets, who may burn tokens, paying only when changing chain state, explorers for linked deployments, and how local, test, and production networks relate.

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Jarosław Pałka - new java.io.File(`geecon.json`); is this really that simple?
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Jarosław Pałka - new java.io.File(`geecon.json`); is this really that simple?.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Jarosław Pałka presents a comprehensive analysis of Java file I/O operations, deconstructing the hidden complexity behind what appears to be simple file read/write code. The talk traces execution from high-level Java APIs through JNI layers to underlying operating system calls, exposing multiple buffer copies, memory allocations, and performance pitfalls.

## Key Topics

**File vs File Descriptor**: The File class in Java is not an OS file descriptor but a wrapper for path manipulation. The actual file descriptor is represented by FileDescriptor, which stores an integer representing the OS-level file descriptor. FileDescriptor implements reference counting to track multiple streams using the same descriptor; when the count reaches zero, the descriptor can be garbage collected.

**FileInputStream/FileOutputStream Implementation**: Standard streams maintain a hard-coded 8KB buffer in native code. Writes exceeding 8KB trigger additional memory allocation on the C heap. The write path involves multiple copies: Java buffer → JNI buffer → C buffer → page cache → storage. This design protects against garbage collection by copying data to stable C-allocated memory, preventing the JNI code from accessing memory that could be moved by GC.

**FileChannel as Superior Alternative**: FileChannel maintains an internal cache of buffers at multiple sizes, avoiding redundant allocation on each operation. The configurable JDK NIO max cache buffer size parameter (e.g., 128KB) allows tuning. FileChannel's stack trace shows most operations occur in Java with only one native call at the end, compared to multiple native calls in the standard stream approach. Buffer caches are thread-local and evicted via least-recently-used algorithm.

**Vectored I/O**: FileChannel supports scatter-gather operations with read/write methods accepting multiple byte buffers. Java arbitrarily limits this to 16 buffers, despite modern operating systems supporting 1,024+ buffers. This limitation stems from legacy code checking for a fixed maximum value.

**Memory-Mapped Files**: Enable file access as a byte array with random access capabilities. The operating system handles paging, allowing access to files larger than physical memory. Critical limitation: Java's ByteBuffer uses integer indexing, restricting each mapped region to 2GB maximum. Workarounds include using Unsafe to call the private native method and access the pointer, or creating multiple ByteBuffers over the same file. Memory-mapped files provide unpredictable performance due to OS-controlled flush timing similar to garbage collection pauses. Used effectively in Cassandra and Neo4j for indexes and data storage.

## Technical Details

**Linux I/O Stack**: File operations traverse the virtual file subsystem, which queues requests for drivers. The page cache mechanism avoids redundant storage reads by caching file portions in memory. The I/O scheduler merges sequential read requests and reorders them to minimize disk seek time, particularly critical for spinning drives. Direct I/O (O_DIRECT flag) bypasses the page cache, useful for databases implementing their own caching strategies.

**Zero-Copy Optimization**: The sendfile system call transfers file data directly to network sockets without copying to application memory. Java's FileChannel.transferTo and transferFrom methods expose this capability. This technique is extensively used in Apache Kafka because the log format matches network packet format exactly, allowing direct disk writes from network packets.

**Direct I/O Limitations**: While Linux supports O_DIRECT, Java lacks official API support. The sun.nio package provides unofficial access to direct I/O, but this is a private, unsupported API with no guarantee of stability. This creates a barrier to fully utilizing database-appropriate I/O modes.

## Takeaways

- For writes exceeding 8KB, prefer FileChannel over FileInputStream/FileOutputStream
- Configure BufferedInputStream/BufferedOutputStream buffer sizes appropriately; default 8KB is often insufficient
- Use FileChannel with vectored I/O for multi-buffer operations, accounting for the 16-buffer limitation
- Memory-mapped files excel in database and index storage scenarios but are limited to 2GB per mapping
- Direct I/O is feasible through sun.nio package APIs for applications requiring data integrity guarantees
- Understanding the OS I/O stack (page cache, scheduler, system calls) enables informed optimization decisions
- Simple file operations involve substantial hidden complexity with multiple buffer copies and system call overhead

talks.title: GeeCON 2018: Daniel Sawano - Creating secure software - benefits from cloud thinking
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2018: Daniel Sawano - Creating secure software - benefits from cloud thinking.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Daniel Sawano from Avanza Bank (Stockholm) presents how cloud-native principles can improve application security regardless of deployment location. He draws from 12-factor app methodology and cloud-native thinking to propose three key architectural changes: configuration management, stateless processes, and logging-as-a-service, culminating in the 3 R's of enterprise security framework.

## Key Topics

### Configuration in Environment
Instead of hardcoding secrets or storing them in configuration files on disk, move passwords and access keys to environment variables. This shifts secret management responsibility to the platform/centralized service, reduces exposure to developers, enables audit trails, and enables ephemeral secrets (short-lived credentials stored only in RAM). While the platform must still protect secrets at rest, this design pattern forces intentional security thinking.

### Stateless Processes
Run multiple instances of the application as stateless processes communicating only through backing services (databases, caches, message queues). This approach enables:
- **Availability**: Kill off compromised instances without data loss
- **Integrity**: Replace bad instances with fresh ones
- Separation of deployment (privileged user) from runtime (dedicated unprivileged user per application)
- Principle of least privilege: processes have only necessary permissions

### Logging as a Service
Instead of logging to disk files, send logs to a centralized logging service. This solves security challenges:
- **Confidentiality**: Service enforces authorized access (addresses GDPR concerns about sensitive data in logs)
- **Integrity**: Logs can be treated as read-only, digitally signed to detect tampering
- **Availability**: No disk space issues; dedicated team manages storage and rotation

### The 3 R's of Enterprise Security
Justin Smith (Pivotal) coined this framework inverting traditional enterprise security (minimize change) to maximize change as a defense against Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). Time favors attackers; constant change starves them.

**Rotate** (every few minutes/hours):
- Secrets expire quickly, limiting attack window
- Use services like HashiCorp Vault to inject new credentials
- Applications can passively receive rotated secrets or actively fetch them
- Apply to passwords, tokens, certificates

**Repave** (at least hourly):
- Recreate servers/containers from fresh base images
- Kills any malicious software; completely destroy instances (including temp files)
- Use rolling deployments for zero downtime
- Deploy even without code changes for security benefit

**Repair** (within hours of patch release):
- Deploy patches as new known-good states
- Always recreate from scratch, not incremental updates
- Monitor and update third-party dependencies
- Use CI/CD integration (e.g., Jenkins plugins) to detect dependency vulnerabilities
- Automated processes enable fast verification

## Technical Details
The CIA security model (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) frames analysis. Design patterns mentioned include wrapper objects for sensitive data and secure toString() methods to prevent accidental log leakage. For legacy applications with connection pools, compromise by allowing longer password validity (e.g., one hour) while still repaving to retain some security benefit. Admin tasks should become dedicated APIs running as separate processes, not terminal/SQL commands, limiting scope and keeping administration logic aligned with application code.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Jarek Ratajski - Walking in Code
talks.teaser: Presents a VR prototype that turns Java classes and PMD code smells into a walkable 3D space.
talks.summary:
The presenter, a Java developer, opens with a complaint about flat screens and keyboards as limits on how programmers work, and argues for coding while standing or walking. They explain choosing an HTC Vive headset for room-scale movement and why they wanted to see a codebase in 3D space instead of a flat editor.

The prototype runs PMD over a project and places each class as a node in space, grouping classes from the same package into clusters and linking imports with lines. Positions come from a physics simulation in which springs pull connected classes together while repulsion pushes unrelated ones apart. Viewers switch between code-smell measures such as cyclomatic complexity, see taller or redder blocks for worse code, and pull a trigger to open a class's source. The presenter built it on a browser-based VR framework over WebGL, which they found easier to start with than Unity or Unreal, and showed a live demo with audience members taking turns in the headset.

The presenter reports that editing code in VR is still unsolved, since virtual keyboards and speech recognition handled Java poorly, and that small code text is hard to read at the headset's resolution. The tool is presented as an early prototype that already helps in navigating an unfamiliar project, with better displays and input methods expected to improve it.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Bruno Bossola - Distributed Systems explained (with NodeJS)
talks.teaser: Walks through CAP trade-offs and consistency models with live Node.js demos of two-phase commit, sloppy quorum, and Raft.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why organizations scale by composing many modest machines instead of one supercomputer, then narrows the discussion to distributed storage: growing capacity without a single huge disk, staying online when parts fail, and keeping replicas from diverging. Partitioning spreads different data across nodes for speed and partial fault isolation; replication copies data so reads can survive outages but introduces stale reads when copies lag.

The middle develops strong, weak, and eventual consistency in plain terms, links them to availability and latency, and states the CAP theorem: under network partition, systems choose consistency or availability. Classic CA databases rely on strict quorums and two-phase commit; AP designs (as in large e-commerce carts) favor responsiveness and reconcile later; CP designs use majority quorums, with ZooKeeper-style examples and Raft leader election sketched as a simpler consensus path.

The closing section is a hands-on tour of a small REST key-value cluster in Node.js: a CA store that halts writes when a peer drops; an AP store with sloppy quorums, timestamps, and repair; and a CP Raft implementation with leaders, ticks, terms, and recovery after partitions simulated with firewall rules. Practitioners leave with interview-ready vocabulary, paper references such as Dynamo, and encouragement to read the published code and reproduce partition experiments locally.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Daniel Sawano/Daniel Deogun - Cracking the code to secure software
talks.teaser: Shows developers how good domain design can remove injection flaws, shared-state problems and accidental data leaks.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security bugs feel mysterious to developers, yet many of them can be handled with the same design principles used for ordinary bugs. The speakers start with cross-site scripting and a retail case where a negative quantity entered in a shopping cart gave buyers an unintended discount for years. They explain that quantity was modelled as a plain integer, which does not behave like a real order quantity. Their remedy is the domain primitive: a small immutable type that enforces business rules when it is created. Applied to a phone number field, the same idea rejects script input before it reaches the page, while output escaping remains as a second layer of defence.

The second part covers mutable state, using the confidentiality, integrity and availability model to frame why shared mutable state causes trouble. For an order that moves through a lifecycle, the speakers separate reads from writes. Reads use immutable entity snapshots that always remain valid, and writes go through a separate update path, with consumers reaching eventual consistency. They also discuss how invariants that span time can be handled with saga-style approaches.

The final part looks at accidental leakage of sensitive data into logs, sessions or serialised output, which often appears as a domain evolves. A read-once pattern marks a sensitive value so that a second read throws an exception, which exposes unintended uses in tests or production. The speakers close by summarising their three patterns and answering questions about persistence and consistency.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Mihail Mateev - Dealing with CosmosDB
talks.teaser: Surveys Cosmos DB multi-model APIs, global replication, consistency choices, and when to use it for IoT and gaming workloads.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the assumption that most attendees have little hands-on experience with Cosmos DB. The presenter frames it as a multi-API software-as-a-service datastore spanning document, MongoDB-compatible, Gremlin graph, and enhanced table models under one account abstraction, contrasted with Amazon RDS for relational SaaS and with DynamoDB, Cloudant, and CouchDB as conceptual peers.

Core themes include global replication, aggressive latency and SLA claims, and tunable consistency in the spirit of the CAP theorem. Document DB is highlighted for SQL-like querying over JSON, automatic indexing on every field (with cost and write-performance implications), and abstractions from account through collections to documents, stored procedures, triggers, and user-defined functions. Partitioned versus single-partition collections, request units, gateway versus direct connectivity, TCP versus HTTP, etag-based optimistic concurrency, and failover behavior across regions receive practical emphasis, including warnings that partitioned tiers can become expensive without careful sizing.

The close skips deeper MongoDB API material for time but points to a public SQL playground, GitHub tooling such as DocumentDB Studio, SDK samples across common languages, and a brief live demo of creating a partitioned collection. Practitioners should leave with a decision-oriented picture: strong fits for globally distributed mission-critical apps, IoT operational data, retail, e-commerce, and gaming when scale and availability matter, but not as cheap bulk archival storage.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Lukas Jungmann - Java EE 8 finally final! Now what?
talks.teaser: Outlines Java EE 8 final features across web, JSON, and CDI specs, and explains Oracle's handoff of the platform to Eclipse.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how Java EE 8 work began in 2014, slipped behind other priorities for roughly a year, and shipped in July 2017 after a 2016 replan and community survey. Survey feedback favored web-tier updates and deprioritized management, JMS, and MVC; MVC finished as its own spec but does not ship on the Java EE 8 platform.

The middle walks through modernization themes: JSON-P 1.1 (pointer, patch, merge patch, collectors, streaming for large documents), JSON-B binding atop JSON-P with customization parallels to JAXB, JAX-RS 2.1 reactive clients using CompletionStage, server-sent events, Servlet 4 and HTTP/2, JSF 2.3 touches, CDI 2.0 observer ordering and async events, Bean Validation alignments with Java SE 8, the new Java EE Security API (identity store, authentication mechanism, security context), and JPA 2.2 maintenance such as repeatable annotations and limited java.time support tied to JDBC.

GlassFish 5 is noted as the open reference implementation. The close covers the in-flight move of Java EE development to the Eclipse Foundation, likely EE4J naming, initial transfer candidates EclipseLink and Yasson, goal of a binary-compatible EE 8–equivalent release, and that Java EE 9 timing now depends on the Eclipse community rather than a fixed Oracle schedule.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Jacek Kunicki - Tame Your Data with Akka Streams and Java 8
talks.teaser: Shows how Akka Streams and Java 8 backpressure tame fast producers while importing gzipped CSV pairs into Cassandra.
talks.summary:
The session opens with reactive stream processing and backpressure: when a fast producer meets a slow consumer, the consumer signals demand so it is not flooded. Akka Streams terminology—source, flow, sink, and graph—is introduced, along with lazy recipe-style graphs and the default actor-based materializer.

The worked example imports gzipped semicolon-separated files whose lines share IDs in pairs. The speaker builds parsing with asynchronous CompletionStage logic and Vavr Try for invalid lines, then streams bytes through framing, flatMapConcat for ordered file concatenation, mapAsync for parsing, grouped pairs, and mapAsyncUnordered averaging with a default when both values are invalid. Flows compose type-safely; a sink with mapAsync persists to Cassandra via a repository, using materialized CompletionStage and Keep.right. A custom GraphDSL balancer parallelizes per-file processing before runWith executes the pipeline.

Practitioners see when to preserve order versus use unordered async stages, how sinks differ from flows, and how to reuse flows as workers in a balance–merge graph. Invalid lines are logged and folded into averages without aborting the import.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Quentin Adam - Deep dive and learn about your Operating System
talks.teaser: Maps container hype to Linux process isolation, namespaces, cgroups, and the security gaps versus hardware virtualization.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a hosting operator’s perspective: when Docker popularized containers, many developers treated them as iron boxes without understanding decades of Linux kernel work on processes, scheduling, and isolation. The speaker walks through why operating systems isolate processes in the first place—dependency clashes, cross-process security, and fair use of CPU and other resources—and how early chroot jails helped with dependencies but broke easily and interacted badly with privilege boundaries.

The core technical thread ties containers to three kernel mechanisms: namespaces that reshape what a process sees, cgroups that limit resource usage rather than acting as strong security boundaries, and capabilities that split traditional root power. Live-style explanation shows that a containerized process still appears on the host process list, shares one kernel with neighbors, and inherits kernel-wide weaknesses such as shared entropy pools and historic privilege-escalation bugs. The talk contrasts this with virtualization paths (KVM, hardware-assisted separation), argues production performance is often I/O-bound, and warns about operational pitfalls—including PID 1 inside containers, glibc versus application runtimes, and risky minimal images such as Alpine’s libc choices.

Practitioners are urged to treat containers as weak isolation, avoid running untrusted workloads on a shared kernel, pair container use with real virtualization when needed, collaborate with operations before production cutovers, and study low-level Linux behavior rather than trusting product marketing. Audience questions reinforce nesting Docker inside VMs, avoiding databases in containers, and learning through daily Linux use plus kernel-oriented reading.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Kevlin Henney
talks.teaser: A stack provides a path from clearer requirements to examples of state, concurrency, and inheritance.
talks.summary: The speaker uses a stack to connect requirements writing, behavioral specifications, data structures, and programming paradigms. Attendees learn how use cases and tests can describe behavior with concrete examples, and how mutable, persistent, and message-based stacks shape reasoning about state, concurrency, and inheritance.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Jakub Fojtl - Infinispan in the world dominated by raft
talks.teaser: Contrasts Infinispan's availability-first grid with Raft CP stores for on-site enterprise distributed workflows.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from enterprise print workflow software that must stay highly available on customer premises rather than in a managed cloud. He argues that teams outgrowing a single relational database often reach for Raft-backed stores by default, then walks through why that choice is not always appropriate when write volume and partition tolerance matter more than strong serializability on every update.

A compressed tour of Infinispan covers its in-memory data grid model, peer nodes, Hot Rod clients, JGroups clustering, and distribution modes, especially distributed consistent hashing with configurable owners. He contrasts Raft leader replication and majority health requirements with Infinispan's AP behavior, linear write scaling, and split-brain rebalancing. Operational guidance centers on merge policies he finds inadequate without application logic, warnings against coordinating with physical clocks, and an append-only event model that mixes ordered, commutative, and order-agnostic event types so writes avoid cross-node coordination.

The architecture shifts partial failure handling to clients: UUID keys, operation IDs for idempotent retries, and microservice failover that replays missing writes after HTTP failures leave half-finished records. A Spring demo on three local nodes shows a failed job write on one node, empty reads that discard orphans, and a successful retry that completes the stored job. Closing lessons urge matching datastore CAP tradeoffs to the workload, minimizing coordination end to end, and designing reads that tolerate incomplete writes.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Piotr Jagielski - Sequencing Dance Music
talks.teaser: Explores live-coded dance music with Clojure, Overtone, and Leipzig through REPL workflows and demos.
talks.summary:
The presentation positions REPL-driven development as the natural way to build a hobby music project in Clojure. After a short language tour—editor-linked evaluation, map-based HTTP responses, threading macros, and parentheses-aware editing—it moves to sound synthesis with Overtone and melodic structure with Leipzig, treating notes and phrases as plain data.

Demonstrations walk through defining filtered, enveloped instruments, building G minor phrases from scales, layering kick-snare-hi-hat patterns typical of dance music, tempo-matching sampled breaks, and mixing melodies with beats. A custom library extends the same model for drum parts and time-stretched samples. Live performance uses atoms, swap, and reset on track state so looped playback can pick up revised code on the next cycle.

Later sections import MIDI into playable sequences, mix results in the REPL, and show a ClojureScript and React browser table that mirrors song state over WebSockets for editing and playback. The talk closes with pointers to SuperCollider, Sonic Pi, Tidal Cycles, and similar live-coding tools, a prepared performance, and brief Q&A on DSL limits, workflow, safety when code fails, and exporting WAV recordings via Overtone.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Todd Montgomery - Making It Count: Quality is Not Optional
talks.teaser: GeeCON Prague 2017: Todd Montgomery - Making It Count: Quality is Not Optional.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk from GeeCON Prague 2017, Todd Montgomery discusses software quality, safety, and accountability, drawing from his early career researching safety-critical NASA systems (including the Space Shuttle and International Space Station). Montgomery argues that quality cannot be treated as an afterthought or patched into a system late in development; rather, safety is an emergent property that depends fundamentally on quality, and quality relies on engineering pride, ownership, and responsibility.

### Key Topics
- **Safety as an Emergent Property**: Reflecting on the 1986 Space Shuttle Challenger disaster and subsequent National Research Council report co-authored by Nancy Leveson, Montgomery highlights that safety cannot simply be designed into isolated components. Instead, it must emerge from the system as a whole. NASA established Independent Verification and Validation (IV&V) facilities to scrutinize software and mission risk independently.
- **The Fallacy of "Non-Functional" Requirements**: Classifying aspects like performance, robustness, safety, stability, and security as "non-functional" requirements devalues them. Montgomery explains that these are really unspoken or incomplete functional requirements that teams mistakenly ignore until a crisis occurs.
- **Reactive Fixes vs. Root Causes**: When quality failures emerge, organizations commonly react by throwing testers at the problem, slapping patches on issues, mandating source code reviews, and holding bug triage meetings. Montgomery terms these reactive steps placebos that fail to solve the underlying root cause.
- **Dogma and Lack of Silver Bullets**: Software quality does not stem from choosing Agile over Waterfall, adopting specific frameworks, selecting functional versus object-oriented paradigms, or picking specific programming languages. Quoting Fred Brooks, Montgomery emphasizes that there is no silver bullet, and treating methodologies dogmatically is the antithesis of quality.
- **Engineering Accountability and Legal Precedents**: The era of software engineering evading legal accountability through end-user license agreement (EULA) disclaimers is ending. Citing the criminal prosecution and 40-month prison sentence of a Volkswagen engineer in the diesel emissions scandal, Montgomery argues that software engineers will increasingly be held accountable for decisions and ethics, just like traditional electrical or civil engineers.

### Technical Details & NASA Case Study
Montgomery shares lessons from evaluating NASA software systems to illustrate practical approaches to quality:
- **Assumptions and Edge Cases**: In one case involving a shuttle GPS tracking unit that was flown without prior IV&V, an analyst discovered a critical defect simply by asking the engineer to articulate baseline assumptions. The engineer had hard-coded an assumption that no more than 12 satellites would ever be visible at once. At high altitudes, more satellites become visible, causing memory corruption when writing past array bounds.
- **Specifications as Communication**: Exhaustive binders of specifications are far less valuable than the collaborative thinking that produces them. A specification can be an email exchange, structured documentation, or executable specifications such as Test-Driven Development (TDD) or Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) test suites.

### Takeaways
- Software quality cannot be outsourced to tools, languages, or processes; it is driven by personal commitment, team pride, accountability, and a sense of ownership.
- Early requirements analysis—specifically having domain experts conduct conversational interviews with developers to probe assumptions—yields the highest return on investment.
- Developers should strive to develop good engineering "taste" and craftsmanship, ensuring quality throughout the system down to variable naming and maintainability, even in areas end users will never directly see.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Anton Arhipov - TestContainers - integration testing without the hassle
talks.teaser: GeeCON Prague 2017: Anton Arhipov - TestContainers - integration testing without the hassle.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON Prague 2017 presentation, Anton Arhipov from ZeroTurnaround introduces the Testcontainers Java library and explains how it simplifies integration testing. Integration testing is critical because unit tests alone—even with 100% code coverage—fail to detect bugs arising from real external interactions, such as network protocols, driver behavior, and database engine quirks. Arhipov illustrates this with an incident where moving from Java 1.4 to 1.5 modified the `BigDecimal.toString()` implementation, causing an Oracle database driver to insert millions of euros instead of cents because the test suite relied on an in-memory mock database rather than a real database.

### Key Topics
- **Challenges of Integration Testing**: Setting up testing environments is traditionally difficult due to complex manual configurations, long onboarding times, resource contention, and slow feedback cycles. Running concurrent tests often causes collisions over static ports or local resources.
- **Requirements for Effective Integration Tests**: Modern integration test suites require reproducible environments across developer machines (Mac, Linux, Windows) and continuous integration (CI) systems, automatic resource isolation, ease of maintenance, and testing against real dependencies rather than mocks.
- **Docker and Testcontainers**: Testcontainers acts as a wrapper around the `docker-java` library, providing JUnit rules and fluent Java APIs to manage container lifecycles directly within JUnit tests. It automates container discovery, pulling images, port mapping, and teardown.

### Technical Details
- **Dynamic Port Mapping**: Instead of hardcoding port bindings that cause collisions during parallel execution, Testcontainers dynamically binds container ports (e.g., Redis port 6379 or Jetty port 8080) to random, sequential local host ports, accessible programmatically via helper methods.
- **GenericContainer and MockServer**: For dependencies without dedicated modules (such as Redis or PostgreSQL), users can instantiate `GenericContainer`. The talk demonstrates mocking third-party microservices over the network using MockServer inside a container, avoiding in-process JVM mocking.
- **Testing JVM Agents**: Arhipov demonstrates how ZeroTurnaround tests monitoring agents that instrument bytecode. Testing involves packaging a lightweight Groovy test script using the Spark framework and embedded Jetty, mounting the local agent JAR and Groovy scripts into a Groovy Docker container via classpath resource mapping, configuring `JAVA_OPTS` to pass `-javaagent`, waiting for readiness via a wait strategy, and asserting against HTTP response headers with a Feign client.

### Takeaways
Testcontainers eliminates the need for proprietary setup scripts and manual wiki-driven environment setups. By running disposable, containerized dependencies on demand directly from JUnit, teams achieve isolated, reliable, and cross-platform integration tests that closely mirror production environments.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Chris Thalinger - Twitter's quest for a wholly Graal runtime
talks.teaser: Reports on running the Graal JIT compiler in Twitter production, with the bugs found, CPU savings measured, and tuning tried.
talks.summary:
Chris Thalinger, from Twitter's VM team, explains why the company moved production services from the C2 JIT compiler to Graal. C2 is old and intricate, so a change in one area often breaks another, and little new optimization work had appeared in years. Running a new compiler at Twitter's scale was also a way to test its maturity, with the broader aim of cutting infrastructure costs.

Several bugs surfaced during the rollout. One method could not compile because it used locks, a gap in static class initialization needed a small fix, and a crash that appeared only after days of uptime traced back to a snippet interacting with heap-profiling instrumentation. A byte-swap intrinsic bug, caught by unit tests, needed changes across several files. On the tweet service, benchmarks on dedicated machines receiving identical requests showed about 11 percent less CPU time than C2, with roughly 2.5 percent fewer garbage collection cycles and about 40 megabytes of extra compiler state. Manually raising inlining thresholds added a further couple of percent. Most of the workload was Scala, so the gains on pure Java code were less certain.

Remaining work includes porting the hand-written string intrinsics that Intel built for C2, which Graal needs to match performance on string-heavy code. Official support is limited: JDK 9 includes the required JVMCI interface in an unsupported way, and Oracle signaled experimental Linux support. The takeaway for practitioners is to test Graal on their own workloads, since the savings can be significant depending on fleet size.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Jaroslav Tulach - JavaScript & co. for Java Developers
talks.teaser: Compares Java and JavaScript evolution, speed, and standards, then demonstrates GraalVM polyglot interop for browser and server workloads.
talks.summary:
The presenter frames the session around a historical split: most of the audience identifies as Java-first, while JavaScript now dominates the browser and much of the client stack. Drawing on roughly twenty years with NetBeans—from early student work through Swing adoption and open sourcing—he sketches how Java’s client vision stalled as applets faded, Swing tooling proved heavy, and JavaFX stumbled before HTML and JavaScript engines matured.

The middle of the talk contrasts the two ecosystems on performance, governance, and UI patterns. Prime-number benchmarks pit browser engines, Nashorn, and GraalVM against Java, arguing that modern JavaScript is no longer inherently slow. He walks through JCP versus ECMAScript politics, ASM.js-style extensions, invokedynamic’s JVM cost, and why HTML won as a rendering platform. Live demos include transpiling Java to run NetBeans-like tooling in the browser, an MVVM sample binding Java models to HTML, and GraalVM running Node.js while debugging Ruby, JavaScript, and Java in one process—with notes on numeric precision and async boundaries between languages.

The closing argument is that polyglot development is unavoidable: teams either transpile Java to JavaScript for the web and Node-style servers, or standardize on GraalVM and Truffle for fast multi-language VMs with direct compiler cooperation. He briefly mentions native-image startup wins and API-style patterns (configuration objects, builders) for crossing language boundaries, and invites practitioners to experiment with the open Graal stack rather than assuming Java must stay invisible behind REST on the server.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Jakub Dżon - High request rate system architecture - an Ad Tech case study
talks.teaser: A case study explains how a demand-side ad platform reaches six-figure QPS while staying within sub-150ms bid deadlines.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by situating a demand-side platform in the ad-exchange ecosystem among SSPs, exchanges, and creatives, and by defining queries per second as the central throughput measure. The team at Codewise faced volatile traffic between roughly 15,000 and over 150,000 bid requests per second, plus hard exchange limits near 150 milliseconds, auto-scaling without over-provisioning, fault tolerance, billing safety, maintainability, and fast partner onboarding.

The walkthrough covers an evolving Volume DSP layout: edge traffic servers parsing OpenRTB JSON, bidders matching campaigns, Eureka discovery, TCP between services, and async paths through Kafka (later Amazon Kinesis) into storage and budget tracking. Concrete pivots include Jackson streaming over data bind for parsing throughput, Jetty replaced by Netty on traffic nodes, one-thread-per-request handling to cut thread-pool queuing, a homegrown circuit breaker instead of Hystrix, Hazelcast for cross-datacenter cache logic, and splitting win-notification traffic onto dedicated Netty endpoints.

Closing material maps initial requirements to outcomes: proven peak production throughput, latency under 100 milliseconds on the response path, multi-datacenter AWS deployment with regional endpoints, Dockerized Java services, metrics-first observability, and JSON-driven exchange onboarding without redeploys. Remaining pain points include partner-specific integration quirks, latency tuning, and Hazelcast replication.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Martin Hochel
talks.teaser: Walks through building scalable enterprise React apps with TypeScript, covering tooling, Redux data flow, dependency injection and testing.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a software engineer, argues that TypeScript makes large JavaScript codebases easier to manage, since type annotations flag mistakes such as adding a number to a string and allow gradual adoption. React is presented as a component library where each element is a function of its props, with JSX compiled into plain function calls and a virtual DOM that re-renders only the changed parts.

The middle section covers the setup used for a production app. Yarn manages dependencies and tasks, webpack bundles the code, and Create React App scaffolds new projects. Prettier, TSLint, and Husky with lint-staged run on each commit, while commitizen enforces conventional commit messages that drive changelogs and version bumps through standard-version. For architecture, smart container components hold logic while presentational components only render, and services are injected through a provider pattern and higher-order components so they are easy to mock. Application state lives in a Redux store, and redux-observable epics handle side effects by calling injected services and emitting new actions. Backend models are generated from a Swagger definition, so a backend change surfaces as a compile error.

For testing, Jest covers components with snapshot tests, and TestCafe runs browser end-to-end tests written in TypeScript that reuse the generated models. The speaker closes with takeaways: keep data flow one-directional, separate a service layer, and split components clearly. There is no silver bullet, and in the Q&A the speaker says Angular can suit teams that want a complete framework, while the architecture carries over to any renderer.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Peter Hilton - How to write maintainable code
talks.teaser: Practical guidance on naming, comments, duplication, and lean documentation targets slower decline into unmaintainable legacy code.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing maintainability as the decisive factor on long-lived projects, using humor and an inverted checklist—borrowed from satirical writing on unmaintainable code—to surface habits like sloppy naming, mixed paradigms, and endless experimentation without cleanup. A Luxembourg bilingual-newspaper analogy and multilingual codebases illustrate how flexibility without discipline becomes an incomprehensible mess, with fallout that includes rising fix costs, unhappy teams, hiring friction, and a downward spiral the speaker labels legacy hell.

The core turns toward positive practice: consistent style despite change, strong naming backed by dictionaries and thesaurus work, recognition of naming smells, safe rename refactors, and explanatory tests that document intent. Comments are treated as first-class code to maintain; abstraction is tempered by a rule of three before extracting shared logic. The speaker sketches a subjective clean-code percentage curve that inevitably slides after deadlines, argues that very large in-house codebases (~100,000 lines) accelerate that slide, and recommends pair programming, review, the Boy Scout rule, and deliberate refactoring time that grows with codebase age.

Documentation advice favors minimum viable artifacts—often a clear README plus targeted deep docs when one area is genuinely complex—rather than encyclopedic specs. The closing message is to recognize bad patterns, write clean code, invest extra effort for longevity, and keep maintaining both code and comments; a brief Q&A affirms design patterns can help when applied thoughtfully.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Andrea Provaglio
talks.teaser: Explains how agility depends on leaders who influence people, decentralize decisions and build trust within teams.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who coaches organizations on becoming more agile, separates agility from agile as a set of named practices. Agility means knowing that you do not know, and still working productively while uncertain. Drawing on a complexity framework, he argues that software and markets are complex rather than merely complicated, so small experiments and frequent feedback matter. He suggests organizations should resemble living systems more than machines, with decisions pushed toward the people doing the work.

The middle of the talk separates management, which uses organizational resources to complete a defined task, from leadership, which creates change by influencing people. Leadership does not depend on a formal role: anyone can lead for a while, then step back and follow, and good leaders grow others. Self-awareness is treated as the foundation, because you cannot communicate with or lead others without first knowing what you feel and think. He also contrasts accountability, reporting upward, with responsibility, which people can only take on for themselves.

The closing section covers truthfulness and trustworthiness. Being truthful means stating real deadlines and making actions match stated values, such as praising teamwork while paying individual bonuses. Trustworthiness means teammates can admit mistakes without being attacked, keeping problems visible. The takeaway is to lead by example and to ask which kind of leader you want to be, since that choice is yours. In the Q&A he notes that managers can also lead if they know which hat they are wearing.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Thompson/Montgomery - Design process behind the fastest Messaging System
talks.teaser: Explains how the Aeron messaging transport was designed, covering data structures, flow control, lock-free agents and Java I/O.
talks.summary:
Martin Thompson and Todd Montgomery explain how they designed Aeron, a fast messaging transport, and why they built it around modern multi-core machines and unreliable networks. Their starting point is that networks can drop, duplicate and reorder messages, so the wire protocol and the data structures that hold messages have to be designed together as one system. They chose an append-only stream that is effectively immutable, tracked by a term and an offset, so that the data layout matches what goes on the wire and old data can be reclaimed once it has been consumed.

The middle of the talk covers flow control and congestion control, which the transport treats as first-class concerns. The receiver advertises a window that can be managed by different strategies, including a cubic-style option, and congestion control can be switched off where capacity is planned in advance. Work is split across agents that run non-blocking duty cycles and batch their work on each pass, and counters kept in memory-mapped files give the team visibility into internal state. The speakers also describe Java I/O problems they ran into, including buffer design, lock contention in channels and selectors, DNS lookups inside the security manager on UDP sends, and the cost of one system call per message.

They close with results from early adopters such as Onyx and Akka, which reported higher throughput after moving to the transport, and with figures for single-digit microsecond round trips between machines and millions of messages per second. Their takeaways are to build telemetry in from the start, to avoid locks and layers that do not earn their cost, and to stay willing to revisit and rewrite code.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Robert Munteanu - Scaling up development of a modular code base
talks.teaser: Outlines patterns for modular development and deployment across repos, aggregate builds, IDE setup, and developer communication.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames modular development as distinct from modular deployment, using a matrix of how independently code is written versus how it is shipped. He argues that deploying many units while developing in one repository is especially painful, and that teams should treat modularity as a spectrum rather than a checkbox.

The middle of the session walks through four pillars. Source control covers monorepos versus many repositories, client-side orchestration with repo-style manifests, and migrating history when splitting a monorepo. Build and CI discusses Maven reactor limits, artifact repositories for distributed builders, and automating large Jenkins fleets with job DSL. IDE setup compares heavy Eclipse provisioning with sharing formatter and commit preferences via Maven plugins. Communication contrasts one broad dev channel with filtering versus many channels that fragment expertise.

Live demos show Docker-seeded Jenkins spawning per-module jobs, Eclipse importing shared coding standards on project load, and shell automation generating a repo manifest from GitHub. The closing message is to script glue between off-the-shelf SCM, build, IDE, and chat tools, score each pillar honestly, and automate as repository count grows.

talks.title: GeeCON Prague 2017: Aki Salmi - Live Coding: CQRS + Event Sources system
talks.teaser: A live-coded walkthrough builds a conference feedback app using CQRS patterns and an event-sourced event store.
talks.summary:
The session introduces command-query responsibility segregation and event sourcing, then spends most of the time implementing them in a small conference session feedback application. Commands cover creating sessions, registering participants, and submitting star ratings; a query exposes aggregated feedback for organizers and speakers.

Work proceeds in test-driven steps: wiring a create-session command handler and REST route, projecting read models by replaying stored events such as session created and session rated, and folding in registration and rating flows. The presenter uses acceptance tests as a script, names an event store “schedule,” and walks through loading history, applying events to build averages, and publishing uncommitted domain changes. A register command illustrates how one handler can coordinate multiple aggregates loaded from the event stream.

Step four covers where validations belong—controller input checks, command-handler application rules, and domain invariants such as rating only after registration—without further live coding. The close recaps separating writes from reads, rebuilding state from events, and using a conventional database as the event store in production systems.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Łukasz Byczyński - Build backend UI like a rockstar with Vaadin 8
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Łukasz Byczyński - Build backend UI like a rockstar with Vaadin 8.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Marcin Grzejszczak - Consumer-Driven Contracts to enable API evolution
talks.teaser: Shows how Spring Cloud Contract turns consumer-written agreements into shared WireMock stubs and generated producer tests.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting producer-owned APIs with a consumer-driven model, where the teams that call a service define scenario-based agreements rather than full schemas. It frames two pain points: integration tests that rely on consumer-written HTTP or messaging stubs can pass while production breaks on wrong URLs, topics, or serialization, and producers rarely shape APIs around real consumer needs.

After walking through WireMock JSON stubs and typical failure modes, the speaker demos a beer-ordering microservice pair. The consumer clones the producer repository, writes Groovy DSL contracts for grant and reject cases, publishes stub artifacts to Maven local, and runs tests via Stub Runner on port 8090. Refactoring drops an unnecessary name field; contracts gain regex matchers for age. On the producer side, Maven generates REST tests from those contracts; implementing a small person-checking service makes them pass. CI then publishes stubs to Nexus so consumers can test against remote artifacts instead of fantasized mocks.

The close covers optional dedicated contract repos, AsciiDoc living documentation, Rest Docs verification, Stub Runner Boot for non-JVM clients, and Dalston-era plug-ins including stubs-per-consumer and classpath retrieval. Practitioners gain a workflow where shared producer stubs stay trustworthy and API evolution follows negotiated, executable contracts.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Jarosław Ratajski - Ratpack
talks.teaser: Compares a non-blocking Java web server, Ratpack, with blocking Spring code using live demos of thread limits and deadlocks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a deliberately naive recursive Fibonacci service. When each request calls the same server over HTTP, the blocking, servlet-style version runs out of its thread pool and deadlocks. A rough benchmark on a virtual machine then suggested that a single thread, and later two threads, could serve concurrent load better than a 200-thread pool, with around four or five threads giving the best results.

The speaker explains the non-blocking model, where work is queued as tasks on an event loop and a thread is not held while waiting on I/O. He notes that this also makes CPU cache use more efficient and gives developers more control over how many cores each kind of work gets. He argues that many Java framework features hide behaviour, including annotations, reflection, thread-locals and classpath scanning, and contrasts them with explicit, function-based configuration. Ratpack's JSON handling, WebSocket support and immutable game state are shown through a multiplayer Pong demo. Blocking JDBC access is kept off the event loop by delegating it to a separate executor, and security checks are written as higher-order functions rather than annotations.

Near the end, the speaker explains that Ratpack's server can be started in tests, so endpoints are tested over real HTTP. He compares it with Spring 5's functional web style and suggests that its promise-heavy Java code looks awkward compared with Scala or Haskell. His takeaway is to consider explicit, non-blocking designs for services used by mobile clients, rather than relying on traditional Java EE or Spring stacks.
