talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Ondrej Mihalyi - 5 ways to improve your Java EE applications in reactive way.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Josh Long
talks.teaser: Builds a non-blocking Spring service with Reactor, reactive MongoDB, streamed events and a reactive client.
talks.summary:
The talk is a live-coding walkthrough by a Spring developer advocate on building reactive web applications with Spring 5 and Spring Boot 2.0, which were still at milestone stage. The starting point is that splitting systems into small services makes moving data between them hard when each call blocks a thread. The speaker explains that the Java standard library has no way to return an unbounded stream of asynchronous values, and that the Reactive Streams specification fills that gap with publisher, subscriber, subscription and processor types. Project Reactor builds on it with Mono and Flux.

Using these types, the speaker builds a movie service backed by reactive MongoDB. Sample records are written and read back, showing that nothing runs until a subscription is made. A Flux that emits a value every second is zipped with a stream of movie events to produce a continuous feed. The service is exposed through WebFlux as ordinary JSON endpoints and as server-sent events, first with annotated controllers and then with functional routing. A separate WebClient application consumes both the list and the event stream.

The final section adds security with the Spring Security 5 milestone, using a reactive authentication manager, an in-memory user store and HTTP basic authentication with a role check, so that unauthenticated requests get a 403. The takeaway is that a reactive application only stays reactive if every layer, including security and data access, is non-blocking, and the same event-based model carries through the whole stack.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Marcus Jura - Lagom: Building reactive mircoservices with ease
talks.teaser: Shows how the Lagom framework builds resilient, reactive microservices using CQRS, event sourcing and live demos.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Lagom, a microservices framework for the JVM aimed at teams that want resilient, highly scalable service-based systems. The speaker starts from a common failure pattern: a web gateway calls a downstream building services component, and when that service is slow or unavailable, timeouts and cascading failures can spread through the whole system.

To contain this, the talk walks through a circuit breaker placed between the gateway and the downstream service. The breaker stops calls to a failing service and lets requests through again once the service is available. For communication between services, the talk then turns to a message broker, with Apache Kafka as the publish-subscribe component, so that services publish and consume events rather than depending only on direct synchronous calls.

The later part covers event sourcing, where state changes are kept as events in an event log and rebuilt from data stores and snapshots. The speaker discusses how consistency is handled across services in this model. The session is pitched at an intermediate level and includes live demos showing how these pieces fit together in Lagom.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Gary Crawford - Build the right thing: survive the accelerating rate of business change
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Gary Crawford - Build the right thing: survive the accelerating rate of business change.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Jakub Pilimon - Event Sourcing and CQRS with Spring Stream
talks.teaser: Walks through event sourcing and CQRS with live Java demos, Kafka, and Spring Cloud Stream scaling patterns.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting Hibernate’s dirty checking with persisting domain changes as timestamped JSON deltas that can rebuild state at any past moment, yielding an audit trail and avoiding ORM impedance mismatch. It explains why mixing ORM persistence with hand-raised domain events creates two sources of truth, and how event-sourced tests assert exactly which deltas were emitted.

CQRS is introduced as separate write and read models, using Twitter’s read/write scaling problems as analogy. The shop demo wires domain events through Spring Cloud Stream channels and Kafka: multiple consumer groups replay from the beginning, enable horizontal read scaling and failover, support experimental consumer groups for production testing and gradual rollout, and shard hot streams via partition keys.

The architecture splits a write-side event store, command handling, and thin read projections. Drawbacks include broken relational joins, snapshot coupling when projections change, immutable events requiring compensation rather than SQL fixes, and painful event versioning. Q&A covers compensation events, HTTP caching of immutable event feeds, and why snapshots do not replace retaining the full event log.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Wojciech Seliga - colonialism of XXI century
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Wojciech Seliga - Developer plantations - colonialism of XXI century.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that software development has become a commodity, drawing a parallel between Central European IT outsourcing and colonial-era economies that exported raw resources. The speaker points to fast coding bootcamps, graduates with little hands-on experience, and a steady supply of cheaper workers moving east as signs that writing code alone no longer sets a professional apart. He compares developers who stick to one tool with a bricklayer who builds everything from brick, and cites job losses in banking, law and driving as warnings.

The middle section makes the case for product engineering: understanding the customer's real problem, the business context and the "why" before choosing a technology. Using the five-whys technique, he shows how a stated request can hide a different root cause. From his own experience, a business team that dictated detailed specs was won over over roughly two years, when his team shared knowledge and taught them to make changes themselves, turning a troubled project into a successful one.

He closes with practical steps: seek direct contact with users and business people, check whether your company offers a career path into business, and push to join decisions rather than only implementing specs. Real end-user feedback, he argues, is the most important loop for verifying a product, more than tests or continuous integration. He urges engineers in the region to move up the value chain while there is still demand for them.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Zach Holman
talks.teaser: Uses real outages, a database wipe and a repository breach to show how teams can handle mistakes and rebuild trust.
talks.summary:
Zach Holman, a former GitHub engineer, looks at how teams should react to the mistakes they inevitably make. He opens with his own errors, including shipping a build in development mode to GitHub Enterprise customers, and with a 2010 incident where a continuous integration run used production credentials and emptied a database, which was wiped a second time after the restore. He also cites a GitLab data loss, where open incident updates helped keep users onside.

The middle of the talk covers a 2012 breach in which an outside researcher used unguarded database attributes to write data into the Rails repository. GitHub's response was split into parallel tracks: an immediate fix, a longer-term push toward secure-by-default code, a disclosure policy for researchers, and a team that reviewed logs to find any other misuse. Holman also describes a botched pricing change for organization accounts that was reversed with new payment tiers, and argues that a postmortem should apologize, show understanding, and state concrete fixes. For severe events he recommends a small group of senior, cross-functional people for high-stakes decisions.

His takeaways are to test backups and keep them isolated from production, separate the people posting status updates from those debugging, measure impact with data, and offer generous make-goods to affected customers. He argues that processes are usually built from earlier failures, so teams should turn each painful lesson into a durable safeguard.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Cyrille Martraire - DDD beyond the infamous repository pattern
talks.teaser: Clarifies core DDD ideas beyond repositories, covering ubiquitous language, modeling in code, and bounded contexts for practitioners.
talks.summary:
Teams often reduce Domain-Driven Design to generic repositories or glorified data access and overlook modeling that reflects the business. The session recenters DDD on ubiquitous language, making domain terms first-class in code, and on separating tactical patterns from the strategic work of understanding the problem space.

Examples from legacy modernization and fleet fuel-card monitoring show how mismatched vocabulary between business and engineering meetings breeds churn, how code gravity draws unrelated concerns into growing classes, and how to place behavior in the domain model using value objects, entities, aggregates, and domain services. Repositories are described as specialized domain services for persistence, not the heart of the design, with adapters and persistence ignorance keeping databases and middleware at the edges.

The latter half turns to strategic design and bounded contexts: billing, shipping, and catalog concerns in e-commerce evolve on different schedules and should not be forced into one coupled model. Deliberate duplication across contexts can preserve autonomy better than synchronized schemas. Listeners are pointed toward the classic pattern catalog while being warned that frameworks cannot substitute for domain learning or for choosing context boundaries that match how the business actually changes.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Grzegorz Gubiński
talks.teaser: A Sabre team experiment blends evidence-based management and 4DX to turn retrospectives into lasting habits.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a retrospective from 2009, when delivery actions succeeded but working agreements and habits did not. That gap raised how to choose the right habits and know they stick long enough to matter.

The middle connects evidence-based management for software organizations—twelve agility-index style measures across current value, time to market, and ability to innovate—with the four disciplines of execution: one wildly important goal, leading versus lagging indicators, visible scoreboards, and a cadence of accountability. Examples include stabilizing releases through hypotheses about testing environments and unit testing, plus a Sabre team targeting predictability with an acceptance-rate lagging measure and a daily in-progress-tasks-per-person leading indicator.

Practitioners should leave with practical guidance: align team-level goals with product goals, write hypotheses openly, pick indicators that are cheap to calculate, review scoreboards daily, and keep the process engaging. Experiments may fail to hit expected outcomes yet still teach whether behavior correlates with larger measures.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Ondrej Mihalyi - 7 simple steps to boost your team work
talks.teaser: Seven habits from real project experience show how to motivate, empower, and socialize development teams beyond formal agile ceremonies.
talks.summary:
The speaker contrasts this session with his usual Java and Payara technical material and frames software delivery as work that depends on people, not solo heroics. He polls the room on Scrum use, then sets Scrum aside as an organizational tool while focusing on motivation, empowerment, and everyday collaboration drawn from a project that used the acronym CBN and built shared identity through a team logo.

He walks through practical patterns: broad access and shared documentation wikis paired with forcing knowledge into people's heads through demos and emails; real face-to-face social time such as post-lunch chats and a magnetic office board; pairing, shared laptops, and short-term seating changes for intense sprint pushes; and spreading business context so the team can challenge written requirements while respecting constraints. He stresses regular, time-boxed rituals like stand-ups, planning, and releases so momentum does not fade back into isolated screen work, plus Jenkins button-push automation and respectful cooperation with operations teams.

He closes by urging periodic process review to drop cumbersome habits, and suggests inviting a more experienced colleague to meetings for guiding questions. Practitioners should treat certified frameworks as optional: basic teamwork habits, he argues, matter more than strict process adherence.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Andrew Sorensen - Sound Synthesis in the Computational Crucible
talks.teaser: Traces live-coded concert culture and builds a digital synthesizer from sample callbacks through filters, delay, and FM sound.
talks.summary:
The session opens outside typical conference fare: live coding as performance art, with code on screen and audiences worldwide, including robotic pianos driven entirely from software. Andrew Sorensen recounts Australia’s early stored-program computer SILLIAC (referred to in speech as Zurich/C SIRAC), whose control-panel speaker began as a debug aid and by 1950–51 was used to play popular tunes via programmed pulses—music sampled in a live piece layered over archival remarks from designer Trevor Pearcey.

The core is a from-scratch digital audio walkthrough at 44,100 samples per second per channel. Starting from an audio callback that returns values between 1.0 and −1.0, the demo moves through white noise, gain, silence, periodic impulses (linking back to those early machine beeps), rhythm turning into pitch, summing ratios for harmony, and pulse width changing timbre without shifting pitch. A short delay line repeats random noise chunks so the ear hears pitched material; a trivial low-pass average models a plucked string decaying from broadband noise, then MIDI-note playback, simple delay-based “reverb,” and finally a Yamaha DX7-style FM oscillator mixed with the string for polyphony.

The close argues for hearing every change while coding: no audio libraries, iterative tweaking in the room, and treating computation as a crucible—like older experimental science—for discovering how digital structures become audible instruments listeners could replicate afterward.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Henning Schwentner - The Next Big Thing for Java
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Henning Schwentner - Value types - The Next Big Thing for Java.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the difference between objects, which have an identity and a lifecycle, and values, which are immutable and have no identity. The speaker points out that Java only has eight primitive types that behave as true values. User-defined values have to be simulated with value-based classes, which still live behind references. That costs memory, makes arrays of them scattered on the heap, and means the equality operator does not compare them as expected.

The speaker then presents Project Valhalla as the planned fix: user-defined value types that can be declared directly in the language. The syntax shown is a placeholder, and the rules sketched include final fields, constructor initialization, and equals and hashCode based only on fields. Open questions include how values are created, what their default values are, how they interact with generics and erasure, and how boxing would work. The talk compares this with C++ stack variables and C# structs, which the speaker notes can carry mutable state.

The main argument is about domain-driven design. A bank account that stores its balance as a plain integer becomes a richer model once money is an amount type holding a value and a currency, with methods that enforce the same-currency rule. Teams often drop back to primitives for performance, which makes the model anemic again. Value types would let developers keep the rich model and fast execution together. The Q&A confirmed that operator overloading is not planned for Java.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Charles Oliver Nutter
talks.teaser: Shows how to call native POSIX and C libraries from Java without writing JNI, using the JNR libraries behind JRuby.
talks.summary:
Charles Oliver Nutter explains why calling native C and POSIX code from the JVM is hard. While building JRuby, he needed operating-system features such as file metadata, process control and terminal handling that standard Java APIs did not provide. He describes Java Native Interface code as cumbersome, with generated headers, platform-specific build toolchains and the need to unpack native binaries from a jar at runtime.

He then walks through the Java Native Runtime (JNR) project, which lets developers declare native functions as Java interfaces and bind them without hand-written JNI. Its layers include a low-level foreign function interface library, POSIX bindings, generated sets of preprocessor constants, and channel-based libraries for native I/O, UNIX sockets and interactive subprocesses. Code examples cover a getpid call and a gettimeofday call with a struct. He reports that a getpid call runs roughly 10 times faster than with JNA, and that skipping error-code preservation gains about 25%.

The talk closes with the limits of the current approach, since JNI overhead remains even for trivial calls. He points to a proposed standard foreign function interface for the JVM, tracked as JEP 191 and now part of Project Panama, as the longer-term fix. The practical takeaway is that developers who need native calls today can use JNR instead of hand-written JNI, while watching Panama for built-in support.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Jakub Marchwicki - Java9 and REPL. Forget debugging, welcome joy and productivity.
talks.teaser: The session demonstrates Java 9 JShell for interactive coding, new API exploration, and quick Spark and Spring prototypes.
talks.summary:
The presentation positions JShell as the JDK’s read-eval-print loop for Java: code is typed, compiled, and printed immediately, with deeper hooks into the platform than older Java shells. The speaker outlines why that matters for onboarding newcomers without a sandbox class and public static void main, for trying unfamiliar libraries, for rapid prototyping, and for running against a full Maven classpath via a build plugin.

Most of the session is live terminal work. Basics include variables, imports, history search, shift-tab Javadoc, and editing snippets with /edit. The demo then walks Java 9 stream helpers such as Optional.stream and takeWhile, experiments with the incubating HTTP client against a simple JSON service, and assembles a small Spark Java todo UI with REST endpoints and in-memory storage, saving and reloading shell history. Maven is used to launch a similar app on another port, and Spring 5 manual bean registration is explored in the same REPL style.

Practitioners hear that sustained JShell use encourages more deliberate coding, and that integrations exist or are emerging in NetBeans, IntelliJ, and Maven, even when the niche “build the server entirely in the shell” path is not for everyone. Slides and examples are offered via the speaker’s GitHub account.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Nikita Lipsky - JIT vs. AOT: Unity And Conflict of Dynamic and Static Compilers
talks.teaser: Compares Java JIT and AOT compilation on myths, class loaders, performance, startup, and protecting bytecode from decompilers.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through ahead-of-time versus just-in-time compilation for Java, using Excelsior JET as the concrete JVM example. It opens by separating compile-time and runtime on the diagram of HotSpot versus an AOT-capable JVM, then tackles widespread beliefs that reflection, dynamic loading, or “write once, run anywhere” block static compilation. Most classes are fixed before launch; the serious obstacle is custom class loaders in frameworks such as Java EE, OSGi, and Eclipse RCP, where the compiler must name loaders, partition classes, and load precompiled natives by matching loader identity at runtime. Tomcat and Eclipse RCP are cited as supported targets.

Motivation shifts to deployment: native binaries resist decompilation better than jars plus obfuscators, though obfuscator exclude lists break when APIs change. Startup benchmarks on RSS-style apps show AOT closing much of the gap with C++ after startup profiling and sequential preloading, even though larger native images can offset gains from skipping JVM warmup. On performance, managed-language checks limit parity with C, yet whole-program static analysis can devirtualize and optimize hot patterns such as collection iteration without running the program—at a cost in compile time and disk-backed global analysis that JIT engines avoid.

JIT remains strong for profile-guided optimization, hot traces, and servers whose execution stabilizes under load; AOT can reuse those profiles offline for steadier latency and faster cold starts across microservices. Embedded and mobile constraints favor avoiding runtime compilation for battery and policy reasons, with notes on iOS, Android tooling, and Java 9’s experimental HotSpot AOT. The close argues both models persist, combined where each fits best.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Avishai Ish-Shalom

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Adam Dubiel - HTTP clients: silent heroes of distributed systems
talks.teaser: Explains what sits under RestTemplate and Jersey, and how pools, timeouts, and thread models shape microservice reliability.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that teams overfocus on HTTP client APIs while ignoring the shared implementations underneath. Walking through RestTemplate and Jersey call stacks, the speaker shows both paths end at HttpURLConnection, and that async wrappers often land in the same place with different method names.

Using Groovy tests against a localhost service with artificial delay, he contrasts HttpURLConnection keep-alive behavior with Apache HttpClient’s default pool of two connections per route, which caused eight of ten parallel calls to fail until pool limits were raised. He ties this to measuring available, leased, and pending pool slots, then covers connection and socket read timeouts, demonstrating how JVM defaults can wait tens of seconds and how Apache’s async client may only enforce short read timeouts if the background eviction interval is tuned—not merely by setting the timeout property.

He closes with blocking versus NIO thread models, warning that callback work on scarce I/O threads blocks the whole client, and revisits API choice only after picking an implementation. Q&A notes Allegro’s default of async Apache HttpClient, optional shared factories with sane pools and timeouts, and freedom for teams that configure alternatives themselves.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Tomasz Borek
talks.teaser: Explains why a dedicated Java training program for newcomers can ease hiring, and what worked and failed in running one.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who has run a Java training program for newcomers, argues that teaching new hires alongside regular project work is hard to sustain. Someone has to prepare lessons, set tasks and verify what was learned, and that takes time most developers do not have. Without a dedicated teacher, the strongest colleague quietly becomes the informal mentor and loses productive hours.

The format he described was a three-month course of about eight hours a day, split into a foundations month, an intermediate month and a closing month, with a project each month. Students worked with tests, Maven and Git, and groups were kept to around 12 people, since he found larger ones hard to handle. He used strict rules, retrospectives, one-on-one talks and recognition, and brought in outside interviewers for the monthly assessments so that he stayed out of grading. He was candid about failures: introducing tools late, letting a task deadline slide, and guessing at the cause of students' problems instead of asking.

His closing points were to extend the trial period so hiring rests on observed work, to make students use the IDE and language specification rather than asking the teacher, and to let learners hit a mistake before correcting it. He suggested a gentler first language such as Python, and argued that graduates of such a program can later become the colleagues who train others.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Dalibor Topić - Onward to New Shores with Project Jigsaw and JDK 9
talks.teaser: Shows how JDK 9's module system, jlink runtimes and compact strings shrink, secure and speed up Java applications.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by addressing the recurring claim that Java is about to die, arguing that the platform has become steadier, with more predictable update and release schedules. It then introduces Project Jigsaw, the OpenJDK effort with three goals: making the platform smaller, safer and faster, while adding a module system that helps developers build libraries and complex applications.

The middle section is a live demo. A small modular application depends on a library module, both are packaged as modular JAR files, and the jlink tool assembles a custom runtime that contains only the modules the application needs. The runtime shrinks from around 30 megabytes to just over 20 megabytes after compression and stripping debug information. The speaker also covers an official Oracle server JRE Docker image, the Portola port of the JDK to the Alpine Linux distribution, and better container-aware resource detection. For internal APIs that were once used freely, the talk shows how a static dependency analysis tool reports reliance on JDK internals, and it describes the experimental ahead-of-time compiler and compact strings, which store single-byte characters more efficiently.

The closing part encourages developers to try JDK 9 builds, check their own code and third-party dependencies for internal API use, and report problems on the OpenJDK mailing lists. It also invites participation in quality outreach, where open source projects test early builds before general availability.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Simon Ritter - 55 New Features In JDK 9
talks.teaser: A rapid tour groups JDK 9 changes across modularity, APIs, performance, and tooling for developers planning migration.
talks.summary:
The presenter races through fifty-five additions slated for JDK 9’s late-July release, grouping them so a packed room can see what matters before upgrade day. He opens with the Java platform module system: ninety-four modules replacing the monolithic runtime, stronger encapsulation of non-public APIs such as sun.misc.Unsafe, and command-line escapes like --add-exports, --add-opens, and --permit-illegal-access for backward compatibility. He also covers jlink for slim custom runtimes and notes that JCP politics delayed but did not cancel the JSR 376 public review.

Most of the session is a fast inventory of developer-facing changes: immutable collection factories, stream dropWhile and takeWhile, parallel Files.lines, JShell for quick experiments, reactive Flow APIs, CompletableFuture delays and timeouts, richer @Deprecated metadata, small Project Coin language tweaks, multi-release JARs, Unicode and standards updates, and a long list of JVM tuning moves including G1 as the default collector, compact strings, unified logging, and graphics pipeline improvements. Variable handles and related APIs are framed as supported replacements for unsafe tricks.

The close emphasizes housekeeping—new version numbering, flattened JDK layout, searchable Javadoc, removed legacy tools and six APIs, CMS deprecation, and incubator modules such as HTTP/2. The practical message is to test applications early, expect friction only if code leaned on internal APIs or odd reflection, and treat modular runtimes as optional for many classpath-based apps.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Piotr Przybył - Graylog: one tool to log 'em all
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Piotr Przybył - Graylog: one tool to log 'em all.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At GeeCON 2017, Piotr Przybył presented an overview and practical demonstration of Graylog, an open-source log aggregation and analysis platform. He distinguished debugging (evaluating running program state at breakpoints in an IDE) from logging, which is post-factum or post-mortem and relies exclusively on recorded logs. Przybył emphasized that in non-ideal real-world environments, centralized remote logging is critical for post-incident diagnostics, system visibility, and handling multi-instance or microservice architectures.

### Key Topics
- **Architecture and Deployment**: Graylog is distributed as a single fat JAR embedding a Grizzly/Jersey REST server and a React.js web client. State and configuration metadata are stored in MongoDB, while log message indexing and searching are handled by Elasticsearch. Deployment options range from virtual machine appliances (such as Oracle VirtualBox) to production tarballs and orchestration scripts.
- **Ingestion and Inputs**: Graylog utilizes inputs that collect and interpret specific log formats, such as standard syslog over UDP or the Graylog Extended Log Format (GELF).
- **Application Integration**: Java applications can integrate with Graylog without code modifications using SLF4J, Logback, and appenders like logstash-gelf. Przybył demonstrated capturing per-thread contextual data via Mapped Diagnostic Context (MDC), including user identities and instance IDs.
- **Log Organization and Processing**: Using features like Streams, Extractors (e.g., regex-based field cleanup), and Pipelines with staged rules, incoming logs can be filtered, mutated, and routed based on conditions like CIDR IP matching.
- **Alerting and Dashboards**: Graylog allows defining stream-based alert conditions (such as specific field values like HTTP 500 status codes, or message counts drops to zero) to trigger notifications via email, HTTP requests, or external monitoring systems.

### Technical Details
- **Timezone Pitfalls**: A critical troubleshooting point highlighted is mismatched timezones. Devices emitting logs without explicit timezone data (such as routers sending syslog via UDP) are interpreted by Graylog in UTC. If the sending device uses local time without an offset, logs appear as timestamps from the future and will not show in default relative searches.
- **Processing Pipelines**: Przybył demonstrated solving timezone mismatches using a processing pipeline rule. Stages execute in ascending numerical order, where an earlier stage can halt subsequent processing. The rule parsed the router's raw timestamp, formatted it with the `Europe/Warsaw` (Europe/Krakow) timezone, and replaced the original timestamp field without modifying application code.
- **Distributed Tracking via MDC**: In a simulated microservice setup running across multiple GlassFish instances behind a round-robin load balancer, MDC fields (`username`, `instance`, `response_code`) were exported into Graylog via GELF. This allowed tracing a single user's actions across multiple backend nodes, displaying chronological surrounding messages and diagnosing intermittent HTTP 500 errors.
- **Internal Components**: Graylog utilizes Apache Shiro for role-based access control, Google Guice (Juice) for dependency injection and multi-bindings plugins, Airline for CLI command parsing, and Swagger for browsing the underlying REST API.

### Takeaways
Centralized logging with Graylog provides unified search across distributed applications and hardware devices where manual log gathering via SSH/SCP is impractical. For sizing, performance testing in pre-production is required, and adding RAM typically provides more immediate performance gains than adding Graylog nodes. When compared to the ELK stack, Graylog was chosen by the speaker due to its GPL license and its purpose-built, log-focused web UI.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Sebastian Malaca - Do you really know how to create your objects?
talks.teaser: Contrasts Spring field injection with constructors and method injection so required and optional dependencies stay visible during reviews.
talks.summary:
Malaca opens by asking how developers create objects and notes that frameworks often wire components without explicit constructors. He argues that field injection prevents marking dependencies as final, allows invalid partially wired instances, and ties object creation to the container so plain construction or alternate libraries become awkward even in tests.

He walks through code-review pain when @Autowired hides required versus optional semantics, especially when the required attribute is never set explicitly. Subclass constructor injection with Spring can mislead readers into assuming all dependencies arrive through the constructor. He discusses optional dependencies, runtime setters, delayed null checks inside methods, context-dependent validity, and when validation or factories belong in the class versus elsewhere. Drink-themed examples illustrate named constructors, factories that hide complexity, and builders that enforce prerequisites at build time.

He closes by urging teams to keep constructors and method injection for clarity, avoid heavy logic in constructors, use factories and named constructors to embed context, reserve builders for complex valid objects, and place test-only builders and factories in test code rather than production packages.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Pavel Lahoda - Advanced Android Annotations for AAA Mobile applications
talks.teaser: Shows how to build compile-time annotation processors for Android, generating interfaces and networking code from annotations.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a basic point: an annotation does nothing on its own, so something has to process it. It contrasts runtime processing through reflection, which carries a performance cost, with compile-time processing, which generates code during the build. It also warns that removing a null check after adding a nullability annotation can leave a crash risk, because the annotation is not enforced under default settings.

It then walks through setting up an annotation processor inside an Android project. The steps are a separate Java library module, a class extending the processor base, a registration file in the resources folder, and Gradle changes so the processor output is packaged and compiled. A first example uses a contract annotation on methods to generate interfaces for MVP-style presenter contracts automatically, including methods that belong to more than one contract. A second example builds on a networking library: a remote data annotation with a URL generates the request handling, and success and error callbacks are checked at compile time, so the build fails if a required callback is missing.

The talk also reviews established libraries that use the same technique, such as Dagger and Butter Knife, and cautions that some uses add complexity without benefit, such as heavy annotation-based languages or generated Parcelable boilerplate where plain serialization would do. The takeaways are to understand the generated code, to use the compiler to enforce contracts, and to remember that processors can be unit tested as normal Java, while debugging them means attaching a debugger.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: DuyHai Doan - Big Data 101, all the foundations you need to bootstrap a new project
talks.teaser: Foundational distributed-system ideas help practitioners judge big-data marketing and choose sharding, replication, and consistency wisely.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing big-data projects as distributed systems problems, so vendor slides and benchmarks can be read critically instead of taken at face value. It walks through why physical clocks drift, how local ordering differs from global ordering, and how Lamport clocks and vector clocks relate to detecting conflicts without necessarily resolving them. Latency is tied to real network physics; failure is treated through timeouts, heartbeats, and the limits of naive ping logic. Consensus is introduced via validity, termination, and agreement, with two-phase commit, three-phase commit, and quorum-based protocols such as Paxos, Raft, and ZooKeeper sketched as the usual toolbox.

The middle sections apply those ideas to data sharding and replication. Hash versus range-style partition keys, statistical balance versus hot spots, and costly rebalancing are spelled out with interactive true-or-false prompts. Symmetric versus asymmetric replicas are compared through message loss, overload, crash, and buffered-write scenarios that expose subtle inconsistency. CAP is presented as a partition-time trade-off rather than a simple triangle label, with tunable consistency levels and the coordination cost of stronger guarantees illustrated using Apache Cassandra consistency levels and lightweight transactions.

The close contrasts pure master–slave, sharded primaries, and marketed “masterless” designs, including documentation inconsistencies the speaker highlights in the wild. Masterless benefits come with harder reasoning, weaker global ordering, and last-write-wins timestamp pitfalls when clocks skew. Practitioners should verify claims with their own measurements, match consistency choices to application needs, and expect to pay latency and coordination tax when they demand strong agreement across replicas.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Jacek Kunicki - Tame Your Data with Akka Streams and Java 8
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a CSV import pipeline with Akka Streams in Java, covering framing, parsing, averaging and Cassandra storage.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Akka Streams, a Scala library with a Java API, for building data processing pipelines. It explains the source, flow and sink model and why reactive streams add backpressure, so a slow consumer can signal how much data it can take. It also notes that Akka Streams pipelines are lazy recipes that run only when a materializer executes them, and that the library is not distributed by default.

The worked example imports semicolon-separated sensor readings from compressed CSV files into Cassandra. Each line is parsed into either a valid or invalid reading, and the pipeline splits byte streams on newlines, turns each file into a source of readings, and averages each pair of readings per ID. A pair with no valid values receives a default value. The speaker contrasts ordered and unordered async stages, and wraps storage in a sink whose completion can be awaited.

The talk closes by wiring the pieces into a complete importer and adding a custom load-balancing graph stage that distributes files across workers using the graph DSL. The import runs against a Cassandra container, and invalid lines are logged along the way. The main takeaway is that the Java API works well for this kind of pipeline, though the Scala version is more concise.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Yegor Bugayenko - What this InterruptedException is about?
talks.teaser: Explains how Java's InterruptedException works and why developers must restore the interrupt flag after catching it.
talks.summary:
The session targets a gap the presenter sees in everyday Java code: many developers catch InterruptedException, log it, and keep going, which breaks cooperative thread shutdown. After a short slide setup, most of the time is live coding in Java 8.

Starting from a background worker thread and daemon versus non-daemon behavior, the talk contrasts brutal Thread.stop() with polite shutdown using a die flag, then the built-in interrupt mechanism. Demos show how sleep and other blocking calls consult the interrupt flag, how interrupted() clears that flag when throwing, and why a mere break or stack trace leaves the worker ignoring later stop requests. The central fix demonstrated is calling Thread.currentThread().interrupt() after a catch so upstream code still sees an pending interrupt.

Closing guidance favors declaring throws InterruptedException instead of catching when possible; when catching is unavoidable, always re-assert the flag; and for long CPU-bound loops, poll isInterrupted() so interrupt() takes effect promptly. The presenter notes on the order of three hundred JDK blocking APIs use this exception, and briefly discusses design trade-offs in audience Q&A.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Krzysztof Kaczmarek-12 ways Software Engineers to make client presentations a disaster
talks.teaser: Maps twelve recurring mistakes that wreck developer client demos, from misplaced apologies to asking whether the audience liked the show.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a live force-and-balance demonstration to argue that small adjustments matter, then frames client work as a pairing of solid delivery and persuasion that the audience should sell, not assume will sell itself. The core is a numbered tour of presentation anti-patterns: treating the relationship as friendship instead of solving stated business goals, failing to project leadership and confidence, leading with apologies, and skipping a clear agenda with an exit time. Further items warn against drowning stakeholders in code and diagrams, note-taking from the podium, scripted monotone updates, conflating personal ego with professional pushback, and boasting about effort instead of outcomes.

Later mistakes cover reactive “yes” answers to shallow design complaints, leaving clients to guess what feedback is useful, and closing with pleas for approval rather than expert judgment. Examples draw on agency demos, distributed teams, and search-feature pitches. Audience questions widen “client” to managers and peers and revisit how to state schedule risk without over-explaining internals.

Practitioners should treat review meetings as trust maintenance: set expectations early, speak to business effect, guide critique toward decisions that matter, and reserve honest status updates for facts rather than performance.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: J.Marchwicki/J.Pałka - Stages of maturity on the way to microservices
talks.teaser: Argues that teams should build maturity in deployment, failure handling and culture before moving from a monolith to microservices.
talks.summary:
The speakers present their own, deliberately opinionated view of microservices, starting from why many organisations adopt them. Legacy systems often reach a point where nobody wants to touch the core code that earns money, so teams look to new architectures to fence off risk and ship new features elsewhere. Without first checking readiness, the move tends to multiply existing deployment pain across many services.

The talk then walks through the maturity a team should reach first. Releases should be frequent and cheap, deployment and rollback should be automated, and configuration should stay out of the code. Environments and infrastructure should behave like production, and developers should understand their framework and runtime rather than treat them as black boxes. Remote calls should never be treated as local, and circuit breakers, timeouts and contracts can be added to an existing monolith. Culture matters as much as tooling: accepting failure without blame, making decisions from measured data, owning products rather than projects, and logging and monitoring with the on-call engineer in mind.

The closing advice is to adopt changes that help whatever the architecture. Publish events from the existing application, use consumer-driven contracts for external integrations, and centralise logs so problems can be found quickly. These steps prepare a team for microservices, or show that a well-run monolith may be enough.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Lieven Doclo - Implementing Clean Architecture using Kotlin
talks.teaser: Delivers a Kotlin walkthrough of clean architecture with a live property-management demo and swappable persistence backends.
talks.summary:
The session opens by situating clean architecture as a blend of hexagonal, onion, screaming architecture, and older patterns, crediting Robert C. Martin’s 2012 formulation. The speaker outlines control flow from consumers through application APIs into domain logic and persistence, stressing dependency inversion so callers stay unaware of storage details. Use cases express intent; gateways and presenters keep domain models from leaking into REST controllers, with a pragmatic warning that mapping compromises become technical debt.

The core is a Spring Boot property management example in Kotlin. A create-building use case starts with request and response models, a controller with its own JSON payload, and a mock implementation before a real domain Building, entity gateway, and in-memory map store. A second use case lists building names. The speaker then plugs in Spring Data MongoDB by implementing the same gateway interface, showing that controllers and application code stay unchanged when persistence shifts.

The close recaps keeping application and domain layers free of framework annotations, deferring technology choices to infrastructure, and organizing code into modules so dependencies enforce boundaries. Kotlin extension methods map domain objects for MongoDB only where that module depends on persistence. A brief Q&A touches on layered mocking for tests and how DCI’s business emphasis relates to use cases.

talks.teaser: Contract checks, fallbacks, monitoring and automation help keep microservices in a public cloud maintainable.
talks.summary: The speaker describes the maintenance challenges of microservices in a public cloud, including availability, service communication, testing and performance. Attendees learn why business boundaries and asynchronous communication can reduce dependencies, how contract verification and fallback behavior help systems handle failures, and why monitoring and automation support reliable operations at scale. The talk also considers when microservices may not be a useful choice.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: M.Laskowski/T.Michalak - When Vert.x & RxJava meet
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: M.Laskowski/T.Michalak - When Vert.x & RxJava meet.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At GeeCON 2017, speakers Maciej Laskowski and Tomasz Michalak from Cognifide presented an open-source integration framework called Knot.x (referred to throughout as Knot.x / notX). The project addresses the challenges of building high-traffic, dynamic digital platforms—such as e-commerce websites receiving upwards of 750 million requests per month—where content managed by business teams in a CMS must be integrated seamlessly with multiple backend services. Instead of forcing the CMS to process external data or relying solely on fragile client-side front-end calls, the speakers designed Knot.x as an asynchronous, non-blocking integration layer utilizing Eclipse Vert.x and RxJava.

### Key Topics
- **Integration Architectures**: The trade-offs between traditional CMS-driven integration (scalability limitations, licensing, difficult upgrades) and client-side front-end integration (exposing internal services, fragmented visitor performance). Knot.x sits between both as a dedicated integration layer combining CMS layout authoring with service data.
- **Eclipse Vert.x Core Concepts**: How Vert.x leverages the reactor pattern, single-threaded event loops (one per CPU core), Verticles, and an event-driven model to handle high concurrency without blocking threads.
- **Clustered Event Bus**: Vert.x's lightweight, distributed messaging system using Hazelcast by default, enabling horizontal scaling and automatic load balancing across separate servers without changing application code.
- **Reactive Programming with RxJava**: Addressing "callback hell" resulting from cascading asynchronous handler callbacks by using RxJava's `Observable`, `Single`, and operators like `zip` to execute service calls concurrently and combine their outputs.
- **Knot.x Framework Architecture**: Declarative endpoint configurations, dynamic templating using Handlebars snippets, mocking engines for rapid prototyping, and pluggable modules (REST, SOAP, databases, authentication).

### Technical Details
- **Vert.x Architecture**: Uses non-blocking handlers invoked by event loops. On multi-core CPUs, Vert.x spins up multiple event loops (e.g., eight loops on an eight-core processor) to fully utilize CPU hardware while enforcing that blocking operations must never run on the event loop.
- **Avoiding Callback Hell**: When orchestrating multiple dependencies (e.g., personalized search requiring both a user-profile service and an Elasticsearch engine), standard nested callbacks force sequential calls or complex synchronization. RxJava's `Observable.zip` operator allows simultaneous calls to both services, merging their streams cleanly before invoking downstream business logic. Reactive streams handle events through `onNext`, `onError`, and `onCompleted` callbacks.
- **Live Demonstration & Scalability**: The presenters demonstrated Knot.x running as a standalone fat JAR. They showcased switching between local mock servers and live external endpoints (Google Books API) purely through configuration changes. They then demonstrated clustering using the `--cluster` flag, running a core Knot.x instance on one node and scaling a dedicated search module across a second instance with automatic load balancing over the Hazelcast-backed distributed event bus. Finally, they attached an HSQL database adapter Verticle communicating over the event bus using Handlebars snippet bindings (`knotx adapters service books DB`).
- **Resilience and Error Handling**: In response to an audience question regarding service failures, the speakers outlined fallback strategies: returning an HTTP 503 error, degrading gracefully by omitting or stubbing individual component data, or using Vert.x circuit breakers and service discovery.

### Takeaways
Knot.x demonstrates how pairing Vert.x's distributed event-driven vertical scaling with RxJava's functional reactive stream composition creates a resilient, modular integration layer. This architecture allows engineering teams to decouple content editing from backend data sources, scale individual service modules across machines, and prototype against mock endpoints without code alterations.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Mark West-Building a Smart Security Camera with Raspberry Pi Zero,Node.js and The Cloud
talks.teaser: Shows how a Raspberry Pi Zero camera paired with cloud image recognition filtered out false motion alerts.
talks.summary:
The speaker wanted an early warning for a secluded back garden after burglaries nearby, and agreed quick, cheap and portable requirements with his wife, who acted as project manager. The first version used a Raspberry Pi Zero with a camera module mounted inside a window, running open-source motion detection software that emailed snapshots. Cats, shadows and rain soon triggered hundreds of alerts a day, so the system needed to recognise people rather than any movement.

Rather than train a neural network or use face detection, he sent snapshots to Amazon Recognition, a hosted image analysis service. On AWS, each upload to S3 started a Step Functions workflow, Lambda functions called Recognition, and an email went out through SES only when a person label appeared. Images were archived and an error handler emailed him about failures. Test costs for about 8,000 pictures came to just over a dollar, with a monthly estimate near eight dollars once free-tier credits ended.

Recognition gave consistent results on repeated images and still detected people in partial or poor-quality frames, which removed the false alarms. Drawbacks were that it is a black box with no way to give feedback when it misses, it struggled with noisy images, and output quality depends on which motion frames get uploaded, a trade-off between cost and hit rate. Writing Step Functions definitions in JSON was error-prone, and heavy cloud use brings vendor lock-in and ongoing charges. A viewer reported that a similar camera helped police catch a burglar in the act.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Michał Płachta - A Pragmatist’s Guide to Functional Geekery
talks.teaser: Explores practical functional programming in Java with Vavr, using a playful domain model to teach futures, ADTs, and type classes.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that Java 8 lambdas and streams help but leave mutable collections and blocking habits intact, while Scala and libraries such as Vavr embed immutability, higher-order functions, and richer types in everyday APIs. Through a tongue-in-cheek “Twitter for a galaxy far away” MVP focused on follower counts, the speaker walks from naive blocking calls on futures toward non-blocking composition with map, flatMap, and forEach.

Each production incident becomes a typing exercise. Ambiguous zeros yield Option; exceptions that never reach forEach yield Try; combined loading, failure, and success states become a custom algebraic data type handled with pattern matching. A political censorship feature turns mutable rule spaghetti into a list of filter objects reduced by folding, with manipulation limits tracked in a small status type. A closing segment separates domain data from JSON serialization using type classes so HTTP handlers stay free of annotation clutter.

Practitioners leave with a reusable pattern: model states and errors as data, compose asynchronous pipelines without blocking threads, and keep serialization as evidence supplied elsewhere. Sample code exists in parallel Java and Scala implementations tied to the same fictional product.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Jeroen Resoort - Having fun
talks.teaser: A developer demonstrates Amazon Alexa features and walks through building custom skills with the Skills Kit and AWS Lambda.
talks.summary:
The session opens with what Amazon Echo and Alexa are: a hands-free speaker tied to voice services for music, jokes, smart-home hooks, news flashes, and third-party skills. The presenter notes regional availability, compares Alexa with Google Home, Siri, and Cortna, and flags the tradeoff of an always-on microphone on the internet before turning to custom skill development.

The core walkthrough covers the Alexa developer console: invocation names, intents, sample utterances, and slots so fuzzy phrasing still maps to actions. Backend logic runs on AWS Lambda (with a nod to the free tier), using JSON interaction models and session attributes to carry state across turns. Live demos include a GeeCON information and news skill, a times-tables quiz that stores answers in session data, and a brief text-adventure style game; troubleshooting covers intent name mismatches and precise invocation wording.

Practitioners leave with a concrete path from blank skill to testable Lambda handler, patterns for slots and sessions, and awareness of publishing choices between private skills and the public marketplace—plus the reminder that a voice assistant in the home is both a convenience layer and a networked sensor.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Matt Raible - Building a PWA
talks.teaser: Walks through building a progressive web app with an Ionic Angular front end and a Spring Boot API.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through building a progressive web app with an Ionic and Angular front end backed by a Spring Boot API. It opens with mobile performance: developers often test on fast machines, so pages feel fine to them but slow for users on weak connections. The speaker recommends mobile-first design and the PRPL pattern (push, render, pre-cache, lazy-load) to load pages faster.

The demo starts on the server, where a Spring Boot project exposes a beer entity through a Spring Data REST repository, and a command-line runner seeds an in-memory H2 database. A controller adds a route that returns only the good beers. On the Ionic side, the speaker generates a page and a provider service, fixes a missing HTTP module and a cross-origin error, and adds Giphy images. A modal lets users add and edit entries.

The progressive web app section covers three requirements: HTTPS, offline loading through a service worker, and a web app manifest that lets the browser install the app. The Ionic starter already includes a service worker, and a missing manifest icon is added. Lighthouse audits the result. Android prompts installation, while Safari lacks support. Attempts to deploy to Cloud Foundry and build for iOS were shown live, and the iOS build needed signing in Xcode. The takeaway is that existing Angular apps can become installable PWAs.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Steve Poole - The Anatomy of Java Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Outlines how Java bugs, deserialization, and dependencies chain into exploits and changes teams need in design, patching, and scanning.
talks.summary:
The session frames vulnerabilities as ordinary bugs that attackers chain into availability, integrity, or code-execution outcomes, set against organized cybercrime economics rather than lone hackers. A staged URL-encoding and Windows path example shows how percent-encoding mistakes can intersect with extension loading—without naming a specific JVM fix—to illustrate that serious issues rarely look like obvious smoking guns in source.

The middle maps how the industry finds and discusses flaws: CVE listings, vendor CPU streams, scoring that assumes reasonable posture, and the tension between educating developers and giving exploit writers instant ammunition. For Java, much historical CVE weight sits in applets and untrusted code, but server-side risks persist through deserialization (including commons-library gadget chains), permissive trust managers, dependency blindness, crafted untrusted input, image parsers, and exposed debug surfaces such as JMX.

Practitioners are urged to stay patched, segment access, reduce overly flexible configuration and class loading, validate every inbound datum, use secure-coding guidance and scanning across dependencies and containers, and treat responsible disclosure as mandatory when they find issues in shared platforms.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Charles Oliver Nutter
talks.teaser: Walks through HotSpot diagnostic flags, bytecode, inlining, and assembly to show how common Java constructs compile and optimize.
talks.summary:
Charles Oliver Nutter frames the JVM as a hidden layer most Java developers ignore until performance or odd behavior forces a deeper look. He outlines how source becomes bytecode, how the interpreter hands hot methods to the JIT, and how tiered compilation balances startup against stronger server-side optimization.

Using small programs and tools such as javap, -XX:+PrintCompilation, -XX:+PrintInlining, and -XX:+PrintAssembly with diagnostic unlocks, he walks from Hello World through loop compilation logs, inlining graphs, and trimmed x86 output. Examples cover static versus lazily initialized final fields, synchronized method overhead and locking in native code, a JRuby case where a volatile field initialization showed up as costly lock-related instructions, string switch lowering via hash codes and follow-up switches, and lambda invokedynamic paths that block inlining through utilities like Collections.sort.

The closing message is that every language feature carries a runtime cost the JIT may or may not erase within your application's lifetime. Practitioners who profile code but still hit mystery slowdowns gain a repeatable path: correlate compile events, inspect inlining decisions, and read assembly when higher-level tools stay silent.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Nitsan Wakart - Using FlameGraphs To Illuminate The JVM
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Nitsan Wakart - Using FlameGraphs To Illuminate The JVM.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Michael Plöd - Caching for Business Applications: Best Practices and Gotchas
talks.teaser: Surveys layering, consistency tradeoffs, and rollout discipline for caching in typical enterprise Java business applications.
talks.summary:
The presenter argues that caching in ordinary business software is neither solved nor interchangeable with the patterns used at massive social platforms. Teams serving banks or insurers usually face predictable load shapes, so copying internet-scale stacks or caching aggressively without analysis often creates consistency gaps, JVM garbage-collection pain, or replication storms on the network.

The middle of the session walks through where to place caches in a conventional n-tier Java stack, why local in-heap caches should persist as long as possible, and how clustered nodes diverge when addresses or entities change. Invalidation strategies are favored over full replication; small heap-bound caches with eviction can stall real production systems, while moving to distributed grids such as Hazelcast trades latency for capacity and demands operations expertise early.

Closing points stress picking read-heavy, expensive integration data, refusing hand-rolled cache code, introducing caches only after fixing application inefficiencies, preferring optimized serializers, considering off-heap storage only when growth warrants it, and treating unprotected cache contents as an audit risk. JCache and Spring Cache abstractions are offered as ways to keep providers swappable without drowning business logic in infrastructure APIs.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Konrad Malawski - The best is yet to come
talks.teaser: Tours the Akka toolkit's evolution, from actors and clustering to streams, typed actors and the Artery remoting layer.
talks.summary:
The talk reviews the state of the Akka toolkit in 2017, explaining where its modules came from and what they contribute. Akka is presented as a set of building blocks for reactive systems rather than a framework, with the actor model at its core. Actors only send and receive messages and create children, and remote interaction is handled much like local interaction. Early sections cover Erlang-inspired failure handling, binary serialization preferred over Java's built-in mechanism for speed and security, and futures. The speaker argues that circuit breakers handle failure but do little for flow control, which motivated streams.

Cluster sharding routes messages by key and restarts actors on another node after failure, while persistence uses event sourcing so state can be rebuilt by replaying events. Akka HTTP, a streaming-first rewrite of spray, models HTTP elements as types and supports server-side push, and HTTP/2 lets many streams share one connection. Reactive Streams adds backpressure through a permit-based scheme heading into JDK 9. Distributed Data lets developers pick how consistent each write must be. Typed actors, a UDP-based remoting layer that the speaker says gives about a tenfold performance gain, and compression round out the technical material.

The closing part covers a connector community for databases and queues, monitoring built into the streams infrastructure, and commercial tracing tools. The speaker asks the audience for feedback on typed actors and multi-data-center use cases.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Dan Heidinga - OpenJ9: Under the hood of the next open source JVM
talks.teaser: A walkthrough of OpenJ9 internals covers class loading, ROM and RAM classes, interpretation, JIT tiers, and shared caches.
talks.summary:
The presentation starts from a trivial Hello World service and asks what the JVM actually does after compile and jar steps. It traces startup through the invocation API and a minimal JNI launcher, then centers on how OpenJ9 organizes runtime data so algorithms stay straightforward.

Class files with awkward variable layouts become ROM classes with fixed headers, self-relative pointers for position-independent sharing, and separate RAM classes for live resolution, vtables, and JIT entry points. The speaker links class loaders and heap mirrors, thread lists for stop-the-world events, interpreter stack state without frame pointers, profiling that feeds the JIT, and tiered recompilation from cold through scorching compiles. Shared class caches reuse ROM data and ahead-of-time JIT bodies to cut startup time and memory footprint.

The close ties OpenJ9 to Eclipse OMR reusable GC and compiler components, explains swapping HotSpot while keeping OpenJDK libraries and tools, and argues open collaboration, JVM competition, and cross-platform runtimes matter. Q&A clarifies retained OpenJDK pieces, OMR garbage collectors sourced from J9, ended multi-VM-in-one-process support, and where J9 aims on startup and memory versus other JVMs.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Charlie Gracie - Eclipse OMR your (J)VM toolkit
talks.teaser: GeeCON 2017: Charlie Gracie - Eclipse OMR your (J)VM toolkit.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this GeeCON 2017 presentation, Charlie Gracie, a senior software developer at IBM and garbage collection architect for the IBM J9 JVM, introduces the Eclipse OMR project. Originally originating internally as the "Open Managed Runtime," the project does not provide a managed runtime itself, nor is it linked to the Eclipse IDE. Instead, it is an open-source (dual-licensed under Apache v2 and EPL v1) toolkit hosted by the Eclipse Foundation consisting of language-agnostic components extracted from IBM's J9 JVM. The goal of Eclipse OMR is to provide reusable virtual machine building blocks—such as platform abstraction, threading, garbage collection, JIT compilation, and diagnostic tooling—allowing language runtimes to share robust, high-performance runtime infrastructure without imposing language semantics.

### Key Topics
- **Rationale and Mission**: Modern cloud platforms rely heavily on multiple language runtimes (e.g., Java, Node.js, Ruby). While runtimes share common architecture components (bytecode interpreters, memory managers, platform layers, diagnostic services), their implementations are typically siloed, requiring repetitive effort to exploit modern hardware capabilities. Eclipse OMR aims to eliminate duplication by providing a modular, language-agnostic toolkit without fracturing existing runtime communities.
- **Component Decoupling**: Unlike approaches like running languages entirely atop the JVM or CoreCLR, OMR does not impose an execution model or object semantics. Components can be consumed independently (e.g., swapping a single-threaded GC for a parallel GC, adding platform portability, or integrating a JIT compiler) via lightweight glue layers.
- **OMR Architecture**: The toolkit contains 800,000–900,000 lines of code across several core modules:
  - *Port and Thread Libraries*: Abstract OS and platform calls across supported architectures (x86, Power, z/Architecture/s390, ARMv7) and operating systems (Linux, Windows, AIX, z/OS).
  - *Garbage Collector (GC)*: Scales from a simple mark-sweep GC (which can be brought up in under 100 lines of glue code) up to parallel, generational, concurrent, or region-based collection.
  - *Compiler Framework and JITBuilder*: An extensible intermediate language (IL) compiler backend derived from IBM compilers, complemented by JITBuilder—a high-level API wrapper that simplifies JIT generation without requiring deep compiler IL knowledge.
  - *RAS and Diagnostic Tooling*: Lightweight event tracing into rolling buffers, Diagnostic Data Router (DDR) for post-mortem structure inspection and core dump analysis, and verbose GC output compatible with tools like GC Memory Visualizer and IBM Health Center.

### Technical Details & Case Studies
Gracie reviews several integration prototypes demonstrating OMR's practical impact:
- **Base9**: A minimal educational stack-based interpreter supporting primitive types, used to demonstrate OMR JIT integration. Implementing JIT compilation via JITBuilder achieved over a 100x speedup on benchmarks such as Fibonacci in under a day of work.
- **SOM++**: A minimal Smalltalk C++ virtual machine. Integrating OMR's parallel GC delivered an immediate >2x throughput improvement. Later adding JITBuilder yielded a 3x to 30x speedup across the benchmark suite in roughly 3–4 weeks of development.
- **Lua (PUC-Rio)**: Integrating OMR JIT required fewer than 50 lines changed in Lua itself and roughly 2,000 lines of JITBuilder code to map opcodes. To combat the performance penalty of dynamic typing ("death of a million type checks"), developers implemented type specialization guards, dropping benchmarks like Mandelbrot from 17 minutes to approximately one minute.
- **OpenJ9**: IBM consumes OMR back into its production J9 development stream on an hourly basis. Gracie notes IBM plans to open-source the remaining JVM components under the OpenJ9 project.

### Takeaways
Eclipse OMR provides a modular, production-hardened foundation for building or modernizing virtual machines. Rather than rewriting complex memory managers, platform abstraction layers, and JIT compilers from scratch, language developers can integrate OMR components incrementally using C or C++ glue code while retaining existing language semantics and tooling compatibility. Next steps for the project include improving open documentation, expanding multi-platform testing infrastructure, and growing community engagement across academic and research groups.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Geertjan Wielenga - True JavaScript Confessions of a Java Developer!
talks.teaser: Ten lessons help enterprise Java teams adopt browser front ends without replacing stable backends.
talks.summary:
Mobile browsers pushed business software toward JavaScript on the front end while Java still suits long-lived enterprise backends reached via REST. The speaker argues against wholesale rewrites, using air traffic control and similar cases where desktop tools should stay primary while phones and manager dashboards add notifications, charts, and stats.

The middle walks through ten lessons: resist hype, mine HTML5 for validation and datalists, use JavaScript libraries such as Response JS for DOM-level responsive behavior, choose stable libraries over the latest frameworks, design loose coupling with ES6 modules or RequireJS, accept ecosystem churn, and evaluate vendor stacks including Oracle JET with internationalization and chart components. Corporate open-source frameworks from PayPal, IBM, Salesforce, and others signal mature options for charts, modularity, and accessibility.

Practitioners should supplement rather than replace proven systems, match framework lifetimes to how often they can refactor, and optionally treat JavaScript as a compilation target via GWT, Vaadin, DukeScript, or Codename One when teams prefer Java for logic or views.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Alexander Gallego - Distributed Stream Processing Over Thousands Of Datacenters
talks.teaser: Explains how Akamai built a stream processing engine that schedules and secures workloads across thousands of edge data centers.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at building distributed stream processing on Akamai's edge, where the platform runs across tens of thousands of small data centers close to users instead of a few large ones. The speaker, who previously was CTO of a C++ stream processing company called Concorde, explains why that setting changes the design: bandwidth and latency between nodes vary widely, so the usual assumptions from cloud environments do not hold.

The architecture is built on Apache Mesos with multi-tenant clusters and containers for isolation. Operators can change a running pipeline, including hot code deployment and dynamic topology changes, without taking the cluster down. A per-tenant auto-scaler adjusts instance counts against latency or throughput targets, and a C++ proxy sidecar handles sockets, retries and memory so user code can be written in several languages. On the security side, each container receives an ephemeral certificate, so its access expires when the container dies, and scheduling respects legal data-residency constraints. Distributed tracing tags packets across the processing graph so that trends in latency become visible.

Performance figures shared include about 1.2 million messages per box on Amazon instances, low p99 latencies, and a round trip of 17 microseconds between two machines using a user-level TCP/IP stack. The talk closes by noting that delivery guarantees such as exactly-once or at-least-once can be chosen per pipeline, and by describing future work on hierarchical scheduling across geographic regions. The takeaway for practitioners is that at edge scale, placement, tracing and security have to be designed in from the start rather than added later.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Ensar Basri Kahveci - Distributed Systems Theory for Mere Mortals
talks.teaser: Maps distributed-systems theory to practical choices in clustering, failures, clocks, consensus limits, and CAP trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames why organizations adopt multi-node designs for scalability and fault tolerance, using an in-memory data grid as a recurring example of partitioning, replication, elasticity, and recovery after partial failures. It walks through foundational models: synchronous versus asynchronous interaction (and partial synchrony in real deployments), crash, omission, crash-recover, and Byzantine failure classes, and why physical clocks drift while Lamport and vector clocks support causal ordering in cluster management.

The middle develops the consensus problem, safety versus liveness, the FLP impossibility result in asynchronous settings, and how failure detectors and timing assumptions reopen the design space. It compares two-phase commit, three-phase commit, and majority-based approaches, noting blocking behavior, failure sensitivity, and familiar algorithms used in production coordination stacks, plus the cost of strong consistency coordination at scale.

The close applies the CAP principle under network partitions, treating consistency and availability as spectrums rather than binaries. The product side is described as favoring availability with primary-copy asynchronous replication, accepting replication lag and stickiness constraints. The closing message is that distributed fundamentals now matter beyond dedicated databases—to web, mobile, and any architecture with replicated state.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Bruno Bossola - Distributed Systems explained (with NodeJS)
talks.teaser: Walks through CAP theorem trade-offs with live Node.js demos of CA, AP, and CP replicated key-value stores.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by explaining why teams turn to distributed programming when a single machine cannot provide enough storage and throughput, then focuses on replicated storage rather than distributed computation. It defines scalability, availability, and consistency—including strong, weak, and eventual models—and introduces the CAP theorem: under network partition, a system cannot simultaneously provide strong consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.

The core maps those trade-offs to familiar architectures. Classical CA relational designs use two-phase commit and strict quorums where every node must agree. AP systems, illustrated with Amazon Dynamo-style reasoning, sacrifice consistency during failures and rely on sloppy quorums plus read repair, as in Cassandra-like behavior. CP systems keep consistency across partitions but may reject requests when a majority is unavailable, using leader election and heartbeat-driven consensus similar to Raft.

Live demos on a four-node Node.js key-value store show strict quorum blocking on a slow peer, AP writes succeeding with partial acknowledgements and background repair, and CP operation through leader changes, partition isolation, and catch-up replication. The closing advice is to internalize CAP when choosing or operating data stores, study interactive Raft material, and experiment with the published demo repository.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Krzysztof Kudryński/Błażej Kubiak
talks.teaser: Shows how a drone with one camera learns depth with a neural network to steer around obstacles.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a project in which a small Parrot AR.Drone flies from a user's click on a target in the camera image, with the software working out the control commands itself. The speakers began with tracking, using OpenCV methods such as mean shift and optical flow to keep the drone oriented toward a chosen region, and then added forward motion. Avoiding obstacles with a single camera was the harder problem, because structure-from-motion reconstruction becomes unreliable when the drone flies straight at an object or only rotates.

Their answer was to train a deep convolutional network to predict a depth map from one image. Training data came from flying toward a pillar placed three to four meters away, with the relative depth normalized to that known distance. They started from a pretrained ResNet-50 model, removed its fully connected layers and added upscaling layers. The model was about 200 megabytes and took around five minutes to load, with an estimate taking roughly 30 seconds on a CPU, while a GPU needed about 100 milliseconds. The system was split into Python, Java and C++ components connected over the network.

The live demo worked after a difficult recording day, showing the drone steering around obstacles toward a tracked window. The speakers closed with a sofa-classification exercise in which the audience acted as the network, illustrating how an ambiguous training set teaches the wrong features. The practical takeaway is that training data design matters as much as the architecture, and that a learned model can be far costlier to build than a handcrafted rule.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Kamil Owczarek - Akka Typed: A fresh look at the Actor model
talks.teaser: Attendees see untyped versus Akka Typed actors, vending FSMs, and compile-time safety against classic pitfalls.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the 1973 actor-model idea—message-driven entities that send, spawn children, or change behavior—and why multi-threaded APIs often trade correctness for complexity. It contrasts classic untyped Akka (partial functions on any message, actor systems, ping-pong demos) with Akka Typed, where behaviors are typed functions that return the next behavior and guardian actors must be supplied explicitly.

The middle section centers on behavior variants: stateless loops, stateful finite-state machines modeled as a vending machine with idle, ordered, and awaiting-payment states, full behaviors handling lifecycle signals alongside commands, guardian hierarchies that spawn typed children, and tap behaviors that intercept traffic. Examples highlight unit-testable state transitions, typed actor references, and a more functional style without sprawling receive blocks.

The close covers practical wins: fewer non-exhaustive match and wrong reply-type failures, explicit reply targets instead of fragile sender semantics in async aggregates, and smoother dynamic behavior changes. The speaker notes Akka Typed’s API is still evolving, interoperability with untyped actors exists with module gaps, and long-term plans may elevate typed actors without deprecating classic APIs soon. Practitioners gain a mental model for choosing behaviors and typing boundaries in new actor code.
