talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Rod Johnson - Simplification and Automation in Java: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow
talks.teaser: A historical tour of enterprise Java simplification leads into demos of automated project creation and library upgrades across services.
talks.summary:
The talk opens on how enterprise Java moved from painful J2EE complexity—too many artifacts, ceremony, and vendor-driven “necessary complexity”—toward POJOs, Spring, and lessons about when code generation helps versus when it masks duplication. It traces convention over configuration from Ruby on Rails through Maven and Spring Boot, plus process gains from GitHub, CI/CD, and more standardized deployment, while noting tradeoffs as monoliths gave way to microservices, fragmentation across languages, and “pets versus cattle” operational strain.

Rod Johnson argues the next step combines code simplification with process automation and “process as code.” He demonstrates Atomist: generating working projects from seed Git repositories via transformations rather than opaque templates, wiring new repos to Slack channels, adding Travis CI from chat, and propagating seed changes to downstream services through branches and pull requests only when builds pass.

Practitioners hear a concrete workflow for industrialized service creation and evolution—library releases that rev POMs, upgrade dependents, open PRs or raise issues on failure—and a model linking Slack, GitHub, builds, and multi-language project structure. The close points to broader industry movement in this space and Spring Boot–oriented automation products.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: Anton Arhipov
talks.teaser: Demonstrates TestContainers for spinning up real Docker dependencies during Java integration and acceptance tests.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that unit tests alone often miss real-world failures: full coverage can still break once networking, databases, or the filesystem enter the picture. At ZeroTurnaround, testing JRebel and XRebel meant exercising full framework lifecycles inside application servers, which pushed the team toward heavyweight integration setups rather than narrow unit checks.

He lays out requirements—reproducible environments on developer laptops and CI, isolation so parallel runs do not clash on ports, realism, cross-platform support, and quick onboarding—and explains how raw Docker and Compose help but still fight CI when ports are fixed. The core of the session is TestContainers: a Java library that discovers Docker, starts throwaway images, and tears them down with the JVM. He walks through generic containers, bundled database images, Compose-backed stacks, Spring Boot tests with real databases plus a MockServer stand-in for sibling microservices, Selenium browsers (including recorded runs), and custom containers that launch JVMs with Java agents for instrumentation checks.

Practitioners should leave with a concrete pattern: treat dependencies as disposable containers in JUnit, keep tests isolated while still hitting real protocols, and reuse the same recipes locally and on build servers. The closing message is that ZeroTurnaround merged its in-house Docker test runner into the open TestContainers project so others can adopt the same workflow.

talks.title: GeeCON 2017: James Lewis - Betting on performance: a note on hypothesis-driven performance testing
talks.teaser: Shows hypothesis-driven performance testing via telemetry, simple probes, and deploys checked with lightweight benchmarks.
talks.summary:
James Lewis contrasts end-of-cycle, heavyweight performance testing with a hypothesis-driven loop inspired by Richard Feynman's description of science. Long delivery lead times block fast feedback, so he argues teams need instrumentation, telemetry, visualization, rapid continuous delivery, and simple probes such as Apache Bench, Siege, and Vegeta rather than only enterprise load suites.

He walks through prerequisites—correlated request timing, circuit breakers, hardware visibility, automated pipelines, canary and blue-green deploys—and then a publishing-platform rebuild that started near 35-second median page loads on expensive XSLT over large XML in S3. Sequential experiments scaled transform capacity, colocated compute with data in AWS, tightened transforms using dashboards, and only then tried caching—learning that a front proxy improved latency but hurt change agility, so cache moved nearer storage while staying near target latencies.

Practitioners should embed early performance ratchets in CI, document decisions when possible, and treat failed guesses as data. Q&A covers higher percentiles, automated versus manual probes, architecture decision records, warmup pitfalls, and risks of replaying production traffic into test environments.
